physics/optics:
What is Optics?

Optics is the branch of physics that studies light and its interactions with matter. It is divided into geometrical optics (ray optics) and physical optics (wave optics). For NEET, key topics include reflection and refraction, lenses and mirrors, optical instruments, interference, diffraction, and polarization. Understanding ray diagrams and wave properties is essential.

Key Concepts

Reflection: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection. Mirror Formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, where f is focal length, v is image distance, u is object distance. Magnification m = -v/u. Snell's Law: n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2. Lens Formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u. Lensmaker's formula: 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2). Critical Angle: sin C = 1/n (for total internal reflection). Young's Double Slit Experiment: Fringe width β = λD/d.

Solved Examples

Example 1
An object is placed 15 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the position and nature of the image.

a) 30 cm, real b) -30 cm, real c) 6 cm, virtual d) -6 cm, virtual
Solution: Using mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. u = -15 cm, f = -10 cm. 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/10 - (-1/15) = -1/10 + 1/15 = (-3 + 2)/30 = -1/30. So v = -30 cm. Negative sign indicates image is real and in front of the mirror. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 2
Light travels from air (n = 1) to water (n = 4/3). If the angle of incidence is 45°, find the angle of refraction.

a) 32.1° b) 28.6° c) 36.8° d) 41.2°
Solution: Using Snell's law: n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2. 1 × sin45° = (4/3) × sinθ2. sinθ2 = (3/4) × sin45° = (3/4) × 0.707 = 0.530. θ2 = sin-1(0.530) = 32.1°. Hence option (a) is correct.
Example 3
In Young's double slit experiment, the slit separation is 0.5 mm and the screen is 1 m away. If the wavelength of light used is 500 nm, find the fringe width.

a) 0.5 mm b) 1.0 mm c) 1.5 mm d) 2.0 mm
Solution: Fringe width β = λD/d = (500 × 10-9 × 1)/(0.5 × 10-3) = (500 × 10-9)/0.5 × 10-3 = 1000 × 10-6 = 1.0 × 10-3 m = 1.0 mm. Hence option (b) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For lenses and mirrors, memorize sign conventions: distances in direction of incident light are positive.
  • In refraction problems, always draw the normal at the point of incidence to avoid errors.
  • For total internal reflection, check if the light is traveling from denser to rarer medium and incidence angle > critical angle.
  • In interference, for dark fringes (destructive), path difference = (2n - 1)λ/2.
Pro Tip
For NEET, practice drawing accurate ray diagrams for lens and mirror problems. A good ray diagram can help you verify your calculated answers and catch sign convention errors quickly.

physics/electrostatics:
What is Electrostatics?

Electrostatics deals with stationary electric charges, the forces between them, and the electric fields they produce. Key topics for NEET include Coulomb's law, electric field and potential, Gauss's law, capacitors, and dielectrics. Understanding charge interactions and electric field concepts is fundamental for this topic.

Key Concepts

Coulomb's Law: F = kq1q2/r2, where k = 1/(4πε0) = 9 × 109 Nm2/C2. Electric Field: E = F/q = kQ/r2. Electric Potential: V = kQ/r, and potential difference ΔV = W/q. Gauss's Law: ΦE = &oblique8;E·dA = Qenc/ε0. Capacitance: C = Q/V. For parallel plate capacitor: C = ε0A/d. Energy stored in capacitor: U = (1/2)CV2 = Q2/(2C).

Solved Examples

Example 1
Two charges of +2 μC and +8 μC are placed 10 cm apart. Find the point on the line joining them where the electric field is zero.

a) 2.5 cm from smaller charge b) 3.33 cm from smaller charge c) 4 cm from smaller charge d) 5 cm from smaller charge
Solution: Let x cm from the 2 μC charge. The electric field is zero when E1 = E2. k(2)/x2 = k(8)/(10 - x)2. Taking square roots: √2/x = √8/(10 - x). √2/x = 2√2/(10 - x). 1/x = 2/(10 - x). 10 - x = 2x, so 3x = 10, x = 3.33 cm. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 2
A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.1 m2 separated by 2 mm. Find its capacitance. (ε0 = 8.85 × 10-12 C2/Nm2)

a) 44.25 pF b) 88.5 pF c) 22.125 pF d) 442.5 pF
Solution: C = ε0A/d = (8.85 × 10-12 × 0.1)/(2 × 10-3) = (8.85 × 10-13)/(2 × 10-3) = 4.425 × 10-10 F = 442.5 pF. Hence option (d) is correct.
Example 3
Find the potential at a distance of 30 cm from a point charge of 5 μC.

a) 1.5 × 105 V b) 1.5 × 104 V c) 4.5 × 105 V d) 4.5 × 104 V
Solution: V = kQ/r = (9 × 109 × 5 × 10-6)/(0.3) = (45 × 103)/0.3 = 1.5 × 105 V. Hence option (a) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For electric field zero problems, use the ratio method: the point is closer to the smaller charge.
  • For capacitors in series, use 1/Ceq = 1/C1 + 1/C2 + ...; for parallel, Ceq = C1 + C2 + ...
  • In problems involving dielectric insertion, remember that capacitance increases by factor K (dielectric constant).
  • For work done in moving a charge between two points, use W = q(VB - VA).
Pro Tip
For NEET, always convert all units to SI (meters, Coulombs, etc.) before plugging into formulas. Charge is typically given in μC, so remember to multiply by 10-6 to convert to Coulombs.

physics/magnetism:
What is Magnetism?

Magnetism deals with magnetic fields, their sources, and their effects on moving charges and magnetic materials. For NEET, key topics include Biot-Savart law, Ampere's circuital law, force on a current-carrying conductor, magnetic moment, Earth's magnetism, and electromagnetic induction. This topic bridges electricity and magnetism, forming the basis of electromagnetism.

Key Concepts

Biot-Savart Law: dB = (μ0/4π)(Idl × r)/r3. Magnetic field due to straight conductor: B = (μ0I)/(2πr). Force on a moving charge: F = q(v × B). Force on a current-carrying conductor: F = I(L × B). Ampere's Law: &oblique8;B·dl = μ0Ienc. Magnetic moment: M = IA for a current loop. Faraday's Law: Induced emf ε = -dΦB/dt. Lenz's Law: Induced current opposes the change causing it.

Solved Examples

Example 1
A long straight wire carries a current of 5 A. Find the magnetic field at a distance of 2 cm from the wire. (μ0 = 4π × 10-7 Tm/A)

a) 5 × 10-5 T b) 2.5 × 10-5 T c) 1 × 10-4 T d) 4 × 10-5 T
Solution: B = (μ0I)/(2πr) = (4π × 10-7 × 5)/(2π × 0.02) = (20π × 10-7)/(0.04π) = (20 × 10-7)/(0.04) = 5 × 10-5 T. Hence option (a) is correct.
Example 2
A proton enters a magnetic field of 0.2 T with a velocity of 106 m/s perpendicular to the field. Find the radius of its circular path. (mp = 1.67 × 10-27 kg, q = 1.6 × 10-19 C)

a) 2.6 cm b) 5.2 cm c) 1.3 cm d) 10.4 cm
Solution: For circular motion in magnetic field, qvB = mv2/r. r = mv/(qB) = (1.67 × 10-27 × 106)/(1.6 × 10-19 × 0.2) = (1.67 × 10-21)/(3.2 × 10-20) = 0.052 m = 5.2 cm. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 3
A circular coil of radius 5 cm has 100 turns and carries a current of 2 A. Find the magnetic field at its center.

a) 8π × 10-4 T b) 4π × 10-4 T c) 2π × 10-3 T d) 8π × 10-3 T
Solution: B at center of circular coil = (μ0NI)/(2r) = (4π × 10-7 × 100 × 2)/(2 × 0.05) = (8π × 10-5)/(0.1) = 8π × 10-4 T. Hence option (a) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For magnetic field direction, use the right-hand thumb rule: thumb points in direction of current, fingers curl in direction of magnetic field.
  • For force between two parallel current-carrying wires, currents in same direction attract, opposite directions repel.
  • In electromagnetic induction, the induced emf is maximum when the coil rotates perpendicular to the magnetic field.
  • For a solenoid, B = μ0nI, where n is number of turns per unit length.
Pro Tip
For NEET, learn Fleming's left-hand rule (for force on current-carrying conductor) and right-hand rule (for induced current in generators). These mnemonics save time in the exam and reduce sign errors.

Magnetic Materials and Hysteresis Loops

Magnetic materials are classified by their response to an applied magnetic field. Diamagnetic substances develop a weak magnetisation opposite to the field, with a relative permeability slightly less than one. Paramagnetic materials align their atomic dipoles with the field, giving a permeability marginally greater than one. Ferromagnetic materials exhibit strong, cooperative alignment of magnetic domains, producing permeabilities that can reach several thousand. The macroscopic behaviour of a ferromagnet is captured by its hysteresis loop, a plot of magnetic flux density B versus magnetic field strength H for a complete magnetisation cycle. The loop encloses an area proportional to the energy dissipated as heat per unit volume per cycle, known as hysteresis loss. Key points on the loop include the saturation flux density Bs, where all domains are aligned; the remanent flux density Br, the flux remaining after the external field is removed; and the coercive field Hc, the reverse field required to bring the flux back to zero. Soft magnetic materials such as silicon‑steel have narrow loops, low Hc and low hysteresis loss, making them suitable for transformer cores and inductors. Hard magnetic materials like Alnico or rare‑earth alloys possess wide loops, high Hc and high Br, serving as permanent magnets. The Steinmetz equation, Ph = kh f Bmaxn, quantifies hysteresis loss per unit volume, where f is frequency, Bmax the peak flux density, and n ≈ 1.6–2.0 for typical electrical steels. Eddy‑current loss, another core loss component, scales with the square of frequency and the square of lamination thickness; therefore, thin insulated laminations are used to suppress it. Understanding the shape and parameters of the hysteresis loop is essential for designing efficient magnetic circuits, selecting core material for a given operating frequency, and estimating temperature rise in transformers and rotating machines.

Motional Electromotive Force and Faraday's Law in Moving Media

When a conductor moves through a magnetic field, the magnetic component of the Lorentz force acts on the free charges, creating a potential difference known as motional emf. For a straight rod of length L moving with velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, the emf induced between its ends is ε = B L v. This result follows directly from the magnetic force q(v × B) on a charge q and the definition of emf as work per unit charge. In a more general situation, the emf around a closed loop C moving and deforming in a time‑varying magnetic field is given by the flux rule ε = − dΦB/dt, where ΦB = ∫S B·dA is the magnetic flux through any surface S bounded by C. The total time derivative includes both the explicit time variation of B and the change of flux due to the motion of the boundary. The equivalence of the motional emf expression and the flux rule can be demonstrated by applying the Leibniz integral rule to the moving surface. A classic illustration is the sliding rod on parallel rails forming a rectangular circuit; as the rod moves, the area of the loop increases, the flux increases, and an emf appears that drives a current. The direction of the induced current is given by Lenz’s law: it opposes the change in flux, which in this case means the magnetic force on the current‑carrying rod opposes the external pulling force. In rotating machines, the same principle generates alternating emf in the armature windings. For a coil of N turns rotating at angular speed ω in a uniform field B, the instantaneous emf is ε = N B A ω sin(ωt), where A is the coil area. This sinusoidal emf is the basis of AC generators. The concept of motional emf also underlies electromagnetic flow meters, where the voltage induced across a conducting fluid moving in a pipe is proportional to the flow velocity.

Worked Example: Motional EMF in a Rotating Rod
A conducting rod of length 0.5 m rotates about one end in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.3 T. The rod makes 60 revolutions per second. Calculate the emf induced between the fixed end and the free end of the rod.
The rod sweeps out a circular area. For a small element at distance r from the pivot moving with speed v = ω r, the motional emf contributed is dε = B v dr = B ω r dr. Integrating from 0 to L gives ε = ∫0L B ω r dr = ½ B ω L². The angular speed ω = 2π × 60 = 120π rad/s. Substituting B = 0.3 T, L = 0.5 m: ε = ½ × 0.3 × 120π × (0.5)² = 0.15 × 120π × 0.25 = 4.5π ≈ 14.1 V. The emf between the ends is approximately 14.1 V.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem involves a moving conductor, first decide whether the flux‑rule (ε = −dΦ/dt) or the direct motional‑emf formula (ε = ∫ (v × B)·dl) is simpler. For straight rods moving uniformly, the direct formula often yields the answer in one step. For rotating or deforming loops, the flux rule with a clear choice of surface avoids sign errors. Always draw the velocity, field, and length vectors to apply the right‑hand rule for the direction of induced current.

AC Circuit Resonance, Power Factor, and Phasor Analysis

In a series RLC circuit driven by a sinusoidal voltage v(t) = Vm sin(ωt), the steady‑state current is i(t) = Im sin(ωt − φ), where φ is the phase angle between voltage and current. The impedance Z = R + j(ωL − 1/ωC) combines resistance R, inductive reactance XL = ωL, and capacitive reactance XC = 1/ωC. The magnitude of impedance is |Z| = √[R² + (XL − XC)²] and the phase angle satisfies tan φ = (XL − XC)/R. Resonance occurs when XL = XC, i.e. ω0 = 1/√(LC). At resonance the impedance is purely resistive (Z = R), the current amplitude is maximum (Im = Vm/R), and the voltage across L and C can be Q times the source voltage, where the quality factor Q = ω0L/R = 1/(ω0CR). The bandwidth Δω = ω0/Q defines the frequency range over which the power delivered to the resistor is at least half its maximum value. Power factor cos φ = R/|Z| indicates the fraction of apparent power that is real power. A lagging power factor (φ > 0) means the circuit is inductive; a leading power factor (φ < 0) means it is capacitive. Power factor correction is achieved by adding a parallel capacitor to an inductive load, bringing the overall φ closer to zero and reducing the current drawn from the supply for the same real power. Phasor diagrams provide a geometric representation: voltage phasors for R, L, and C are drawn with appropriate phase shifts, and their vector sum equals the source voltage phasor. This visual method simplifies the analysis of series and parallel combinations, especially when multiple frequencies are present. In three‑phase systems, balanced loads allow per‑phase analysis using the same phasor techniques, with line‑to‑line voltages √3 times the phase voltages and a 30° phase shift.

Electromagnetic Wave Propagation, Polarization, and Poynting Vector

Maxwell’s equations in free space predict transverse electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. For a plane wave propagating in the +z direction, the electric and magnetic fields can be written as E(z,t) = E₀ cos(kz − ωt) x̂ and B(z,t) = B₀ cos(kz − ωt) ŷ, with E₀ = c B₀ and k = ω/c. The fields are perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation, confirming the transverse nature. The instantaneous Poynting vector S = (1/μ₀) E × B represents the power flux density (W/m²). For the plane wave above, S = (E₀²/μ₀c) cos²(kz − ωt) ẑ. The time‑averaged intensity I = ⟨S⟩ = ½ ε₀ c E₀² = ½ (E₀²/μ₀c). In a dielectric medium with relative permittivity εr and permeability μr, the wave speed becomes v = c/√(εrμr) and the intrinsic impedance η = √(μ/ε). Polarization describes the orientation of the electric field vector. Linear polarization occurs when E oscillates along a fixed direction. Circular polarization results from two orthogonal linear components of equal amplitude and a 90° phase difference; the tip of the E vector traces a helix. Elliptical polarization is the general case with unequal amplitudes or a phase difference other than 90°. Polarization can be produced by reflection (Brewster’s angle), by passage through anisotropic crystals (birefringence), or by antenna geometry. At a dielectric interface, the Fresnel equations give the reflection and transmission coefficients for s‑ (perpendicular) and p‑ (parallel) polarizations. Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a higher‑index medium to a lower‑index medium at an incidence angle greater than the critical angle θc = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁). In waveguides and optical fibres, boundary conditions quantise the allowed modes, each with a distinct field distribution and cutoff frequency. The concept of group velocity vg = dω/dk becomes important for pulses, as it determines the speed of energy and information transfer, which can differ from the phase velocity vp = ω/k in dispersive media.

Displacement Current and the Complete Set of Maxwell's Equations

Ampere’s circuital law in its original form, ∮ B·dl = μ₀ Ienc, fails for time‑varying electric fields because it does not account for the current that “flows” through a capacitor gap. Maxwell introduced the displacement current density Jd = ε₀ ∂E/∂t, so that the generalized Ampere‑Maxwell law reads ∮ B·dl = μ₀ (Icond + ε₀ dΦE/dt), where ΦE = ∫ E·dA is the electric flux through the surface bounded by the loop. This term restores continuity of current: in a charging capacitor, the conduction current in the leads equals the displacement current between the plates, ensuring that the magnetic field around the loop is uniquely defined regardless of the chosen surface. The four Maxwell equations in differential form are: ∇·E = ρ/ε₀ (Gauss’s law), ∇·B = 0 (no magnetic monopoles), ∇×E = −∂B/∂t (Faraday’s law), and ∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀ ∂E/∂t (Ampere‑Maxwell law). Together they imply the wave equation ∇²E − μ₀ε₀ ∂²E/∂t² = 0 in source‑free regions, confirming electromagnetic wave propagation. The displacement current is essential for the self‑consistency of the theory; without it, the divergence of the Ampere‑Maxwell law would give ∇·J = 0, contradicting charge conservation ∇·J + ∂ρ/∂t = 0. In materials, the equations incorporate polarization P and magnetisation M through D = ε₀E + P and H = B/μ₀ − M, leading to the macroscopic forms ∇·D = ρfree, ∇·B = 0, ∇×E = −∂B/∂t, ∇×H = Jfree + ∂D/∂t. The boundary conditions at interfaces follow from the integral forms: the tangential component of E is continuous, the normal component of D jumps by the free surface charge, the tangential component of H jumps by the free surface current, and the normal component of B is continuous. These conditions are used to derive reflection and transmission coefficients for waves at dielectric and conducting boundaries, and to analyse waveguides, cavities, and radiation from antennas.

  • Confusing the direction of induced emf in motional problems: always apply the right‑hand rule to v × B, not the left‑hand rule.
  • Assuming the resonance frequency of a parallel RLC circuit is the same as the series formula; the parallel resonant frequency shifts when the resistance is not negligible.
  • Neglecting the phase angle when calculating real power; using P = VI instead of P = VI cos φ leads to overestimation.
  • Treating the Poynting vector as instantaneous power flow in a standing wave; the time‑averaged Poynting vector is zero for a pure standing wave.
  • Forgetting that the displacement current term is required for consistency with charge conservation, not merely a mathematical convenience.
  • Using the free‑space wave speed c in a dielectric without adjusting for the refractive index n = √(εrμr).
  • Misapplying the Fresnel equations by swapping s and p polarizations or using the wrong angle (incidence vs. transmission).

These advanced topics deepen the conceptual framework needed for high‑level problem solving and should be revisited regularly during preparation.
physics/modern-physics:
What is Modern Physics?

Modern physics covers the revolutionary developments in physics from the early 20th century, including quantum mechanics, relativity, atomic and nuclear physics. For NEET, key topics include photoelectric effect, Bohr's atomic model, radioactivity, nuclear fission and fusion, and dual nature of matter. These concepts explain phenomena at atomic and subatomic scales.

Key Concepts

Photoelectric Effect: Einstein's equation: hf = φ + KEmax, where φ is work function. Threshold frequency f0 = φ/h. Bohr's Model: Angular momentum mvr = nh/2π, Energy En = -13.6/n2 eV, Radius rn = 0.529 n2/Z Å. de Broglie Wavelength: λ = h/p = h/(mv). Radioactive Decay: N = N0e-λt, half-life T1/2 = 0.693/λ. Mass-Energy Equivalence: E = mc2. Nuclear Binding Energy: Δm × c2.

Solved Examples

Example 1
The work function of a metal is 2.3 eV. Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on it. Find the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons. (h = 6.63 × 10-34 Js, c = 3 × 108 m/s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10-19 J)

a) 0.8 eV b) 1.1 eV c) 1.5 eV d) 2.3 eV
Solution: Energy of photon E = hc/λ = (6.63 × 10-34 × 3 × 108)/(400 × 10-9) = 4.97 × 10-19 J = 4.97 × 10-19/1.6 × 10-19 = 3.1 eV. KEmax = E - φ = 3.1 - 2.3 = 0.8 eV. Hence option (a) is correct.
Example 2
In a hydrogen atom, find the energy of the electron in the second excited state (n = 3).

a) -3.4 eV b) -1.51 eV c) -0.85 eV d) -13.6 eV
Solution: En = -13.6/n2 eV. For n = 3, E3 = -13.6/9 = -1.51 eV. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 3
A radioactive sample has a half-life of 5 days. How much fraction of the sample remains after 15 days?

a) 1/2 b) 1/4 c) 1/8 d) 1/16
Solution: Number of half-lives n = t/T1/2 = 15/5 = 3. Fraction remaining = (1/2)n = (1/2)3 = 1/8. Hence option (c) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For photoelectric effect, remember that intensity affects number of photoelectrons (current), not their kinetic energy.
  • For atomic spectra, the number of spectral lines when an electron drops from n to 1 is n(n-1)/2.
  • In radioactive decay, after n half-lives, remaining fraction = (1/2)n and decayed fraction = 1 - (1/2)n.
  • For binding energy calculations, mass defect Δm is converted to energy using 1 amu = 931 MeV.
Pro Tip
For NEET, memorize the key constants: h = 6.63 × 10-34 Js, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10-19 J, 1 amu = 931 MeV/c2. Also remember that the ground state energy of hydrogen is -13.6 eV.

Foundations of Physical Chemistry: Mole Concept and Stoichiometry

1.1 The Mole as a Bridge Between Microscopic and Macroscopic Worlds

The mole is the fundamental counting unit that allows chemists to translate the number of atoms, molecules, or ions in a sample into a measurable mass. One mole of any substance contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities, a value fixed by the 2019 redefinition of the SI base units. Because the molar mass of an element expressed in grams per mole is numerically equal to its atomic weight, the relationship n = m/M connects the mass m of a sample to the amount of substance n. This equivalence makes it possible to weigh out reactants in the laboratory while knowing precisely how many particles will take part in a reaction.

1.2 Avogadro’s Law and the Molar Volume of Gases

Avogadro’s hypothesis states that equal volumes of all gases, measured at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of particles. At standard temperature and pressure (0 °C, 1 atm) one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.414 L, a value that follows directly from the ideal‑gas equation PV = nRT. Real gases deviate from this volume because of intermolecular forces and finite molecular size; the deviation is quantified by the compressibility factor Z = PV/RT. Understanding these deviations is essential when high‑precision gas‑phase stoichiometry is required, for example in the calibration of gas‑chromatography standards.

1.3 Stoichiometric Calculations and Limiting Reagents

Balanced chemical equations provide the mole ratios that govern how reactants combine and products form. When the initial amounts of reactants are known, the limiting reagent is identified by comparing the mole ratio of each reactant to its stoichiometric coefficient; the reactant that yields the smallest amount of product controls the theoretical yield. The percent yield, calculated as (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100 %, reveals the efficiency of a process and is a key metric in both laboratory synthesis and industrial production. Mastery of these calculations enables a student to predict the mass of product obtainable from a given mass of starting material, a skill tested repeatedly in quantitative problems.

Atomic Structure and Quantum Mechanics

2.1 The Development of the Quantum Model

The failure of classical physics to explain black‑body radiation, the photoelectric effect, and atomic line spectra led to the quantum hypothesis introduced by Max Planck in 1900 and extended by Albert Einstein in 1905. Niels Bohr’s 1913 model quantised the angular momentum of the electron in hydrogen, reproducing the Rydberg formula for spectral lines. However, the Bohr model could not account for the fine structure of spectra or the behaviour of multi‑electron atoms. The Schrödinger equation, published in 1926, replaced the notion of defined orbits with wavefunctions ψ that describe the probability density of finding an electron in a region of space. The solutions to this equation are characterised by four quantum numbers: principal (n), azimuthal (l), magnetic (mₗ), and spin (mₛ), which together define the unique state of each electron in an atom.

2.2 Electron Configurations and the Periodic Table

The Aufbau principle, guided by the (n + l) rule, dictates the order in which atomic orbitals are filled as the atomic number increases. Hund’s rule states that electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing, maximising total spin and lowering electron‑electron repulsion. The Pauli exclusion principle forbids two electrons in the same atom from having identical sets of four quantum numbers. These rules generate the periodic recurrence of chemical properties because elements in the same group share similar valence‑electron configurations. Exceptions such as chromium (3d⁵4s¹) and copper (3d¹⁰4s¹) arise from the extra stability associated with half‑filled and fully‑filled d subshells.

2.3 Spectroscopic Evidence for Quantised Energy Levels

Atomic emission and absorption spectra provide direct experimental proof of quantised energy levels. When an electron transitions from a higher energy level E₂ to a lower level E₁, a photon of frequency ν = (E₂ − E₁)/h is emitted; the reverse process absorbs a photon of the same frequency. The Lyman, Balmer, and Paschen series of hydrogen correspond to transitions ending at n = 1, 2, and 3 respectively. In multi‑electron atoms, the presence of screening and penetration modifies the effective nuclear charge experienced by each electron, shifting line positions and giving rise to the complex spectra used in analytical techniques such as atomic absorption spectroscopy.

Example 1
A 0.500 g sample of an unknown metal M reacts completely with excess hydrochloric acid to produce 0.0250 mol of H₂ gas. The reaction follows the equation 2 M + 6 HCl → 2 MCl₃ + 3 H₂. Determine the molar mass of M and identify the metal from the periodic table.
Solution: From the stoichiometry, 3 mol H₂ are produced per 2 mol M, so moles of M = (2/3) × 0.0250 mol = 0.01667 mol. Molar mass = mass ÷ moles = 0.500 g ÷ 0.01667 mol = 30.0 g mol⁻¹. The element with a molar mass close to 30 g mol⁻¹ that forms a +3 oxidation state is aluminium (Al, 26.98 g mol⁻¹) but the calculated value is slightly higher; considering experimental uncertainty, the metal is most likely aluminium.
Exam‑Day Insight
When a problem gives a gas volume at non‑standard conditions, always convert to moles using the ideal‑gas law before applying stoichiometric ratios; this avoids the common mistake of using 22.4 L mol⁻¹ at the wrong temperature or pressure.

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

3.1 Ionic, Covalent, and Metallic Bonding

Ionic bonds arise from the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the transfer of electrons from a low‑ionisation‑energy metal to a high‑electron‑affinity non‑metal. The lattice energy, which can be estimated by the Born‑Landé equation, quantifies the stability of the resulting crystal. Covalent bonds involve the sharing of electron pairs between atoms; the degree of sharing is described by electronegativity differences, with a difference greater than about 1.7 indicating predominant ionic character. Metallic bonding is characterised by a delocalised “sea” of valence electrons that holds positively charged metal ions together, giving rise to properties such as electrical conductivity, malleability, and metallic lustre.

3.2 Valence‑Shell Electron‑Pair Repulsion Theory and Molecular Geometry

The VSEPR model predicts the three‑dimensional arrangement of electron domains around a central atom by minimising repulsions between bonding pairs and lone pairs. The order of repulsion strength is lone‑pair–lone‑pair > lone‑pair–bonding‑pair > bonding‑pair–bonding‑pair. Consequently, molecules such as CH₄ (four bonding pairs) adopt a tetrahedral geometry with bond angles of 109.5°, while NH₃ (three bonding pairs, one lone pair) is trigonal pyramidal with a reduced angle of about 107°, and H₂O (two bonding pairs, two lone pairs) is bent at roughly 104.5°. The model also rationalises the shapes of species with expanded octets, such as SF₆ (octahedral) and XeF₄ (square planar).

3.3 Hybridisation and the Description of σ and π Bonds

Hybridisation mixes atomic orbitals on the same atom to form a set of equivalent hybrid orbitals that can form σ bonds directed in space. sp hybridisation yields two linear orbitals (180°), sp² gives three trigonal‑planar orbitals (120°), and sp³ produces four tetrahedral orbitals (109.5°). Unhybridised p orbitals overlap side‑by‑side to form π bonds, which are weaker than σ bonds and restrict rotation about the bond axis. In ethene (C₂H₄) each carbon is sp² hybridised; the C=C double bond consists of one σ bond from sp²–sp² overlap and one π bond from p–p overlap. In ethyne (C₂H₂) each carbon is sp hybridised, giving a triple bond composed of one σ and two π bonds.

Thermodynamics and Energy Changes

4.1 The First Law: Conservation of Energy

The first law of thermodynamics states that the internal energy U of an isolated system is constant; for a closed system, the change in internal energy ΔU equals the heat q added to the system plus the work w done on the system (ΔU = q + w). In chemistry, work is most often pressure‑volume work w = −PΔV, so at constant pressure the heat exchanged equals the enthalpy change ΔH = ΔU + Δ(PV). Enthalpy is a state function, meaning its value depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path taken. This property allows the use of Hess’s law to calculate ΔH for a reaction by summing the enthalpy changes of a series of steps that lead from reactants to products.

4.2 Enthalpy Changes in Chemical Reactions

Standard enthalpy of formation ΔH_f° is defined as the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states at 1 bar and a specified temperature (usually 298 K). The standard reaction enthalpy ΔH_rxn° can be obtained from Σ n ΔH_f°(products) − Σ m ΔH_f°(reactants). Exothermic reactions have negative ΔH (heat released), while endothermic reactions have positive ΔH (heat absorbed). Calorimetry, either constant‑pressure (coffee‑cup) or constant‑volume (bomb), provides experimental ΔH or ΔU values. The temperature dependence of ΔH is described by Kirchhoff’s law: ΔH(T₂) = ΔH(T₁) + ∫ΔC_p dT, where ΔC_p is the difference in heat capacities between products and reactants.

4.3 The Second Law: Entropy and Spontaneity

The second law introduces entropy S, a measure of the number of microscopic configurations consistent with a macroscopic state. For any spontaneous process in an isolated system, the total entropy change ΔS_total > 0. In a non‑isolated system, the Gibbs free energy G = H − TS combines enthalpy and entropy to predict spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure: a process is spontaneous if ΔG < 0, non‑spontaneous if ΔG > 0, and at equilibrium if ΔG = 0. The standard Gibbs energy of formation ΔG_f° allows calculation of ΔG_rxn° analogously to ΔH_rxn°. The relationship ΔG° = −RT ln K links thermodynamics to chemical equilibrium, where K is the equilibrium constant.

Chemical Equilibrium and Kinetics

5.1 Dynamic Equilibrium and the Equilibrium Constant

At equilibrium the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant in time. The equilibrium constant K_c is expressed in terms of molar concentrations, while K_p uses partial pressures for gas‑phase reactions; they are related by K_p = K_c(RT)Δn_gas, where Δn_gas is the change in moles of gas. The reaction quotient Q has the same form as K but uses instantaneous concentrations; comparing Q to K predicts the direction in which the system will shift to reach equilibrium (Q < K → forward, Q > K → reverse). Le Chatelier’s principle states that a system at equilibrium will respond to a change in concentration, pressure, or temperature by shifting in a direction that counteracts the imposed change.

5.2 Reaction Rates and Rate Laws

The rate of a reaction is defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time. For a reaction aA + bB → products, the differential rate law is rate = k[A]^x[B]^y, where x and y are the reaction orders with respect to A and B, determined experimentally. The overall order is x + y. The rate constant k varies with temperature according to the Arrhenius equation k = A exp(−E_a/RT), where A is the pre‑exponential factor and E_a is the activation energy. A plot of ln k versus 1/T yields a straight line of slope −E_a/R, providing a method to determine E_a from kinetic data.

5.3 Integrated Rate Laws and Half‑Life

Integration of the differential rate law gives concentration‑time relationships that are linear for specific orders. For a first‑order reaction, ln[A] = −kt + ln[A]0; a plot of ln[A] versus t is linear with slope −k. The half‑life t1/2 = ln 2/k is independent of initial concentration, a hallmark of first‑order kinetics. For a second‑order reaction with a single reactant, 1/[A] = kt + 1/[A]0, and the half‑life depends on the initial concentration as t1/2 = 1/(k[A]0). Zero‑order reactions show a linear decrease in concentration with time, [A] = −kt + [A]0, and their half‑life is t1/2 = [A]0/(2k). Recognising the linear form appropriate to the order allows rapid determination of k from experimental data.

5.4 Catalysis and Reaction Mechanisms

A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, increasing the rate without being consumed. Homogeneous catalysts exist in the same phase as the reactants, while heterogeneous catalysts operate at a phase boundary, often a solid surface. The catalytic cycle involves adsorption of reactants, reaction on the surface, and desorption of products. Enzymes are biological catalysts that exhibit high specificity and operate under mild conditions; their kinetics are described by the Michaelis–Menten equation v = (V_max[S])/(K_m + [S]). Understanding the elementary steps of a mechanism, identifying the rate‑determining step, and applying the steady‑state approximation for reactive intermediates are essential for deriving rate laws that match experimental observations.

Mastery of these interconnected topics equips a student to analyse any physicochemical problem by moving fluidly between quantitative calculations and conceptual reasoning.
chemistry/organic-chemistry:
What is Organic Chemistry?

Organic chemistry is the study of carbon-containing compounds, their structure, properties, reactions, and synthesis. For NEET, key topics include IUPAC nomenclature, isomerism, reaction mechanisms (SN1, SN2, E1, E2), functional group transformations, hydrocarbons, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids, and biomolecules. Understanding reaction mechanisms and electron movement is crucial.

Key Concepts

IUPAC Nomenclature: Identify the longest carbon chain, number the carbons to give the lowest locants to substituents, name substituents alphabetically. Isomerism: Structural isomers (chain, position, functional group) and stereoisomers (geometrical and optical). Reaction Mechanisms: SN1 (unimolecular, carbocation intermediate, racemization) and SN2 (bimolecular, backside attack, inversion). Markovnikov's Rule: In addition of HX to alkenes, the hydrogen adds to the carbon with more hydrogen atoms. Electrophilic Substitution: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution reactions (nitration, halogenation, sulfonation).

Solved Examples

Example 1
What is the IUPAC name of CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-COOH?

a) 3-methylbutanoic acid b) 2-methylbutanoic acid c) 3-methylpentanoic acid d) 2-methylpentanoic acid
Solution: The longest chain containing the carboxylic acid group has 4 carbons (butanoic acid). Numbering starts from the carbon of COOH. The methyl group is on carbon 3. So the name is 3-methylbutanoic acid. Hence option (a) is correct.
Example 2
Which of the following shows optical isomerism?

a) CH3OH b) CH3CH(OH)COOH c) CH3COOH d) CCl4
Solution: Optical isomerism occurs in molecules with a chiral carbon (carbon with four different groups). In CH3CH(OH)COOH, the central carbon (CH) has four different groups: H, OH, CH3, and COOH. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 3
When propene reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxide, the product is:

a) 1-bromopropane b) 2-bromopropane c) 1,2-dibromopropane d) 1,3-dibromopropane
Solution: In the presence of peroxide, the addition of HBr to alkenes follows anti-Markovnikov rule (peroxide effect). The Br adds to the terminal carbon. So propene forms 1-bromopropane. Hence option (a) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For distinguishing SN1 vs SN2: SN1 favors tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents; SN2 favors primary substrates and polar aprotic solvents.
  • For geometrical isomerism, if two identical groups are on the same side of the double bond, it is cis; on opposite sides, it is trans.
  • In naming organic compounds, aldehydes and carboxylic acids always get priority in numbering (lowest locant).
  • For the peroxide effect, remember that it only works with HBr, not HCl or HI.
Pro Tip
For NEET organic chemistry, make flashcards for named reactions (Friedel-Crafts, Aldol condensation, Cannizzaro, etc.) with reagents, conditions, and mechanisms. Review them regularly to build speed in identification-based questions.

Connect concepts to real-world applications: Why sky is blue (Rayleigh scattering), how pressure cookers work, why apples turn brown (oxidation).

chemistry/inorganic-chemistry:
The Periodic Table and Periodic Properties

1.1 Historical Development and Modern Form

The periodic table arranges elements in order of increasing atomic number so that elements with similar chemical properties fall in the same vertical group. Dmitri Mendeleev's 1869 table left gaps for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties with remarkable accuracy, but the modern form follows Henry Moseley's 1913 discovery that atomic number, not atomic mass, is the fundamental ordering principle. The long form of the table contains eighteen groups and seven periods, with the f-block elements placed separately at the bottom to keep the table's width manageable. Each period corresponds to the filling of a principal quantum shell, while each group reflects a common valence electron configuration that dictates chemical behaviour.

1.2 Periodic Trends in Atomic and Ionic Radii

Atomic radius decreases across a period because the nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same principal shell, so the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outermost electrons rises steadily. Down a group, a new principal shell is added, which outweighs the increased nuclear charge and causes the radius to increase. Ionic radii follow the same trends, but cations are always smaller than their parent atoms because the loss of electrons reduces electron-electron repulsion and often removes an entire shell, while anions are larger because added electrons increase repulsion without increasing nuclear charge. For isoelectronic species such as N3-, O2-, F-, Na+, Mg2+, and Al3+, the radius decreases as nuclear charge increases, giving the order N3- > O2- > F- > Na+ > Mg2+ > Al3+.

1.3 Ionization Energy, Electron Affinity, and Electronegativity

First ionization energy generally increases across a period because the increasing effective nuclear charge holds electrons more tightly, and it decreases down a group because the outermost electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded. Exceptions occur at Group 13 (B, Al, Ga) where removal of a p-electron is easier than removal of an s-electron from the preceding Group 12 element, and at Group 16 (O, S, Se) where electron-electron repulsion in a paired p-orbital lowers the energy needed to remove one electron. Electron affinity becomes more exothermic across a period and less exothermic down a group, though the trend is less regular because of small orbital sizes and repulsion effects. Electronegativity, measured on the Pauling scale, follows the same periodic pattern as ionization energy; fluorine (3.98) is the most electronegative element and caesium (0.79) the least, and the difference in electronegativity between bonded atoms determines the ionic character of the bond.

1.4 Metallic Character and Oxidation States

Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group, mirroring the trends in ionization energy and electronegativity. Elements on the left of the table lose electrons readily to form cations, while those on the right gain electrons to form anions. Transition metals exhibit variable oxidation states because the (n-1)d and ns orbitals are close in energy, allowing different numbers of electrons to be lost or shared. The highest oxidation state of a transition metal usually equals its group number up to manganese (Group 7, +7 in MnO4-), after which the increasing nuclear charge makes higher oxidation states less stable. In the p-block, the inert pair effect makes the oxidation state two less than the group valence increasingly stable down Groups 13-16, so Tl(I) is more stable than Tl(III), Pb(II) more stable than Pb(IV), and Bi(III) more stable than Bi(V).

Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure

2.1 Ionic Bonding and Lattice Energy

Ionic bonds form when the electronegativity difference between two atoms is large enough (typically >1.7 on the Pauling scale) that electron transfer creates oppositely charged ions held together by electrostatic attraction. The stability of an ionic compound is quantified by its lattice energy, the energy released when gaseous ions combine to form one mole of solid crystal. The Born-Landé equation shows that lattice energy is proportional to the product of the ionic charges and inversely proportional to the sum of the ionic radii, so compounds with small, highly charged ions such as MgO (Mg2+ and O2-) have very high lattice energies and high melting points. The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to relate lattice energy to measurable quantities: enthalpy of formation, enthalpy of atomization, ionization energies, electron affinities, and enthalpy of sublimation, allowing lattice energies to be determined indirectly.

2.2 Covalent Bonding and Lewis Structures

Covalent bonds arise from the sharing of electron pairs between atoms of similar electronegativity. A Lewis structure represents valence electrons as dots and shows how atoms achieve noble-gas configurations by sharing. The octet rule works well for second-period elements but fails for molecules with odd numbers of electrons (NO, NO2), electron-deficient species (BF3, BeCl2), and expanded octets in third-period and heavier elements (PF5, SF6, XeF4) where d-orbitals or, more accurately, hypervalent bonding involving three-centre four-electron bonds can accommodate extra electrons. Formal charge, calculated as valence electrons minus non-bonding electrons minus half the bonding electrons, helps select the most plausible Lewis structure; the structure with formal charges closest to zero and negative charges on the more electronegative atoms is preferred.

2.3 VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry

The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) model predicts molecular shapes by assuming that electron pairs around a central atom arrange themselves to minimize repulsion. The order of repulsion strength is lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair, so lone pairs occupy more space and compress bond angles. The steric number (number of sigma bonds plus lone pairs) determines the electron-pair geometry: 2 gives linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral, 5 trigonal bipyramidal, and 6 octahedral. The molecular geometry is the shape of the atoms only; for example, four electron pairs with one lone pair (steric number 4, one lone pair) give a tetrahedral electron-pair geometry but a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry (NH3, bond angle 107°), while two lone pairs give a bent geometry (H2O, bond angle 104.5°). In trigonal bipyramidal arrangements, lone pairs always occupy equatorial positions to minimize 90° repulsions, leading to seesaw (SF4), T-shaped (ClF3), and linear (XeF2) molecular geometries.

2.4 Hybridization and Orbital Overlap

Hybridization mixes atomic orbitals on the same atom to form equivalent hybrid orbitals that overlap more effectively with orbitals on neighbouring atoms. The number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed, and the hybridization scheme corresponds to the steric number from VSEPR: sp (linear, 180°), sp2 (trigonal planar, 120°), sp3 (tetrahedral, 109.5°), sp3d (trigonal bipyramidal), and sp3d2 (octahedral). Sigma bonds form by head-on overlap of hybrid orbitals or s-orbitals, while pi bonds form by sideways overlap of unhybridized p-orbitals. In ethene (C2H4), each carbon is sp2 hybridized; three sp2 orbitals form sigma bonds (two C-H and one C-C), and the remaining p-orbitals overlap to form a pi bond, giving a rigid planar structure. In ethyne (C2H2), sp hybridization leaves two p-orbitals for two pi bonds, producing a linear molecule with a short, strong triple bond.

2.5 Molecular Orbital Theory for Homonuclear Diatomics

Molecular orbital (MO) theory treats electrons as delocalized over the entire molecule, forming bonding, antibonding, and non-bonding orbitals from linear combinations of atomic orbitals. For homonuclear diatomics of the second period, the ordering of MOs depends on the energy gap between 2s and 2p orbitals. For Li2 to N2, the order is σ2s, σ*2s, π2px=π2py, σ2pz, π*2px=π*2py, σ*2pz; for O2 and F2, the σ2pz drops below the π2p orbitals because of reduced s-p mixing. Bond order = ½ (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons) predicts stability and bond length: N2 (bond order 3) has a very short, strong triple bond; O2 (bond order 2) is paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons in degenerate π* orbitals, a result MO theory explains but Lewis structures cannot; F2 (bond order 1) has a weak single bond; Ne2 (bond order 0) does not exist.

Example 1
Predict the shape and bond angle of ClF3 using VSEPR theory, and state the hybridization of the central chlorine atom.
Solution: Chlorine in ClF3 has seven valence electrons. Three are used to form sigma bonds with three fluorine atoms, leaving four electrons (two lone pairs). The steric number is therefore 5 (three bond pairs + two lone pairs), giving a trigonal bipyramidal electron-pair geometry. To minimize repulsion, the two lone pairs occupy equatorial positions, resulting in a T-shaped molecular geometry. The bond angles are slightly less than 90° and 180° due to lone pair-bond pair repulsion being stronger than bond pair-bond pair repulsion. The hybridization corresponding to steric number 5 is sp3d. Thus ClF3 is T-shaped with sp3d hybridization.
Exam Insight
In NEET, questions on VSEPR often ask for the shape of ions such as ICl4- or XeF4. Remember that for steric number 6 with two lone pairs, the lone pairs occupy opposite axial positions in the octahedral electron-pair geometry, giving a square planar molecular geometry. The bond angles are exactly 90° because the lone pairs are trans to each other and their repulsions cancel in the equatorial plane.

Coordination Compounds

3.1 Werner's Coordination Theory

Alfred Werner's 1893 coordination theory revolutionized the understanding of complex compounds by proposing that metal ions exhibit two types of valence: primary valence (oxidation state), satisfied by anions, and secondary valence (coordination number), satisfied by ligands attached directly to the metal ion in a fixed geometry. Werner's experiments with cobalt(III) chloride-ammonia complexes, such as CoCl3·6NH3 (which precipitates all three chlorides as AgCl), CoCl3·5NH3 (two chlorides precipitated), and CoCl3·4NH3 (one chloride precipitated), demonstrated that only the chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are ionizable. He also resolved optical isomers of [Co(en)3]3+ and geometric isomers of [Co(NH3)4Cl2]+, proving that coordination compounds have definite three-dimensional structures, not chain structures as previously believed.

3.2 Nomenclature and Isomerism

IUPAC nomenclature for coordination compounds follows a systematic order: ligands are named alphabetically before the metal, with prefixes di-, tri-, tetra-, penta-, hexa- for simple ligands and bis-, tris-, tetrakis- for complex ligand names. Anionic ligands end in -o (chloro, cyano, hydroxo), neutral ligands keep their common names (aqua, ammine, carbonyl, nitrosyl), and cationic ligands end in -ium. The metal name takes its element name for cationic or neutral complexes and the -ate suffix for anionic complexes (ferrate, cuprate, cobaltate), with the oxidation state in Roman numerals in parentheses. Isomerism in coordination compounds includes structural isomerism (ionization, hydrate, linkage, coordination, and coordination position isomerism) and stereoisomerism (geometric and optical). Geometric isomerism arises in square planar (MA2B2 type) and octahedral (MA4B2, MA3B3) complexes; optical isomerism occurs in octahedral complexes lacking a plane of symmetry, such as [M(AA)3] and [M(AA)2B2] (cis form), where AA is a bidentate ligand like ethylenediamine.

3.3 Crystal Field Theory and Spectrochemical Series

Crystal Field Theory (CFT) treats ligands as point negative charges that split the degenerate d-orbitals of the central metal ion. In an octahedral field, the five d-orbitals split into a lower-energy t2g set (dxy, dyz, dzx) and a higher-energy eg set (dz2, dx2-y2), with a splitting energy Δo. In a tetrahedral field, the splitting is inverted and smaller (Δt ≈ 4/9 Δo). The magnitude of Δo depends on the metal ion (increasing down a group and with higher oxidation state) and the ligand. The spectrochemical series orders ligands by field strength: I- < Br- < SCN- (S) < Cl- < NO3- < F- < OH- < C2O42- < H2O < NCS- (N) < NH3 < en < bipy < phen < NO2- < PPh3 < CN- < CO. Strong-field ligands cause large splitting and favour low-spin configurations; weak-field ligands cause small splitting and favour high-spin configurations.

3.4 Magnetic Properties and Colour

The magnetic behaviour of a complex depends on the number of unpaired electrons. High-spin complexes follow Hund's rule, maximizing unpaired electrons, while low-spin complexes pair electrons in the lower t2g orbitals before occupying eg. For example, [Fe(CN)6]4- (d6, strong field) is low-spin t2g6eg0 with no unpaired electrons (diamagnetic), whereas [Fe(H2O)6]2+ (d6, weak field) is high-spin t2g4eg2 with four unpaired electrons (paramagnetic). The spin-only magnetic moment μ = √[n(n+2)] BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons, gives a good approximation for first-row transition metals. Colour arises from d-d transitions: absorption of visible light promotes an electron from t2g to eg, and the complementary colour is observed. The wavelength absorbed corresponds to Δo; thus [Ti(H2O)6]3+ (d1) absorbs at about 20,000 cm-1 (green-yellow) and appears purple. Charge-transfer transitions, where an electron moves from ligand to metal (LMCT) or metal to ligand (MLCT), are often more intense and account for the deep colours of MnO4- (purple) and [Fe(phen)3]2+ (red).

s-Block Elements

4.1 Group 1: Alkali Metals

The alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr) have a single ns1 valence electron, which they lose readily to form M+ ions, giving them a uniform +1 oxidation state. Their low ionization energies and low electronegativities make them the most electropositive elements. Lithium shows anomalous behaviour due to its small size and high charge density: it forms a stable nitride (Li3N) directly with nitrogen, its carbonate and fluoride are sparingly soluble, and it forms covalent organolithium compounds. The standard electrode potentials (E° M+/M) become more negative down the group (Li -3.04 V, Na -2.71 V, K -2.93 V, Rb -2.98 V, Cs -3.03 V), but lithium's highly negative value is due to its large hydration enthalpy rather than a low ionization energy. All alkali metals react vigorously with water to give MOH and H2, with reactivity increasing down the group. They form ionic oxides (M2O), peroxides (M2O2), and superoxides (MO2); the larger cations stabilize the larger anions, so Li forms mainly the oxide, Na forms the peroxide, and K, Rb, Cs form superoxides.

4.2 Group 2: Alkaline Earth Metals

The alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra) have an ns2 configuration and predominantly show a +2 oxidation state. Their first ionization energies are higher than those of alkali metals, but the second ionization energy is compensated by the high lattice energies or hydration enthalpies of the M2+ compounds. Beryllium is anomalous: it forms covalent compounds, its oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric, and it does not react with water even at high temperatures. Magnesium reacts slowly with hot water, while Ca, Sr, Ba react readily with cold water. The solubility of hydroxides increases down the group (Be(OH)2 and Mg(OH)2 are sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)2 is quite soluble), while the solubility of sulfates and carbonates decreases down the group due to the faster decrease in hydration enthalpy compared to lattice energy. Thermal stability of carbonates and nitrates increases down the group because larger cations stabilize the large anions better; BeCO3 is unstable, MgCO3 decomposes at 540°C, CaCO3 at 900°C, and BaCO3 at 1360°C.

4.3 Anomalous Behaviour and Diagonal Relationship

Lithium and magnesium exhibit a diagonal relationship due to their similar charge densities (Li+ 76 pm, Mg2+ 72 pm) and electronegativities (Li 0.98, Mg 1.31). Both form nitrides on heating in nitrogen, both form covalent organometallic compounds, both have carbonates that decompose on heating, and both have hydroxides and fluorides that are sparingly soluble. Beryllium and aluminium show a similar diagonal relationship: both form amphoteric oxides and hydroxides, both form covalent halides that are Lewis acids, both form complex ions like [BeF4]2- and [AlF6]3-, and both are rendered passive by concentrated nitric acid due to a protective oxide layer. These relationships arise because moving down a group increases size while moving across a period decreases size, so the two effects partially cancel along the diagonal.

p-Block Elements

5.1 Group 13: Boron Family

Group 13 elements (B, Al, Ga, In, Tl) have an ns2np1 configuration. Boron is a non-metal with a high ionization energy and forms only covalent compounds; it is electron-deficient and acts as a Lewis acid, forming adducts with Lewis bases (BF3·NH3) and complex anions like [BF4]-. Aluminium is a metal but forms a protective oxide layer (Al2O3) that makes it corrosion-resistant. The +3 oxidation state is common for B, Al, Ga, In, but the inert pair effect makes +1 increasingly stable down the group; Tl(I) is more stable than Tl(III), and Tl+ resembles alkali metal ions in size and chemistry. The trihalides are Lewis acids, with acid strength order BF3 < BCl3 < BBr3 (due to pπ-pπ back-bonding in BF3 reducing electron deficiency). Boron forms unusual hydrides (boranes) like B2H6 with three-centre two-electron bonds, and borax (Na2B4O7·10H2O) gives a bead test for metal ions.

5.2 Group 14: Carbon Family

Group 14 (C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb) shows a transition from non-metal to metal. Carbon's unique ability to catenate (form C-C bonds) leads to the vast field of organic chemistry. The +4 oxidation state dominates for C and Si, but the inert pair effect makes +2 increasingly stable for Ge, Sn, and Pb; Pb(II) is more stable than Pb(IV), and PbO2 is a strong oxidizing agent. All elements form tetrahalides (MX4), but stability decreases down the group; PbI4 does not exist. The dioxides (CO2, SiO2, GeO2, SnO2, PbO2) show decreasing acidity: CO2 and SiO2 are acidic, GeO2 and SnO2 are amphoteric, PbO2 is weakly acidic. Silicates, based on the SiO44- tetrahedron, form the bulk of the Earth's crust; they polymerize by sharing corners to give chains, sheets, and three-dimensional frameworks (zeolites).

5.3 Group 15: Nitrogen Family

Group 15 (N, P, As, Sb, Bi) has ns2np3 configuration. Nitrogen differs sharply from the others: it is a diatomic gas (N≡N, bond energy 945 kJ/mol), forms multiple bonds readily (pπ-pπ), and shows oxidation states from -3 to +5. Phosphorus exists as P4 tetrahedra (white P) and polymeric forms (red, black P). The hydrides (NH3, PH3, AsH3, SbH3, BiH3) show decreasing thermal stability and basicity down the group; NH3 is a strong ligand and hydrogen-bonds, while PH3 is a weak ligand and does not hydrogen-bond. Oxides include N2O, NO, N2O3, NO2, N2O5 for nitrogen and P4O6, P4O10 for phosphorus. The oxoacids of nitrogen (HNO2, HNO3) and phosphorus (H3PO2, H3PO3, H3PO4) show varying oxidation states and reducing/oxidizing properties; H3PO2 (hypophosphorous acid) is a strong reducing agent due to two P-H bonds.

5.4 Group 16: Oxygen Family

Group 16 (O, S, Se, Te, Po) has ns2np4. Oxygen is a diatomic gas with strong pπ-pπ bonding; it shows -2 oxidation state (except in OF2 and peroxides) and does not expand its octet. Sulphur forms S8 rings and catenates extensively (S-S bonds up to 20 atoms). The hydrides H2O, H2S, H2Se, H2Te show decreasing bond angles (104.5°, 92°, 91°, 90°) and increasing acidity. Oxides: SO2 (bent, reducing agent), SO3 (trigonal planar, anhydride of H2SO4). Sulphuric acid is manufactured by the Contact process (V2O5 catalyst, 450°C, 2 atm). The oxoacids of sulphur include H2SO3, H2SO4, H2S2O3 (thiosulphuric), H2S2O7 (disulphuric), and peroxoacids like H2SO5 (peroxymonosulphuric, Caro's acid).

5.5 Group 17: Halogens

Group 17 (F, Cl, Br, I, At) are the most electronegative elements, needing one electron to complete an octet.
chemistry/environmental-chemistry:
What is Environmental Chemistry?

Environmental chemistry studies the chemical processes occurring in the environment and the impact of human activities on natural systems. For NEET, key topics include air pollution, water pollution, soil pollution, ozone layer depletion, greenhouse effect, and waste management. Understanding the causes, effects, and control measures of environmental issues is essential.

Key Concepts

Air Pollution: Major pollutants include CO, SO2, NOx, particulate matter (PM2.5, PM10), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Greenhouse Effect: Gases like CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs trap heat in the atmosphere, causing global warming. Ozone Depletion: CFCs release chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone: Cl + O3 → ClO + O2, ClO + O → Cl + O2. Water Pollution: BOD (Biochemical Oxygen Demand) measures organic pollution. Higher BOD indicates more pollution. Photochemical Smog: Formed by reaction of NOx and VOCs in sunlight, producing ozone and PAN (peroxyacyl nitrate).

Solved Examples

Example 1
Which of the following is primarily responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer?

a) CO2 b) SO2 c) CFCs d) CH4
Solution: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are the primary cause of ozone depletion. When CFCs reach the stratosphere, UV radiation breaks them down, releasing chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone molecules. Hence option (c) is correct.
Example 2
What is the permissible level of lead in drinking water as per WHO standards?

a) 0.05 ppm b) 0.5 ppm c) 1.0 ppm d) 5.0 ppm
Solution: The WHO permissible limit for lead in drinking water is 0.05 ppm (parts per million). Lead is toxic and can cause neurological damage, especially in children. Hence option (a) is correct.
Example 3
Which gas is mainly responsible for the greenhouse effect?

a) O2 b) N2 c) CO2 d) Ar
Solution: Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the primary greenhouse gas responsible for global warming. It traps infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface, preventing heat from escaping into space. Although methane and CFCs are more potent per molecule, CO2 is the most abundant. Hence option (c) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For identifying acid rain, remember that pH of normal rain is about 5.6 (due to dissolved CO2). Acid rain has pH < 5.6 due to HNO3 and H2SO4.
  • Catalytic converters in vehicles convert CO to CO2, NOx to N2, and unburnt hydrocarbons to CO2 and H2O.
  • Eutrophication occurs when excess nutrients (phosphates, nitrates) enter water bodies, causing algal blooms.
  • The ozone layer is located in the stratosphere, between 15-35 km above Earth's surface.
Pro Tip
For NEET, remember key environmental acts and years: Water Act (1974), Air Act (1981), Environment Protection Act (1986). Also know the major air quality index (AQI) parameters and their health effects for application-based questions.

biology/cell-biology:
What is Cell Biology?

Cell biology is the study of the structure, function, and behavior of cells, the fundamental units of life. For NEET, key topics include cell theory, prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells, cell organelles (nucleus, mitochondria, ER, Golgi apparatus, ribosomes, lysosomes), cell membrane structure (fluid mosaic model), and cell division (mitosis and meiosis). Understanding the molecular machinery within cells is crucial.

Key Concepts

Cell Theory: All living organisms are composed of cells; the cell is the basic structural and functional unit; all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Cell Membrane: Fluid mosaic model by Singer and Nicolson. Phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins. Mitochondria: Powerhouse of the cell, site of aerobic respiration, has double membrane with cristae, contains its own DNA. Endoplasmic Reticulum: RER (rough with ribosomes for protein synthesis) and SER (smooth for lipid synthesis). Golgi Apparatus: Modifies, sorts, and packages proteins. Lysosomes: Suicidal bags containing hydrolytic enzymes. Cell Division: Mitosis (equational division for growth) and Meiosis (reduction division for gamete formation).

Solved Examples

Example 1
Which organelle is responsible for the synthesis of ATP?

a) Nucleus b) Ribosome c) Mitochondria d) Lysosome
Solution: Mitochondria are known as the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through oxidative phosphorylation during cellular respiration. They have a double membrane and contain enzymes for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain. Hence option (c) is correct.
Example 2
How many daughter cells are produced after one cycle of meiosis?

a) 2 haploid cells b) 4 haploid cells c) 2 diploid cells d) 4 diploid cells
Solution: Meiosis consists of two successive divisions (meiosis I and meiosis II) without DNA replication in between. Starting from one diploid parent cell, four genetically distinct haploid daughter cells are produced. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 3
Which of the following is not a membrane-bound organelle?

a) Nucleus b) Mitochondria c) Ribosome d) Golgi apparatus
Solution: Ribosomes are non-membrane bound organelles composed of rRNA and proteins. They are the site of protein synthesis and can be found free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough ER. All other options (nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi apparatus) have membrane-bound structures. Hence option (c) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For identifying stages of mitosis: remember PMAT (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase).
  • In meiosis, crossing over occurs during pachytene stage of prophase I.
  • Plant cells can be distinguished from animal cells by the presence of cell wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole.
  • The endomembrane system includes the ER, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, and vacuoles (but not mitochondria or chloroplasts).
Pro Tip
For NEET, focus on the differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Key points: prokaryotes lack a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, have 70S ribosomes, and have circular DNA. These contrasting features are frequently tested.

biology/genetics-evolution:
What is Genetics and Evolution?

Genetics is the study of genes, heredity, and genetic variation in living organisms. Evolution explains how populations of organisms change over generations through the process of natural selection. For NEET, key topics include Mendelian genetics, molecular basis of inheritance (DNA replication, transcription, translation), gene regulation, mutation, and the evidence and mechanisms of evolution.

Key Concepts

Mendel's Laws: Law of Segregation (alleles separate during gamete formation), Law of Independent Assortment (genes on different chromosomes assort independently). DNA Structure: Double helix by Watson and Crick, complementary base pairing (A-T, G-C), antiparallel strands. Central Dogma: DNA → mRNA → Protein. Transcription: DNA to mRNA by RNA polymerase. Translation: mRNA to protein by ribosomes. Hardy-Weinberg Principle: p + q = 1, p2 + 2pq + q2 = 1. Natural Selection: Darwin's theory - organisms with favorable traits survive and reproduce more.

Solved Examples

Example 1
In a cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt), what proportion of offspring will be homozygous tall?

a) 1/4 b) 1/2 c) 3/4 d) 1
Solution: Using a Punnett square for Tt × Tt: TT (homozygous tall), Tt (heterozygous tall), Tt (heterozygous tall), tt (dwarf). The genotypes are in the ratio 1:2:1. Homozygous tall (TT) = 1/4. Hence option (a) is correct.
Example 2
If a population has 16% recessive phenotype, what is the frequency of the dominant allele? (Assuming Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium)

a) 0.4 b) 0.6 c) 0.8 d) 0.2
Solution: Recessive phenotype frequency q2 = 0.16, so q = √0.16 = 0.4. Since p + q = 1, p = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6. The frequency of the dominant allele is 0.6. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 3
Which enzyme is responsible for unwinding the DNA double helix during replication?

a) DNA polymerase b) DNA helicase c) DNA ligase d) RNA primase
Solution: DNA helicase is the enzyme that unwinds the DNA double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs, creating the replication fork. DNA polymerase synthesizes new strands, DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments, and RNA primase synthesizes RNA primers. Hence option (b) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For monohybrid cross problems, the phenotypic ratio is 3:1 and genotypic ratio is 1:2:1 in F2 generation.
  • For dihybrid cross, the phenotypic ratio is 9:3:3:1 if genes are on different chromosomes.
  • In DNA, the number of hydrogen bonds: A-T pair has 2 bonds, G-C pair has 3 bonds.
  • For evolution, remember homology (same structure, different function) indicates common ancestry; analogy (different structure, same function) indicates convergent evolution.
Pro Tip
For NEET, master Punnett square problems by practicing various cross types (monohybrid, dihybrid, test cross, back cross). Also understand pedigree analysis as it is a common application question in genetics.

biology/plant-physiology:
What is Plant Physiology?

Plant physiology is the study of how plants function, including their metabolism, growth, development, and responses to environmental stimuli. For NEET, key topics include photosynthesis, respiration, transpiration, mineral nutrition, plant growth regulators (phytohormones), and photoperiodism. Understanding how plants convert light energy into chemical energy is fundamental.

Key Concepts

Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 12H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2 + 6H2O. Light reactions produce ATP and NADPH; dark reactions (Calvin cycle) fix CO2. C3 vs C4 Plants: C3 plants use RuBisCO and have photorespiration; C4 plants use PEP carboxylase and have Kranz anatomy. Transpiration: Loss of water vapor through stomata, driven by the transpiration pull-cohesion tension mechanism. Plant Hormones: Auxin (cell elongation), Gibberellin (stem growth), Cytokinin (cell division), Abscisic acid (stress response), Ethylene (fruit ripening).

Solved Examples

Example 1
Which pigment is the primary light-absorbing pigment in photosynthesis?

a) Chlorophyll a b) Chlorophyll b c) Xanthophyll d) Carotene
Solution: Chlorophyll a is the primary photosynthetic pigment that directly participates in the light reactions. It acts as the reaction center in both photosystem I and photosystem II. Accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, carotenoids) absorb light and transfer energy to chlorophyll a. Hence option (a) is correct.
Example 2
Which plant hormone promotes fruit ripening?

a) Auxin b) Gibberellin c) Cytokinin d) Ethylene
Solution: Ethylene (C2H4) is the plant hormone responsible for fruit ripening. It is a gaseous hormone that also promotes senescence and abscission. It is commercially used to ripen fruits like bananas and tomatoes. Hence option (d) is correct.
Example 3
The opening and closing of stomata is regulated by:

a) Auxin b) Abscisic acid c) Gibberellin d) Cytokinin
Solution: Abscisic acid (ABA) is the stress hormone that causes stomatal closure under water-deficit conditions. ABA triggers the efflux of potassium ions from guard cells, reducing turgor pressure and closing the stomatal pore. Hence option (b) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For C3 vs C4 comparison: C4 plants have higher photosynthetic efficiency at high temperatures and low CO2 concentrations.
  • Photorespiration occurs only in C3 plants and reduces photosynthetic efficiency by consuming O2 instead of CO2.
  • Casparian strips in the endodermis of roots regulate the apoplastic movement of water and minerals.
  • Essential plant nutrients are classified as macronutrients (C, H, O, N, P, K, Ca, Mg, S) and micronutrients (Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, Mo, B, Cl, Ni).
Pro Tip
For NEET, remember the key differences between C3 and C4 plants: C4 plants have Kranz anatomy, higher optimum temperature, higher water use efficiency, and include crops like maize, sugarcane, and sorghum.

biology/human-physiology:
What is Human Physiology?

Human physiology is the study of how the human body functions, including the mechanisms of various organ systems and their coordination. For NEET, key topics include digestion and absorption, respiration and gas exchange, circulation (heart and blood vessels), excretion and osmoregulation, nervous system, endocrine system, and reproduction. Understanding homeostasis and feedback mechanisms is essential.

Key Concepts

Digestive System: Mouth (amylase), stomach (pepsin, HCl), small intestine (trypsin, lipase, maltase). Villi and microvilli increase surface area for absorption. Respiratory System: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli. Oxygen transport: 97% bound to hemoglobin, 3% dissolved. CO2 transport: 70% as bicarbonate, 23% bound to hemoglobin, 7% dissolved. Circulatory System: SA node is the pacemaker. Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. Excretory System: Nephron is the functional unit. Ultrafiltration, reabsorption, and secretion. Endocrine System: Hypothalamus-pituitary axis, feedback regulation. Nervous System: Neuron structure, synapse, action potential propagation.

Solved Examples

Example 1
Which enzyme is responsible for the digestion of proteins in the stomach?

a) Trypsin b) Pepsin c) Lipase d) Amylase
Solution: Pepsin is the proteolytic enzyme secreted by chief cells of the gastric glands in the stomach. It acts on proteins in an acidic medium (pH 1.5-2.0) and breaks them down into peptides. Trypsin acts in the small intestine. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 2
Which part of the brain is responsible for maintaining balance and coordination?

a) Cerebrum b) Cerebellum c) Medulla oblongata d) Hypothalamus
Solution: The cerebellum is the part of the hindbrain that coordinates voluntary movements, balance, posture, and motor learning. It receives input from sensory systems and the spinal cord to fine-tune motor activity. Hence option (b) is correct.
Example 3
The hormone that regulates blood sugar level is secreted by which gland?

a) Thyroid b) Adrenal c) Pancreas d) Pituitary
Solution: The pancreas secretes insulin (by beta cells of islets of Langerhans) which lowers blood glucose, and glucagon (by alpha cells) which raises blood glucose. These hormones maintain blood sugar homeostasis. Hence option (c) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For the cardiac cycle: remember Lub (atrioventricular valve closure) and Dub (semilunar valve closure).
  • For the nephron: Proximal convoluted tubule is the major site of reabsorption (glucose, amino acids, 65% of Na+, water).
  • In the nervous system, the resting membrane potential is -70 mV maintained by Na+/K+ ATPase pump.
  • For hormone classification: Peptide hormones act via second messengers (cAMP); steroid hormones act directly on DNA.
Pro Tip
For NEET, focus on the hypothalamus-pituitary-target organ axis. Understand the feedback mechanisms: negative feedback (most common) and positive feedback (e.g., oxytocin in childbirth, LH surge in ovulation).

biology/ecology:
What is Ecology?

Ecology is the study of interactions between organisms and their environment, including both biotic and abiotic factors. For NEET, key topics include ecosystem structure and function, energy flow, biogeochemical cycles (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus), population ecology, community ecology, biodiversity and conservation, and environmental issues. Understanding ecological principles is crucial for addressing environmental challenges.

Key Concepts

Ecosystem Components: Abiotic (light, temperature, water, soil) and Biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers). Energy Flow: 10% law (Lindemann) - only 10% of energy is transferred to the next trophic level. Biogeochemical Cycles: Carbon cycle (reservoir: atmosphere), Nitrogen cycle (fixation, nitrification, assimilation, ammonification, denitrification), Phosphorus cycle (sedimentary, no atmospheric component). Population Ecology: Exponential growth (J-shaped) and logistic growth (S-shaped). Carrying capacity K. Biodiversity: Species richness, endemic species, biodiversity hotspots. Conservation: In situ (national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves) and ex situ (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks).

Solved Examples

Example 1
According to the 10% law of energy transfer, if plants have 1000 J of energy, how much energy will be available at the tertiary consumer level?

a) 100 J b) 10 J c) 1 J d) 0.1 J
Solution: Energy transfer follows the 10% law: Producers (1000 J) → Primary consumers (100 J) → Secondary consumers (10 J) → Tertiary consumers (1 J). At each level, only 10% of energy is passed to the next trophic level. Hence option (c) is correct.
Example 2
Which of the following is not a greenhouse gas?

a) CO2 b) CH4 c) N2 d) CFCs
Solution: Nitrogen (N2) is not a greenhouse gas. Greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs, water vapor) trap infrared radiation and contribute to global warming. N2 makes up 78% of the atmosphere but does not absorb infrared radiation. Hence option (c) is correct.
Example 3
What type of population growth curve shows a population reaching carrying capacity?

a) J-shaped b) S-shaped c) Linear d) Exponential
Solution: Logistic growth follows an S-shaped (sigmoid) curve. Initially, growth is exponential, but as resources become limited, the growth rate slows down and eventually stabilizes at the carrying capacity K. The J-shaped curve represents exponential growth without resource limitation. Hence option (b) is correct.

Shortcut Techniques

  • For ecological pyramids: Pyramids of number can be inverted (tree-single tree supports many herbivores). Pyramids of biomass are usually upright. Pyramids of energy are always upright.
  • Keystone species have a disproportionately large effect on their ecosystem relative to their abundance (e.g., tiger, sea otter).
  • Biodiversity hotspots meet two criteria: at least 1500 endemic plant species and at least 70% habitat loss.
  • In nitrogen cycle, Rhizobium (symbiotic) and Azotobacter (free-living) are nitrogen-fixing bacteria.
Pro Tip
For NEET, understand the difference between in situ and ex situ conservation. In situ (within natural habitat) includes national parks, sanctuaries, and biosphere reserves. Ex situ (outside natural habitat) includes zoological parks, botanical gardens, and gene banks.
