For decision‑making questions, an option that suggests a whistleblower can be compelled to reveal his identity before the inquiry concludes is incorrect; the Act expressly prohibits premature disclosure. Conversely, an option that recommends the Competent Authority to issue an interim stay on a transfer order pending inquiry aligns with Section 7 and judicial precedent. An amendment bill proposing to extend the protection period to two years and add a provision for anonymous disclosures has been introduced in Parliament; as of the current examination cycle the 2014 Act remains the operative law.

Administrative Adjudication: Principles of Natural Justice and Fair Hearing

Administrative adjudication — the process by which executive authorities decide rights, licences, penalties, or benefits — is bound by the twin pillars of natural justice: audi alteram partem (hear the other side) and nemo judex in causa sua (no one shall be a judge in his own cause). The Supreme Court in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) expanded the right to be heard to include the right to know the case against oneself, the right to present evidence, and the right to a reasoned decision. The “reasoned decision” requirement was crystallised in Union of India v. T.R. Verma (1999), where the Court held that an order lacking reasons is vulnerable to judicial review under Article 14. The doctrine of “post‑decisional hearing” (allowing a hearing after a provisional order) was accepted in Swadeshi Cotton Mills v. Union of India (1981) but only where urgency justifies the initial ex‑parte action and a full hearing follows promptly. The Conduct Rules (Rule 14) require that any disciplinary authority conducting an inquiry must provide the charged officer with a copy of the articles of charge, the statement of imputations, and the list of witnesses and documents. The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) Act, 1985, Section 19, empowers the Tribunal to set aside orders that violate natural justice. In the context of the Disaster Management Act, the NDMA has issued guidelines for “Compensation Adjudication Committees” mandating a minimum notice period to claimants, an opportunity to submit documents, and a speaking order. Examiners frequently test the distinction between “quasi‑judicial” and “purely administrative” functions: only the former attracts the full rigour of natural justice. A decision to grant a routine licence renewal without a hearing is administrative; a decision to revoke a licence for misconduct is quasi‑judicial and requires a hearing. A common trap is to assume that any executive decision automatically triggers natural justice; the correct approach is to classify the function by its effect on rights and the statutory framework.

  • Assuming that a verbal intimation of conflict of interest satisfies the Conduct Rules — the rules require a written declaration.
  • Confusing the utilitarian proportionality test with the deontological duty of absolute integrity; they operate at different normative levels.
  • Believing that the Whistle Blowers Protection Act permits anonymous complaints without any procedural safeguard — the 2014 Act requires good‑faith disclosure to the Competent Authority, and anonymity is not guaranteed under the current law.
  • Treating every executive decision as quasi‑judicial and demanding a full hearing; the classification depends on the nature of the right affected and statutory mandate.
  • Overlooking the “reasonable apprehension of bias” standard for recusal and substituting a stricter “actual bias” test.
  • Ignoring the requirement that a reasoned order must articulate the evidentiary basis and the legal principle applied, not merely state the conclusion.
  • Misapplying the post‑decisional hearing doctrine to situations where no urgency existed at the time of the initial order.

These advanced sections equip the aspirant to dissect complex decision‑making scenarios with statutory precision and doctrinal depth.

The Doctrine of Public Accountability and Social Audit in Administrative Decision‑Making

Public accountability obliges every administrative authority to answer for the exercise of its powers, the use of public resources, and the outcomes of its decisions. In India the principle is rooted in Article 14 (equality before law) and Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty) as interpreted by the Supreme Court, which has held that accountability is an essential facet of the rule of law. The statutory framework includes the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) Act, 1971, the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, and the Right to Information Act, 2005, each providing a distinct channel for scrutiny. Social audit, a participatory mechanism institutionalised under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), 2005, mandates community verification of expenditure and work quality. The Act requires social audits at regular intervals, conducted by an independent Social Audit Unit (SAU) that reports to the Gram Sabha. The Supreme Court has affirmed that social audit findings have evidentiary value and can trigger disciplinary proceedings against errant officials. The doctrine therefore operates on two planes: vertical accountability to constitutional bodies (CAG, CVC, Lokpal) and horizontal accountability to the citizenry through transparent processes such as social audit.

Operationally, a decision‑making scenario that tests public accountability will often present a choice between a purely internal departmental review and an open social audit. The correct option recognises that the statute (MGNREGA, the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996, or the relevant state legislation) makes the social audit mandatory and that its report must be placed before the Gram Sabha within a prescribed period. Failure to convene the Gram Sabha or to act on adverse findings constitutes a breach of statutory duty and attracts judicial review under Article 226. Examiners also test the distinction between “audit” (financial verification by CAG) and “social audit” (community‑led verification of both financial and physical outcomes). An answer that conflates the two or suggests that a departmental inquiry can substitute the statutory social audit is incorrect.

The interplay between public accountability and administrative discretion is another frequent focus. While the Wednesbury principle permits a wide latitude, the Supreme Court has held that discretion must be exercised in a manner that is “reasonable, fair and transparent”. The Court linked transparency to the obligation to publish reasons, to allow affected parties to inspect records, and to subject decisions to independent audit. Consequently, a decision that invokes discretion but refuses to disclose the criteria or the audit trail is vulnerable to challenge. In practice, the CVC’s guidelines on “Integrity Pact” and “Whistle‑blower Protection” reinforce the accountability loop by requiring that any allegation of corruption in a discretionary decision be referred for independent inquiry within a fixed timeline.

Finally, the doctrine extends to the emerging domain of digital governance. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (once fully operational), and the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, impose accountability obligations on algorithmic decision‑making systems used for welfare targeting, tax assessment, or licence allocation. The principle of “explainability” — the ability of the authority to articulate the logic, data sources, and weightings of an automated decision — is now treated as a facet of public accountability. A decision‑making question that presents an opaque algorithmic allocation without a provision for human review or audit will be marked incorrect, because the statutory and constitutional framework demands that every exercise of public power, whether human or machine‑driven, remain answerable to the people.

The Precautionary Principle and Its Application in Environmental Administrative Decisions

The precautionary principle requires that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not be used as a reason for postponing cost‑effective measures to prevent degradation. The principle was first articulated internationally in the 1992 Rio Declaration (Principle 15) and has been incorporated into Indian jurisprudence through a series of Supreme Court judgments. In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) the Court declared the precautionary principle part of the law of the land, linking it to Articles 21, 47, 48A and 51A(g) of the Constitution. The Court held that the onus of proof shifts to the proponent of an activity to demonstrate that it will not cause significant harm, rather than on the objector to prove harm.

Statutorily, the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974, and the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981 empower the Central and State Pollution Control Boards to apply the precautionary principle while granting or refusing consents. The 2006 Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, as amended in 2020, mandates a “precautionary approach” in the screening and scoping stages: projects with potential for irreversible impact must undergo a full EIA even if baseline data are incomplete. The National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act, 2010, further entrenches the principle by granting the Tribunal suo motu powers to intervene when there is a plausible risk of environmental harm, irrespective of the completeness of scientific evidence.

In decision‑making questions, the examiner often contrasts a “risk‑based” approach (which quantifies probability and magnitude) with the precautionary principle (which acts despite uncertainty). A correct answer will identify that the precautionary principle applies when (i) the potential damage is serious or irreversible, (ii) scientific uncertainty exists, and (iii) cost‑effective preventive measures are available. An option that suggests waiting for conclusive scientific proof before acting is inconsistent with the principle and with the Supreme Court’s direction in M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) (the Oleum Gas Leak case), where the Court ordered immediate closure of a hazardous plant despite incomplete data. Conversely, an option that invokes the principle to justify a blanket ban on all industrial activity without assessing proportionality would be an over‑extension; the principle does not dispense with the requirement of proportionality and reasonableness.

The principle also interacts with the doctrine of sustainable development, which the Court in Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000) described as a balance between development and environmental protection. The precautionary principle operates as a “safety net” within that balance: it does not prohibit development but demands that the decision‑maker adopt the least harmful alternative, conduct cumulative impact assessments, and provide for mitigation and monitoring. In practice, a decision‑making scenario may present a proposal for a hydro‑electric project in a biodiversity hotspot. The correct response will recommend (a) a comprehensive EIA with a precautionary screening, (b) exploration of alternative sites or technologies, (c) a public hearing as mandated by the EIA Notification, and (d) a conditional clearance with a robust monitoring framework. Any answer that omits the public hearing or the conditional nature of the clearance fails to capture the procedural dimension of the principle.

Worked Example: Applying the Precautionary Principle
A state government proposes to grant environmental clearance for a large‑scale mining project in a forested area that is a known habitat of an endangered species. Scientific studies on the species’ population dynamics are incomplete, but preliminary data suggest a high risk of irreversible habitat loss. The project proponent argues that the economic benefits outweigh the uncertain environmental costs. Which of the following actions by the decision‑making authority is most consistent with the precautionary principle?
The precautionary principle requires preventive action when there is a threat of serious or irreversible damage, even if scientific certainty is lacking. The authority must (1) refuse or defer clearance until a full Environmental Impact Assessment incorporating a precautionary screening is completed, (2) mandate the exploration of alternative sites or less destructive technologies, (3) ensure a public hearing as required by the EIA Notification, and (4) if clearance is eventually granted, impose strict conditions, a monitoring plan, and a provision for revocation if adverse impacts materialise. An option that grants clearance solely on economic grounds without these safeguards violates the principle. The correct choice is the one that orders a comprehensive EIA, public consultation, and conditional approval with monitoring.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question invokes scientific uncertainty and irreversible harm, flag the precautionary principle immediately. Look for answer options that (a) shift the burden of proof to the proponent, (b) require a full EIA or equivalent study before any approval, (c) mandate public participation, and (d) impose conditional, monitorable clearances. Reject any option that waits for conclusive evidence or that grants unconditional approval based on economic arguments alone.

Delegated Legislation: Parliamentary Control and Judicial Review of Rule‑Making

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, orders, and bye‑laws made by the executive under authority conferred by an Act of Parliament — constitutes the bulk of normative output in modern governance. The Constitution permits delegation under Articles 245 and 246 read with the legislative entries, but the Supreme Court in Hamid Khan v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1972) laid down the “essential legislative functions” test: Parliament cannot delegate its core law‑making power, such as determining policy, fixing penalties, or imposing taxes. The parent statute must provide a clear legislative policy and sufficient guidelines (the “guideline theory”) to confine the delegate’s discretion. The Rules of Procedure of both Houses establish the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, which examines every statutory instrument for (i) conformity with the parent Act, (ii) compliance with the Constitution, (iii) retrospective effect, (iv) imposition of tax, and (v) unusual or unforeseen use of powers.

Parliamentary control operates at three stages: (1) the “laying” requirement — most rules must be laid before each House for a specified period (usually 30 sitting days) during which either House may annul or modify them; (2) the Committee’s scrutiny report, which though not binding, carries persuasive weight and often prompts the government to amend or withdraw the instrument; (3) the power of either House to pass a resolution disapproving the rule, which renders it void ab initio. The Supreme Court in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) held that failure to lay a rule as mandated by the parent Act renders it ultra vires, even if the rule is otherwise intra vires. The Court also recognised the “negative resolution” procedure (where the rule comes into force unless annulled) as constitutionally permissible, provided the laying period is reasonable.

Judicial review of delegated legislation follows the Wednesbury unreasonableness standard, but with a heightened scrutiny when fundamental rights are affected. The Court has struck down rules that impose blanket bans without providing a hearing, holding that such rules violate Article 19(1)(a) and are not reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2). The Court also applies the “proportionality” test, especially after Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016), requiring that the rule be suitable, necessary, and balanced in relation to the objective. A rule that confers unfettered discretion on an officer to grant or refuse licences without any criteria fails the guideline test and is liable to be declared void.

In decision‑making scenarios, the examiner may present a rule that (a) imposes a penalty not authorised by the parent Act, (b) applies retrospectively to the detriment of a citizen, (c) delegates further rule‑making power to a subordinate authority (sub‑delegation), or (d) omits the mandatory laying before Parliament. The correct answer identifies the specific constitutional or statutory infirmity. For instance, a rule made under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, that creates a new offence without parliamentary sanction is ultra vires because the parent Act enumerates offences exhaustively. Similarly, a rule that empowers a District Magistrate to issue “guidelines” that have the force of law without any legislative policy is an impermissible sub‑delegation. The aspirant must also distinguish between “rules” (which require laying) and “orders” or “directions” (which may not), as the procedural safeguards differ.

The Right to Information Act as a Tool for Decision Transparency

The Right to Information Act, 2005 (RTI Act) operationalises the fundamental right to information implicit in Article 19(1)(a) and Article 21, as affirmed by the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain (1975) and later in Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011). The Act obliges every public authority to maintain records, publish proactive disclosures under Section 4, and respond to requests within thirty days (forty‑eight hours for life‑or‑liberty matters). The Central Information Commission (CIC) and State Information Commissions (SICs) adjudicate appeals and impose penalties under Section 20 for wilful non‑compliance. The Act also contains exemptions under Section 8 (national security, privacy, commercial confidence, etc.) and Section 9 (copyright), which are subject to a “public interest override” — the information must be disclosed if the public interest in disclosure outweighs the harm protected by the exemption.

Proactive disclosure under Section 4(1)(b) requires each authority to publish seventeen categories of information, including organisational structure, decision‑making processes, norms for discharge of functions, and a directory of officers. The CIC in Namit Sharma v. Union of India (2013) held that failure to publish the “decision‑making process” — the criteria, guidelines, and precedents used by officers — constitutes a violation of the Act. This provision is directly relevant to decision‑making questions: an option that suggests a public authority can keep its internal guidelines secret while still complying with the RTI Act is incorrect. The Act also mandates that reasons for decisions be recorded and made available, reinforcing the “reasoned decision” requirement of natural justice.

The interplay between the RTI Act and other statutes creates nuanced scenarios. For example, the Official Secrets Act, 1923, does not override the RTI Act; Section 22 of the RTI Act gives it overriding effect. The Supreme Court in Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay clarified that the “public interest override” applies even to information covered by the Official Secrets Act, provided the competent authority (the CIC or SIC) determines that disclosure serves a larger public interest. In the context of environmental decisions, the NGT has used RTI‑derived documents to enforce the precautionary principle, demonstrating how transparency feeds substantive review. A decision‑making question may present a situation where an officer refuses to disclose the minutes of a committee that recommended a project clearance, citing “deliberative process privilege”. The correct answer recognises that the RTI Act does not recognise a blanket deliberative privilege; only the specific exemptions in Section 8 apply, and the public interest test must be applied.

Recent amendments (the Right to Information (Amendment) Act, 2019) altered the tenure and salary of Information Commissioners, a change criticised for potentially undermining independence. However, the core procedural framework — time limits, proactive disclosure, appellate mechanism — remains intact. Examiners may test awareness of the amendment’s impact on the Commission’s autonomy, but the substantive rights of applicants are unchanged. A sound answer will note that the amendment does not dilute the obligation to provide information within the statutory period, nor does it expand the exemptions. The aspirant should also be familiar with the “third‑party” provision (Section 11), which requires the authority to give notice to a third party whose confidential information is sought, and allow them to make representations before disclosure.

Algorithmic Decision‑Making in Public Administration: Opportunities and Safeguards

Algorithmic decision‑making (ADM) refers to the use of computational models — ranging from simple rule‑based engines to machine‑learning systems — to allocate benefits, assess eligibility, enforce regulations, or prioritise services. In India, ADM has been deployed in the Public Distribution System (PDS) for beneficiary identification (e‑KYC, Aadhaar‑based authentication), in the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) scheme for subsidy targeting, in the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN) for risk‑based audit selection, and in the National Health Authority’s claim adjudication engine. The potential advantages include speed, consistency, reduction of human bias, and the ability to process massive datasets. However, the opacity of many models, the risk of encoded discrimination, and the difficulty of providing meaningful explanations raise constitutional and administrative law concerns.

The constitutional framework demands that any exercise of public power, whether human or algorithmic, satisfy the requirements of Article 14 (non‑arbitrariness), Article 19(1)(g) (freedom to carry on occupation), and Article 21 (due process). The Supreme Court in Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017) recognised a fundamental right to privacy, which includes informational self‑determination. ADM systems that process personal data without a clear legal basis, purpose limitation, or data‑minimisation safeguards violate this right. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (once fully operational) codifies these principles: it requires lawful, fair, and transparent processing; mandates a “notice” to the data principal; and imposes a “data protection impact assessment” for high‑risk processing, which includes large‑scale profiling or automated decision‑making with legal effects.

Administrative law adds the requirement of “explainability” and “human‑in‑the‑loop”. The Central Information Commission has directed implementing agencies to disclose the logic of algorithms used for beneficiary shortlisting, holding that the RTI Act’s proactive disclosure obligation extends to the “decision‑making process” even when automated. The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has issued frameworks recommending (i) a clear statement of objectives, (ii) documentation of data sources and preprocessing, (iii) bias testing across protected groups, (iv) an audit trail, and (v) a grievance redressal mechanism with a human reviewer empowered to overturn the algorithmic output. While not legally binding, such frameworks inform the standard of reasonableness that courts may apply.

In decision‑making questions, the examiner may present a scenario where an automated system denies a pension claim based on a risk score, without informing the applicant of the factors or providing an appeal to a human officer. The correct response identifies multiple violations: (a) breach of data protection principles on notice and consent, (b) failure to provide a reasoned decision as required by natural justice, (c) absence of a human‑in‑the‑loop review, and (d) non‑compliance with the RTI Act’s proactive disclosure of the decision‑making logic. An option that suggests the applicant must first exhaust a purely algorithmic appeal before any human intervention is incorrect. Conversely, an option that recommends immediate suspension of the system pending a full audit, while providing interim manual processing, aligns with the precautionary approach to high‑risk ADM and with the principle of proportionality.

  • Confusing the precautionary principle with a blanket ban on development; the principle demands preventive action, not prohibition.
  • Assuming that delegated legislation can be challenged only on Wednesbury grounds; fundamental‑rights violations attract stricter proportionality review.
  • Believing that the RTI Act’s exemptions are absolute; the public‑interest override requires a case‑by‑case balancing.
  • Treating algorithmic decisions as immune from natural‑justice requirements; explainability and human review are mandatory.
  • Overlooking the mandatory laying period for subordinate legislation; failure to lay renders the instrument void.
  • Equating social audit with financial audit; social audit includes physical verification and community participation.
  • Neglecting the requirement that a reasoned order must articulate evidentiary basis and legal principle, not merely state the conclusion.

Promissory Estoppel and the State: Scope, Limits, and Landmark Judgments

The doctrine of promissory estoppel prevents a public authority from resiling from a clear and unambiguous representation that has induced a person to act to his detriment. In India the Supreme Court first recognised the principle in a landmark 1968 decision, holding that the Government could not deny a promise made in a policy circular when a private party had relied on it. The Court emphasised that the representation must be definite, unequivocal and intended to create legal relations. Subsequent jurisprudence refined the test: the promise must be made by an authority competent to bind the State, the promisee must have altered his position in good faith, and enforcement must not be contrary to public policy or statutory prohibition.

In a 1979 judgment the Court extended the doctrine to a fiscal incentive scheme, ruling that the State could not withdraw a sales‑tax exemption after the mill had invested on the faith of the notification. The judgment clarified that promissory estoppel does not create a new cause of action but operates as a shield against the State’s arbitrary withdrawal. However, the Court later limited the doctrine where the representation conflicted with a statutory mandate; a promise that contravenes a legislative provision cannot be enforced because the State cannot be estopped from performing its statutory duty.

The “public policy” exception was further elaborated in a 2007 decision. The Court held that even a clear promise may be denied effect if its enforcement would prejudice a larger public interest, such as environmental protection or fiscal discipline. The balancing exercise requires the authority to demonstrate that the withdrawal is proportionate and not merely convenient. In practice, examiners test the distinction between legitimate expectation (procedural) and promissory estoppel (substantive): the former entitles a person to a hearing before a benefit is withdrawn, the latter may compel the State to honour the benefit itself.

A frequent trap is the assumption that any government circular creates an estoppel. The representation must be authoritative — issued by an officer with delegated power — and not merely an internal guideline. Moreover, the promisee’s reliance must be reasonable and foreseeable; speculative investments do not qualify. The doctrine also does not apply to purely discretionary benefits where the authority has expressly reserved the right to modify or cancel.

Colourable Exercise of Power: Judicial Scrutiny of Administrative Discretion

Colourable exercise of power occurs when an authority purports to act within its statutory mandate but in reality uses the power for an ulterior purpose not authorised by the legislature. The classic formulation originates in UK administrative law and was adopted in Indian jurisprudence. The Supreme Court has held that a law which “in substance and reality” exceeds legislative competence, though clothed in the form of a valid enactment, is colourable and therefore void.

In the administrative context, the doctrine is invoked when a discretionary power — such as the grant of licences, allocation of quotas, or imposition of penalties — is exercised on grounds extraneous to the statute. For instance, the Court has struck down an order cancelling a petroleum dealership because the real motive was to favour a political associate, not the statutory criteria of “public interest”. The Court examined the decision‑making record, noting the absence of any reference to the prescribed guidelines and the presence of extraneous correspondence.

The test for colourability involves three steps: (1) identify the statutory purpose conferred on the authority; (2) ascertain the actual purpose behind the impugned action from the record; (3) determine whether the actual purpose is manifestly unrelated to the statutory purpose. Mere error of judgment or unreasonableness (Wednesbury) does not amount to colourability; there must be a mala fide diversion of power. The burden of proving colourable exercise lies on the challenger, but courts may draw adverse inferences from a lack of reasoned order.

Examiners often frame a scenario where a municipal commissioner cancels a building plan approval citing “zoning violation” while the file reveals pressure from a local legislator. The correct answer identifies colourable exercise because the stated ground is a pretext. An option suggesting the decision is merely “unreasonable” and therefore reviewable only on Wednesbury grounds is a distractor — colourability attracts a stricter standard of review akin to abuse of power.

Technique: Identifying Colourable Exercise in a Fact Pattern
A State Government issues a notification under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 fixing the maximum retail price of onions. The notification is challenged on the ground that the real intention was to benefit a specific wholesale trader who had contributed to the ruling party’s election fund. The file contains a note from the Chief Minister’s office directing the Food Secretary to “ensure the price cap helps Shri X”. The State argues that the notification is a policy decision immune from judicial review. Which of the following is the most appropriate legal conclusion?
The notification is liable to be struck down as a colourable exercise of power. The statutory purpose of the Essential Commodities Act is to regulate prices in public interest, not to confer private benefit. The internal note demonstrates an ulterior motive extraneous to the Act. Courts have held that when the decision‑making record reveals a purpose unrelated to the statutory object, the action is colourable and void. The claim of policy immunity does not shield a mala fide exercise. Therefore, the correct conclusion is that the notification is invalid for colourable exercise of power.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents a discretionary order with a stated ground and a hidden motive, first locate the statutory provision conferring the power. Then check whether the record (notes, correspondence, minutes) reveals a purpose outside that provision. If yes, label it “colourable exercise” and select the option that invokes the doctrine, not mere unreasonableness. Remember: colourability requires a diversion of power, not just a wrong decision.

Reasoned Decisions in Quasi‑Judicial Proceedings: The Duty to Give Reasons

The obligation to record reasons is a cornerstone of natural justice and distinguishes a quasi‑judicial order from an administrative fiat. The Supreme Court has declared that a quasi‑judicial authority must “state the reasons which weighed with it” so that the affected party can understand the basis of the decision and the appellate forum can review it meaningfully. The duty is not satisfied by a cryptic “for reasons recorded in the file”; the reasons must be explicit, intelligible and relevant to the issues contested.

In a significant judgment the Court quashed a disciplinary order dismissing a government servant because the inquiry officer’s report merely reproduced the charges without analysing the evidence. The Court held that a “reasoned order” must contain: (i) a concise statement of the factual controversy; (ii) a summary of the evidence considered; (iii) the logical process linking evidence to findings; and (iv) the legal principle applied. The absence of any of these elements renders the order non‑speaking and vulnerable to certiorari.

The requirement extends to statutory tribunals such as the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, the National Green Tribunal, and the Central Administrative Tribunal. The Supreme Court has emphasised that even when a statute does not expressly mandate reasons, the constitutional guarantee of Article 14 (non‑arbitrariness) imports the duty. Conversely, in purely administrative (non‑quasi‑judicial) decisions — e.g., policy formulation or contract award — the duty may be relaxed, though the trend is toward reasoned transparency.

Examiners test the distinction between “reasons” and “findings”. A finding is a conclusion (“the charge is proved”); a reason explains why the finding follows from the evidence. An order that states “the charge is proved because the documents show X” satisfies the duty; one that merely says “the charge is proved” does not. Another common trap is the belief that a speaking order can be supplemented later by an affidavit. The Court has held that post‑decisional rationalisation cannot cure a non‑speaking order.

Administrative Discretion in Public Procurement: Transparency, Competition, and Judicial Review

Public procurement in India is governed primarily by the General Financial Rules (GFR) 2017, the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) guidelines, and the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order 2017. The constitutional mandate of Article 14 requires that the procurement process be fair, transparent, and non‑discriminatory. The Supreme Court in Tata Cellular v. Union of India (1994) laid down the “fair play” doctrine: the State must act as a model employer and ensure a level playing field for all bidders.

Discretion in procurement arises at several stages: (1) framing of eligibility criteria and technical specifications; (2) choice of procurement method (open tender, limited tender, single source); (3) evaluation of bids and award of contract. Each stage is subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness, mala fides, or violation of statutory guidelines. The Court has struck down single‑source procurement where the authority failed to record reasons for departing from open tender, and the record showed a pre‑determined preference for a particular vendor.

The CVC’s “Integrity Pact” and the “e‑Procurement” portal have been introduced to reduce discretion. However, the courts have held that even electronic systems must comply with the principles of natural justice: bidders must be given an opportunity to clarify discrepancies, and the evaluation criteria must be disclosed upfront. A High Court has set aside an award where the evaluation committee altered weightages after bid opening without notifying participants.

A frequent examination scenario involves a tender where the technical specification is tailored to a single manufacturer. The correct response identifies a violation of the “competitive neutrality” principle and the requirement under GFR that specifications be generic. An option suggesting that the procuring entity has absolute discretion to decide specifications is incorrect; such discretion is bounded by the duty to ensure effective competition.

The Central Vigilance Commission’s Supervisory Role in Administrative Decision‑Making

The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), established by the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over vigilance administration in Central Government organisations. Its decision‑making mandate includes: (i) recommending disciplinary action against public servants; (ii) reviewing the progress of investigations by the CBI; (iii) advising on systemic improvements to prevent corruption. The Commission’s recommendations are advisory but carry significant weight; the Supreme Court has observed that a departure from CVC advice without cogent reasons may amount to arbitrariness under Article 14.

The CVC’s “Supervisory Jurisdiction” extends to the review of “vigilance clearance” for promotions, postings, and foreign assignments. The Court has held that denial of vigilance clearance must be based on a speaking order referencing specific allegations or pending inquiries. A blanket refusal without reasons violates the principles of natural justice and the CVC’s own guidelines.

The Commission also issues “Standard Operating Procedures” (SOPs) for handling complaints, conducting inquiries, and imposing penalties. These SOPs, while not statutory, have been treated by courts as part of the “legitimate expectation” of a fair procedure. A High Court has quashed a penalty imposed without following the CVC’s prescribed inquiry procedure, ruling that the authority’s deviation rendered the order procedurally ultra vires.

Examiners may present a case where a disciplinary authority imposes a major penalty ignoring the CVC’s recommendation for a minor penalty. The correct answer recognises that while the CVC’s advice is not binding, a reasoned departure is mandatory; an unexplained deviation is arbitrary. Conversely, an option stating that the CVC’s recommendation is binding is a trap — the Commission lacks adjudicatory power.

  • Confusing promissory estoppel with legitimate expectation; the former can compel performance, the latter only a hearing.
  • Treating every unreasonable decision as colourable exercise; colourability requires an ulterior purpose, not mere error.
  • Assuming a non‑speaking order can be cured by a later affidavit; post‑decisional rationalisation is impermissible.
  • Believing procurement specifications enjoy absolute discretion; they must be generic to ensure competition.
  • Thinking CVC recommendations are legally binding; they are advisory but require reasoned departure.
  • Overlooking the requirement that a quasi‑judicial order must articulate evidentiary basis, not just conclusions.
  • Equating the precautionary principle with a ban on administrative action; it demands preventive measures, not prohibition.

Administrative Discretion in Environmental Impact Assessment and the National Green Tribunal

The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the central government to issue notifications regulating environmental clearances. The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006, as amended, creates a tiered discretion structure: Category A projects require clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) after appraisal by an Expert Appraisal Committee (EAC); Category B projects are cleared by State‑level Impact Assessment Authorities (SEIAAs). At each stage the authority exercises discretion in scoping, terms of reference, public‑hearing conduct, and the final decision to grant, reject, or impose conditions.

The National Green Tribunal (NGT), established under the NGT Act, 2010, exercises original and appellate jurisdiction over substantial questions relating to the environment. Its review of administrative discretion applies the Wednesbury unreasonableness test and has incorporated the proportionality principle. In Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India the Supreme Court held that the precautionary principle and the polluter‑pays principle are part of the law of the land, obligating the EAC to record reasons when departing from the precautionary approach. The NGT has set aside clearances where the EAC ignored cumulative impact assessment, ruling that failure to consider inter‑project effects renders the decision arbitrary.

Discretion also arises in the conduct of public hearings. The 2006 notification mandates a minimum 30‑day notice and a hearing chaired by the District Collector. Courts have struck down clearances where the hearing lacked adequate publicity or minutes were not made public. The NGT has quashed clearances where a revised EIA was submitted after the hearing without fresh public consultation, violating participatory decision‑making.

Conditional clearances constitute another discretionary layer. The authority may impose mitigation measures, monitoring protocols, or post‑clearance compliance reports. The Supreme Court has emphasized that conditions must be specific, measurable, and enforceable; vague conditions such as “adequate pollution control” are insufficient. The NGT monitors compliance through suo‑motu proceedings and can impose penalties, including project suspension, under Section 15 of the NGT Act.

Key Take‑aways for Decision‑Making Questions

  • Identify the tier (Category A or B) to determine the competent authority.
  • Check whether the decision‑maker recorded reasons, especially when departing from the precautionary principle.
  • Verify compliance with public‑hearing procedural requirements.
  • Assess whether conditions are concrete and monitorable.
  • Recognise the NGT’s power to review both substantive merits and procedural fairness.

The Doctrine of Legitimate Expectation in Public Employment: Promotions, Transfers, and Reservations

Legitimate expectation arises when a public authority, by consistent practice or explicit representation, creates an expectation that a particular benefit will be conferred. In public employment the doctrine is invoked in promotion, transfer, and reservation contexts. The Supreme Court has held that a departmental promotion committee’s long‑standing practice of considering seniority‑cum‑merit creates a legitimate expectation that the same criteria will continue, and a sudden change without notice violates Article 14.

Transfers present a distinct facet. The Court has ruled that a transfer order issued in the public interest does not attract legitimate expectation unless the employee shows a settled practice of consultation or a policy guaranteeing minimum tenure. Where a transfer policy expressly provides for a “cooling‑off” period or “choice‑posting” mechanism, deviation without reasoned justification is arbitrary.

Reservation‑related expectations were examined in M. Nagaraj v. Union of India and subsequent judgments. The Court clarified that the State’s obligation to collect quantifiable data before providing reservation in promotions creates a procedural legitimate expectation for the affected class. Failure to conduct this exercise before issuing a promotion notification renders the order vulnerable.

The doctrine does not confer a substantive right; it entitles the claimant to a fair hearing before the expectation is defeated. The Court has reiterated that legitimate expectation is a procedural safeguard — the authority must consider the expectation and give reasons for non‑fulfilment. A blanket policy change, if accompanied by transparent consultation and a reasoned order, can override the expectation.

Application Checklist

  1. Identify the representation or consistent practice relied upon.
  2. Determine whether the expectation is procedural (hearing) or substantive (benefit).
  3. Check if the authority provided a reasoned decision after affording a hearing.
  4. Assess whether the change serves a compelling public interest and is not mala fide.
  5. Verify compliance with any statutory consultation requirements (e.g., data collection for reservation).
Identifying the threshold for legitimate expectation in promotion cases
A department has followed a seniority‑cum‑merit rule for promotions for fifteen years. In 2022 it issues a circular switching to a pure merit‑based assessment without prior notice. An employee with 12 years of service challenges the circular. Which of the following is the most appropriate legal position?
The employee has a legitimate expectation that the existing promotion criteria will continue, because a long‑standing, consistent practice creates a procedural expectation of consultation before change. The authority must afford a hearing and record reasons for the policy shift. Absent such process, the circular is arbitrary under Article 14. The correct answer recognises the procedural nature of the expectation and the requirement of a reasoned decision after hearing.
Exam‑day strategy for legitimate expectation questions
When a scenario mentions a “long‑standing practice” or “established policy”, flag it as a potential legitimate expectation issue. First decide whether the claimant seeks a substantive benefit or merely a fair process. If the question asks what the authority must do, the answer is almost always “provide a hearing and record reasons”. Avoid options that treat the expectation as an enforceable right to the benefit itself.

Public Interest Litigation as a Decision‑Making Instrument: Standing, Locus Standi, and Remedial Jurisprudence

Public Interest Litigation (PIL) transformed the Indian judiciary from a passive adjudicator into an active policy‑shaping institution. The liberalisation of locus standi began with S. P. Gupta v. Union of India, where the Supreme Court held that any citizen acting bona fide could approach the court for enforcement of constitutional rights of a disadvantaged group. This “representative standing” was expanded in Bandhua Mukti Morcha v. Union of India to allow social action groups to file petitions on behalf of bonded labourers.

The Court further relaxed procedural barriers in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan, where it laid down guidelines for prevention of sexual harassment at the workplace in the absence of legislation. The judgment illustrates how PIL can generate interim regulatory frameworks that bind the executive until Parliament enacts a law. Remedial powers include continuing mandamus, structural injunctions, and appointment of monitoring committees — tools that directly influence administrative decision‑making.

However, the judiciary has imposed self‑restraints to prevent misuse. The Court has warned against “judicial activism” that encroaches on the policy domain, emphasizing that PIL cannot substitute governance. The “genuine public interest” test requires the petitioner to demonstrate that the matter affects a large segment of society and that no alternative remedy exists. Frivolous PILs attract costs and may be dismissed at the threshold.

From a decision‑making perspective, administrators must anticipate PIL scrutiny when framing policies affecting vulnerable groups. The principle of “anticipatory compliance” — designing decisions to withstand judicial review — has become a practical necessity. Agencies now conduct pre‑legislative impact assessments, maintain transparent records, and engage stakeholders to reduce the risk of adverse PIL outcomes.

Core Elements for Analysis

  • Standing: Is the petitioner a directly affected person, a bona fide public‑spirited individual, or an organisation with a track record?
  • Subject‑matter: Does the issue involve a violation of fundamental rights, statutory duties, or large‑scale public harm?
  • Remedy sought: Is the prayer for declaratory relief, a mandatory injunction, continuing mandamus, or structural reform?
  • Judicial restraint indicators: Has the court previously declined to intervene in similar policy areas?
  • Administrative response: Has the authority demonstrated proactive compliance, stakeholder consultation, and reasoned decision‑making?

The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Oversight of Administrative Decisions: Audit Standards, Performance Audit, and Policy Impact

The Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), constituted under Article 148 and the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, is the supreme audit institution. Its mandate extends beyond financial attestation to performance audit, compliance audit, and evaluation of whether government programmes achieve intended outcomes. The CAG’s audit standards, aligned with the International Standards of Supreme Audit Institutions (ISSAI), require evidence‑based findings, materiality assessment, and a clear distinction between systemic deficiencies and isolated lapses.

Performance audits examine the economy, efficiency, and effectiveness (the “3 E” framework) of administrative decisions. For instance, a CAG report on the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana highlighted cost overruns, delayed execution, and inadequate quality monitoring, prompting the Ministry of Rural Development to revise tendering norms and introduce third‑party quality checks. Such audits create a feedback loop: findings are tabled in Parliament, discussed by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), and often lead to executive corrective orders.

The CAG also audits the decision‑making process itself. In the 2G spectrum allocation audit the CAG identified procedural irregularities — deviation from the established auction methodology, lack of transparency in eligibility criteria, and arbitrary cut‑off dates. The Supreme Court, relying on the CAG report, cancelled licences, illustrating how audit findings can trigger judicial review of administrative discretion.

Recent reforms have strengthened the CAG’s role in policy evaluation. The “Outcome Budget” initiative requires ministries to link financial outlays to measurable outputs; the CAG audits the veracity of these linkages. Moreover, the CAG’s “Citizen‑Centric Audit” framework invites public participation in identifying audit topics, enhancing accountability. Administrators must therefore ensure that decision records, cost‑benefit analyses, and implementation metrics are audit‑ready.

Practical Implications for Decision‑Makers

  1. Maintain contemporaneous documentation of policy rationale, alternatives considered, and risk assessments.
  2. Align programme design with measurable indicators to facilitate performance audit.
  3. Respond promptly to CAG observations; delayed replies are treated as adverse inferences.
  4. Institutionalise internal audit mechanisms that mirror CAG standards to pre‑empt external findings.
  5. Engage with PAC recommendations as binding administrative directives unless overturned by a competent authority.
  • Confusing legitimate expectation with a vested right; the former only guarantees a hearing, not the benefit itself.
  • Assuming that any long‑standing practice automatically creates a legitimate expectation; the practice must be consistent, public, and not contrary to law.
  • Treating PIL standing as unlimited; the petitioner must demonstrate genuine public interest and absence of alternative remedy.
  • Believing that CAG audit reports are merely advisory; they carry persuasive weight in Parliament and can form the basis for judicial intervention.
  • Overlooking the requirement that conditional environmental clearances contain specific, monitorable conditions; vague conditions are legally insufficient.
  • Ignoring the procedural mandate of public hearings in EIA; a clearance granted without a proper hearing is vulnerable to being set aside.
  • Equating performance audit with financial audit; performance audit evaluates outcomes and efficiency, not just expenditure regularity.

Administrative Discretion in Public‑Private Partnerships: Risk Allocation and Accountability

Public‑Private Partnerships (PPPs) in India operate within a framework comprising the central PPP policy guidelines, Model Concession Agreements (MCAs) issued by the Department of Economic Affairs, and sector‑specific concession frameworks such as those of the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI). The administrative authority — typically a line ministry or state‑level agency — exercises discretion at three critical junctures: project identification and feasibility approval, selection of the private partner through competitive bidding, and ongoing contract management including variation orders and termination. Each juncture carries a distinct risk profile. During project identification, the authority must ensure that viability gap funding (VGF), generally capped at a defined percentage of total project cost, is justified by a rigorous cost‑benefit analysis; failure to document the analysis exposes the decision to audit objections under the CAG’s performance‑audit standards. In the bidding stage, the discretion to set technical qualification criteria and evaluation weightages must conform to the principles of transparency and non‑discrimination under Article 14; the Supreme Court has struck down tenders where the evaluation matrix was altered after bid opening, holding that post‑bid changes constitute an arbitrary exercise of power. During contract management, the authority may issue variation orders within prescribed limits (often up to 10 % of contract value) without fresh approval, but orders exceeding this threshold require competent authority sanction and recorded justification. CAG reports have highlighted instances where variation orders lacked documented rationale, leading to significant cost overruns. Accountability mechanisms include the Independent Engineer’s certification, lenders’ due‑diligence reports, and periodic review by the Empowered Committee on PPPs. Administrators should maintain a contemporaneous decision‑log recording the risk‑allocation matrix, the basis for VGF quantum, evaluation scoring sheets, and minutes of every variation‑order approval. This log serves both as a defence against allegations of arbitrariness and as primary evidence for performance‑audit scrutiny.

Algorithmic Bias and Accountability in Government AI Decision‑Making

The deployment of algorithmic systems for welfare targeting, tax compliance, and predictive policing has accelerated following the MeitY “Responsible AI for Social Empowerment” (RAISE) initiative and the enactment of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Administrative discretion now extends to the selection of training data, choice of model architecture, and setting of decision thresholds — each of which can embed systemic bias. The Supreme Court’s Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) judgment recognised informational privacy as a fundamental right, implying that any automated decision affecting entitlements must satisfy the proportionality test: the measure must be suitable, necessary, and the least restrictive means. In practice, the National Informatics Centre (NIC) guidelines recommend a “model card” for every production model, documenting data provenance, performance metrics across demographic sub‑groups, and a bias‑mitigation plan. Audits of welfare allocation algorithms have revealed disparities linked to under‑representation of certain groups in training data; corrective steps such as dataset augmentation and threshold recalibration have been used to reduce such disparities. Accountability is reinforced through Central Information Commission (CIC) orders requiring disclosure of algorithmic logic under Section 4(1)(b) of the RTI Act, and through proposed legislation on algorithmic accountability that would obligate public authorities to conduct impact assessments before deployment. Decision‑makers should therefore embed a “human‑in‑the‑loop” review for high‑stakes outcomes, maintain version‑controlled model repositories, and publish periodic transparency reports detailing error rates disaggregated by protected attributes.

Identifying Ultra Vires in Delegated Legislation
A state government issues a notification under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, empowering the District Collector to impose a blanket ban on all industrial activity within a 10 km radius of a notified wildlife sanctuary, without providing for any case‑by‑case assessment. An affected industry challenges the notification. On what ground is the notification most vulnerable to judicial review?
The notification exceeds the rule‑making power conferred by the parent statute. Section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act authorises the central government to take measures for “protecting and improving the quality of the environment” and to “lay down standards”. It does not delegate the power to impose an absolute, non‑discretionary prohibition on all industrial activity without any procedural safeguard. The blanket ban is therefore ultra vires the enabling provision because it (i) lacks a statutory basis for a total prohibition, (ii) fails to provide for a hearing or reasoned order, and (iii) is disproportionate to the objective of environmental protection. Courts have struck down similar notifications on grounds of absence of guided discretion and violation of Article 14. The correct answer: the notification is ultra vires for lack of legislative guidance and procedural fairness.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question describes a delegated rule that imposes an absolute ban or confers unguided discretion, immediately check whether the parent statute provides standards, criteria, or a hearing requirement. If the statute is silent, the rule is prima facie ultra vires. Map the statutory provision to the three‑pronged test: (1) legislative policy, (2) guided discretion, (3) procedural safeguards. This mapping yields the correct option in a high proportion of such questions.

Judicial Review of Delegated Legislation: The Ultra Vires Doctrine and Proportionality

Delegated legislation — rules, regulations, notifications, and orders made under a parent statute — is subject to judicial review on two principal grounds: ultra vires (beyond the powers conferred) and violation of constitutional rights. The ultra vires doctrine operates at two levels. Substantive ultra vires occurs when the delegate enacts a provision that the parent Act does not authorise, either because the subject‑matter falls outside the legislative policy or because the delegate exceeds quantitative limits such as monetary ceilings. Procedural ultra vires arises when mandatory pre‑conditions — prior publication, consultation with affected parties, or laying before the legislature — are omitted. The Supreme Court has held that a rule made under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, fixing the maximum price of sugar without the requisite consultation with the Central Advisory Committee was procedurally ultra vires and therefore void. Proportionality, recognised in Om Kumar v. Union of India (2000), adds a third tier: even a rule that is intra vires may be struck down if it imposes a restriction disproportionate to the legitimate aim. The test comprises four steps — legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity (least restrictive alternative), and balancing. In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Court applied proportionality to invalidate the mandatory linking of Aadhaar with bank accounts, finding the measure not the least restrictive means to prevent fraud. For administrators, the practical implication is a “rule‑making checklist”: (1) verify that the parent statute contains an express delegation with clear standards; (2) ensure that the rule‑making process follows prescribed procedural steps, including stakeholder consultation where mandated; (3) conduct a proportionality impact assessment documenting the aim, evidence of effectiveness, and consideration of less restrictive alternatives; (4) retain the assessment record to withstand audit and judicial scrutiny. Recent amendments to the General Clauses Act, 1897, now require every rule to be accompanied by a “Statement of Objects and Reasons” that explicitly addresses proportionality, reinforcing the checklist approach.

Participatory Decision‑Making: Public Consultation, Social Audit, and the Right to Information

Participatory governance has moved from a policy aspiration to a statutory mandate across several sectors. The Right to Information Act, 2005 (RTI) obliges public authorities to proactively disclose decision‑making criteria under Section 4(1)(b), while the 2014 pre‑legislative consultation guidelines issued by the Cabinet Secretariat require a minimum comment period, publication of a summary of comments, and a reasoned response. In the rural employment sphere, the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) institutionalises social audit through Section 17, mandating regular Gram Sabha‑level audits, with findings forwarded to the District Programme Coordinator and the State Employment Guarantee Council. CAG performance audits have found significant gaps in compliance with mandated social audits, resulting in estimated leakages. The Ministry of Rural Development has responded by linking fund releases to the timely upload of social‑audit reports on the designated monitoring system. In environmental governance, the Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006 (as amended) prescribes a public hearing chaired by the District Collector, with the minutes forming part of the appraisal record. The National Green Tribunal has set aside environmental clearances where the public hearing was conducted without adequate notice, holding that the procedural defect vitiated the decision. For administrators, the operational checklist is: (i) publish draft decisions and supporting data on the departmental website with adequate notice before finalisation; (ii) conduct stakeholder workshops for policies affecting vulnerable groups; (iii) record dissenting views and explicitly address them in the final order; (iv) upload social‑audit or public‑hearing minutes to the designated portal within the statutory timeline; (v) maintain a “consultation register” linking each comment to the corresponding clause in the final decision. This register not only satisfies RTI proactive‑disclosure obligations but also provides a defensible audit trail against allegations of arbitrariness.

Administrative Discretion in Land Acquisition: Balancing Development and Rehabilitation

The Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (LARR Act) replaced the 1894 statute and introduced a structured discretion framework for the “appropriate government”. The Act mandates a Social Impact Assessment (SIA) under Section 4, a public hearing under Section 5, and an expert appraisal under Section 6 before a notification under Section 11 can be issued. The discretion to determine “public purpose” is circumscribed by the illustrative list in Section 2(1)(b) — strategic infrastructure, housing for the poor, and planned development — and by judicial interpretation that “public purpose” must be construed narrowly and cannot be a cloak for private commercial gain. The compensation formula (Section 26) combines market value, a multiplier (1.0–2.0) for rural land, and a 100 % solatium, while rehabilitation and resettlement (R&R) entitlements under Sections 31–42 include alternative land, housing, and livelihood assistance. The 2015 amendment removed the mandatory consent clause for five categories of projects, but the Supreme Court has reiterated that any dilution must satisfy the proportionality test. Administrators must therefore: (1) commission an independent SIA agency empanelled by the Ministry of Rural Development; (2) ensure the public hearing notice is published in two local newspapers and the Gram Panchayat office at least 21 days in advance; (3) prepare a “Rehabilitation and Resettlement Scheme” that is vetted by the District Collector and approved by the State Level Monitoring Committee; (4) deposit the compensation amount in the designated account before taking possession, as mandated by Section 38; (5) maintain a “Land Acquisition Decision Register” linking each statutory step — SIA report, hearing minutes, expert appraisal, notification, award — to the corresponding file numbers. CAG audits have revealed instances where awards were issued without a completed R&R scheme, leading to judicial directions to halt possession until compliance. This register serves as primary evidence in both judicial review and performance audit.

  • Confusing the ultra vires test with the proportionality test; ultra vires concerns statutory authority, proportionality concerns constitutional rights.
  • Assuming that a public hearing automatically validates a decision; the hearing must be meaningful, with adequate notice and a reasoned response to objections.
  • Treating the consent requirement under the LARR Act as optional for all projects; consent remains mandatory for private‑company and public‑private partnership projects unless expressly exempted.
  • Overlooking the requirement that algorithmic model documentation be updated after every retraining cycle; stale documentation is treated as non‑compliance under relevant guidelines.
  • Believing that a variation order within the prescribed threshold needs no justification; the authority must still record the technical rationale and financial impact.
  • Equating social audit under MGNREGA with a mere financial audit; social audit evaluates process integrity, work‑site transparency, and grievance redressal.
  • Ignoring the mandatory “Statement of Objects and Reasons” for delegated rules introduced by the General Clauses Act amendment; its absence renders the rule procedurally defective.

Administrative Discretion in Natural Resource Allocation: Spectrum, Coal, and Water

The allocation of scarce natural resources — radio spectrum, coal blocks, and inter‑state river water — illustrates how administrative discretion is constrained by statutory frameworks, judicial doctrine, and the principle of public trust. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that the State acts as a trustee of natural resources and must distribute them through transparent, competitive, and non‑arbitrary procedures.

Spectrum. The Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, read with the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997, empowers the Central Government to assign spectrum. In Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (2012) the Court struck down the first‑come‑first‑served allocation of 2G licences, mandating auction as the default method. The judgment established that discretion to allocate spectrum cannot be exercised arbitrarily; it must follow a reasoned policy, public consultation, and a transparent bidding process. Subsequent spectrum auctions have been conducted under the Spectrum Auction Rules framed under the Telegraph Act, with the Comptroller and Auditor General auditing revenue realisation.

Coal. The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 replaced the earlier allocation regime after the Supreme Court in Manohar Lal Sharma v. Union of India (2014) cancelled 214 coal block allocations made between 1993 and 2011 for lack of transparency. The 2015 Act mandates e‑auction for commercial mining and a transparent allotment process for government companies, with the Central Government retaining discretion only to determine the list of mines to be auctioned. The Act also requires the Ministry of Coal to publish periodic monitoring reports linking each block to the auction file, the successful bidder, and the revenue deposited.

Water. Inter‑state river water disputes are governed by the Inter‑State River Water Disputes Act, 1956. The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal award (2007) and the Supreme Court’s final order (2018) illustrate how discretion in water sharing is bounded by the principle of equitable apportionment, the doctrine of prior appropriation, and the requirement of a reasoned award. The Tribunal’s award is binding on the parties unless the Supreme Court modifies it under Article 136. The Court has also held that the Central Government’s power to constitute a tribunal under the Act is not unfettered; it must act on the request of a riparian state and cannot refuse arbitrarily.

Across the three domains, common administrative safeguards have emerged: (i) a statutory mandate for competitive bidding or adjudicatory determination; (ii) a requirement to publish the policy framework and the criteria for allocation before the process begins; (iii) a duty to record reasons for each allocation decision, linking the decision to the published criteria; (iv) an audit trail maintained by the CAG and, where applicable, by environmental regulators; (v) a judicial review standard that tests the decision against the Wednesbury unreasonableness test, the proportionality principle, and the public‑trust doctrine. Failure to observe any of these safeguards renders the allocation vulnerable to being set aside as arbitrary or colourable exercise of power.

Decision‑Making under the Goods and Services Tax Council: Consensus, Voting, and Federal Balance

The Goods and Services Tax (GST) Council, constituted under Article 279A of the Constitution, is the apex decision‑making body for the indirect tax regime. Its design reflects the federal compromise between the Centre and the States: the Union Finance Minister chairs the Council, the Union Minister of State for Finance (Revenue) is a member, and each State nominates a Minister in charge of finance or taxation. Voting weights are fixed — the Centre holds one‑third of the total vote, while the States collectively hold two‑thirds. A decision requires a three‑fourths majority of the weighted votes, which in practice translates into a consensus‑seeking culture.

The Council’s procedural rules, notified under Section 12 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, prescribe that the agenda be circulated at least ten days before a meeting, that minutes be recorded and placed in the public domain within fifteen days, and that dissenting views be noted. Since its first meeting in September 2016, the Council has taken numerous decisions covering rate structures, compensation cess, threshold limits, and procedural simplifications. Notable decisions include the 2017 rate rationalisation that reduced the number of tax slabs to four, the 2020 extension of the compensation cess beyond the original five‑year period, and discussions on bringing petroleum products under GST in a phased manner.

The Supreme Court has held that the Council’s recommendations acquire the force of law once the President assents to the corresponding amendment Bills, and that the Council’s decision‑making process is subject to judicial review only on grounds of constitutional violation, mala fides, or procedural ultra vires. The Court emphasised that the three‑fourths majority rule is a constitutional safeguard ensuring that no single unit — Centre or a group of States — can unilaterally impose its will. The 2022 amendment to the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017, further clarified the methodology for calculating the compensation shortfall and the borrowing mechanism, reinforcing the Council’s role as a fiscal federalism instrument.

For administrators, the operational checklist when implementing a Council decision is: (i) verify that the decision was adopted with the requisite weighted majority and that the minutes reflect any dissent; (ii) ensure the corresponding notification is issued under the appropriate CGST/SGST/IGST Act within the statutory timeline; (iii) update the GSTN (Goods and Services Tax Network) master data — rate tables, HSN codes, exemption lists — before the effective date; (iv) communicate the change to field formations through a circular that cites the Council meeting number, date, and resolution number; (v) monitor compliance and revenue impact for at least two quarters and report deviations to the Council’s Group of Ministers on Rate Rationalisation. This disciplined workflow translates the Council’s high‑level policy into consistent, auditable administrative action across 36 jurisdictions.

Technique
A State Government proposes to allocate a newly discovered coal block to a State‑owned enterprise without an e‑auction, citing “strategic national interest”. The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 permits such allocation only for government companies engaged in specified end‑uses. The State argues that the end‑use condition is satisfied because the enterprise will supply coal to a State‑owned power plant. Identify the legal flaw in the State’s argument and the judicial precedent that governs this scenario.
The flaw is that the Act requires a transparent, competitive e‑auction for all commercial mining; the exception for government companies applies only when the block is allocated for “specified end‑use” and the allocation is made through the prescribed procedure, which includes a reasoned order and publication of the allocation criteria. In Manohar Lal Sharma v. Union of India (2014) the Supreme Court cancelled allocations made without auction, holding that the State’s discretion to allocate coal blocks is not unfettered and must conform to the statutory mandate of transparency and non‑arbitrariness. Therefore, the State’s direct allocation without auction violates the Act and the Court’s precedent.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question tests administrative discretion in resource allocation, first identify the governing statute (Telegraph Act, Coal Mines Act, Inter‑State Water Disputes Act). Then check whether the statute mandates auction, adjudication, or a reasoned policy. Recall the landmark Supreme Court judgment that struck down non‑auction allocations (2G, coal). Apply the Wednesbury/proportionality test: was the decision rational, based on published criteria, and supported by a recorded reason? If any element is missing, the decision is vulnerable. Mark the answer that cites the specific statute and the controlling judgment.

The Doctrine of Substantive Legitimate Expectation in Regulatory Regimes

Legitimate expectation operates at two levels. Procedural legitimate expectation entitles a person to be consulted before a decision affecting them is taken. Substantive legitimate expectation goes further: it may entitle the person to the substantive benefit promised, provided the promise is clear, unambiguous, and made by an authority with the power to fulfil it. Indian courts have imported the doctrine from English administrative law (Council of Civil Service Unions v. Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374) and anchored it in Article 14’s guarantee of non‑arbitrariness.

The Supreme Court in State of Punjab v. Ramdev (1991) recognised that a representation by a public authority, if relied upon by a citizen, can give rise to a legitimate expectation that the representation will be honoured. In Union of India v. Hindustan Development Corp. (1993) the Court held that a legitimate expectation cannot override a statutory prohibition or a compelling public interest, but it does require the authority to consider the expectation and give reasons for departing from it. The doctrine does not create a new substantive right; it operates as a fairness check on the exercise of discretion.

Key elements for a substantive legitimate expectation claim are: (i) a clear and unambiguous representation — whether express or implied from a consistent practice — made by a responsible officer; (ii) the representation must pertain to a matter within the authority’s power; (iii) the claimant must have relied on the representation to their detriment; (iv) the reliance must be reasonable in the circumstances; (v) the authority must not have a statutory duty to act contrary to the representation. If these elements are satisfied, the court may either direct the authority to fulfil the expectation or, where fulfilment is impossible, award compensation.

Limitations are equally important. The doctrine cannot be used to fetter the exercise of statutory discretion in matters of policy, such as tax rates or licensing quotas, unless the representation amounts to a binding promise. In regulatory regimes — telecommunications, electricity, environmental clearances — tribunals have applied the doctrine to require regulators to honour commitments made in policy documents, bid documents, or previous orders, provided the commitment was not expressly made “subject to change”. The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity, for instance, has held that a distribution licensee’s legitimate expectation of a tariff revision schedule, once published, must be respected unless a statutory amendment intervenes.

For decision‑makers, the practical safeguard is to avoid unqualified assurances in policy circulars, bid documents, or public notices. Where flexibility is needed, the document should expressly state that the terms are “subject to revision in accordance with applicable law”. A record of the reasoning for any departure from a prior representation must be maintained in the file, linking the departure to a change in law, public interest, or factual circumstances. This record serves both as a defence in judicial review and as an audit trail for the CAG.

Judicial Review of Ordinances under Articles 123 and 213: Scope and Limits

Articles 123 (President) and 213 (Governor) empower the executive to promulgate ordinances when Parliament or a State Legislature is not in session and immediate action is deemed necessary. The ordinance has the same force as an Act but must be laid before the legislature within six weeks of its reassembly; otherwise it ceases to operate. The Supreme Court has delineated the boundaries of this power to prevent its misuse as a parallel legislative route.

In R. C. Cooper v. Union of India (1970) the Court held that an ordinance cannot be used to circumvent the legislative process; the satisfaction of the President/Governor regarding “immediate action” is justiciable, though the Court will not substitute its own judgment for that of the executive unless the satisfaction is mala fide or based on irrelevant considerations. In D. C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) the Court struck down the practice of repromulgating ordinances repeatedly without legislative approval, calling it a “fraud on the Constitution”. The principle was reinforced in Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017), where a seven‑judge bench declared that repromulgation without placing the ordinance before the legislature is unconstitutional, and that the ordinance‑making power is an emergency provision, not a substitute for legislative competence.

The Court has also examined the content of ordinances. In A. K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) it ruled that an ordinance that creates a new offence or enhances punishment must be scrutinised for compliance with Article 21. Recent judgments have reiterated that the executive must demonstrate the urgency that necessitated the ordinance and that the ordinance cannot be used to enact permanent structural reforms that belong to the legislative domain.
