The 2022 amendment to the IT Rules introduced a mandatory 72‑hour reporting window for data breaches affecting personal data, aligning with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Non‑compliance attracts penalties up to ₹250 crore under Section 43A of the IT Act.

Sectoral regulators exercise delegated discretion. The Reserve Bank of India’s “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” (2016, updated 2021) mandates a Board‑approved cyber‑risk policy, a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and quarterly penetration testing. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) issued similar guidelines for insurers in 2020. The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) enforces the Unified License conditions requiring licensees to maintain a Security Operations Centre (SOC) and to share incident logs with the NCCC. The National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC), designated under the NCIIPC Act, 2014, identifies CII sectors (power, transport, finance, health, etc.) and issues sector‑specific protection guidelines.

Incident response follows a tiered escalation matrix: Level 1 – the affected entity’s internal SOC; Level 2 – sectoral CERT; Level 3 – NCCC; Level 4 – National Crisis Management Committee (NCMC) chaired by the Cabinet Secretary for incidents of national significance. The 2021 ransomware attack on the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) illustrated the matrix: AIIMS’ SOC escalated to CERT‑In, which coordinated with the NCCC and the Ministry of Health; the NCMC was briefed within 24 hours, leading to a whole‑of‑government containment effort. Decision‑making questions often test the aspirant’s ability to identify the correct escalation level, the statutory reporting deadline, and the authority empowered to issue binding directions. The interplay between the IT Act, sectoral regulations, and the NCSS creates a layered discretion space where procedural compliance and substantive proportionality are both examined.

Situational Judgment: Cyber Incident Escalation
A mid‑size power distribution company detects a sophisticated malware intrusion in its SCADA network at 02:15 hrs. The company’s internal SOC isolates the affected segment but cannot eradicate the malware. According to the NCSS and the IT (CERT‑In) Rules, what is the immediate mandatory action the company must take, and within what time frame?
The company must report the incident to CERT‑In (the sectoral CERT for power is CERT‑Power, which operates under CERT‑In) within six hours of detection, as mandated by the Information Technology (The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team and Manner of Performing Functions and Duties) Rules, 2013. Simultaneously, it must inform the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) because the SCADA system qualifies as Critical Information Infrastructure. The report triggers Level 2 escalation; CERT‑In will coordinate with the NCCC (Level 3) and, if the incident threatens grid stability, the NCMC (Level 4). Failure to report within six hours attracts penal action under Section 43A of the IT Act.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the four‑level escalation matrix (Entity SOC → Sectoral CERT → NCCC → NCMC) and the two statutory reporting windows: six hours for cyber incidents under the CERT‑In Rules and 72 hours for personal‑data breaches under the 2022 IT Rules amendment. When a question describes a sector (banking, power, health), map it to the correct sectoral CERT (CERT‑Fin, CERT‑Power, CERT‑Health) before choosing the answer.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Virtual Digital Assets: The 2023 Bill, Taxation, and Enforcement

The Finance Act, 2023 introduced a comprehensive tax regime for Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs) without enacting a separate legislative framework. Section 115BBH of the Income‑Tax Act, 1961, imposes a flat 30 % tax on income from transfer of VDAs, disallows set‑off of losses against other heads, and permits only the cost of acquisition as deduction. Section 194S mandates a 1 % Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on consideration exceeding ₹10,000 (₹50,000 for specified persons) per transaction, effective 1 July 2023. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) issued Notification No. 13/2023 defining VDAs to include cryptocurrencies, non‑fungible tokens (NFTs), and any other token of similar nature, but explicitly excluding central bank digital currency (CBDC) and loyalty points.

Simultaneously, the Cryptocurrency and Regulation of Official Digital Currency Bill, 2021 (the “Crypto Bill”) lapsed with the dissolution of the 17th Lok Sabha. The government has signalled a consultative approach: the 2023 G20 Presidency produced a “Policy and Regulatory Framework for Crypto‑Assets” that recommends licensing of Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), AML/KYC obligations aligned with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) Travel Rule, and a prohibition on unbacked stablecoins. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) continues to enforce its 2018 circular (upheld by the Supreme Court in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI, 2020) prohibiting regulated entities from dealing in VDAs, while the Enforcement Directorate (ED) investigates money‑laundering cases under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, treating VDA transactions as “proceeds of crime” when linked to predicate offences.

Administrative discretion is exercised at multiple levels: (i) the CBDT determines the threshold for TDS applicability and the valuation methodology for cost of acquisition; (ii) the Financial Intelligence Unit‑India (FIU‑IND) issues guidelines for VASP reporting of suspicious transaction reports (STRs); (iii) the Ministry of Finance, through the Department of Economic Affairs, decides on the licensing regime for VASPs once the Crypto Bill is re‑introduced; (iv) the RBI may issue directions under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, to restrict banking channels for unlicensed VASPs. The Supreme Court’s 2020 judgment struck down the RBI’s blanket ban as disproportionate, but left the door open for proportionate regulation. Consequently, any future licensing framework must satisfy the test of reasonableness under Article 14 and the proportionality standard articulated in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

Enforcement actions illustrate the discretion‑accountability tension. In 2022‑23, the ED attached assets worth ₹1,200 crore in the “CoinSwitch Kuber” investigation, invoking Section 5 of the PMLA. The Delhi High Court, in WazirX v. Union of India (2023), upheld the ED’s provisional attachment but directed that the exchange be given an opportunity to demonstrate legitimate source of funds. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should focus on: (a) the distinction between tax treatment (Income‑Tax Act) and regulatory treatment (pending Crypto Bill); (b) the role of FIU‑IND in AML compliance; (c) the RBI’s residual powers over banking access; and (d) the judicial requirement that any restriction be proportionate and non‑arbitrary.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of 5G Spectrum and the Role of the Telecom Regulatory Authority

The Department of Telecommunications (DoT) conducted the 5G spectrum auction in July‑August 2022, offering 72 GHz across low‑band (600 MHz, 700 MHz), mid‑band (3.3‑3.67 GHz), and high‑band (26 GHz) frequencies. The auction design followed the Simultaneous Multiple Round Ascending (SMRA) format recommended by the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) in its 2021 “Recommendations on Auction of Spectrum in 5G Bands”. TRAI’s discretion encompassed reserve price determination, block size, spectrum cap (50 % per band per licensee), and the introduction of a “spectrum sharing” and “spectrum trading” framework under the Unified License (UL) conditions. The reserve price for the 3.3‑3.67 GHz band was set at ₹317 crore per MHz, a figure derived from the 2021 valuation methodology that incorporated international benchmarks, opportunity cost, and the “willingness‑to‑pay” model.

The auction resulted in total bids of ₹1.5 lakh crore, with Reliance Jio, Bharti Airtel, and Vodafone Idea acquiring the bulk of mid‑band spectrum. Post‑auction, the DoT exercised discretion in granting the “Spectrum Assignment Letter” and in approving the “Spectrum Sharing Agreement” between Jio and Airtel for the 800 MHz band, a first under the 2021 sharing guidelines. The Wireless Planning and Coordination Wing (WPC) monitors compliance with rollout obligations: each licensee must achieve 5G coverage in at least 50 % of the licensed service area within three years and 90 % within five years, failing which the DoT may invoke the “Spectrum Re‑farming” clause.

Judicial review has been limited but instructive. In Cellular Operators Association of India v. Union of India (2023), the Delhi High Court upheld TRAI’s reserve‑price methodology, noting that the authority’s expert discretion in economic valuation is entitled to deference unless shown to be arbitrary. The Supreme Court, in a 2024 special leave petition, declined to interfere with the spectrum cap, reiterating that policy choices on market structure fall within the executive’s domain. However, the Court emphasised that the DoT must publish reasoned orders when invoking penalties for rollout defaults, aligning with the duty to give reasons under Article 14.

For situational‑judgment questions, the decision nodes are: (i) TRAI’s recommendation‑making power versus DoT’s final auction design authority; (ii) the interplay between spectrum sharing/trading rules and the UL conditions; (iii) the rollout obligation timeline and the consequences of non‑compliance; (iv) the standard of judicial review — Wednesbury unreasonableness versus structured proportionality — applied to reserve‑price and cap decisions. Aspirants should be able to trace a scenario (e.g., a new entrant challenging the reserve price) through the administrative hierarchy: TRAI recommendation → DoT acceptance → auction → assignment → rollout monitoring → penalty → judicial review.

Administrative Discretion in Inter‑State Water Dispute Resolution: The Role of the Central Water Commission and Tribunal Awards

The Inter‑State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 (ISRWD Act) provides the statutory architecture for adjudicating disputes between riparian states. Under Section 4, the Central Government may constitute a Water Disputes Tribunal whose award, once published in the Official Gazette, becomes binding on the parties (Section 6). The Central Water Commission (CWC), an attached office of the Ministry of Jal Shakti, performs the technical appraisal: it prepares the “Water Availability Study”, the “Hydrological Data Compendium”, and the “Project Feasibility Reports” that form the evidentiary base for the Tribunal. The CWC’s discretion lies in selecting the hydrological model (e.g., SWAT, MIKE BASIN), defining the baseline period (typically 30 years), and deciding the allocation methodology — whether “equitable apportionment”, “priority of use”, or “historical utilisation”.

Landmark tribunals illustrate the discretion‑outcome link. The Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (constituted 1990, final award 2007, modified by Supreme Court 2018) adopted a “monthly release schedule” based on the 1924 agreement and the 1976 interim order, but the CWC’s 2005 “Cauvery Basin Study” introduced a 10‑year moving average for inflow estimation, which the Tribunal accepted. The Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal‑II (2004‑2010) used the “Principle of Equitable Apportionment” and relied on the CWC’s “Krishna Basin Water Balance” to allocate 811 TMC to Maharashtra, 1,001 TMC to Karnataka, and 1,111 TMC to Andhra Pradesh (later Telangana). The Godavari Water Disputes Tribunal (1969‑1980) applied the “Prior Appropriation” principle for existing projects and “Equitable Apportionment” for future ones, guided by the CWC’s “Godavari Basin Master Plan”.

The 2019 amendment to the ISRWD Act introduced a “Dispute Resolution Committee” (DRC) as a pre‑tribunal conciliation mechanism, chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge, with the CWC providing technical secretariat support. The DRC’s report is non‑binding but influences the Tribunal’s terms of reference. The Ministry of Jal Shakti also exercises discretion in “referring” a dispute to the Tribunal (Section 4) — a political decision that can be delayed, as seen in the Mahanadi dispute (Odisha vs. Chhattisgarh) where the reference was made in 2018 after a decade of negotiations.

Judicial oversight ensures procedural fairness. In State of Karnataka v. State of Tamil Nadu (2018), the Supreme Court held that the Tribunal’s award must be based on “reliable and scientific data” and that the CWC’s methodology is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness. The Court also mandated that the Tribunal provide a “reasoned award” addressing each party’s submissions, reinforcing the duty to give reasons. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should identify: (i) the CWC’s technical discretion in hydrological modelling; (ii) the Tribunal’s legal discretion in choosing allocation principles; (iii) the executive’s political discretion in referring disputes; and (iv) the judicial standard of review — whether the award is “perverse” or “unsupported by evidence”. A typical scenario may ask which body decides the baseline period for inflow data — the answer is the CWC, subject to Tribunal acceptance.

  • Confusing the six‑hour cyber‑incident reporting window under the CERT‑In Rules with the 72‑hour personal‑data breach window under the 2022 IT Rules amendment.
  • Assuming the RBI’s 2018 circular banning crypto dealings remains absolute; the Supreme Court struck it down as disproportionate in 2020.
  • Treating the TRAI’s reserve‑price recommendation as the final auction price; the DoT may modify it before the auction notice.
  • Believing the Inter‑State Water Disputes Tribunal’s award is automatically enforceable without Gazette publication; Section 6 of the ISRWD Act makes publication a condition precedent.
  • Overlooking that the Green Bond Framework requires a second‑party opinion for corporate issuers but not for sovereign issuance, where the DEA’s internal review suffices.
  • Mixing the spectrum cap (50 % per band per licensee) with the spectrum sharing limit (up to 25 % of the shared band) in 5G allocation questions.
  • Assuming the National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change provides loans; it is a grant‑based mechanism with co‑financing requirements.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Forest Rights Act, 2006

The Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act, 2006 (FRA) creates a dual‑layer decision‑making structure. At the village level, the Gram Sabha receives claims, verifies evidence, and passes a resolution recommending recognition. The Sub‑Divisional Level Committee (SDLC) and the District Level Committee (DLC) then examine the Gram Sabha’s recommendation, conduct field verification, and issue the final title. Discretion resides in three distinct stages: (i) the Gram Sabha’s assessment of “traditional occupation” and “community forest resource” claims; (ii) the SDLC’s power to accept, modify, or reject the Gram Sabha resolution under Section 6(2); and (iii) the DLC’s authority to confirm or overturn the SDLC decision under Section 6(3). The Act mandates that the Gram Sabha’s resolution be given “due weight” but does not bind the higher committees, creating a calibrated hierarchy of discretion.

Judicial interpretation has sharpened the limits of this discretion. In Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment & Forests (2013), the Supreme Court held that the Gram Sabha’s consent is a prerequisite for any diversion of forest land under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980, reinforcing the primacy of the community‑level decision. Subsequent rulings have established that the SDLC cannot reject a Gram Sabha recommendation solely on procedural grounds without a substantive review of the evidence, imposing a “reasoned‑decision” requirement. The Ministry of Tribal Affairs issues guidelines (2012, 2014, and subsequent clarifications) that prescribe formats for claim forms, evidence checklists, and timelines — 90 days for SDLC disposal and 180 days for DLC disposal — thereby constraining administrative delay.

Operational discretion also appears in the determination of “critical wildlife habitat” under Section 4(2). The State Government, on the advice of the Chief Wildlife Warden, may notify such areas, which then become ineligible for rights recognition. The Supreme Court has required that such notification be based on “scientific criteria” and subject to public consultation, limiting arbitrary exclusion. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should map the claim‑processing flowchart, identify the statutory timelines, and note the judicial checkpoints that convert discretion into reviewable reasoned orders.

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of Medical Devices: The CDSCO Framework and the Medical Devices Rules, 2017

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organization (CDSCO), under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, regulates medical devices through the Medical Devices Rules, 2017 (MDR). The Rules classify devices into four risk classes — A (low), B (low‑moderate), C (moderate‑high), and D (high) — based on the Global Harmonization Task Force (GHTF) framework. Discretion is exercised at three regulatory gates: (i) the classification decision by the applicant, subject to CDSCO verification; (ii) the grant of a manufacturing or import licence by the State Licensing Authority (SLA) for Class A and B, and by the Central Licensing Authority (CLA) for Class C and D; and (iii) the post‑market surveillance (PMS) and adverse‑event reporting obligations that the licence holder must fulfil.

The CLA’s discretion in granting a licence for Class C and D devices includes the power to demand clinical investigation data, a quality management system certificate (ISO 13485), and a free‑sale certificate from the country of origin. The Rules prescribe a 45‑day timeline for the CLA to process a complete application, extendable by 30 days if additional information is sought. Courts have held that the CLA cannot reject an application on vague “public interest” grounds without a speaking order, reinforcing the duty to give reasons. The Rules also empower the CLA to suspend or cancel a licence for non‑compliance with PMS, subject to a show‑cause notice and an opportunity of hearing — a procedural safeguard rooted in natural justice.

Recent amendments introduced a “regulatory sandbox” for innovative devices, allowing limited‑scale deployment under CDSCO supervision before full licensure. The sandbox decision‑making matrix requires the applicant to define the intended use, risk mitigation plan, and exit criteria. The CDSCO’s discretion to admit a device into the sandbox is guided by an expert committee report, and the final authorisation is published in the Gazette. For exam purposes, candidates should distinguish between the SLA’s and CLA’s jurisdictional thresholds, recall the 45‑day processing norm, and recognise that any adverse‑event reporting failure triggers a mandatory show‑cause procedure before licence suspension.

Worked Scenario
A startup seeks to import a Class C diagnostic kit. The CLA receives the application on 1 January. The applicant submits all required documents except the free‑sale certificate, which is provided on 20 January. The CLA issues a query on 25 January asking for clarification on the sterilisation validation report. The applicant replies on 10 February. Assuming no further queries, on what date must the CLA decide the application under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017?
The 45‑day clock starts when a complete application is received. The application became complete on 20 January (receipt of the free‑sale certificate). The CLA’s query on 25 January does not pause the clock; the Rules allow a 30‑day extension only if the CLA formally extends the period. The applicant’s reply on 10 February is within the original 45‑day window (20 January + 45 days = 6 March). Therefore, the CLA must decide by 6 March. If the CLA invokes the 30‑day extension, the outer limit becomes 5 April, but the extension must be communicated in writing before the original deadline.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a timeline question appears, first identify the “complete application” date, then add the statutory period. Remember that a query from the authority does not automatically extend the deadline unless the Rules expressly provide for an extension and the authority issues a formal extension order. Mark the distinction between SLA (Class A/B) and CLA (Class C/D) jurisdiction — it is a frequent distractor.

Administrative Discretion in the Allocation of Minor Minerals under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957

The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) empowers State Governments to grant quarry leases, mining leases, and composite licences for minor minerals — building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, and sand — under Section 15 and the Minor Mineral Concession Rules framed by each State. Discretion operates at three levels: (i) the identification of “minor mineral” deposits through district‑level surveys conducted by the State Geology and Mining Department; (ii) the grant of a quarry lease by the District Collector or the designated authority after a public notice and objection period; and (iii) the fixation of royalty rates and dead‑rent, which the State Government may revise by notification.

The 2015 amendment to the MMDR Act introduced a mandatory auction for major minerals but left minor minerals to State‑level discretionary allocation, subject to the State’s own auction or e‑tender rules. The Supreme Court has held that even for minor minerals, the allocation process must be “fair, transparent, and non‑arbitrary”, and that the State cannot bypass its own e‑tender rules without a recorded reason. The Court also mandated that the District Collector’s order granting a quarry lease be a speaking order, citing the principles of natural justice.

Environmental clearance adds another discretionary layer. The Environment Impact Assessment (EIA) Notification, 2006, as amended in 2020, exempts minor mineral mining leases up to 5 hectares from prior environmental clearance, but requires a District‑level Environment Impact Assessment Report (DEIAR) and a public hearing for leases above 5 hectares. The State Expert Appraisal Committee (SEAC) exercises discretion in recommending the Terms of Reference (ToR) and in granting the Environmental Clearance (EC). The “precautionary principle” has been read into the EC process, obligating the SEAC to consider cumulative impact even for minor minerals. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should trace the allocation chain from survey → public notice → objection hearing → District Collector’s speaking order → royalty fixation → EC (if applicable), and note the judicial requirement of reasoned orders at each discretionary node.

Decision‑Making in the Enforcement of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988: Role of the Central Vigilance Commission and the Lokpal

The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (PCA) establishes a layered enforcement architecture. The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC), constituted under the Central Vigilance Commission Act, 2003, exercises superintendence over the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) in corruption cases involving Central Government employees. The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013 creates the Lokpal at the Centre and Lokayuktas in States, with jurisdiction over public servants including the Prime Minister (with safeguards), Ministers, and Members of Parliament. Discretion appears in: (i) the CVC’s power to advise the CBI to initiate a preliminary inquiry (PE) or a regular case (RC) under Section 8 of the CVC Act; (ii) the Lokpal’s discretion to order a preliminary inquiry under Section 20, to refer a matter to the CBI or any other agency, or to dismiss a complaint after a prima facie assessment; and (iii) the competent authority’s sanction for prosecution under Section 19 of the PCA, which the Supreme Court in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2014) held must be granted within three months, failing which deemed sanction operates.

The CVC’s advisory role is not binding on the CBI, but the CBI must record reasons for deviating from CVC advice. Courts have quashed CBI closure reports that ignored CVC’s recommendation for a regular case, reinforcing the “reasoned‑deviation” standard. The Lokpal’s inquiry wing, headed by a Director of Inquiry, conducts a preliminary inquiry within 90 days (extendable by 90 days). If a prima facie case exists, the Lokpal may order an investigation by its own prosecution wing or refer to the CBI. The Lokpal’s order is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness under Article 14.

The 2018 amendment to the PCA introduced a “prior approval” requirement for investigating officers before registering an FIR against a public servant for decisions taken in official capacity, unless the decision involves a “demand for undue advantage”. This provision adds a discretionary filter at the registration stage. For exam‑oriented analysis, candidates should map the decision tree: complaint → CVC advice → CBI PE/RC → sanction → prosecution; and parallel Lokpal track: complaint → preliminary inquiry → investigation → prosecution. The key examinable points are the three‑month sanction timeline, the deemed‑sanction rule, and the requirement that any deviation from CVC advice be recorded in writing.

Administrative Discretion in the National Green Tribunal’s Suo Motu Jurisdiction and Environmental Remediation Orders

The National Green Tribunal (NGT), established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010, possesses suo motu powers under Section 14(2) to take cognisance of environmental matters on the basis of newspaper reports, letters, or any other information. The Tribunal’s discretion to invoke suo motu jurisdiction is guided by the “principle of environmental democracy” and the “polluter pays” principle. The Supreme Court has upheld the NGT’s suo motu action against illegal sand mining, stating that the Tribunal’s statutory mandate includes preventive and remedial jurisdiction, not merely adjudicatory.

Once suo motu cognisance is taken, the NGT may constitute an expert committee, direct the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) or State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs) to conduct inspections, and pass interim directions such as stop‑work orders, closure of units, or imposition of environmental compensation. The NGT has imposed substantial environmental compensation on polluters for continuous violation of emission norms, calculated on the basis of the “cost of restoration” methodology. The NGT’s discretion in quantifying compensation is subject to the “reasonableness” test — the amount must be proportionate to the damage and the polluter’s capacity to pay.

The NGT’s appellate decisions are appealable to the Supreme Court under Section 22 of the NGT Act. The Supreme Court has held that the NGT’s suo motu orders are not immune from judicial review but are entitled to “due deference” given the Tribunal’s specialised expertise. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should identify the trigger for suo motu action, the procedural steps (notice, hearing, expert committee report, final order), and the standards of review — proportionality, reasonableness, and adherence to the principles of natural justice. The Tribunal’s power to direct “restoration of ecology” under Section 15(3) is a remedial discretion that goes beyond penal compensation and is a frequent focus of scenario‑based items.

  • Confusing the Gram Sabha’s recommendatory role under the FRA with a binding veto over forest diversion.
  • Assuming the CLA’s 45‑day timeline for Class C/D devices pauses automatically when a query is raised.
  • Treating minor‑mineral allocation as entirely free from auction requirements; many States now mandate e‑tender even for minor minerals.
  • Believing the CVC’s advice to the CBI is binding; the CBI may deviate but must record reasons.
  • Thinking the Lokpal can directly prosecute without a sanction from the competent authority; sanction remains a statutory prerequisite.
  • Assuming the NGT’s suo motu orders are final and non‑appealable; they are appealable to the Supreme Court.
  • Overlooking that environmental compensation under the NGT must be calculated on a restoration‑cost basis, not an arbitrary flat rate.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Fintech Lending Platforms: RBI Guidelines and the Digital Lending Framework

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has progressively tightened the regulatory perimeter around digital lending apps (DLAs) and fintech lending platforms. The Digital Lending Guidelines, 2022 require that all loan disbursements and repayments be routed through the borrower’s bank account, eliminating the “pass‑through” model where fintechs held funds in escrow. Entities must obtain a Certificate of Registration (CoR) as a Non‑Banking Financial Company (NBFC) or partner with a regulated entity; unregistered lending is prohibited. The guidelines mandate a Key Fact Statement (KFS) in a standardized format, a cooling‑off period of at least 24 hours after loan sanction, and a grievance redressal mechanism with a nodal officer. The RBI’s Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2023 also requires disclosure of the all‑in cost of credit (AIC) and algorithmic transparency: the credit‑scoring model must be documented, auditable, and free from discriminatory variables. Non‑compliance attracts penal action under Section 45‑IA of the RBI Act, 1934, including cancellation of CoR and monetary penalties. The Supreme Court in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. Reserve Bank of India (2020) upheld the RBI’s power to issue directions in the interest of the financial system, reinforcing the regulator’s discretion to prescribe technology‑neutral standards. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should map the decision tree: registration → KFS issuance → cooling‑off → disbursement via borrower account → audit of algorithm → periodic reporting to RBI. The examinable nuances are the distinction between “regulated entity” and “technology service provider”, the 24‑hour cooling‑off requirement, and the obligation to store loan data in India.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Seats under the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006: Role of the University Grants Commission

The Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006 mandates 15 % reservation for Scheduled Castes, 7.5 % for Scheduled Tribes, 27 % for Other Backward Classes (non‑creamy layer) and, since the 103rd Constitutional Amendment (2019), 10 % for Economically Weaker Sections (EWS) in all central universities, IITs, IIMs and other centrally funded institutions. The University Grants Commission (UGC) issues Reservation Guidelines that operationalise the Act: they prescribe the roster‑point system, the method for calculating the “creamy layer” income ceiling (currently ₹8 lakh per annum), and the procedure for inter‑category transfers when a reserved seat remains vacant. The UGC’s discretion extends to approving seat‑matrix proposals submitted by each institution, verifying compliance with the post‑matric scholarship linkage, and directing corrective action when the National Commission for Scheduled Castes or National Commission for Scheduled Tribes reports shortfalls. Landmark judicial pronouncements shape this discretion: in Ashoka Kumar Thakur v. Union of India (2008) the Supreme Court upheld the 27 % OBC quota but required the “creamy layer” exclusion; in Jarnail Singh v. Lachhmi Narain Gupta (2018) the Court held that the creamy‑layer concept applies to SC/ST promotions under Article 16(4A), a principle that informs roster management. The 2021 UGC (Reservation in Admission) Regulations introduced a centralised online counselling platform for postgraduate medical seats, reducing institutional discretion. For exam‑oriented analysis, candidates should identify the decision points: (i) preparation of roster by institution, (ii) UGC verification, (iii) handling of vacant reserved seats through “de‑reservation” only after two consecutive counselling rounds (as per medical counselling norms), (iv) EWS quota implementation subject to notified income criteria. The key trap is confusing the UGC’s advisory guidelines with statutory mandates — the Act binds institutions; UGC guidelines are enforceable primarily through funding conditions.

Worked Scenario
A central university receives 1,200 applications for 100 undergraduate seats. The university prepares a roster following the 2006 Act and the 2021 UGC Regulations. After the first counselling round, 5 SC seats and 3 OBC seats remain vacant. The university proposes to fill these seats with general‑category candidates in the second round. Is this permissible?
No. Under the 2006 Act read with the 2021 UGC Regulations, reserved seats that remain vacant after the first counselling round must be carried forward to the second round. De‑reservation (conversion to general category) is allowed only after two consecutive counselling rounds have failed to fill the seat, and only with prior UGC approval. The university’s proposal to fill SC and OBC vacancies with general candidates in the second round violates the statutory roster and the UGC’s mandatory carry‑forward rule.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mentions “vacant reserved seats”, instantly recall the two‑round carry‑forward rule and the requirement of UGC approval for de‑reservation. Mark the answer that references the 2006 Act and the 2021 UGC Regulations; avoid options that allow immediate conversion to general category.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the National Health Mission: Fund Flow, Flexi‑Pool, and State‑Level Decision‑Making

The National Health Mission (NHM), comprising the National Rural Health Mission (NRHM) and the National Urban Health Mission (NUHM), operates through a flexi‑pool financing architecture that grants states considerable discretion in allocating resources across programme components. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare releases funds in two streams: (i) Resource Envelope — a formula‑based allocation using population, health indicators, and performance scores; (ii) Incentive Pool — performance‑linked grants tied to achievements in immunisation, institutional deliveries, and health‑facility accreditation. States prepare an Annual Programme Implementation Plan (APIP) which the Empowered Programme Committee (EPC) at the central level appraises. The EPC’s discretion includes approving re‑appropriation between sub‑components (e.g., shifting funds from infrastructure to human resources) provided the state justifies the change with outcome data. The State Health Society (SHS), chaired by the Chief Secretary, exercises operational discretion: it sanctions district‑level plans, approves procurement of drugs and equipment through the Centralised Procurement Agency, and monitors the Health Management Information System (HMIS) for real‑time expenditure tracking. CAG audit reports have highlighted instances where states diverted flexi‑pool funds to non‑NHM activities, prompting the Ministry to issue directives mandating quarterly fund‑utilisation certificates and a negative list of inadmissible expenditures. Judicial oversight is limited; courts have generally affirmed executive discretion in fiscal federalism matters. For decision‑making items, aspirants should trace the flow: Central release → State Treasury → SHS → District Health Society → Facility. The examinable points are the distinction between Resource Envelope and Incentive Pool, the EPC’s re‑appropriation authority, and the negative‑list compliance requirement.

Decision‑Making under the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016: Powers of the Real Estate Regulatory Authority and Appellate Tribunal

The Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 (RERA) establishes a Real Estate Regulatory Authority (RERA) in each state/UT and a Real Estate Appellate Tribunal (REAT) to adjudicate disputes. The Authority’s discretionary powers include: (i) registration of projects — it may reject or conditionally register a project if the promoter fails to submit approved plans, land title clearance, or the prescribed 70 % escrow account for construction funds; (ii) extension of completion timelines — the Authority can grant extension on grounds of force majeure, subject to promoter’s application and payment of penalty; (iii) imposition of penalties — up to 10 % of the project cost for non‑registration (Section 59), and up to 5 % for contravention of orders (Section 63). The Appellate Tribunal hears appeals against Authority orders within 60 days; its decisions are binding unless challenged in the High Court under Article 226. Landmark judgments clarify the scope: in Newtech Promoters & Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. (Allahabad High Court, 2020) the Court held that the Authority’s power to impose penalty is quasi‑judicial and must adhere to natural justice; in Batra Hospital & Medical Research Centre v. RERA, Delhi (Delhi High Court, 2022) the Court ruled that the 70 % escrow requirement applies to the entire project cost, not phase‑wise. The Act provides for a Central Advisory Council under Section 43 to advise the Ministry on model rules, while state‑level Authorities retain rule‑making discretion under Section 85. For exam scenarios, candidates should map the decision tree: promoter application → Authority scrutiny → registration/conditional registration → compliance monitoring → penalty/adjudication → appeal to REAT → High Court. The key nuance is that the Authority cannot suo motu cancel registration without a show‑cause notice and hearing.

Administrative Discretion in the Enforcement of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002: Role of the Enforcement Directorate and Adjudicating Authority

The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) empowers the Enforcement Directorate (ED) to investigate money‑laundering offences, attach property, and prosecute offenders. The ED’s discretionary steps are: (i) initiation of inquiry — based on a predicate offence FIR, intelligence input, or a reference from a regulator; (ii) provisional attachment — under Section 5, the Director may attach property for 180 days if he has “reason to believe” it is proceeds of crime; (iii) filing of complaint — before the Adjudicating Authority (AA) within 30 days of attachment, seeking confirmation. The AA, a quasi‑judicial body, decides on confirmation after hearing the accused; its order is appealable to the Appellate Tribunal (PMLA) and thereafter to the High Court. The Supreme Court in Vijay Madanlal Choudhary v. Union of India (2022) upheld the constitutional validity of Sections 3, 5, 19, and 45, but read down the “reason to believe” standard to require a prima facie case based on material evidence, not mere suspicion. The Court clarified that the Enforcement Case Information Report (ECIR) is an internal document and not equivalent to an FIR; its supply to the accused is not a precondition for attachment. The 2019 amendment expanded the definition of “proceeds of crime” to include property derived from any criminal activity relating to scheduled offences, widening the ED’s net. For decision‑making questions, aspirants should identify the chain: predicate offence → ECIR → provisional attachment → AA confirmation → prosecution. The examinable traps are: (a) confusing the ED’s investigative discretion with the AA’s adjudicative function; (b) assuming attachment is final — it is provisional and subject to AA confirmation; (c) overlooking the requirement that the predicate offence must be a scheduled offence under the PMLA schedule.

  • Treating the RBI’s digital‑lending cooling‑off period as optional; it is mandatory and non‑waivable.
  • Assuming the UGC can de‑reserve seats after a single counselling round; two rounds and UGC approval are required (per medical counselling norms).
  • Confusing the NHM Resource Envelope with the Incentive Pool; they have distinct allocation formulas and conditionality.
  • Believing the RERA Authority can cancel registration without a show‑cause notice; natural justice mandates a hearing.
  • Thinking the ED’s provisional attachment under PMLA is final; it expires in 180 days unless confirmed by the Adjudicating Authority.
  • Overlooking that the “reason to believe” standard under PMLA requires prima facie material, not mere suspicion.
  • Assuming the 70 % escrow rule under RERA applies phase‑wise; the Delhi High Court clarified it applies to the total project cost.

These advanced sections equip aspirants with the granular statutory and judicial knowledge needed to navigate complex decision‑making scenarios in competitive examinations.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the National Rural Livelihoods Mission

The National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM), launched in 2011 and later subsumed under the Deendayal Antyodaya Yojana – National Rural Livelihoods Mission (DAY‑NRLM), empowers State Rural Livelihoods Missions (SRLMs) to design and execute livelihood‑enhancement programmes for self‑help groups (SHGs). The administrative discretion exercised by SRLMs operates at three tiers: (i) identification and mobilisation of target households through participatory rural appraisal; (ii) allocation of revolving fund and community investment fund across SHGs based on grading criteria; and (iii) selection of livelihood activities — farm, off‑farm, and non‑farm — guided by the District Level Committee (DLC) and the State Level Committee (SLC). The Ministry of Rural Development issues framework guidelines, but the SRLM retains rule‑making power under the NRLM Guidelines to adapt eligibility thresholds, interest subvention rates, and convergence modalities with other schemes such as MGNREGS, PMKSY, and the National Rural Economic Transformation Project.

Judicial scrutiny of this discretion has focused on the transparency of SHG grading and the fairness of fund disbursement. High Courts have held that SRLM decisions denying revolving funds on grounds such as “insufficient credit history” violate natural justice if the SHG is not given an opportunity to present its repayment track record. The Supreme Court has reiterated that while the Mission’s objectives are policy‑driven, administrative orders affecting individual beneficiaries are quasi‑judicial and must satisfy the Wednesbury reasonableness test. Recent amendments to the NRLM Guidelines introduced mandatory social audit at the Gram Panchayat level, requiring the SRLM to publish fund utilisation statements and SHG grading scores on the public portal, thereby converting a purely discretionary allocation into a process subject to public scrutiny.

For decision‑making questions, aspirants should map the decision chain: community mobiliser recommendation → block level verification → DLC approval → SRLM fund release → social audit → grievance redressal through the State Level Ombudsman. The examinable nuance is that the SRLM cannot unilaterally alter the interest subvention ceiling without prior concurrence of the Ministry, and any deviation must be recorded with reasons to survive judicial review.

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of E‑Commerce Marketplaces under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 (CPA) introduced a dedicated regulatory framework for e‑commerce entities through the Consumer Protection (E‑Commerce) Rules, 2020, and subsequent amendments. The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) exercises administrative discretion in three principal domains: (i) registration and classification of e‑commerce entities as marketplace‑based or inventory‑based models; (ii) enforcement of mandatory disclosures — seller details, return‑refund policies, country of origin, and grievance officer contact — under Rule 5; and (iii) imposition of penalties for unfair trade practices, misleading advertisements, and non‑compliance with the “no‑cancellation‑fee” mandate for consumer‑initiated returns.

The CCPA’s discretion is bounded by statutory timelines for issuing show‑cause notices and passing final orders. Courts have upheld the CCPA’s power to direct an e‑commerce platform to delist a seller for repeated violations, but struck down blanket bans on future registration as disproportionate. Recent amendments introduced a “dark‑pattern” prohibition, empowering the CCPA to issue directions against UI designs that manipulate consumer choice. Enforcement orders under this provision have required platforms to redesign checkout flows within specified periods.

Decision‑making scenarios in examinations typically present a fact pattern where a marketplace claims immunity as an intermediary under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000. The correct analytical step is to test whether the entity exercises control over inventory, pricing, or delivery — factors that convert it into an inventory‑based model under the E‑Commerce Rules, thereby attracting full liability under the CPA. The CCPA’s order is appealable to the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) within the prescribed period, and further to the Supreme Court under Article 136. Aspirants must note that the CCPA cannot impose criminal sanctions; its remedies are limited to penalties, corrective advertisements, and directions for compliance.

Technique: Mapping Statutory Decision Trees
A state‑level e‑commerce platform operates a hybrid model: it hosts third‑party sellers but also procures a private‑label range that it stores in its own warehouses and fulfils directly. A consumer files a complaint alleging misleading discount claims on the private‑label products. The CCPA issues a show‑cause notice to the platform. The platform argues it is an intermediary under Section 79 IT Act and therefore not liable. Determine the correct regulatory classification and the CCPA’s permissible order.
Step 1: Identify the model. Because the platform holds inventory, controls pricing, and fulfils orders for its private label, it falls under the inventory‑based definition in the E‑Commerce Rules, irrespective of its marketplace arm. Step 2: Apply CPA liability. Inventory‑based entities are “sellers” under Section 2(31) CPA and are directly liable for unfair trade practices. Step 3: CCPA powers. The CCPA may issue a direction to cease the misleading advertisement, impose a penalty, and order corrective advertisements. It cannot ban the platform’s marketplace operations unless those operations themselves violate the Rules. Step 4: Appeal route. The platform may appeal to NCDRC within the prescribed period. The intermediary defence under Section 79 IT Act fails because the platform is not a pure conduit for the private‑label goods.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a fact pattern mixes marketplace and inventory activities, first isolate the inventory‑based segment; the CCPA’s jurisdiction attaches to that segment alone. Remember the statutory show‑cause and order deadlines — they are frequent “trap” dates in time‑bound questions.

Administrative Discretion in the Allocation of Renewable Energy Certificates and the Role of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission

The Renewable Energy Certificate (REC) mechanism, operationalised under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for Recognition and Issuance of Renewable Energy Certificates) Regulations, 2010 and amended subsequently, grants the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) wide administrative discretion in three areas: (i) accreditation of eligible renewable energy generators — solar, wind, small hydro, biomass — based on capacity, vintage, and grid‑connected status; (ii) determination of the floor and forbearance prices for solar and non‑solar RECs through a price‑discovery formula linked to the weighted average cost of power purchase agreements; and (iii) monitoring compliance of obligated entities — distribution licensees, open‑access consumers, and captive users — with Renewable Purchase Obligations (RPO) prescribed by the respective State Electricity Regulatory Commissions (SERCs).

The CERC’s discretion is exercised through a transparent stakeholder consultation process: draft regulations are published for public comments, followed by a public hearing. The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity has upheld the Commission’s decision to revise solar REC floor prices, finding that the revision was based on a reasoned analysis of market liquidity and the cost of capital, satisfying the proportionality test. Conversely, the Supreme Court has set aside a CERC order that retrospectively cancelled RECs issued to a wind generator on the ground of “non‑compliance with grid code” without affording a hearing, reiterating that quasi‑judicial cancellation requires adherence to natural justice.

Recent amendments introduced a “banking” facility allowing generators to carry forward unsold RECs for a specified period, subject to an annual depreciation factor. The CERC also administers the REC registry, a digital platform that records issuance, transfer, and redemption. For exam purposes, the decision tree is: generator application → CERC accreditation → REC issuance → trading on power exchanges → obligated entity redemption → compliance reporting to SERC. The key trap is confusing the CERC’s price‑setting role (administrative) with the SERC’s RPO target‑setting role (legislative); only the former is subject to judicial review on Wednesbury grounds.

Judicial Review of Administrative Action under Article 21: Right to Life, Personal Liberty, and Procedural Fairness

Article 21 of the Constitution has been interpreted by the Supreme Court as a repository of substantive and procedural due process, extending the scope of judicial review over administrative decisions that affect life, liberty, health, and environment. The landmark Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) established that any law depriving a person of personal liberty must be “fair, just and reasonable”, importing the principles of natural justice into administrative action. Subsequent jurisprudence has applied this standard to a spectrum of administrative domains: (i) preventive detention orders under the National Security Act, 1980 — the Court in A. K. Roy v. Union of India (1982) required the detaining authority to disclose grounds and afford an effective opportunity of representation; (ii) environmental clearances — in Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) the Court held that the precautionary principle and polluter‑pays principle are integral to Article 21, obligating the Ministry of Environment to conduct a rigorous impact assessment before granting clearance; (iii) public health emergencies — during the COVID‑19 pandemic, the Supreme Court in In Re: Distribution of Essential Supplies (2021) mandated that allocation of oxygen and vaccines follow a transparent, non‑arbitrary formula, subject to judicial audit.

The procedural facet of Article 21 demands that administrative orders affecting fundamental rights be preceded by notice, hearing, and reasoned decisions. In K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) the Court recognised privacy as a facet of Article 21, requiring data‑processing authorities to adopt purpose limitation, data minimisation, and accountability — principles later codified in the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The proportionality test, refined in Modern Dental College v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2016), requires that the administrative measure be suitable, necessary, and balanced in its impact on the right. For decision‑making questions, the analytical framework is: identify the right engaged under Article 21 → ascertain whether the administrative action is backed by law → apply the triple‑test of legality, necessity, and proportionality → check for compliance with natural justice (notice, hearing, reasons). The examinable nuance is that the Court does not substitute its policy judgment for that of the executive; it only reviews the decision‑making process for arbitrariness.

Administrative Discretion in the Management of Public Sector Bank Recapitalisation and the Role of the Department of Financial Services

The Department of Financial Services (DFS), Ministry of Finance, exercises administrative discretion in the design and execution of capital infusion programmes for public sector banks (PSBs) under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Acts, 1970/1980 and the subsequent recapitalisation schemes. The discretion operates at three levels: (i) determination of the quantum of capital support for each bank based on the “capital adequacy ratio” (CAR) gap, non‑performing asset (NPA) coverage, and the bank’s business plan — the DFS uses a weighted scoring model approved by the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC); (ii) choice of instrument — equity infusion, recapitalisation bonds, or contingent convertible bonds — each carrying distinct governance conditions such as board restructuring, dividend restrictions, and lending targets for priority sectors; and (iii) monitoring compliance through the “Enhanced Access and Service Excellence” (EASE) reform index, which tracks metrics across governance, risk management, and digital adoption.

The Supreme Court has upheld the government’s discretion to attach performance‑linked conditions to recapitalisation bonds, ruling that such conditions are policy measures within the executive’s fiscal authority and do not violate Article 14 unless they are manifestly arbitrary. Recent packages introduced a “capital buffer” requirement: PSBs receiving infusion must maintain a minimum CET1 ratio and a leverage ratio within a specified timeline. The DFS’s decision to release tranches is contingent on quarterly certification by the bank’s audit committee and an independent external auditor. For exam scenarios, the decision chain is: bank submits capital plan → DFS evaluates against scoring model → FSDC endorsement → Cabinet approval → issuance of recapitalisation bonds → tranche release linked to EASE milestones → parliamentary reporting. The common trap is to treat the DFS’s scoring model as a statutory rule; it is an internal administrative guideline, subject to judicial review only for mala fide or irrationality.

  • Assuming the SRLM can unilaterally change the interest subvention ceiling without Ministry concurrence.
  • Treating an e‑commerce platform’s marketplace arm as a shield for its inventory‑based private label operations.
  • Confusing CERC’s REC price‑setting (administrative) with SERC’s RPO target‑setting (legislative).
  • Believing Article 21 judicial review permits courts to substitute policy choices on environmental clearances.
  • Thinking the DFS’s capital‑scoring model is a binding regulation rather than an internal guideline.
  • Overlooking the mandatory statutory show‑cause and order timelines for CCPA proceedings.
  • Ignoring the requirement of a hearing before CERC cancels already‑issued RECs.
The advanced sections above equip aspirants with the statutory depth, judicial nuance, and decision‑tree mapping needed to tackle high‑difficulty decision‑making questions in competitive examinations.

Administrative Discretion in the Governance of Public Sector Undertakings: Board Autonomy, MoU Targets, and the Role of the Department of Public Enterprises

The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE), under the Ministry of Heavy Industries, exercises administrative discretion over the governance framework of Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs). The discretion operates through three interlocking instruments: (i) the categorisation of CPSEs into Maharatna, Navratna, Miniratna‑I and Miniratna‑II based on net worth, turnover and profit‑before‑tax thresholds revised periodically; (ii) the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) system, introduced in 1987 and refined subsequently, which sets annual performance targets — financial (revenue, profit, return on net worth), non‑financial (project milestones, R&D spend, CAPEX utilisation) and enterprise‑specific (market share, export earnings); and (iii) the delegation of financial powers to boards, where higher‑category CPSEs enjoy progressively larger investment approval limits without prior government clearance, subject to prescribed ceilings.

The MoU evaluation is conducted by an independent External Evaluation Agency (EEA) appointed by DPE; the composite score determines the performance rating (Excellent, Very Good, Good, Fair, Poor) and feeds into the Performance Related Pay (PRP) for executives. Judicial review of DPE decisions is limited to Wednesbury unreasonableness and procedural fairness. In a leading Supreme Court ruling, the Court upheld the government’s power to impose a dividend payout ratio on a Maharatna, holding that the condition was a policy directive within the executive’s fiscal authority and not a violation of Article 14. The Court, however, struck down a directive that mandated a specific vendor without a transparent tender, emphasising that discretion must be exercised through a fair, documented process.

For decision‑making questions, the analytical chain is: identify the CPSE category → ascertain the delegated financial limit → verify whether the board decision falls within the MoU‑approved annual plan → check compliance with the General Financial Rules (GFR) and the DPE’s Guidelines on Corporate Governance for CPSEs → evaluate whether any government directive was issued through a reasoned order after consultation with the board. The common examiner twist is to present a board resolution that exceeds the delegated limit but is later ratified by the administrative ministry; the correct answer is that ratification does not cure an ultra‑vires act unless the competent authority (such as the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs) had prior statutory power to approve such expenditure.

Decision‑Making in Defence Procurement: The Defence Acquisition Procedure, Offset Obligations, and the Role of the Defence Acquisition Council

The Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020, issued by the Ministry of Defence (MoD), replaced the Defence Procurement Procedure (DPP) 2016 and governs all capital acquisitions for the Armed Forces. The apex decision‑making body is the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), chaired by the Defence Minister and comprising the Chief of Defence Staff, the three Service Chiefs, the Defence Secretary, and the Secretary (Defence Production). The DAC accords Acceptance of Necessity (AoN) — the first gateway — after which the procurement moves to the Request for Proposal (RFP) stage. The DAP classifies procurement into “Buy (Indian‑IDDM)”, “Buy (Indian)”, “Buy & Make (Indian)”, “Buy & Make”, and “Buy (Global)”, each with progressively higher indigenous content thresholds.

A critical discretionary element is the offset policy: for contracts above a specified value threshold, the vendor must discharge offset obligations through eligible investments, technology transfer, or export of Indian‑made defence products. The offset fulfilment is monitored by the Defence Offset Management Wing (DOMW) and verified by an independent auditor. The DAC may grant a waiver or reduction of offset only on grounds of national security, strategic necessity, or non‑availability of eligible Indian partners, and such waiver must be recorded in a reasoned order.

Judicial scrutiny of defence procurement is narrow. The Supreme Court has held that the DAC’s AoN is a policy decision protected by the doctrine of non‑justiciability, but the subsequent RFP and contract award are subject to Article 14 review for arbitrariness. The Court mandated that any deviation from the DAP’s prescribed evaluation criteria must be justified in writing and placed before the DAC for post‑facto approval. For exam scenarios, the decision tree is: AoN by DAC → RFP issuance → technical and commercial evaluation → Contract Negotiation Committee (CNC) recommendation → DAC approval of contract → offset clause incorporation → contract signing → DOMW monitoring. The trap is to conflate the AoN (policy) with the contract award (executive action) and to assume that offset compliance is a purely commercial matter beyond judicial reach.

Technique: Decision‑Node Mapping
A CPSE classified as Navratna proposes a joint venture with a foreign firm requiring an equity infusion above its delegated limit. The board approves the proposal and forwards it to the administrative ministry for ratification. The ministry issues a sanction order without referring the matter to the competent authority. In a decision‑making question, which of the following statements is correct?
The correct answer: The board’s approval exceeds the Navratna delegated limit; therefore the proposal required prior approval from the competent authority (such as the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs). Ratification by the administrative ministry cannot cure the ultra‑vires act because the DPE guidelines mandate that any investment above the delegated ceiling be cleared by the competent authority before commitment. The decision‑node map is: (1) Identify CPSE category → Navratna; (2) Check delegated limit; (3) Compare proposed infusion → exceeds limit; (4) Determine required approval → competent authority (CCEA); (5) Conclude that post‑facto ministry sanction is invalid.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a scenario mixes CPSE governance and defence procurement, first isolate the statutory framework (DPE guidelines vs DAP). Then locate the exact decision node — AoN, board limit, offset waiver — and apply the corresponding review standard (Wednesbury for policy, proportionality for contract award). Write the decision chain in bullet form; examiners award marks for structured reasoning more than for a single‑word answer.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban): Beneficiary Selection, Fund Release, and Grievance Redressal

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – Urban (PMAY‑U), launched in June 2015, aims to provide “Housing for All”. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) exercises discretion through the “Housing for All” (HFA) guidelines, which prescribe a four‑step beneficiary identification process: (i) use of the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 data as the primary eligibility filter; (ii) validation by Urban Local Bodies (ULBs) through door‑to‑door surveys; (iii) preparation of a “Beneficiary List” approved by the State Level Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee (SLSMC); and (iv) uploading of the final list on the PMAY‑U MIS portal for Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) of central assistance as per scheme norms for EWS/LIG and MIG categories.

Fund release follows a “first‑come‑first‑served” principle within each vertical (In‑situ Slum Redevelopment, Affordable Housing in Partnership, Beneficiary‑Led Construction, Credit‑Linked Subsidy Scheme). The central share is released in three instalments — on sanction, on grounding (foundation), and on completion — contingent on the ULB submitting utilisation certificates (UCs) and geo‑tagged photographs. The MoHUA may withhold or recall funds if the UC is not furnished within the prescribed period, a discretion upheld by courts as a reasonable condition to prevent fund diversion.

Grievance redressal operates at three tiers: (a) the ULB‑level “Housing Grievance Cell” mandated under the HFA guidelines; (b) the State‑level “PMAY‑U Grievance Redressal Committee” chaired by the Principal Secretary (Urban Development); and (c) the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) portal, where citizens can escalate unresolved complaints. The MoHUA issues a quarterly “Grievance Disposal Report” that feeds into the performance rating of states under the “Housing for All” index. For decision‑making questions, the key analytical steps are: verify whether the beneficiary was identified through SECC‑validated survey → confirm that the SLSMC sanction preceded fund release → check compliance with the instalment-linked UC requirement → assess whether the grievance was addressed within the prescribed timelines. The examiner often tests the distinction between the central assistance (a statutory entitlement once eligibility is proved) and the state‑level top‑up subsidy (a discretionary policy).

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of Medical Education: The National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and the Transition from the Medical Council of India

The National Medical Commission (NMC) Act, 2019, which came into force in September 2020, repealed the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, and dissolved the Medical Council of India (MCI). The NMC comprises four autonomous boards — Under‑Graduate Medical Education Board (UGMEB), Post‑Graduate Medical Education Board (PGMEB), Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), and Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB) — each headed by a president appointed by the Central Government on the recommendation of a Search‑cum‑Selection Committee. The Commission’s discretionary powers include: (i) framing the “Minimum Standards for Medical Colleges” (MSMC) and the “Graduate Medical Education Regulations” (GMER); (ii) granting, renewing, or withdrawing recognition of medical qualifications; (iii) conducting the National Eligibility‑cum‑Entrance Test (NEET‑UG and NEET‑PG) as the sole entrance examination; and (iv) regulating fees for 50 % of seats in private medical colleges and deemed universities through the “Fee Fixation Committee” constituted under the Act.

The transition involved a “Board of Governors” (BoG) appointed in 2018 to supersede the MCI, which exercised interim discretion to approve new colleges and increase seat intake. The Supreme Court upheld the BoG’s decisions, ruling that the interim body acted within the legislative vacuum and its actions were protected by the doctrine of legislative competence. The NMC’s decision‑making is subject to judicial review under Article 14 for arbitrariness; a High Court has quashed a fee‑fixation order that ignored the prescribed “cost‑plus” methodology, emphasising that discretion must be guided by transparent criteria.

For exam purposes, the decision chain is: (1) Identify the relevant board (UGMEB for new college, MARB for assessment, EMRB for ethics); (2) Verify compliance with the MSMC/GMER — infrastructure, faculty‑student ratio, bed strength; (3) Check whether the NEET‑based merit list was followed for admissions; (4) Confirm that fee fixation followed the prescribed formula and was published on the NMC portal; (5) Assess whether any adverse order (de‑recognition, penalty) was preceded by a show‑cause notice and personal hearing as mandated by the Act. The common trap is to treat the NMC’s “advisory” guidelines as binding regulations; only the regulations notified in the Official Gazette have the force of law.

Administrative Discretion in the Management of the National Pension System: Investment Choices, Fund Managers, and Subscriber Grievance Mechanism

The National Pension System (NPS), launched in 2004 for new government recruits and extended to all citizens in 2009, is regulated by the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) under the PFRDA Act, 2013. The system’s architecture gives subscribers two investment choices: (i) “Active Choice”, where the subscriber allocates contributions across three asset classes — Equity (E), Corporate Bonds (C), and Government Securities (G) — within prescribed caps that taper with age; and (ii) “Auto Choice”, a life‑cycle fund that automatically rebalances the asset mix based on the subscriber’s age. Multiple Pension Fund Managers (PFMs) are appointed through a competitive bidding process and are required to maintain daily Net Asset Value (NAV) disclosure.

PFRDA exercises discretion in (a) approving the investment guidelines for each PFM, including sectoral exposure limits; (b) setting the “Performance Benchmark” for each asset class against which PFM returns are measured; and (c) enforcing the “Subscriber Grievance Redressal Mechanism” mandated by the PFRDA (Redressal of Subscriber Grievances) Regulations, which requires each PFM to resolve complaints within 30 days and the NPS Trust to adjudicate appeals within 60 days. The NPS Trust, a statutory body under the PFRDA Act, also monitors the “Investment Management Fee” capped at statutorily prescribed rates for government and private sectors.

Judicial review of PFRDA decisions follows the proportionality test. The Supreme Court has upheld the regulator’s decision to cap equity exposure for younger subscribers, finding the restriction proportionate to the objective of protecting retirement savings from market volatility. For decision‑making questions, the analytical framework is: identify the subscriber’s choice (Active vs Auto) → verify that the PFM’s asset allocation respects the regulatory caps → confirm that the NAV is published daily and the investment management fee is within the statutory ceiling → check whether any grievance was addressed within the prescribed timelines. The examiner often tests the distinction between the PFRDA’s regulatory power (binding) and the NPS Trust’s operational guidelines (administrative).

  • Treating the Defence Acquisition Council’s Acceptance of Necessity as a justiciable contract award rather than a policy gateway.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the National Skill Development Mission

The National Skill Development Mission (NSDM), launched in 2015 under the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), provides the overarching framework for coordinating skill‑training initiatives across central ministries, state governments, and private partners. The Mission’s decision‑making architecture rests on three pillars: the National Skill Development Agency (NSDA) as the nodal policy‑coordination body, the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC) as the public‑private partnership vehicle, and the Sector Skill Councils (SSCs) that define occupational standards and assessment criteria. Administrative discretion is exercised at each level when (a) approving training providers for empanelment under the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY), (b) allocating funds from the Skill Development Fund to states based on a “performance‑linked” formula weighting placement rates, industry partnership depth, and geographic coverage, and (c) granting exemptions from the mandatory 70 % placement target for sectors identified as “strategic” by the NSDA.

Empanelment and Quality Assurance

The NSDC’s Empanelment Committee evaluates training providers against the National Skill Qualification Framework (NSQF) alignment, infrastructure norms, trainer‑to‑trainee ratios, and past placement records. Discretion arises when a provider meets most but not all criteria; the Committee may grant conditional empanelment with a six‑month compliance window. The 2022 amendment to the PMKVY guidelines introduced a “fast‑track” route for providers accredited by the National Accreditation Board for Education and Training (NABET), reducing the Committee’s discretionary margin but preserving a residual power to reject applications on grounds of “public interest” — a term left undefined in the notification.

Fund Allocation and Performance Monitoring

States submit Annual Action Plans (AAPs) appraised by the NSDA’s Project Approval Board. The Board applies a weighted index: 40 % for placement outcomes, 30 % for industry‑linked curriculum adoption, 20 % for coverage of aspirational districts, and 10 % for innovation in delivery (e.g., blended learning). Discretion is evident in the “innovation” weight, where the Board may award bonus points for pilots using augmented‑reality simulators, a criterion not codified in the original PMKVY framework. Audit observations have flagged instances of fund releases without verified placement data, underscoring the risk of unchecked discretion.

Judicial and Institutional Checks

Judicial precedent holds that the NSDC’s conditional empanelment orders are subject to judicial review under Article 14 for arbitrariness, and that the “public interest” clause must be interpreted narrowly, requiring a reasoned order. A Central Vigilance Commission advisory mandated that all discretionary decisions above ₹5 crore be recorded in a searchable digital ledger, a measure aimed at reducing opaque allocations.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Funds under the Fifteenth Finance Commission

The Fifteenth Finance Commission (FFC), constituted under Article 280, submitted its final report for the 2021‑26 award period in October 2020. Its decision‑making framework determines the vertical share of the divisible pool of taxes (41 % to states) and the horizontal distribution among states using a composite index: 45 % weight to population (2011 Census), 15 % to area, 15 % to forest and ecology, 12.5 % to income distance, 10 % to demographic performance, and 2.5 % to tax effort. Administrative discretion enters at three stages: (i) the Centre’s acceptance or modification of the Commission’s recommendations before presidential assent; (ii) the Ministry of Finance’s issuance of “conditional grants” for health, education, and rural infrastructure that attach performance benchmarks; and (iii) the states’ own prioritisation of devolved funds within the broad purpose‑specific envelopes.

Conditional Grants and Performance Benchmarks

The FFC recommended substantial health‑sector grants tied to the achievement of National Health Mission indicators (e.g., institutional delivery rate, immunisation coverage). The Ministry of Finance, exercising discretion, added a “fiscal responsibility” condition requiring states to maintain a debt‑GSDP ratio below 25 % to access the full grant. Instances of grant withholding for non‑compliance have been challenged in courts. The Supreme Court has upheld such withholding, ruling that the condition is a legitimate exercise of the Centre’s fiscal oversight under Article 293, provided the benchmark was published before the award period.

Horizontal Distribution Disputes

States such as Tamil Nadu and Kerala have contested the 15 % weight to forest cover, arguing it penalises high‑performing states with low forest area. The Commission’s rationale — compensating for ecological services — is a policy choice, not a justiciable formula. However, judicial clarification holds that while the Commission’s methodology is not subject to judicial review, the Centre’s implementation must not introduce arbitrary deviations from the recommended shares.

State‑Level Prioritisation

Once devolved, states enjoy discretion in allocating funds across sectors. The FFC’s “untied” component (approximately 30 % of the state share) permits re‑allocation, but the Centre’s “monitoring dashboard” tracks expenditure against the original AAP. Audit reports have flagged diversions of untied grants to revenue expenditure, triggering Centre‑issued advisories to realign spending.

Situational Judgment: Conditional Grant Withholding
A state fails to meet the immunisation coverage target set by the Fifteenth Finance Commission’s health grant. The Centre withholds 40 % of the grant citing the shortfall. The state argues that the target was unrealistic given a recent natural disaster. As an administrative officer advising the Centre, which principle should guide the decision?
The guiding principle is proportionality combined with legitimate expectation. The Centre may enforce conditions only if (1) the benchmark was publicly notified before the award period, (2) the shortfall is not attributable to force‑majeure events recognised under the Disaster Management Act, and (3) the withholding is proportionate to the degree of non‑compliance. Since the disaster qualifies as a force‑majeure event, the Centre should either grant a waiver or reduce the withholding to a level reflecting the actual controllable shortfall, documenting the reasoning in a speaking order.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents a conditional grant dispute, first identify the source of the condition (Commission recommendation vs. Centre’s own add‑on). Then apply the three‑step proportionality test: legality of condition, causality of breach, and proportionality of sanction. Remember that the Commission’s methodology is policy, not law; only the Centre’s implementation is justiciable.

Administrative Discretion in the Enforcement of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019: Central Consumer Protection Authority and District Commissions

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 replaced the 1986 legislation and introduced a three‑tier adjudicatory structure: the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) at the apex, State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions, and District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions. The CCPA, headed by a Chief Commissioner, wields investigative, advisory, and punitive powers. Its discretionary domain includes (a) initiating suo‑motu investigations into unfair trade practices, (b) ordering product recalls, (c) imposing penalties up to ₹10 crore for misleading advertisements, and (d) issuing “cease‑and‑desist” directions to e‑commerce platforms for non‑compliance with the Consumer Protection (E‑Commerce) Rules, 2020.

Investigation and Recall Powers

Section 18 empowers the CCPA to direct the Director‑General of Investigation to conduct inquiries. The Authority may order a recall if a product is found to be “defective” or “hazardous” under Section 2(1)(f). In a notable case, the CCPA ordered the recall of a pressure‑cooker brand after laboratory tests revealed pressure‑release valve failure rates exceeding the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) tolerance. The manufacturer challenged the order, arguing that the CCPA lacked technical expertise. The High Court upheld the recall, noting that the CCPA’s reliance on BIS‑accredited lab reports satisfied the requirement of “reasonable satisfaction” under Section 18(2).

Penalty Determination

Penalties under Section 21 are calibrated by the “gravity of the contravention”, “gain made”, and “loss caused to consumers”. The CCPA’s guidelines introduced a matrix: minor misleading claims attract lower penalties; repeat offences or health‑risk claims attract higher penalties. Discretion is evident in the “gain made” assessment, where the CCPA may estimate revenue attributable to the advertisement using market‑share data. The Supreme Court has held that the matrix is advisory; the Authority must record reasons for departing from it, ensuring the penalty is not arbitrary.

E‑Commerce Liability

The 2020 Rules impose a “duty of due diligence” on marketplace entities to verify seller credentials and product authenticity. The CCPA may issue directions under Section 18(1)(b) for non‑compliance. In a recent case, the CCPA directed a major platform to delist a seller offering counterfeit cosmetics. The platform contended that the Rules only required “reasonable efforts”. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) ruled that “reasonable efforts” is an objective standard; the platform’s failure to deploy automated brand‑verification tools constituted a breach, affirming the CCPA’s direction.
