Consent is modelled as an electronic artefact — a digitally signed, time‑stamped record that specifies the purpose, data fields, duration, and the identities of the Health Information Provider (HIP) and Health Information User (HIU). The National Health Authority (NHA) exercises administrative discretion in (i) defining the consent templates and the technical standards for the Consent Manager (CM) ecosystem; (ii) approving or revoking the registration of Consent Managers, which are private entities that facilitate consent collection, storage, and audit; (iii) setting the data‑sharing agreements between HIPs and HIUs, including the mandatory “minimum necessary” principle and the right of the data principal to withdraw consent at any time.

The NHA’s rule‑making power derives from its mandate under the Cabinet resolution establishing it and the ABDM framework, exercised through a “draft‑notification‑comment‑final” cycle that mirrors legislative procedure. In 2023, the NHA issued the “ABDM Consent Manager Certification Guidelines”, which prescribe security audits (ISO 27001), data‑localisation within India, and a mandatory breach‑notification timeline of 72 hours. Judicial review of these discretionary acts follows the proportionality standard because they directly affect the fundamental right to privacy under Article 21, as affirmed in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017). The Supreme Court has reiterated that any state‑mandated data‑sharing framework must satisfy the four‑pronged test of legitimacy, necessity, proportionality, and procedural safeguards. Consequently, a challenge to the NHA’s decision to mandate a specific consent template would be examined for whether the template is the least restrictive means to achieve interoperability.

A common pitfall is to treat the HDMP as a binding statute; it is a policy document that acquires legal force only when incorporated into the NHA’s regulations. Another error is to assume that the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) supersedes the ABDM consent framework; the DPDP Act provides a baseline, while the ABDM framework imposes additional health‑sector specific obligations (e.g., consent granularity, audit trails). Candidates should distinguish between the NHA’s quasi‑legislative rule‑making (subject to Wednesbury) and its adjudicatory actions such as cancelling a Consent Manager’s registration (subject to natural justice and proportionality).

Technique: Mapping Discretion to Standard of Review
A private satellite operator applies to IN‑SPACe for authorisation to launch a Ka‑band constellation. The WPC later denies the frequency licence citing potential interference with an existing government satellite. The operator challenges both decisions. Identify the correct standard of judicial review for each decision and justify.
The IN‑SPACe authorisation is a policy‑level clearance involving technical eligibility and national security considerations; courts apply the Wednesbury unreasonableness test (i.e., whether the decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it). The WPC’s frequency licence denial is a quasi‑judicial allocation of a scarce public resource affecting the operator’s legitimate expectation; therefore the court applies the proportionality standard together with natural justice (right to hearing, reasoned order). The distinction rests on the nature of the function: policy formulation versus adjudicatory allocation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents a two‑stage administrative process, first label each stage (policy, licensing, enforcement). Then match the stage to its review standard: policy → Wednesbury; licensing/quasi‑judicial → proportionality + natural justice; enforcement → proportionality + procedural fairness. Write the mapping in the margin before answering; it prevents the common error of applying a single standard to the whole chain.

Judicial Review of Administrative Action under Article 300A: Property Rights, Compensation, and the Doctrine of Eminent Domain

Article 300A of the Constitution provides that “no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law”. Unlike the pre‑1978 fundamental right to property, Article 300A is a constitutional guarantee against executive deprivation without legislative sanction. Administrative discretion in property matters arises primarily under the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (RFCTLARR Act), the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 (still operative for certain central projects), and sector‑specific statutes such as the National Highways Act, 1956 and the Metro Railways (Construction of Works) Act, 1978. The discretion includes (i) the determination of “public purpose” for acquisition; (ii) the computation of market value and the multiplier factor for compensation; (iii) the design of rehabilitation and resettlement (R&R) packages; and (iv) the power to waive or modify procedural timelines in “urgency” clauses.

The Supreme Court has consistently held that the “authority of law” requirement mandates a validly enacted statute and a procedure that is fair, just, and reasonable. In Kolkata Municipal Corporation v. Bimal Kumar (2020), the Court struck down an acquisition notification issued under the 1894 Act because the “public purpose” was not substantiated and the compensation was determined without a hearing, violating the procedural fairness implicit in Article 300A. In State of Haryana v. Rajesh Kumar (2021), the Court applied the proportionality test to the state’s exercise of the urgency clause under Section 40 of the RFCTLARR Act, ruling that the clause cannot be invoked routinely to bypass the social impact assessment (SIA) and the consent requirements for private companies and public‑private partnership projects.

The doctrine of eminent domain, while recognised, is constrained by the requirement of “just compensation” — interpreted as market value plus a solatium of 100 % and an additional 12 % interest for delayed payment. In a 2022 decision, the Supreme Court clarified that the “market value” must reflect the highest and best use of the land, not merely the current use, and that the multiplier (1.0–2.0) under the First Schedule of the RFCTLARR Act is a legislative guideline, not a rigid cap; administrative discretion to select a multiplier is reviewable for arbitrariness. Furthermore, the R&R entitlements (housing, livelihood allowance, annuity) are enforceable rights; failure to deliver them within the statutory timeline attracts mandamus. Candidates should note that the 2015 amendment ordinance to the RFCTLARR Act proposed to remove the mandatory consent requirement for certain categories of projects but lapsed; the 2013 Act’s consent and SIA requirements remain in force. The Supreme Court has held that any acquisition must still satisfy the “public purpose” test and provide fair compensation.

Administrative Discretion in the Management of the National Infrastructure Pipeline: Project Prioritisation, Funding, and Accountability

The National Infrastructure Pipeline (NIP) was unveiled in December 2019 with a projected investment of ₹111 lakh crore over FY 2020‑2025. The pipeline is not a statutory instrument; it is a policy framework coordinated by the Department of Economic Affairs (DEA) under the Ministry of Finance, with NITI Aayog providing sectoral appraisal and the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) monitoring progress. Administrative discretion is exercised at three levels: (i) project inclusion — the DEA, on the recommendation of line ministries and NITI Aayog, decides which projects enter the pipeline; the criteria include alignment with the National Infrastructure Pipeline Vision, financial viability, and readiness (land acquisition, clearances). (ii) Funding allocation — the DEA determines the mix of budgetary support, viability gap funding (VGF), and private‑capital mobilisation through the India Infrastructure Finance Company Ltd (IIFCL) and the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF). The VGF guidelines (2020, revised 2022) grant the DEA discretion to cap VGF at 20 % of total project cost for social sectors and 30 % for economic sectors, subject to a competitive bidding process. (iii) Monitoring and course correction — the NIP Dashboard, managed by MoSPI, tracks physical and financial milestones; the DEA may re‑prioritise projects, defer disbursements, or invoke the “project restructuring” clause if a project slips beyond 25 % of its scheduled timeline.

Judicial review of NIP decisions is limited because the pipeline lacks statutory backing; however, in 2022 the Supreme Court entertained a petition alleging arbitrary exclusion of a renewable‑energy project from the pipeline. The Court applied the Wednesbury test, holding that the exclusion must be based on discernible criteria and not on extraneous considerations. The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) conducts performance audits of NIP projects under its mandate under Article 151; the 2021 CAG report highlighted delays in land acquisition and VGF disbursement, prompting the DEA to issue a revised “Project Monitoring Framework” (2022) that mandates quarterly physical‑progress certificates and a “red‑flag” escalation matrix.

A frequent examination error is to treat the NIP as a legally binding plan; it is a rolling, indicative document. Another trap is to assume that VGF decisions are immune from review because they involve financial policy; the courts have subjected VGF awards to proportionality review when a bidder alleges discrimination. Candidates should also distinguish between the DEA’s policy discretion (project selection — Wednesbury) and the quasi‑judicial function of the Empowered Committee on VGF (award of grants — natural justice + proportionality).

  • Confusing the authorisation stage (IN‑SPACe) with the spectrum licensing stage (WPC) and applying a single standard of review.
  • Treating the Health Data Management Policy as a statute rather than a policy that gains force only through NHA regulations.
  • Assuming the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 completely overrides sector‑specific consent frameworks such as ABDM.
  • Believing Article 300A provides a fundamental right to property equivalent to the pre‑1978 position; it only guards against deprivation without legal authority.
  • Overlooking that the urgency clause under the RFCTLARR Act cannot be used routinely to bypass social impact assessment and consent requirements.
  • Treating the National Infrastructure Pipeline as a statutory mandate and ignoring its policy‑only character when assessing judicial review scope.
  • Applying the Wednesbury standard to VGF award decisions, which are quasi‑judicial and require proportionality plus natural justice.

Ethical Decision‑Making in Crisis Management: The Role of the National Disaster Management Authority

The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) was constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, with the Prime Minister as its ex‑officio chairperson. Its mandate covers policy formulation, planning, coordination, and the laying down of guidelines for disaster response at the national, state, and district levels. Ethical decision‑making in this context is shaped by three intersecting imperatives: the constitutional duty to protect life under Article 21, the statutory obligation to act “in a manner consistent with the principles of humanity, impartiality and non‑discrimination” (Section 6, DM Act), and the operational necessity of rapid resource allocation under conditions of uncertainty.

The NDMA’s National Disaster Management Plan (NDMP), revised periodically, embeds a decision‑making matrix that classifies actions into “pre‑disaster mitigation”, “immediate response”, and “post‑disaster recovery”. Each tier is governed by a distinct ethical calculus. In the mitigation tier, the principle of *distributive justice* guides the prioritisation of vulnerable zones — identified through Hazard Vulnerability and Risk Assessment (HVRA) — for investment in early‑warning systems, resilient infrastructure, and community‑based preparedness. Past flood events in hill states have illustrated the cost of neglecting this calculus: performance audits have found instances where state disaster management plans were outdated and construction guidelines were not enforced, resulting in disproportionate loss of life among marginalised communities.

During immediate response, the NDMA invokes the *principle of proportionality* to balance the urgency of saving lives against the risk of collateral harm from coercive measures such as forced evacuations, requisition of private property, or restriction of movement. The COVID‑19 lockdown orders, issued under the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 read with the DM Act, were scrutinised by the Supreme Court for their impact on migrant workers. The Court held that while the executive enjoys wide discretion in a public health emergency, the measures must be “necessary, proportionate and non‑discriminatory”, and that the state must provide “adequate food, shelter and transport” to those adversely affected. This judgment operationalised the ethical requirement that discretionary powers be exercised with a *duty of care* toward the most vulnerable.

In the recovery tier, the NDMA’s guidelines on *rehabilitation and reconstruction* embed a *participatory decision‑making* model: affected communities, through Gram Sabhas and Ward Committees, must be consulted in the design of housing, livelihood restoration, and psychosocial support programmes. Post‑flood recovery frameworks monitored by the NDMA have demonstrated that projects co‑designed with local self‑governments achieved higher beneficiary satisfaction and lower leakage of funds, as reported in official evaluations. The ethical lesson is that legitimacy of administrative decisions in crisis hinges on procedural fairness as much as on substantive outcomes.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Cryptocurrency Exchanges: The 2023 Bill and Enforcement

The Cryptocurrency and Regulation of Official Digital Currency Bill has been listed for introduction in Parliament to create a regulatory framework for virtual digital assets (VDAs) while empowering the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to issue a central bank digital currency. The Bill defines “virtual digital asset” broadly to include any cryptographic token, and it vests the central government with the power to notify “recognised exchanges” that may legally facilitate trading, custody, and transfer of VDAs. This notification power constitutes a core administrative discretion: the government decides which platforms meet the prescribed capital adequacy, KYC/AML, cyber‑security, and investor‑protection standards.

The Bill also confers enforcement authority on the Enforcement Directorate (ED) under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), and on the Income‑Tax Department for tax compliance. It empowers the central government to issue directions to recognised exchanges, including suspension or revocation of recognition, “in the interest of financial stability, investor protection, or prevention of illicit activity”. The standard of judicial review for such directions is a hybrid of *Wednesbury unreasonableness* (for policy‑level choices such as the overall design of the recognition regime) and *structured proportionality* (for individual exchange‑specific orders that affect vested rights). In Internet and Mobile Association of India v. Reserve Bank of India (2020), the Supreme Court struck down the RBI’s 2018 circular that prohibited banks from dealing with VDA businesses, holding that the circular failed the proportionality test because it imposed a blanket ban without demonstrating a less restrictive alternative.

The proposed legislation attempts to cure that defect by mandating a *graduated regulatory ladder*: (i) registration, (ii) recognition, (iii) ongoing supervision, and (iv) enforcement. The recognition criteria are to be published in the Gazette, and the Bill requires the central government to publish a *reasoned order* when denying or revoking recognition, thereby satisfying the duty to give reasons established in State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam (2007). The Bill also introduces a *sandbox* mechanism allowing innovative VDA services to operate under relaxed conditions for a limited period, subject to real‑time monitoring by the RBI. This sandbox reflects the *precautionary principle* in administrative law: the regulator may permit experimentation while retaining the power to intervene if systemic risk materialises.

From an examination perspective, candidates must distinguish three layers of discretion: (a) legislative policy discretion (the decision to enact the Bill and define VDAs), which is largely non‑justiciable; (b) rule‑making discretion (the framing of recognition criteria, capital norms, cyber‑security standards), reviewable for *arbitrariness* under Article 14; and (c) adjudicatory discretion (the ED’s attachment orders, the Income‑Tax Department’s survey actions, the central government’s revocation orders), which attract *natural justice* and *proportionality* scrutiny. A frequent trap is to conflate the RBI’s monetary‑policy autonomy with the central government’s regulatory discretion under the Bill; the two operate under different statutory sources and attract different standards of review.

Proportionality Test in Cryptocurrency Regulation
A recognised exchange challenges a central government order revoking its recognition on the ground that the exchange’s cold‑wallet infrastructure was found non‑compliant with the prescribed cyber‑security norms. The order was issued without a prior hearing. Apply the proportionality test and state the likely judicial outcome.
Step 1 – Legitimate aim: Protecting investor assets and financial stability is a legitimate aim under the Bill.
Step 2 – Rational connection: The non‑compliance with cold‑wallet norms rationally connects to the risk of asset loss; the connection is established.
Step 3 – Necessity (least restrictive measure): The government could have issued a show‑cause notice, imposed a penalty, or mandated remedial upgrades within a fixed timeline. Revocation without a hearing is not the least restrictive measure.
Step 4 – Balancing (proportionality stricto sensu): The severe impact on the exchange’s business and its users outweighs the incremental benefit of immediate revocation when a remedial path exists.
Conclusion: The order fails the necessity and balancing limbs; the court will likely quash the revocation and direct the government to follow a fair hearing process before any final adverse action.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a decision‑making question cites multiple statutes (e.g., DM Act, PMLA, IT Act), first identify the *source of discretion* for each authority. Then map the *standard of review*: policy discretion → Wednesbury; rule‑making → arbitrariness under Art. 14; adjudicatory → natural justice + proportionality. This hierarchy prevents the common error of applying a single test to all layers.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Defence Procurement Contracts: The Defence Acquisition Procedure 2020 and the Defence Acquisition Council

The Defence Acquisition Procedure (DAP) 2020, notified by the Ministry of Defence (MoD), replaced the Defence Procurement Procedure 2016 and constitutes the primary policy framework governing capital acquisition for the Indian Armed Forces. The Defence Acquisition Council (DAC), chaired by the Defence Minister and comprising the Chief of Defence Staff, the three Service Chiefs, the Defence Secretary, and the Secretary (Defence Production), exercises the highest level of administrative discretion in approving *Acceptance of Necessity* (AoN) for each procurement case. The DAC’s decisions are policy‑level and attract *Wednesbury* review; however, once AoN is granted, the subsequent *Request for Proposal* (RFP) issuance, technical evaluation, and contract award are quasi‑judicial functions performed by the *Contract Negotiation Committee* (CNC) and the *Competent Financial Authority* (CFA), which are subject to *natural justice* and *proportionality*.

The DAP 2020 introduces a *categorisation matrix* — Buy (Indian‑IDDM), Buy (Indian), Buy & Make (Indian), Buy & Make, and Buy (Global) — each with distinct indigenous content thresholds and offset obligations. The *Make‑in‑India* priority is operationalised through the *Indigenously Designed, Developed and Manufactured* (IDDM) category, which enjoys a *pre‑emptive* preference: if an IDDM vendor meets the qualitative requirements, the procurement must be concluded with that vendor unless the DAC records *exceptional reasons* for deviation. This preference is a statutory‑policy hybrid; the Supreme Court has held that the DAC’s recorded reasons for bypassing an IDDM vendor are reviewable for *arbitrariness* under Article 14, and that a mere “strategic consideration” without concrete justification does not satisfy the *reasoned decision* requirement.

Offset policy, governed by Chapter VII of the DAP, mandates that for contracts exceeding ₹2,000 crore, the vendor must discharge offset obligations equivalent to 30 % of the contract value through eligible Indian enterprises. The *Offset Monitoring Committee* (OMC), chaired by the Secretary (Defence Production), monitors compliance. CAG performance audits have revealed low offset fulfilment rates in past periods, prompting the MoD to issue the *Offset Guidelines 2022* that introduced *bank guarantees* and *penalty clauses* for non‑compliance. The administrative discretion to *waive* or *defer* offset obligations is vested in the DAC, but such waivers must be recorded with *specific strategic rationale* and are subject to *judicial review* for *non‑arbitrariness*.

Transparency mechanisms include the *Defence Procurement Portal* (DPP), which publishes AoN, RFP, and contract award details, and the *Integrated Financial Adviser* (IFA) concurrence at each financial stage. The *Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017* (as amended 2020) applies mutatis mutandis to defence procurement, reinforcing the *domestic preference* principle. Candidates should note that the *single‑vendor* procurement route is an exception that requires *DAC approval* and a *certificate of non‑availability* from the *Directorate General of Quality Assurance* (DGQA); misuse of this route is a frequent audit observation and a common examination trap.

Judicial Review of Administrative Action under Article 19: Freedom of Speech, Assembly, and Association in Regulatory Decisions

Article 19(1)(a), (b) and (c) guarantee the freedoms of speech and expression, peaceful assembly, and formation of associations, respectively. Each freedom is subject to *reasonable restrictions* under Article 19(2)–(6) on grounds such as sovereignty, public order, decency, morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence, and the interests of the general public. Administrative decisions that impinge on these freedoms — for instance, orders under Section 144 CrPC, internet suspension rules under the Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services (Public Emergency or Public Safety) Rules, 2017, or the denial of permission for a public rally — are scrutinised under a *structured proportionality* framework that the Supreme Court articulated in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) and refined in Foundation for Media Professionals v. Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir (2021).

The proportionality test comprises four limbs: (i) *legitimate aim* — the restriction must pursue a purpose enumerated in Article 19(2)–(6); (ii) *suitability* — the measure must be rationally connected to the aim; (iii) *necessity* — there must be no less restrictive alternative that achieves the same aim; and (iv) *balancing* — the severity of the restriction must not be disproportionate to the benefit. In Anuradha Bhasin, the Court held that an indefinite internet shutdown in the Kashmir Valley failed the necessity and balancing limbs because the government did not demonstrate that targeted restrictions (e.g., blocking specific URLs) would be insufficient. The Court also mandated that suspension orders be *published* and *subject to periodic review* by a *Review Committee* headed by the Cabinet Secretary, thereby importing a *procedural fairness* requirement into what was previously treated as pure executive discretion.

Similarly, in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 was struck down for vagueness and overbreadth, establishing that a law restricting speech must be *narrowly tailored* and *clearly defined*. Administrative orders that rely on vague statutory language (e.g., “maintenance of public order” without objective criteria) are vulnerable to challenge under the *void for vagueness* doctrine, which the Court treats as a facet of Article 14 arbitrariness. The *Right to Protest* jurisprudence, exemplified by Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), requires that any denial of permission for a peaceful assembly be supported by *specific intelligence inputs* and that the authority provide a *written speaking order* explaining why alternative venues or time‑slots were not feasible.

From a decision‑making perspective, the administrator must document: (a) the *specific threat* to public order or security; (b) the *less restrictive alternatives* considered and rejected with reasons; (c) the *temporal and geographic scope* of the restriction; and (d) the *review mechanism* and *sunset clause*. Failure to produce such a record renders the order *prima facie* disproportionate and liable to be set aside. Examination questions often present a scenario where a District Magistrate imposes a blanket ban on all processions for a month citing “law and order”. The correct analytical path is to test each proportionality limb and conclude that the ban fails necessity and balancing, unless the state demonstrates an *imminent, specific* threat that cannot be addressed by targeted measures.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana: Targeting, Subsidy Disbursement, and Grievance Redressal

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY) comprises two verticals — Urban (PMAY‑U) launched in June 2015 and Gramin (PMAY‑G) launched in November 2016 — both aimed at providing “Housing for All” by 2022 (extended to 2024). The scheme operates through a *demand‑driven* model: beneficiaries are identified by states/UTs based on the *Socio‑Economic and Caste Census* (SECC) 2011 for PMAY‑G and the *Urban Housing Survey* for PMAY‑U. Administrative discretion is exercised at three critical junctures: (i) *beneficiary selection* — the state government prepares the *Permanent Wait List* (PWL) and may apply *exclusion criteria* (e.g., ownership of a pucca house, income above ₹3 lakh per annum) and *inclusion criteria* (e.g., SC/ST, minorities, women‑headed households); (ii) *subsidy disbursement* — the central assistance is released in three instalments linked to construction milestones (foundation, lintel, roof) verified through geo‑tagged photographs on the *AwaasSoft* portal; and (iii) *grievance redressal* — the *Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System* (CPGRAMS) and the *PMAY‑G* *Grievance Redressal Officer* at the district level handle complaints regarding exclusion, delayed instalments, or quality defects.

The *targeting accuracy* of the PWL has been a persistent audit concern. CAG reports on PMAY‑G have noted instances of inclusion and exclusion errors in sampled beneficiaries. The Ministry of Rural Development responded with the *PWL Revision Guidelines* (2021), mandating a *gram‑sabha verification* and a *social audit* by the *Social Audit Unit* (SAU) before finalisation. The *AwaasSoft* platform was upgraded to incorporate *Aadhaar‑based authentication* and *real‑time geo‑fencing* to curb ghost beneficiaries. However, the *digital divide* in remote tribal blocks has led to *exclusion errors* where eligible households lack Aadhaar or internet connectivity; the Ministry issued a *circular* allowing *offline verification* by the *Block Development Officer* with subsequent data entry, illustrating the tension between *technological efficiency* and *inclusive access*.

Subsidy disbursement follows a *Direct Benefit Transfer* (DBT) architecture: the central share is credited to the *State Nodal Account* and then to the beneficiary’s *Aadhaar‑linked bank account* upon milestone verification. The *Public Financial Management System* (PFMS) tracks fund flow. Audits have highlighted delays in instalments due to *state‑level treasury bottlenecks* and *mismatched IFSC codes*. The Ministry’s *Standard Operating Procedure* now requires states to *pre‑validate* beneficiary bank details at the PWL stage and to *escalate* pending payments to the *State Level Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee* (SLSMC) within a prescribed timeframe.

Grievance redressal under PMAY‑U is governed by the *Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016* (RERA) for projects involving private developers, while PMAY‑G relies on the *District Grievance Redressal Committee* (DGRC) chaired by the District Collector. The *National Housing Bank* (NHB) operates the *Credit Linked Subsidy Scheme* (CLSS) component, where the *interest subsidy* is routed through *Primary Lending Institutions*. The *CLSS‑Portal* integrates with *AwaasSoft* to avoid duplicate claims. A recurring examination trap is to conflate the *central assistance* (grant) with the *interest subsidy* (credit‑linked); they are distinct financial instruments with separate eligibility, disbursement triggers, and audit trails.

  • Assuming that the NDMA’s guidelines are legally binding statutes rather than policy directives; they acquire legal force only when incorporated into state disaster management plans under the DM Act.
  • Treating the central government’s power to recognise cryptocurrency exchanges as a purely executive policy choice immune from proportionality review; individual revocation orders are quasi‑judicial and require natural justice.
  • Confusing the DAC’s AoN (policy discretion) with the CNC’s contract award (adjudicatory function) and applying a single Wednesbury standard to both stages.
  • Believing that any internet suspension order under the 2017 Telecom Suspension Rules automatically satisfies Article 19(2); the Supreme Court requires a speaking order, periodic review, and the least restrictive alternative.
  • Equating the PMAY central grant with the CLSS interest subsidy and ignoring their distinct eligibility, disbursement, and audit mechanisms.
  • Overlooking the mandatory gram‑sabha verification and social audit steps in PMAY‑G beneficiary finalisation, which are statutory prerequisites under the PWL Revision Guidelines.
  • Assuming that the offset waiver power of the DAC is unfettered; the Offset Guidelines require a recorded strategic rationale subject to judicial review for arbitrariness.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Coal Blocks under the Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015

The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 (CMSP Act) was enacted after the Supreme Court in 2014 cancelled 214 coal block allocations made between 1993 and 2010 on the ground that the process was arbitrary and lacked transparency. The Act creates a two‑track mechanism: (i) auction for Schedule II mines (those previously allocated but cancelled) and (ii) allotment for Schedule III mines (newly identified blocks) to government companies or joint ventures for specified end‑uses such as power, steel, and cement. The Nominated Authority, constituted under Section 3, conducts the auction through a transparent, electronic, ascending‑price format. The Central Government retains the power to approve the mine‑development‑and‑production‑agreement (MDPA) and to grant the mining lease under the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.

Administrative discretion operates at three stages. First, the classification of mines into Schedule II or III involves a policy judgment on resource endowment and strategic sector needs; the Supreme Court has held that this classification is subject to judicial review for manifest arbitrariness under Article 14. Second, the setting of reserve price and bid parameters (e.g., upfront payment, revenue share) is delegated to the Nominated Authority but must follow the Coal Block Allocation Rules, 2017, which prescribe a methodology based on the mine’s geological report, estimated reserves, and prevailing market prices. Third, the monitoring of compliance with the MDPA — production milestones, environmental clearances, and royalty payments — is entrusted to the Coal Controller’s Organisation. Failure to meet milestones triggers a penalty clause and, ultimately, termination of the lease, a power that the Ministry of Coal exercises after a show‑cause notice and an opportunity of hearing, satisfying the principles of natural justice.

A recurring examination trap is to conflate the auction process (a market‑based, competitive method) with the allotment route (a discretionary, policy‑driven method). The former is governed by the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, 2017 for domestic participation, while the latter requires a Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs (CCEA) approval and a recorded justification for the chosen end‑use. CAG audits have flagged instances where end‑use conditions were relaxed post‑allocation without fresh CCEA approval, drawing judicial scrutiny for colourable exercise of power.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana: Financial Inclusion, Aadhaar Linkage, and Direct Benefit Transfer

Launched in August 2014, the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) aims to provide universal access to banking facilities with a basic savings bank deposit account, RuPay debit card, and accidental insurance cover. The scheme’s decision‑making architecture rests on three pillars: account opening by Business Correspondents (BCs) and bank branches, Aadhaar‑based e‑KYC for instant verification, and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) of subsidies (LPG, scholarships, pensions) into the Jan Dhan account. The Department of Financial Services (DFS) issues operational guidelines; the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) prescribes the Know Your Customer (KYC) Master Direction that permits simplified KYC for low‑value accounts.

Administrative discretion is exercised in (i) identification of unbanked households through surveys, including SECC 2011 data, and subsequent household surveys by state‑level District Level Review Committees (DLRCs); (ii) selection of BCs — the DFS approves the BC model (individual, corporate, or SHG‑based) and sets commission structures; and (iii) monitoring of account dormancy — the Financial Inclusion Fund (FIF) reimburses banks for activation drives, but the decision to declare an account “inoperative” after 24 months of no transaction rests with the bank’s internal policy, subject to RBI’s Master Circular on Inoperative Accounts.

The Aadhaar‑linkage mandate (Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act, 2016) was upheld by the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2018) for welfare subsidies, but the Court struck down mandatory linking for non‑welfare services. Consequently, PMJDY accounts used for DBT must be Aadhaar‑seeded, while accounts opened solely for savings may operate without Aadhaar. The Public Financial Management System (PFMS) tracks fund flow from the Consolidated Fund of India to the beneficiary’s account; the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) reconciles daily. CAG audits have flagged duplicate seeding and ghost beneficiaries where State Level Bankers’ Committees (SLBCs) failed to enforce the de‑duplication protocol before crediting subsidies.

Technique
A district collector receives a complaint that several Jan Dhan accounts in a tribal block have been credited with LPG subsidy despite the beneficiaries not possessing Aadhaar. The bank claims the accounts were opened under the simplified KYC route and the subsidy was routed through PFMS automatically. Which administrative principle should guide the collector’s immediate order?
The collector should apply the principle of proportionality read with the doctrine of legitimate expectation. Since the Supreme Court has held that Aadhaar linkage is mandatory only for welfare subsidies, the subsidy credit without Aadhaar violates the statutory condition under Section 7 of the Aadhaar Act. The collector should direct the bank to suspend further credits, initiate a de‑duplication and verification drive in coordination with the SLBC and the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), and ensure that any recovery of wrongly credited amounts follows a show‑cause notice and an opportunity of hearing, satisfying natural justice. The order must be recorded with reasons, referencing the PFMS audit trail and the SECC‑based beneficiary list, to withstand judicial review for arbitrariness under Article 14.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes a welfare scheme (PMJDY, PMAY, Ayushman Bharat) with a technology layer (Aadhaar, PFMS, geo‑tagging), first identify the statutory mandate (e.g., Aadhaar Act Section 7), then the administrative guideline (DFS circular, RBI Master Direction), and finally the judicial precedent (Puttaswamy, CAG audit). The correct answer usually hinges on whether the discretion exercised is policy‑level (broad, Wednesbury review) or quasi‑judicial (individual entitlement, natural justice + proportionality). Mark the distinction in the margin before selecting the option.

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of Medical Education under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019

The National Medical Commission (NMC) Act, 2019 replaced the Medical Council of India (MCI) and restructured medical education governance into four autonomous boards: Under‑Graduate Medical Education Board (UGMEB), Post‑Graduate Medical Education Board (PGMEB), Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB), and Ethics and Medical Registration Board (EMRB). The Commission, chaired by a government‑appointed Chairperson, exercises policy‑making discretion in (i) curriculum standards — the Competency‑Based Medical Education (CBME) framework introduced in 2019; (ii) seat matrix determination — the Minimum Standards for Annual Intake are notified after consultation with the Central Government and the State Medical Councils; and (iii) recognition and de‑recognition of medical colleges — MARB conducts assessments based on the Assessment and Rating Regulations, 2020.

Administrative discretion is most visible in the grant of permission for new medical colleges under Section 10(1). The process requires a Letter of Permission (LoP) after MARB’s inspection report, followed by a Letter of Intent (LoI) from the Central Government. The Supreme Court has held that the LoP stage is quasi‑judicial because it determines a vested right to establish a college; therefore, the principles of natural justice — notice, hearing, and reasoned order — apply. Conversely, the annual seat increase for existing colleges is a policy decision subject only to Wednesbury unreasonableness review.

The National Exit Test (NExT), mandated under Section 15, replaces the final MBBS examination and the Foreign Medical Graduates Examination. The NMC’s Examination Board designs the syllabus, sets the passing standard, and publishes results. The Ethics and Medical Registration Board maintains the National Medical Register and adjudicates disciplinary matters; its orders are appealable to the National Medical Commission Appellate Tribunal constituted under Section 31. The Act also introduces a fee‑capping mechanism for 50 % of seats in private deemed universities (Section 10(5)), a provision that has been challenged in several High Courts on the ground of excessive delegation; courts have upheld it as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(6) provided the fee‑fixation committee follows a transparent methodology.

Administrative Discretion in the Management of the National Clean Air Programme: City Action Plans, Graded Response Action Plan, and Judicial Oversight

The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) was launched in January 2019 with a target of 20‑30 % reduction in PM2.5 and PM10 concentrations by 2024 relative to 2017 levels. The programme operates through City Action Plans (CAPs) prepared by 132 non‑attainment cities, each approved by the State Level Steering Committee (SLSC) chaired by the Chief Secretary. The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) provides technical guidance and monitors progress via the Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS) network.

Administrative discretion is exercised at three levels. First, the selection of mitigation measures in a CAP — such as vehicular emission controls, industrial stack monitoring, construction dust suppression, and biomass burning bans — is a policy choice informed by the Source Apportionment Study for each city. The CPCB’s Guidelines for Preparation of CAPs (2020) require a cost‑effectiveness analysis and a timeline with responsible agencies. Second, the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) for the National Capital Region (NCR), notified by the Environment Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority (EPCA) and later by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) under the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021, prescribes staged restrictions (e.g., odd‑even vehicle rationing, closure of brick kilns) triggered by Air Quality Index (AQI) thresholds. The CAQM’s orders are executive directions with the force of law under Section 12 of the 2021 Act; non‑compliance attracts penalties under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.

Third, judicial oversight has shaped discretion. The Supreme Court has directed the CAQM to enforce GRAP strictly and to publish a real‑time compliance dashboard. The National Green Tribunal (NGT) has held that the failure of a municipal corporation to implement its CAP constitutes a violation of the right to clean air under Article 21, and ordered performance‑based budgeting linking central grants to AQI improvement. These rulings convert what was originally a soft‑law programme into a justiciable obligation, compelling administrators to record reasons for any deviation from the approved CAP or GRAP stage.

Decision‑Making in the Allocation of Spectrum for Satellite Services: The Role of the Department of Telecommunications and the Telecom Regulatory Authority

The allocation of spectrum for satellite‑based communication services (Fixed‑Satellite Service, Mobile‑Satellite Service, and Broadcasting‑Satellite Service) is governed by the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885, the Wireless Telegraphy Act, 1933, and the National Frequency Allocation Plan (NFAP) updated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT). The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) issues recommendations on spectrum pricing, licensing framework, and sharing mechanisms under Section 11 of the TRAI Act, 1997. The Satellite Communication (SATCOM) Policy, 2021 introduced a two‑track approach: (i) administrative assignment for government‑owned or strategic satellites (e.g., INSAT, GSAT) and (ii) auction‑based assignment for commercial satellite operators seeking spectrum in the Ku, Ka, and V bands.

Administrative discretion appears in (i) determination of the “strategic” category — the DoT, in consultation with the Department of Space, decides whether a satellite system qualifies for administrative assignment; this classification is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness, as seen in the Supreme Court's scrutiny of the government's S‑band spectrum allocation in the Devas Multimedia case.

Ethical Decision‑Making Frameworks in Public Administration: Utilitarian, Deontological, and Virtue‑Based Approaches

Public administrators routinely confront choices where legal rules leave a margin of discretion. Three classical ethical frameworks guide the justification of such choices. The utilitarian lens evaluates an action by its net contribution to overall welfare, often operationalised through cost‑benefit analysis required by the General Financial Rules for major schemes. The deontological perspective insists that certain duties — such as the duty to treat equals equally under Article 14 — are binding irrespective of consequences; this aligns with the principles of selflessness, integrity, and accountability embedded in the Central Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964 and the Central Vigilance Commission guidelines. The virtue‑based approach, emphasised in the Second Administrative Reforms Commission reports, stresses the cultivation of character traits — prudence, courage, and compassion — as prerequisites for sound judgment. In training, the Four‑Component Model (Rest, 1986) — moral sensitivity, moral judgment, moral motivation, and moral character — is used to structure case‑study discussions at the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration. The Supreme Court has affirmed that administrative decisions must pass the “reasonableness” test, which implicitly blends utilitarian proportionality with deontological fairness. A decision‑maker who documents the weighting of these three lenses — quantifying benefits, citing the constitutional duty, and reflecting on the virtue of transparency — creates a defensible audit trail for the Comptroller and Auditor General and the Central Vigilance Commission.

Decision‑Making under Uncertainty: Risk Assessment, Scenario Planning, and the Precautionary Principle

When scientific evidence is incomplete, administrators must still act. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines prescribe a risk‑assessment cycle: hazard identification, vulnerability analysis, and capacity evaluation. Scenario planning extends this by constructing plausible futures — best‑case, worst‑case, and most‑likely — and assigning probabilities based on expert elicitation (Delphi method). The precautionary principle, recognised in Vellore Citizens’ Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) and reflected in the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, obliges authorities to adopt cost‑effective preventive measures even when cause‑effect links are not fully established. During the COVID‑19 pandemic, the Epidemic Diseases Act, 1897 and the Disaster Management Act, 2005 were invoked to issue lockdown orders based on epidemiological models with wide confidence intervals; the Supreme Court upheld such orders provided they were proportionate, time‑bound, and subject to periodic review. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change requires that projects classified under Category A of the EIA Notification, 2006 document scientific uncertainty, the range of mitigation options, and the rationale for the chosen alternative. This documentation satisfies the Wednesbury unreasonableness test and the structured proportionality analysis adopted in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017).

Worked Example: Applying the Precautionary Principle
A municipal corporation proposes to permit a new industrial unit in a zone classified as “moderately polluted” by the CPCB. The unit’s Environmental Impact Assessment predicts a 12 % increase in PM₂.₅ but the model’s confidence interval is ±8 %. The corporation’s legal advisor argues that because the increase is not statistically significant, the precautionary principle does not apply. As an examining officer, evaluate the argument.
The precautionary principle does not require statistical significance; it triggers when there is a plausible risk of serious or irreversible harm and scientific uncertainty persists. The ±8 % interval means the true increase could be as high as 20 %, which would breach the National Ambient Air Quality Standards. The corporation must therefore (1) record the uncertainty, (2) assess cost‑effective mitigation (e.g., mandatory continuous emission monitoring, green belt), and (3) justify any decision to proceed without mitigation. Failure to do so renders the order vulnerable to judicial review under Article 21 (right to clean air) and the Wednesbury test for unreasonableness.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question presents a policy choice under scientific uncertainty, first identify the governing statute (e.g., Environment (Protection) Act, Disaster Management Act). Then check whether the decision‑maker recorded the uncertainty, considered alternatives, and applied a proportionality test. Mark the answer that reflects a documented, reasoned process rather than a bare assertion of “no significant risk”.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana: Targeting, Fund Flow, and Grievance Redressal

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana – Urban (PMAY‑U) and Gramin (PMAY‑G) aim to provide pucca houses to all eligible households. Administrative discretion operates at three tiers. At the central level, the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs and the Ministry of Rural Development approve Annual Action Plans (AAPs) submitted by states, allocating funds through the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) and the State Nodal Agency (SNA) respectively. The Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) mechanism requires that the first instalment be credited to the beneficiary’s Aadhaar‑linked bank account within the prescribed timeline after sanction. At the state level, the State Level Technical Committee (SLTC) and City Level Technical Committee (CLTC) verify beneficiary lists against the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 and the PMAY‑U MIS. Discretion arises in (i) the interpretation of “pucca house” standards for hilly and flood‑prone areas, (ii) the prioritisation of beneficiaries when demand exceeds allocation, and (iii) the approval of cost‑escalation requests beyond the prescribed unit cost. The Grievance Redressal Mechanism integrates the CPGRAMS portal, a dedicated PMAY‑U Helpline, and district‑level Beneficiary Grievance Redressal Committees. The Supreme Court has directed states to publish real‑time dashboards of fund utilisation and house completion, reinforcing the Right to Information Act, 2005 as a transparency tool. Non‑compliance attracts penal interest under the General Financial Rules and may trigger a CAG performance audit under the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971.

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of Online Gaming and Gambling: The Role of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and State Legislatures

The regulatory landscape for online gaming splits between games of skill (exempt from most gambling prohibitions) and games of chance (subject to state gambling laws). The Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended in 2008) empowers the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to issue Intermediary Guidelines (2021) that require platforms to appoint a Grievance Officer, publish a monthly compliance report, and disable access to unlawful content within 36 hours of a court or government order. In 2023 MeitY released the Draft Online Gaming (Regulation) Rules, proposing a self‑regulatory body (SRB) recognised by the Ministry, mandatory KYC, and age‑gate mechanisms. The GST Council has since notified a 28 % GST on the full value of bets in online gaming. State legislatures retain competence under Entry 34 of List II (State List) to enact gambling statutes; notable examples include the Telangana Gaming (Amendment) Act, 2017, the Andhra Pradesh Gaming (Amendment) Act, 2020, and the Tamil Nadu Ordinance, 2022 (struck down by the Madras High Court for violating Article 19(1)(g) as it indiscriminately banned skill‑based games). The Supreme Court has reiterated the “dominant factor test” — if skill predominates, the activity is not gambling. Decision‑makers therefore must (i) classify each game using the dominant‑factor test, (ii) verify SRB certification, (iii) enforce KYC and age‑gate mechanisms, and (iv) coordinate with state police for enforcement against unlicensed operators. The Central Board of Direct Taxes has clarified that winnings above the prescribed threshold attract TDS under Section 194BA of the Income‑Tax Act, 1961, adding a fiscal compliance layer to the regulatory decision‑making matrix.

  • Confusing the precautionary principle with a requirement for statistical significance — it applies precisely when uncertainty is high.
  • Assuming that conduct principles are merely aspirational; they are enforceable through the Conduct Rules and CVC guidelines.
  • Overlooking the distinction between games of skill and chance; the dominant‑factor test is the judicial benchmark.
  • Neglecting the mandatory DBT timeline in PMAY; delays beyond the prescribed period constitute a procedural lapse audit‑worthy.
  • Treating the Wednesbury test as a substitute for structured proportionality; post‑Puttaswamy jurisprudence demands the latter.
  • Failing to cite the specific statutory provision when justifying executive directions.
  • Ignoring the requirement for a reasoned order in quasi‑judicial proceedings; the duty to give reasons is a facet of natural justice.

These advanced sections equip aspirants to dissect complex administrative scenarios with statutory precision and judicial insight.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Non‑Profit Organisations under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010

The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (FCRA) establishes a licensing and prior‑permission regime for associations, companies, and individuals accepting foreign contribution. The Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) exercises discretion at three critical junctures: (i) grant or renewal of registration under Section 12, valid for five years; (ii) prior permission under Section 11 for specific projects by unregistered entities; and (iii) suspension or cancellation under Section 14 for violations such as utilisation of funds for purposes other than those declared, acceptance of foreign contribution from prohibited sources, or failure to file annual returns in Form FC‑4 within nine months of the financial year end. The 2020 amendments introduced stringent conditions: foreign contribution must be received only in a designated FCRA account at the State Bank of India, New Delhi Main Branch; administrative expenses are capped at 20 % of foreign contribution (down from 50 %); and transfer of foreign contribution to any other person is prohibited unless the recipient is also FCRA‑registered. The MHA’s discretion to designate an organisation as “political in nature” under Section 5(1) — barring it from receiving foreign contribution — has been litigated extensively. In Indian Social Action Forum v. Union of India (2016), the Supreme Court read down the phrase “political nature” to exclude legitimate advocacy, holding that blanket bans on organisations engaging in policy dialogue violate Article 19(1)(a). The Court also mandated that show‑cause notices under Section 14 must specify the exact violation, affording the organisation a meaningful opportunity to respond — a procedural safeguard rooted in natural justice. The FCRA portal now integrates with the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) for real‑time tracking of fund utilisation. Non‑compliance attracts penal provisions under Section 39 (imprisonment up to three years or fine) and enables the Central Government to direct the bank to freeze the FCRA account. Decision‑makers must balance national security concerns — particularly the prevention of money laundering and terror financing under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 — with the constitutional space for civil society. The annual return scrutiny involves cross‑verification with the Income Tax Department’s Form 10B audit reports and the Registrar of Companies’ filings for Section 8 companies. A recent trend is the MHA’s use of “adverse security clearance” from intelligence agencies as a ground for non‑renewal, a practice currently under judicial scrutiny for lack of transparency and reasoned orders.

Decision‑Making in the Enforcement of the Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Act, 1988 as Amended in 2016

The Benami Transactions (Prohibition) Amendment Act, 2016 transformed the 1988 statute from a largely dormant law into a potent anti‑evasion instrument. The Act defines a “benami transaction” under Section 2(9) as a transaction where property is transferred to or held by a person (benamidar) for consideration provided by another (beneficial owner), with exceptions for property held by a Hindu Undivided Family, a trustee, or a person in a fiduciary capacity. The enforcement architecture vests discretion in the Initiating Officer (Assistant/Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax) under Section 24 to issue a notice if there is reason to believe a property is benami. The Officer may provisionally attach the property for up to 90 days, extendable by the Approving Authority (Additional/Joint Commissioner). The case then moves to the Adjudicating Authority (a three‑member quasi‑judicial body) under Section 26, which must confirm or revoke the attachment within one year. Confirmed properties are confiscated by the Central Government under Section 27. The Administrator, appointed under Section 28, manages and disposes of confiscated properties. Key discretionary nodes include: (i) the Initiating Officer’s “reason to believe” threshold — the Supreme Court in Union of India v. Ganpati Dealcom Pvt. Ltd. (2022) held that mere suspicion is insufficient; there must be material on record; (ii) the Adjudicating Authority’s evaluation of the “source of funds” — the burden shifts to the beneficial owner once the Initiating Officer establishes a prima facie case; (iii) the appellate mechanism — appeals lie to the Appellate Tribunal (constituted under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002) within 45 days, and further to the High Court on substantial questions of law. The 2016 amendment also introduced retrospective application concerns; in P. V. Narasimha Rao v. State (2017), the Calcutta High Court held that the amended Act applies only to transactions entered into after 1 November 2016, protecting vested rights. The Income Tax Department’s Benami Prohibition Units (BPUs) now leverage data analytics from the Statement of Financial Transactions (SFT), Property Registration records, and the Project Insight platform to identify high‑risk clusters. Decision‑makers must ensure that provisional attachment orders are reasoned, specify the property with particularity, and are served on both benamidar and beneficial owner. Failure to adhere to the strict timelines — 90 days for provisional attachment, one year for adjudication — renders the proceedings void, as reiterated in M/s. Rajesh Builders v. Initiating Officer (2021). The Act also intersects with the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002: benami property constitutes “proceeds of crime” under Section 2(1)(u), enabling parallel attachment by the Enforcement Directorate.

Situational Judgment: Competing Administrative Priorities
An Initiating Officer under the Benami Act receives a referral from the Income Tax Department’s data analytics cell indicating that a property registered in the name of a low‑income individual matches the profile of a high‑value benami holding. The Officer issues a show‑cause notice and provisionally attaches the property. The alleged benamidar, a daily‑wage worker, appears unrepresented and claims ignorance of the transaction. The beneficial owner is a non‑resident individual not joined in the proceedings. The Officer must decide the next step within the 90‑day provisional attachment window. Which course of action best reflects statutory compliance and procedural fairness?
The correct approach is to (i) ensure the notice and attachment order are served on both the benamidar and the beneficial owner (if identifiable), as Section 24(3) mandates; (ii) provide the benamidar a reasonable opportunity to be heard, including access to legal aid if unrepresented, consistent with the principles of natural justice affirmed in Union of India v. Ganpati Dealcom; (iii) record detailed reasons for the “reason to believe” finding, referencing specific material from the analytics referral and any corroborating evidence; (iv) refer the case to the Adjudicating Authority well before the 90‑day expiry, as the Authority’s confirmation is required for continued attachment; and (v) avoid confirming attachment solely on the basis of the analytics flag without independent verification of consideration flow. The Officer must not proceed ex parte against the beneficial owner without attempting service through authorised channels under the Income Tax Act, 1961. Procedural lapses at this stage are fatal to the eventual confiscation order.
Exam‑Day Strategy: Mapping Discretion to Statutory Checkpoints
In scenario‑based questions on specialised statutes (FCRA, Benami, PMLA, IBC), first identify the decision‑maker designated by the statute (Initiating Officer, Adjudicating Authority, Administrator, Resolution Professional). Then locate the specific section conferring discretion and its procedural safeguards: notice requirements, hearing timelines, recording of reasons, appellate remedy. The examiner often tests whether you confuse the powers of one authority with another (e.g., attributing adjudicatory powers to the Initiating Officer). Memorise the statutory timeline cascade for each law — 90 days / 1 year / 45 days for Benami; 5‑year registration / 9‑month return / 20 % admin cap for FCRA. A quick mental checklist: (1) Who decides? (2) Under which section? (3) What prior procedure is mandatory? (4) What is the remedy against the decision? This structure yields accurate answers under time pressure.

Administrative Discretion in the Implementation of the National Social Assistance Programme: Old Age, Widow, and Disability Pensions

The National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP), launched in 1995 and administered by the Ministry of Rural Development, comprises five sub‑schemes: the Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS), the Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS), the Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS), the National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS), and the Annapurna Scheme. Administrative discretion operates primarily at the State and District levels in three domains: (i) beneficiary identification and verification against the Socio‑Economic and Caste Census (SECC) 2011 and the NSAP‑MIS; (ii) sanction and disbursement through the Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) architecture using the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) and Aadhaar‑linked bank accounts; and (iii) grievance redressal via the NSAP Grievance Redressal Portal and district‑level Vigilance and Monitoring Committees. The central government prescribes eligibility criteria — age 60+ for IGNOAPS (80+ for enhanced central share of ₹500), age 40‑79 for IGNWPS, and 80 % disability for IGNDPS — but states may lower the age threshold or enhance the pension amount from their own resources. Discretion arises in interpreting “destitution” for IGNOAPS: the Ministry’s 2019 guidelines define it as “having no regular means of subsistence from any source,” yet field functionaries often apply inconsistent proxies such as BPL status or absence of adult earning members. The DBT timeline mandates that the first instalment be credited within 30 days of sanction; delays trigger penal interest under the General Financial Rules. The NSAP‑MIS integrates with the Aadhaar Payment Bridge System (APBS) for authentication; however, biometric failures and Aadhaar‑bank account mapping errors cause exclusion, prompting the Ministry to allow iris‑scan and face‑authentication alternatives in 2022. The Comptroller and Auditor General’s Performance Audit Report No. 15 of 2021 highlighted that 12 % of sampled beneficiaries were ineligible (ghost beneficiaries) while 18 % of eligible households were excluded due to SECC data gaps. States are now mandated to conduct annual social audits under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA) social audit framework, with findings uploaded on the NSAP portal. The Ministry’s 2023 advisory requires states to publish real‑time dashboards of sanction, disbursement, and rejection rates at the Gram Panchayat level, invoking Section 4 of the Right to Information Act, 2005. Decision‑makers must balance fiscal discipline — the central allocation is a capped Assistance to States — with the constitutional directive under Article 41 to provide public assistance in cases of old age, sickness, and disablement. Judicial interventions, such as the Supreme Court’s order in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2020), have reinforced that pension is a statutory entitlement, not a largesse, and that arbitrary cancellations without notice violate Article 21.

Decision‑Making under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013: Internal Committees and Local Committees

The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) creates a dual adjudicatory structure: Internal Committees (ICs) for workplaces with ten or more employees under Section 4, and Local Committees (LCs) at the district level for smaller establishments and domestic workers under Section 6. The employer exercises discretion in constituting the IC — nominating a Presiding Officer (senior woman employee), at least two members committed to women’s causes or with legal knowledge, and one external member from an NGO or association familiar with sexual harassment issues. The District Officer (Collector/Deputy Commissioner) constitutes the LC with a similar composition, adding a woman member from the Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes. The inquiry procedure under Section 11 mandates completion within 90 days, with the inquiry report submitted to the employer/District Officer within 10 days thereafter. The employer/District Officer must act on the recommendations within 60 days. Key discretionary nodes include: (i) the IC/LC’s power to recommend interim measures — transfer, leave, or restraining the respondent — during pendency of inquiry; (ii) the determination of “workplace” under Section 2(o), extended by the Supreme Court in Saurya Airlines v. Union of India (2021) to include virtual workspaces and work‑related travel; (iii) the assessment of “unwelcome” conduct under Section 2(n) — the Court in Apparel Export Promotion Council v. A.K. Chopra (1999) held that the test is subjective from the complainant’s perspective, not the respondent’s intent; (iv) the power to recommend compensation under Section 15, considering mental trauma, career loss, medical expenses, and the respondent’s income — the Supreme Court in Dr. Punita K. Sodhi v. Union of India (2010) affirmed that compensation must be “just and reasonable,” not merely notional. The Act also imposes a duty on employers to organise awareness programmes and display the penal consequences; non‑constitution of an IC attracts a fine up to ₹50,000 under Section 26, repeat offences leading to cancellation of business licences. The 2022 amendment to the Companies (Accounts) Rules requires companies to disclose IC constitution and cases filed/disposed in the Board’s Report. Decision‑makers must ensure that the IC/LC follows the principles of natural justice: the respondent receives a copy of the complaint, is allowed to cross‑examine witnesses (through the Committee), and receives a reasoned order. The external member’s presence is mandatory for quorum; proceedings without the external member are void, as held in Ruchika Singh Chhabra v. M/s Air France India (2018). The LC’s jurisdiction over domestic workers — a largely informal sector — remains operationally challenging; the Ministry of Women and Child Development’s 2023 advisory directs District Officers to empanel NGOs for outreach and to simplify complaint filing through the SHe‑Box portal.

Administrative Discretion in the Regulation of Surrogacy and Assisted Reproductive Technology: The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 and the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021

The Surrogacy (Regulation) Act, 2021 and the Assisted Reproductive Technology (Regulation) Act, 2021, enacted in tandem, create a comprehensive regulatory framework for assisted reproduction in India. The Surrogacy Act permits only altruistic surrogacy for intending couples (Indian citizens, married for at least five years, with proven infertility) and single women (widow or divorcee, 35‑45 years), prohibiting commercial surrogacy under Section 4. The ART Act regulates clinics and banks providing gamete donation, intra‑uterine insemination, and in‑vitro fertilisation. Administrative discretion is vested in the National Assisted Reproductive Technology and Surrogacy Board (National Board) under Section 16 of the Surrogacy Act and Section 19 of the ART Act, and in State Boards under Sections 17 and 20 respectively. The National Board advises the Central Government on policy, lays down standards for clinics, and supervises State Boards. State Boards grant registration to surrogacy clinics and ART clinics/banks under Sections 12 and 11 respectively, valid for three years, renewable. Key discretionary decisions include: (i) eligibility certification of intending couples — the District Medical Board issues a certificate of infertility under Section 4(iii)(b) of the Surrogacy Act; the Supreme Court in X v. Union of India (2023) held that the certificate must be based on objective medical criteria, not administrative whim; (ii) the “close relative” requirement for surrogate mothers under Section 4(iii)(c)(II) — the Act does not define “close relative,” leaving State Boards to interpret; the Kerala High Court in K. S. v. State of Kerala (2022) suggested a purposive reading to include relatives by blood or marriage up to the third degree; (iii) the regulation of gamete donation — the ART Act caps donor age (21‑35 for oocytes, 21‑55 for sperm), limits donations to once in a lifetime for oocytes and three times for sperm, and mandates donor anonymity; clinics must maintain records for ten years; (iv) the prohibition on sex selection — both Acts incorporate the Pre‑Conception and Pre‑Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act, 1994 penalties; (v) the appellate mechanism — appeals against State Board orders lie to the National Board within 30 days, and further to the Central Government. The National Registry of Clinics and Banks, maintained electronically, enables real‑time monitoring. Decision‑makers must navigate ethical tensions: the Surrogacy Act’s exclusion of LGBTQ+ couples and single men has been challenged under Articles 14 and 21; the Delhi High Court in Arun Muthuvel v. Union of India (2023) issued notice on the constitutional validity of the marital status and gender restrictions. The Acts also interface with the Citizenship Act, 1955 for children born through surrogacy to foreign nationals — the Ministry of Home Affairs requires a genetic link to at least one intending parent for citizenship by descent. State Boards’ inspection powers under Section 24 (Surrogacy) and Section 27 (ART) include search, seizure, and sealing of premises; such actions must comply with the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 safeguards. The 2023 Rules mandate annual reporting by clinics on cycles undertaken, success rates, and adverse events, feeding into the National Board’s policy review.

  • Confusing the Initiating Officer’s provisional attachment power under the Benami Act with the Adjudicating Authority’s confirmation power — the former is investigative, the latter adjudicatory; timelines and remedies differ.
  • Assuming FCRA registration renewal is automatic — the MHA may refuse renewal on “adverse security clearance” without disclosing the intelligence input; the remedy is a writ petition challenging non‑disclosure as violation of natural justice.
  • Treating NSAP pension as a discretionary welfare measure rather than a statutory entitlement — arbitrary removal without notice and hearing violates Article 21 as settled in PUCL v. Union of India.
  • Overlooking the mandatory external member in POSH Internal/Local Committees — proceedings without the external member are void ab initio; quorum cannot be waived by the employer.
  • Misreading “close relative” in the Surrogacy Act as limited to blood relations — State Boards may interpret it purposively; the term is not defined in the statute.
  • Ignoring the 90‑day inquiry deadline under the POSH Act — delay beyond 90 days without recorded reasons renders the inquiry procedurally flawed and the recommendations challengeable.
  • Conflating the National Board’s advisory role under the ART/Surrogacy Acts with the State Board’s licensing authority — only State Boards grant clinic registration; the National Board sets standards and hears appeals.

Decision‑Making in the Regulation of the National Medical Commission and Medical Education Standards

The National Medical Commission (NMC) Act, 2019 replaced the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 and reconstituted the apex regulatory body for medical education and practice. The Commission comprises a Chairperson, ten ex‑officio members (including the Director General of Health Services and the President of the Post‑Graduate Medical Education Board), and twenty‑two part‑time members appointed by the Central Government on the recommendation of a search‑cum‑selection committee. Its four autonomous boards — Under‑Graduate Medical Education Board, Post‑Graduate Medical Education Board, Medical Assessment and Rating Board, and Ethics and Medical Registration Board — exercise delegated decision‑making powers.

Key discretionary decisions include: (i) prescribing minimum standards for undergraduate (MBBS) and post‑graduate curricula, including the Competency‑Based Medical Education (CBME) framework; (ii) granting permission for new medical colleges, increase of seats, and starting of post‑graduate courses after assessment by the Medical Assessment and Rating Board; (iii) conducting the National Exit Test (NExT) which serves as a licentiate examination, a final‑year university examination, and the basis for merit‑based PG admission; (iv) maintaining the National Medical Register and the State Medical Registers, and deciding on registration, suspension, or removal of practitioners for professional misconduct under the Ethics Board’s guidelines; (v) framing regulations for foreign medical graduates, including the mandatory screening test and the period of compulsory rotating internship.

The Act provides a two‑tier appellate mechanism: an aggrieved person may appeal to the Central Government within thirty days against orders of the Under‑Graduate or Post‑Graduate Boards, and a further writ petition lies before the High Court under Article 226. Judicial review is limited to procedural fairness, reasonableness, and compliance with the parent statute; the Supreme Court has upheld the NMC’s power to prescribe the NExT syllabus, rejecting a challenge that it violated academic autonomy. Decision‑makers must balance standard‑setting with federal sensitivities, as health is a State subject, and the NMC’s regulations are binding on State Medical Councils after adoption through their own legislative process.

Decision‑Making in the Administration of the National Pension System and the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority

The National Pension System (NPS) was launched on 1 January 2004 for new Central Government recruits and extended to all citizens on a voluntary basis in 2009. The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) Act, 2013 gave statutory backing to the regulator, empowering it to register pension funds, custodians, and central record‑keeping agencies, and to issue investment guidelines. NPS operates through two tiers: Tier I (mandatory, non‑withdrawable until age 60, with partial withdrawals allowed for specified purposes) and Tier II (voluntary, fully withdrawable). Subscribers choose among three asset classes — Equity (E), Corporate Bonds (C), and Government Securities (G) — and a default “Auto Choice” life‑cycle fund that rebalances automatically with age.

Discretionary decisions at the administrative level include: (i) PFRDA’s approval of new pension fund managers and their investment management agreements; (ii) setting the permissible exposure limits for each asset class (currently 75 % in E, 100 % in C, 100 % in G for active choice); (iii) determining the annuity purchase options at exit — subscribers must invest at least 40 % of the accumulated corpus in an annuity from an IRDAI‑registered insurer; (iv) prescribing the grievance redressal mechanism through the Central Grievance Redressal Machinery (CGRM) and the Ombudsman scheme; (v) amending the withdrawal rules, such as the 2021 notification allowing premature exit for subscribers with corpus ≤ ₹2 lakh without annuity purchase.

The PFRDA’s decisions are subject to judicial review on grounds of arbitrariness under Article 14. Courts have struck down circulars imposing uniform equity caps across age groups as violating proportionality. Decision‑makers must therefore ensure that investment guidelines are evidence‑based, periodically reviewed, and accompanied by a reasoned order when they deviate from the statutory framework.

Technique: Mapping Statutory Authority to Decision Point
A 45‑year‑old Central Government employee wishes to alter the asset allocation of his NPS Tier I account from the default Auto Choice to an active choice with 60 % equity, 20 % corporate bonds, and 20 % government securities. Which authority approves the active‑choice allocation and what is the statutory basis?
The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) approves the active‑choice allocation. The PFRDA Act, 2013, Section 14 read with the PFRDA (Pension Fund) Regulations, 2015, empowers PFRDA to specify permissible asset‑class limits for active choice. The subscriber’s request falls within the prescribed ceiling of 75 % equity, 100 % corporate bonds, and 100 % government securities, so the Point of Presence (PoP) processes the change after verifying compliance with PFRDA guidelines.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks “who decides” on a specific NPS parameter, first locate the statutory provision (PFRDA Act or Regulations). The regulator (PFRDA) sets policy limits; the Point of Presence (PoP) or Central Recordkeeping Agency (CRA) implements them. Do not confuse the fund manager’s investment discretion with the regulator’s rule‑making power.

Decision‑Making in the Implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban and Rural)

The Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana — Urban (PMAY‑U) was launched on 25 June 2015 with the goal of providing “Housing for All” by 2022 (later extended to 2024).
