1. The Eight Parts of Speech and Their Functions

1.1 Nouns: Naming the World Around Us

Every English sentence begins with the need to name something, and the noun fulfills that need by identifying persons, places, animals, things, or abstract ideas. A common noun such as city or river labels a general class, while a proper noun like Delhi or Ganga singles out a unique entity and therefore always carries an initial capital letter. Collective nouns such as team, committee, or flock denote a group regarded as a single unit, yet they create persistent agreement problems because the same word can take a singular verb when the group acts in unison (The committee has submitted its report) and a plural verb when the members act individually (The committee are divided in their opinions). Abstract nouns name qualities, actions, or states that cannot be perceived by the senses — honesty, growth, childhood — and they never take a plural form. Material nouns such as gold, water, or cotton denote substances and are typically uncountable, though they may become countable when referring to distinct varieties (Indian teas versus tea as a substance). Countable nouns admit numbers and the indefinite article (a book, three books), whereas uncountable nouns require quantifiers such as some, much, or a piece of to express quantity. Recognising these sub-classifications is not merely taxonomic; it determines article choice, verb agreement, and the quantifiers that may precede the noun, all of which are tested directly in error-spotting and sentence-improvement items.

1.2 Pronouns: Standing in for Nouns

Pronouns reduce repetition by substituting for nouns already mentioned or easily inferred, but their utility depends on strict agreement in number, gender, and person with their antecedents. Personal pronouns distinguish three persons — first (I, we), second (you), and third (he, she, it, they) — and each person has distinct subject, object, and possessive forms; confusing he with him or his with he is a frequent source of case errors. Reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, himself) must reflect back to a noun or pronoun in the same clause (She prepared herself), and they cannot stand alone as subjects or objects unless used emphatically (The director himself approved the plan). Demonstrative pronouns (this, that, these, those) point to specific items and imply proximity or distance in space, time, or discourse. Relative pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, that) introduce adjective clauses and must match their antecedents in animacy and case: who for people as subjects, whom for people as objects, whose for possession, and which or that for things. Interrogative pronouns (who, whom, whose, which, what) launch questions and follow the same case distinctions. Indefinite pronouns such as everyone, somebody, each, neither are grammatically singular even when they convey plural meaning, so they demand singular verbs and singular possessive pronouns (Each of the students has submitted his or her assignment). Mastery of pronoun case, antecedent clarity, and number agreement eliminates a large proportion of the sentence-correction errors that appear in competitive examinations.

1.3 Verbs: Action, State, and the Engine of the Sentence

The verb is the only part of speech that can constitute a predicate by itself, and every finite clause must contain a finite verb form that marks tense, number, and person. Main verbs express the core action (run, write, build) or state (be, seem, become), while auxiliary verbs — be, do, have — help form continuous, perfect, and passive constructions as well as questions and negatives. Modal auxiliaries (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must, ought to) convey modality such as ability, permission, obligation, or probability, and they never change form for person or number. Transitive verbs require a direct object to complete their meaning (She wrote a letter), whereas intransitive verbs do not (The child sleeps); many verbs function both ways depending on context (He runs a business versus He runs every morning). The distinction between finite and non-finite verb forms is structural: a finite verb (writes, wrote, will write) can serve as the main verb of an independent clause, while infinitives (to write), gerunds (writing), and participles (written, writing) cannot stand alone as predicates and therefore appear in phrases or dependent clauses. Tense, aspect, and voice together locate the action in time, depict its internal structure, and indicate whether the subject performs or receives the action; errors in tense sequencing, inappropriate passive voice, or confusion between been and being in perfect continuous forms are staples of grammar testing.

1.4 Adjectives and Adverbs: Modification and Degree

Adjectives qualify nouns or pronouns by answering the questions which one?, what kind?, or how many?; they appear attributively before the noun (a red balloon) or predicatively after a linking verb (The balloon is red). Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, or entire sentences, answering how?, when?, where?, to what extent?, or why?. The majority of adverbs are formed by adding -ly to an adjective (quick → quickly), but flat adverbs such as fast, hard, early, late retain the same form as their adjective counterparts, and misidentifying them leads to errors like He runs quick instead of He runs quickly. Both adjectives and adverbs exhibit three degrees of comparison: positive (tall, quickly), comparative (taller, more quickly), and superlative (tallest, most quickly). One-syllable modifiers typically take -er and -est; two-syllable modifiers vary (happier but more careful); modifiers of three or more syllables always use more and most. Irregular forms such as good → better → best, bad → worse → worst, little → less → least, and much/many → more → most must be memorised. Double comparatives (more better) and double superlatives (most tallest) are ungrammatical. The placement of only, even, merely, and similar focusing adverbs changes the meaning of a sentence dramatically (Only she loves him versus She only loves him versus She loves only him), making adverb position a favourite testing point.

1.5 Prepositions, Conjunctions, and Interjections: Connecting and Expressing

Prepositions establish relationships of space, time, direction, agency, or manner between a noun or pronoun (the object of the preposition) and other words in the sentence. English prepositions are highly idiomatic; in denotes enclosure or large time spans (in the box, in July), on denotes surface contact or specific days (on the table, on Monday), and at denotes precise location or clock time (at the door, at 5 p.m.). The choice between between (two distinct entities) and among (more than two or a collective mass) is frequently tested, as is the distinction between since (point in time) and for (duration) with perfect tenses. Conjunctions join grammatical units of equal or unequal rank. Coordinating conjunctions — and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet — link words, phrases, or independent clauses of equal status and are remembered by the acronym FANBOYS. Subordinating conjunctions — because, although, if, since, while, unless, until — introduce dependent clauses and signal logical relationships such as cause, contrast, condition, or time. Correlative conjunctions — either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also, both…and — work in pairs and require parallel structure in the elements they connect. Interjections (Wow! Alas! Hurrah! Oh!) express sudden emotion and stand grammatically apart from the sentence, usually followed by an exclamation mark or a comma; they carry no syntactic function but appear in direct-speech narration and dialogue-based comprehension passages.

2. Sentence Architecture: Subjects, Predicates, and the Clause

2.1 The Subject-Predicate Relationship

Every complete sentence divides naturally into a subject — the person, place, thing, or idea that the sentence is about — and a predicate — everything that is said about the subject, always containing at least one finite verb. The simple subject is the head noun or pronoun stripped of modifiers (The bright morning star → star), while the complete subject includes all its modifiers. Similarly, the simple predicate is the verb or verb phrase alone (shines), and the complete predicate encompasses the verb plus objects, complements, and adverbial modifiers. Inverted order places the predicate or part of it before the subject (Into the room rushed the children, Rarely have I seen such courage), a structure common in literary writing and in questions. Compound subjects joined by and normally take a plural verb (Ravi and Priya are coming), but when the parts refer to the same person or thing, or express a single idea, the verb is singular (Bread and butter is his favourite snack). With correlative conjunctions (either…or, neither…nor) the verb agrees with the nearer subject (Neither the manager nor the employees are responsible). Indefinite pronouns such as each, every, either, neither take singular verbs even when followed by a plural noun in a prepositional phrase (Each of the boys has a bicycle). Understanding these agreement rules is essential because subject-verb disagreement is the single most tested error category in objective English papers.

2.2 Phrases: Word Groups Without Subject-Verb Pairing

A phrase is a group of related words that functions as a single part of speech but lacks a subject-finite verb combination; therefore it can never stand alone as a sentence. Noun phrases (the ancient banyan tree) act as subjects, objects, or complements. Verb phrases consist of a main verb plus its auxiliaries (has been waiting) and function as the predicate. Prepositional phrases begin with a preposition and end with its object (in the garden, after the meeting); they function adjectivally (The book on the table) or adverbially (We met after the meeting). Participial phrases use a present participle (walking down the street) or a past participle (exhausted by the journey) and function as adjectives; when they appear at the start of a sentence they must modify the grammatical subject, otherwise a dangling modifier results (Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful — incorrect because trees cannot walk). Gerund phrases (Swimming in the sea) function as nouns. Infinitive phrases (to win the match) can function as nouns, adjectives, or adverbs. Appositive phrases rename a neighbouring noun (My friend, a talented artist, painted this). Absolute phrases (The weather permitting, we shall depart) consist of a noun and a participle and modify the whole sentence. Recognising phrase types enables a candidate to spot misplaced modifiers, ensure parallelism in lists, and reduce wordy clauses to concise phrases during sentence improvement.

2.3 Clauses: The Building Blocks of Complete Thoughts

A clause is a group of words that contains its own subject and finite verb; this subject-verb pairing is what distinguishes a clause from a phrase. An independent (or main) clause expresses a complete thought and can stand alone as a sentence (The sun set). A dependent (or subordinate) clause cannot stand alone because it begins with a subordinating conjunction or a relative pronoun that marks it as incomplete (Because the sun set, who lives next door). Dependent clauses are classified by function: noun clauses act as subjects, objects, or complements (What he said is true); adjective (relative) clauses modify nouns (The book that you gave me); adverb clauses modify verbs, adjectives, or adverbs and answer questions such as when?, where?, why?, under what condition? (We left when the rain stopped). A relative clause may be restrictive (defining, no commas, The student who won the prize) or non-restrictive (non-defining, set off by commas, My brother, who lives in Mumbai, is visiting); the choice affects meaning and punctuation. Conditional clauses introduced by if, unless, provided that follow strict tense sequences: Type 0 (general truths) uses present in both clauses; Type 1 (real possibility) uses present in the if-clause and future in the main clause; Type 2 (unreal present) uses past in the if-clause and would + bare infinitive in the main clause; Type 3 (unreal past) uses past perfect in the if-clause and would have + past participle in the main clause. Mastery of clause types and their punctuation is indispensable for constructing complex sentences and for identifying fragment and run-on errors.

2.4 Classifying Sentences by Structure

Sentences are categorised structurally by the number and type of clauses they contain. A simple sentence contains exactly one independent clause and no dependent clauses (The tiger roared); it may have a compound subject (The tiger and the lion roared), a compound predicate (The tiger roared and prowled), or both, but it remains simple because it has only one subject-verb nexus. A compound sentence contains two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet), a semicolon, or a conjunctive adverb with a semicolon (The tiger roared; however, the deer escaped). A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause (Although the tiger roared, the deer escaped). A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause (Although the tiger roared, the deer escaped, and the monkey chattered). The structural classification determines the punctuation rules that apply: compound sentences require a comma before the coordinating conjunction (unless the clauses are very short and closely related), complex sentences require a comma after an initial dependent clause but not before a final one, and compound-complex sentences combine both conventions. Examiners often test the ability to convert one structural type into another without changing meaning, a skill that demonstrates syntactic flexibility.

Worked Example: Structural Classification and Transformation
Question: Identify the structure of the following sentence and rewrite it as a complex sentence without altering its meaning: "The monsoon arrived late, so the crops failed, and the farmers suffered heavy losses."
Solution: The original sentence contains three independent clauses — "The monsoon arrived late", "the crops failed", and "the farmers suffered heavy losses" — joined by the coordinating conjunctions "so" and "and". There is no dependent clause, so the structure is compound. To convert it into a complex sentence, we must subordinate two of the ideas. One valid version: "Because the monsoon arrived late, the crops failed, causing the farmers to suffer heavy losses." Here "Because the monsoon arrived late" is a dependent adverb clause of reason, "the crops failed" is the independent clause, and "causing the farmers to suffer heavy losses" is a participial phrase modifying the main clause. The meaning is preserved, and the sentence is now complex.
Exam-Day Insight: Spotting Hidden Compounds
When a sentence appears simple but contains a subject-verb pair after a semicolon or a conjunctive adverb (however, therefore, moreover), it is actually compound. Underline every finite verb; if you find more than one independent subject-verb pair not joined by a subordinating conjunction, the sentence is at least compound regardless of how short it looks.

3. Functional Classification: What Sentences Do

3.1 Declarative and Interrogative Sentences

Sentences are also classified by their communicative function, independent of their structural form. A declarative (assertive) sentence makes a statement of fact, opinion, or belief and ends with a full stop (The Parliament passes the bill). It may be affirmative or negative (The bill does not violate the Constitution). An interrogative sentence asks a question and ends with a question mark. Yes-no questions invert the auxiliary and subject (Has the bill been passed?), while wh-questions begin with an interrogative word (When was the bill passed?). Tag questions attach a shortened question to a declarative clause, reversing polarity (The bill was passed, wasn't it?); the tag uses the same auxiliary and a pronoun matching the subject. Indirect questions embed a question within a declarative or interrogative frame without inversion (I wonder when the bill was passed, Can you tell me when the bill was passed?). In examination passages, the shift from direct to indirect speech often requires converting interrogative word order to declarative word order and adjusting pronouns, tenses, and time adverbials.

3.2 Imperative, Exclamatory, and Optative Sentences

An imperative sentence expresses a command, request, advice, or instruction and typically omits the subject you (Close the door, Please be seated). The verb appears in its base form; negative imperatives use do not or don't before the base verb (Do not touch). An exclamatory sentence conveys strong emotion — surprise, joy, anger, sorrow — and ends with an exclamation mark. It often begins with what or how followed by a noun phrase or adjective (What a magnificent building!, How beautifully she sings!). An optative sentence expresses a wish, prayer, or curse and usually begins with may or would that (May you live long!, Would that I were young again!). In formal grammar, optatives are a subset of exclamatories, but competitive examinations treat them as a distinct category. Transformation exercises frequently require changing a declarative into an exclamatory (It is a very hot day → What a hot day it is!) or an imperative into a polite request using a modal (Submit the form → Could you please submit the form?). Recognising the illocutionary force of a sentence helps in selecting the appropriate punctuation and in reporting speech accurately.

3.3 Transformation Between Functional Types

The ability to rewrite a sentence in a different functional form without changing its core meaning is a standard testing objective. Converting an assertive sentence into an interrogative often involves adding a negative tag or using a rhetorical question (Everyone knows the truth → Who does not know the truth?). Turning an interrogative into an assertive may require supplying the implied answer (Is he not a fool? → He is a fool). Imperatives can be reported as infinitives in indirect speech ("Leave the room," he said → He ordered me to leave the room). Exclamatories become declarative clauses with that and an intensifier ("What a tragedy!" she cried → She exclaimed that it was a great tragedy). Optatives are reported with wished or prayed followed by that and a modal ("May you succeed!" → He wished that I might succeed). These transformations rely on a secure grasp of clause structure, tense back-shifting, and pronoun adjustment, all of which are rooted in the foundational concepts covered in the preceding sections.

4. Agreement, Case, and Common Structural Errors

4.1 Subject-Verb Agreement Across Complex Subjects

Agreement errors arise when the verb fails to match the number of its subject, especially when intervening phrases obscure the true head noun. A singular subject takes a singular verb even when followed by a prepositional phrase containing a plural noun (The box of chocolates is open, not are open). Collective nouns take a singular verb when the group acts as a unit (The jury has delivered its verdict) and a plural verb when the members act individually (The jury are arguing among themselves). Nouns plural in form but singular in meaning — news, mathematics, physics, measles, economics, politics — take singular verbs (Mathematics is his favourite subject). Titles of books, films, or organisations are singular even when plural in form (The Canterbury Tales is a classic). Expressions of quantity — a lot of, a number of, the majority of — take their number from the noun that follows: A number of students are absent (plural) versus The number of students is small (singular). Fractions and percentages follow the same rule: Half of the cake is gone, Half of the cakes are gone. In inverted sentences the verb precedes the subject, but agreement remains with the subject (There is a book on the table; There are books on the table). Relative pronouns as subjects take verbs agreeing with their antecedents (He is one of the students who have passed — who refers to students, plural). These rules are not arbitrary; they reflect the logic of reference and are tested in every major English paper.

4.2 Pronoun Case and Reference Clarity

Pronoun case errors occur when a pronoun appears in the wrong case for its syntactic role. Subjective case (I, he, she, we, they, who) is required for subjects and subject complements after linking verbs (It is I, though It's me is accepted in informal usage). Objective case (me, him, her, us, them, whom) is required for direct objects, indirect objects, and objects of prepositions (Between you and me, never Between you and I). Possessive case (my, his, her, our, their, whose) shows ownership and precedes gerunds (His leaving early surprised us). Reflexive pronouns must have an antecedent in the same clause (She hurt herself); using a reflexive without an antecedent (Myself and Rahul went) is a common hypercorrection. Ambiguous reference arises when a pronoun could refer to more than one antecedent (Rahul told Amit that he had failed — who failed?). The remedy is to repeat the noun or restructure the sentence. Vague reference occurs when this, that, which, it refer to an entire clause or an implied idea rather than a specific noun (He missed the train, which annoyed him — which refers to the whole event). Examiners penalise both ambiguous and vague reference because they impair precision.

4.3 Modifier Placement and Dangling Constructions

A modifier must be placed as close as possible to the word it modifies; otherwise the sentence becomes ambiguous or absurd. Misplaced modifiers create unintended meanings: She only ate apples (she did nothing else with apples) versus She ate only apples (apples were the only food). Squinting modifiers sit between two possible heads: Running quickly improves health — does quickly modify running or improves? Dangling modifiers occur when the word modified is absent from the sentence, typically at the beginning: Walking down the road, a dog bit me (the dog was not walking). The correction supplies the appropriate subject: While I was walking down the road, a dog bit me or Walking down the road, I was bitten by a dog. Participial phrases, infinitive phrases, and elliptical clauses are the usual culprits. In sentence-improvement questions, the correct option will always attach the modifier to a logical subject, often by converting the phrase into a clause with its own subject and verb.

4.4 Parallelism in Coordination and Comparison

Parallelism requires that items joined by coordinating conjunctions, correlative conjunctions, or comparison markers share the same grammatical form. In a list, all elements must be nouns, gerunds, infinitives, or clauses — not a mixture (He likes reading, swimming, and to ride → reading, swimming, and riding or to read, to swim, and to ride). With correlatives, the structure after the first correlative must mirror the structure after the second: not only…but also demands not only did he sing but also did he dance (both clauses) or not only singing but also dancing (both gerunds). Comparisons using than or as must compare like with like: The climate of Mumbai is warmer than Delhi (illogical — climate compared to city) → The climate of Mumbai is warmer than that of Delhi or Mumbai is warmer than Delhi. Ellipsis in the second part of a comparison is permitted only when the omitted words are recoverable and the remaining elements are parallel: She runs faster than he (understood runs). Faulty parallelism is a hallmark of poorly constructed sentences and a reliable target for error-detection questions.

The Twelve Tenses

English has three main times (present, past, future) × four aspects (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous) = twelve tenses. Each expresses when an action happens and whether it is complete or ongoing.

TenseFormulaUseExample
Present SimpleV1 (+s/es)Habit, fact, universal truthShe works here. The sun rises in the east.
Present Continuousam/is/are + V1+ingAction happening now, around nowShe is working now.
Present Perfecthas/have + V3Past action with present result, unfinished timeShe has worked here since 2020.
Present Perfect Cont.has/have been + V1+ingAction started in past, still continuingShe has been working here for 3 years.
Past SimpleV2Completed action in pastShe worked here last year.
Past Continuouswas/were + V1+ingOngoing action at a past momentShe was working when I called.
Past Perfecthad + V3Earlier of two past actionsShe had left before I arrived.
Past Perfect Cont.had been + V1+ingOngoing action before another past actionShe had been working for 2 hours when I called.
Future Simplewill/shall + V1Future fact, prediction, decisionShe will join tomorrow.
Future Continuouswill be + V1+ingAction ongoing at a future timeShe will be working then.
Future Perfectwill have + V3Action complete before future timeShe will have finished by 5 pm.
Future Perfect Cont.will have been + V1+ingDuration of action up to future pointShe will have been working for 5 years by 2026.

Key Verbs: V1, V2, V3

  • V1 (base): go, write, eat, see, take, give, know, come, do, make.
  • V2 (past): went, wrote, ate, saw, took, gave, knew, came, did, made.
  • V3 (past participle): gone, written, eaten, seen, taken, given, known, come, done, made.
  • Regular verbs: add -ed (walk → walked, play → played).
  • Irregular verbs: must be memorised (go-went-gone, see-saw-seen).

Signal Words

  • Present Simple: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, every day/week, generally.
  • Present Continuous: now, at present, at the moment, look!, listen!, today (with now).
  • Present Perfect: already, yet, just, ever, never, since, for, today, this week (unfinished).
  • Past Simple: yesterday, last night/week/month/year, ago, in 1999, once, then.
  • Past Perfect: already, before, by the time, when (earlier action), after (earlier action).
  • Future Simple: tomorrow, next week/month/year, soon, in 2026, probably.

Important Rules

  • Since vs For: since = point of time (since 2020, since Monday); for = period of time (for 3 years, for two hours). Used with perfect tenses.
  • Past Perfect for earlier action: When two past actions are mentioned, the earlier one takes Past Perfect (had + V3), the later one Past Simple. "The train had left before I reached the station."
  • No future tense in time/condition clauses: "If it rains, I will stay" (not "If it will rain"). "When he comes, we will start."
  • Present Perfect not used with definite past time: "I have seen him yesterday" (wrong) → "I saw him yesterday" (right).
  • Stative verbs usually not continuous: know, believe, love, hate, want, need, seem, understand — use simple, not continuous ("I know her," not "I am knowing her").
Technique: Choosing the tense
Question: "She ___ (work) here since 2020." Choose correct form.
Answer: "since 2020" = unfinished time starting in past → Present Perfect or Present Perfect Continuous. If focus on result: "has worked." If focus on duration: "has been working." Both acceptable depending on emphasis.
Technique: Earlier of two past actions
Question: "I ___ (reach) the station after the train ___ (leave)."
Answer: Two past actions — train left earlier (Past Perfect: had left), I reached later (Past Simple: reached). "I reached the station after the train had left."

Common Traps

  • Using Present Perfect with "yesterday/last year/ago" — wrong.
  • Using "will" in "if/when" clauses — wrong.
  • Confusing Past Simple and Past Perfect when only one past action is mentioned — use Simple, not Perfect.
  • Using continuous with stative verbs (know, believe, want) — generally wrong.
  • Subject-verb agreement with Present Simple third person singular (he/she/it + s/es).

Memory Tricks

  • 12 tenses: 3 times × 4 aspects. Perfect = completed effect; Continuous = ongoing.
  • Since = point; For = period.
  • V2 = finished past; had + V3 = earlier past.
  • will + V1 = future simple (decision/prediction).
Tense exam strategy
In error spotting, check signal words first (yesterday → past tense; since/for → perfect; every day → present simple). In sentence improvement, choose the tense that matches the time word. Don't overthink — most tense errors are basic form mistakes.

Sequence of Tenses in Reported Speech and Conditional Structures

When a speaker reports an utterance, the tense of the reported clause often shifts back one step in the temporal hierarchy. This backshifting follows a predictable pattern: present simple becomes past simple, present perfect becomes past perfect, past simple becomes past perfect, and future simple (will) becomes would. The rule applies when the reporting verb is in a past tense (said, told, asked) and the reported situation is not a universal truth or a still‑valid fact. For example, “She works here” reported after a past reporting verb becomes “He said she worked here.” If the original statement expresses a timeless fact — “The earth revolves round the sun” — the tense may remain unchanged because the proposition holds irrespective of the reporting time.

Conditional sentences exhibit a parallel tense logic. In the first conditional (real possibility), the if‑clause uses present simple and the main clause uses will + base: “If it rains, we will cancel.” In the second conditional (unreal present), the if‑clause shifts to past simple and the main clause uses would + base: “If it rained, we would cancel.” The third conditional (unreal past) pushes both clauses further back: past perfect in the if‑clause and would have + past participle in the main clause — “If it had rained, we would have cancelled.” Mixed conditionals combine these layers, e.g., “If I had studied harder, I would be a doctor now” (past perfect in the if‑clause, would + base in the main clause) to show a past counterfactual with a present result.

Exceptions arise with modal verbs that lack a past form (must, ought to, should). In reported speech, must often becomes had to when expressing obligation, but remains must when expressing logical deduction: “He must be tired” → “She said he must be tired.” Similarly, should and ought to are unchanged in indirect speech. The verb need behaves like a modal in negative and interrogative contexts (need not, need I?) but follows regular backshifting in affirmative reported clauses (needed to). Understanding these nuances prevents the common error of over‑backshifting modals that are historically present‑tense forms.

Non‑finite Verb Forms: Gerunds, Infinitives, and Participles in Complex Constructions

Gerunds (V‑ing) function as nouns, infinitives (to + V1) as verbal nouns or purpose adjuncts, and participles (present V‑ing, past V3) as adjectival or adverbial modifiers. The choice among them is governed by the matrix verb, the syntactic role, and subtle meaning differences. Verbs of perception (see, hear, watch) take either a bare infinitive or a present participle: “I saw him leave” (complete event) versus “I saw him leaving” (ongoing process). Verbs of preference (like, love, hate, prefer) accept both gerund and infinitive with a shift in focus: “I like swimming” (general enjoyment) versus “I like to swim every morning” (habitual routine).

Control structures determine whether the subject of the non‑finite clause is understood as the matrix subject (subject control) or the matrix object (object control). In “She promised to arrive early”, the understood subject of to arrive is she (subject control). In “She persuaded him to arrive early”, the understood subject is him (object control). Raising verbs (seem, appear, happen) differ: the matrix subject is not the semantic argument of the non‑finite verb — “He seems to know the answer” — the subject he is raised from the embedded clause.

Perfect and progressive non‑finite forms add temporal nuance. The perfect gerund having + V3 indicates anteriority: “Having finished the report, she left.” The perfect infinitive to have + V3 serves a similar function after verbs of expectation or regret: “He claims to have seen the document.” The progressive gerund being + V‑ing and progressive infinitive to be + V‑ing emphasize ongoingness at the reference time: “Being watched made him nervous” and “She appears to be working late.” Passive non‑finite forms (being + V3, to be + V3, having been + V3) allow the logical object to become the subject of the non‑finite clause: “Having been selected, the candidate was interviewed.”

Exam questions frequently test the distribution of gerunds versus infinitives after specific adjectives and nouns. Adjectives such as easy, hard, difficult, impossible license a for‑to infinitive with a passive interpretation: “The problem is easy to solve” (≈ “to solve the problem is easy”). Nouns like decision, attempt, plan, refusal select a to‑infinitive: “His decision to resign surprised everyone.” Conversely, nouns such as habit, chance, opportunity, reason often take a gerund or a prepositional gerund: “There is a chance of winning” or “He has a habit of arriving late.” Mastery of these collocational patterns is essential for sentence‑improvement and error‑spotting items.

Technique: Choosing the Correct Non‑finite Form
Select the appropriate form to complete the sentence: “The manager objected ___ (to propose / to proposing / proposing) the new policy without consultation.”
The verb object is followed by the preposition to and a gerund. Therefore the correct choice is to proposing. The completed sentence reads: “The manager objected to proposing the new policy without consultation.”
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a sentence contains a verb + preposition combination, identify the preposition first; the following verb must be a gerund. For verb‑only patterns, memorise the three major groups: (1) verbs taking only gerund (avoid, enjoy, mind), (2) verbs taking only infinitive (decide, hope, manage), (3) verbs taking both with meaning change (remember, forget, stop, try). Quick classification reduces hesitation in error‑spotting.

Perfect and Progressive Aspects: Interaction with Verb Classes and Aspectual Coercion

The perfect aspect (have + V3) signals that an event is viewed as completed relative to a reference time, while the progressive aspect (be + V‑ing) presents an event as ongoing at that reference time. Their interaction with lexical aspect — the inherent temporal structure of verbs — produces systematic patterns and occasional coercions. Stative verbs (know, believe, love, own) normally resist the progressive because they denote states without internal phases. However, in contexts where a temporary or deliberate interpretation is forced, the progressive appears: “I am loving this concert” (temporary enjoyment) or “He is being difficult” (volitional behaviour). This coercion is a hallmark of advanced usage and is frequently tested in sentence‑improvement items where the simple form would be marked as less appropriate.

Dynamic verbs subdivide into activities (run, write), accomplishments (build a house, write a letter), and achievements (recognise, reach). Activities and accomplishments readily combine with both perfect and progressive: “She has been writing for two hours” (progressive perfect) and “She has written three letters” (perfect). Achievements, being punctual, resist the progressive unless they are reinterpreted as a preliminary phase: “He is reaching the summit” implies the approach, not the instantaneous arrival. The perfect with achievements yields a resultative reading: “He has reached the summit” (current relevance of the achieved state).

Aspectual coercion also operates with the perfect progressive (have been + V‑ing). This form emphasises duration leading up to a reference point and is compatible with activities and accomplishments but odd with achievements unless a preparatory process is implied: “They have been reaching a decision” (extended deliberation). In exam contexts, the presence of duration adverbials (for three hours, since morning) strongly signals the perfect progressive, while result‑oriented adverbials (already, just, yet) favour the simple perfect. Recognising these collocations allows rapid elimination of incorrect tense choices.

Aspect Compatibility by Verb Class
Verb ClassSimple PerfectProgressivePerfect Progressive
State (know, own)NaturalCoerced (temporary)Rare
Activity (run, read)NaturalNaturalNatural
Accomplishment (write a report)NaturalNaturalNatural
Achievement (recognise, arrive)Natural (resultative)Coerced (preparatory)Coerced (extended process)

Modal Verbs and Tense: Perfect, Continuous, and Semi‑modal Patterns

Modal auxiliaries (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must) lack non‑finite forms and do not inflect for person or number. Their temporal reference is conveyed through the following infinitive: bare for present/future, perfect (have + V3) for past, and continuous (be + V‑ing) for ongoing situations. The modal perfect must have + V3 expresses strong deduction about a past event: “She must have left already.” The modal continuous could be + V‑ing indicates a present possibility in progress: “He could be working late.” Combining both yields might have been + V‑ing for a past ongoing possibility: “They might have been waiting for us.”

Semi‑modals (have to, ought to, need to, dare, used to) behave partly like modals and partly like main verbs. Have to forms its past with had to and its perfect with have had to: “I have had to rewrite the report.” Ought to has no past form; past obligation is expressed by should have + V3 or ought to have + V3. Need operates as a modal in negative/interrogative contexts (need not, need I?) but as a main verb elsewhere (needs to, needed to). Dare follows a similar split. Used to exists only in the past and has no perfect or continuous forms; present habitual meaning requires usually + present simple.

Epistemic versus deontic modality further determines tense compatibility. Epistemic modals (expressing likelihood) freely combine with perfect and continuous: “He may have forgotten”, “She must be sleeping.” Deontic modals (expressing obligation/permission) resist the perfect in direct speech but appear in reported contexts: “You must finish” → “He said I must finish” (present obligation reported) versus “He said I had to finish” (backshifted). The modal shall is largely confined to first‑person offers and legalistic future; its past should serves both epistemic and deontic functions. Awareness of these restrictions prevents the common error of writing *“He must have been finished” (incorrect passive with modal perfect) instead of “He must have finished.”

Tense Coordination across Clauses: Rules, Exceptions, and Exam Traps

Complex sentences often contain multiple finite clauses linked by coordination (and, but, or) or subordination (because, although, while, if). The principle of tense harmony states that, unless a clear temporal shift is signalled, clauses sharing the same time frame should maintain consistent tense. In “She arrived early and waited for him”, both verbs are past simple because the events are sequential in the same past narrative. When a subordinate clause expresses a reason or condition that holds at the same time as the main clause, the tense aligns: “He is tired because he worked all night” (past cause, present result) versus “He is tired because he has been working all night” (ongoing cause with present relevance).

Ellipsis and substitution introduce additional constraints. In “She has finished her essay, and he has too”, the auxiliary has is retained to preserve the perfect aspect. Omitting it (*“and he too”) would be ungrammatical in formal writing. Similarly, “I will attend if he does” requires the auxiliary does to match the future simple of the main clause; *“if he will” violates the rule against future tense in conditional clauses. When the subordinate clause is concessive (although, even though), the tense may differ to reflect contrast: “Although he was ill, he attends the meeting” (past illness, present attendance) is acceptable because the concession spans two time frames.

Sequence‑of‑tenses violations frequently appear in error‑spotting items where a past reporting verb is followed by a present tense in the reported clause without a universal‑truth justification. For instance, “He said the sun rises in the east” is correct (timeless fact), but “He said the meeting starts at ten” is questionable unless the meeting is a recurring schedule; the safer form is “He said the meeting started at ten.” Another trap involves the misuse of would in place of used to for past habits: “When we were children, we would play in the park” is acceptable, but “We would live in that house” is not; used to or past simple is required for stative past habits. Mastery of these coordination rules enables rapid identification of the single erroneous verb form in a long sentence.

  • Over‑backshifting modal verbs that lack past forms (must, ought to, should) in reported speech.
  • Using a bare infinitive after a verb that requires a gerund (e.g., *enjoy to swim instead of enjoy swimming).
  • Applying the progressive aspect to stative verbs without a temporary or volitional context.
  • Choosing the simple perfect where a perfect progressive is required by a duration adverbial (for three hours).
  • Writing a future tense (will) inside an if‑clause or time clause instead of the required present form.
  • Omitting the auxiliary in elliptical coordinated clauses, breaking tense harmony.
  • Confusing would for past habits with used to for stative past situations.
grammar/subject-verb-agreement:
Foundations of Concord: Number, Person, and the Basic Rule

1.1 The Concept of Agreement in English

Concord, or subject-verb agreement, is the grammatical principle that requires a finite verb to match its subject in both number and person. In English, this matching is most visible in the present tense, where the verb changes form to signal whether the subject is singular or plural and whether it speaks in the first, second, or third person. The rule operates because the verb carries the primary burden of indicating the action or state of the subject; when the verb form clashes with the subject, the sentence loses clarity and grammatical correctness. Examiners test this principle heavily because it reveals whether a candidate can identify the true subject of a sentence, especially when that subject is separated from the verb by modifiers, phrases, or clauses. A failure of concord often signals a deeper confusion about sentence structure, making it a reliable discriminator in competitive assessments.

1.2 Singular and Plural Verb Forms in the Present Tense

In the simple present tense, the distinction between singular and plural verbs is marked by the presence or absence of the inflectional suffix -s or -es on the main verb. A singular third-person subject — he, she, it, or any singular noun phrase — takes a verb ending in -s (for example, walks, watches, goes, has). All other subjects — first person singular I, second person you, first person plural we, second person plural you, and third person plural they — take the base form of the verb without the suffix (for example, walk, watch, go, have). This asymmetry exists because English historically lost most of its person-and-number endings, leaving only the third-person singular marker as a relic. The verb be is exceptional: it distinguishes am for first person singular, is for third person singular, and are for all plural subjects and for second person singular you. Mastery of these forms is the prerequisite for applying every subsequent concord rule.

1.3 Person Distinctions and Their Effect on Verb Shape

Person determines which verb form the grammar selects once number is established. First person (I, we) and second person (you) always pair with the base verb in the present tense, regardless of whether the subject is singular or plural. Third person is where the singular-plural split occurs: singular third-person subjects require the -s ending, while plural third-person subjects (they or plural nouns) take the base form. This means that the pronoun you, though historically plural, now functions for both singular and plural reference but consistently governs a plural verb form (you are, you go). The practical consequence is that identifying the person of the subject is as important as counting its number; a sentence such as The committee has decided works because committee is treated as a singular third-person entity, whereas The committee are divided works because the same noun is reinterpreted as a plural third-person group. The verb form, therefore, is the surface evidence of a deeper decision about how the subject is conceptualized.

Coordination and the Proximity Principle

2.1 Subjects Joined by Coordinating Conjunctions

When two or more subjects are linked by the coordinating conjunction and, the resulting compound subject is ordinarily plural and therefore takes a plural verb. The logic is additive: Ram and Shyam denotes two distinct individuals, so the verb must be plural (are, go, have). However, this additivity collapses when the two nouns refer to a single person, a single entity, or a single concept. In Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast, the two nouns name one combined dish; in The horse and carriage is waiting, they denote a single conveyance; in The poet and philosopher has arrived, a single individual holds both titles. The grammatical signal of this unity is often the absence of a second article — the poet and philosopher versus the poet and the philosopher — though context can override the article test. Recognizing whether and creates a genuine plurality or a notional singularity is essential for correct verb selection.

2.2 The Proximity Rule with Disjunctive Conjunctions

When subjects are joined by or, either…or, neither…nor, or not only…but also, the verb does not automatically become plural. Instead, English applies the proximity principle: the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. This rule exists because the disjunction presents alternatives rather than a sum; only one of the alternatives is realised, so the verb matches the alternative that is grammatically closest. In Neither the teacher nor the students were present, the plural noun students sits next to the verb, triggering were; reversing the order to Neither the students nor the teacher was present shifts the agreement to the singular teacher. The same principle governs Either the principal or the teachers are responsible versus Either the teachers or the principal is responsible. The proximity rule is a frequent examination target because it tests the candidate's ability to locate the true subject amidst distractors.

2.3 Correlative Constructions and Verb Choice

Correlative pairs such as not only…but also behave identically to either…or and neither…nor with respect to proximity. The verb agrees with the second element, the one immediately preceding it. Thus Not only the students but also the teacher was surprised takes a singular verb because teacher is nearest, while Not only the teacher but also the students were surprised takes a plural verb. A subtle complication arises when the correlative joins noun phrases of different persons: Not only you but also I am to blame sounds awkward because the verb am agrees with I but the construction places you first. Careful writers often rephrase to avoid the clash, but examiners may present the unrevised form to test strict application of the proximity rule. The underlying reason remains the same: the grammar treats the disjunction as offering a single realised subject, and proximity decides which one that is.

Worked Example: Proximity and Person Clash
Select the correct verb form for the sentence: "Neither the director nor the actors ______ satisfied with the rehearsal."
The subject closer to the verb is "the actors", which is plural and third person. By the proximity rule, the verb must agree with "actors". The correct plural verb for third person in the present tense is "were". Therefore the completed sentence reads: "Neither the director nor the actors were satisfied with the rehearsal."
Exam-Day Insight
In multiple-choice questions testing either…or or neither…nor, the distractor option often matches the first subject rather than the second. Train yourself to circle the noun immediately preceding the blank before reading the options; this single habit eliminates the most common proximity trap.

Collective Nouns and the Notion of Unity

3.1 Collective Nouns Acting as a Single Unit

Collective nouns — words such as committee, jury, team, family, audience, government, crowd, flock, herd — denote a group of individuals but can be treated as singular when the group acts as a unified whole. In The committee has submitted its report, the emphasis is on the collective decision; the verb has and the pronoun its both reflect singular agreement. This singular treatment is standard in American English and common in formal British English when the focus is on the group as an institution. The grammatical consequence extends beyond the verb: singular verbs attract singular pronouns (its, itself) and singular determiners (this, that). Candidates must recognise that the singular verb is not an error but a deliberate choice signalling collective unity.

3.2 Collective Nouns Highlighting Individual Members

When the context shifts to the members acting separately or holding differing opinions, the same collective noun takes a plural verb. The committee are divided in their opinions uses are and their because the sentence describes internal disagreement among individuals. British English favours this plural agreement more readily than American English, which often retains the singular even for divided groups. Examination questions set in a British-English framework (as is typical for UPSC and similar Indian competitive exams) expect candidates to detect contextual cues — words such as divided, disagree, argue, differ — that trigger plural agreement. The verb choice, therefore, becomes a diagnostic of meaning: singular for unity, plural for plurality of action.

3.3 Contextual Shifts in Formal and Informal Usage

Certain collective nouns exhibit a strong preference for one number regardless of context. Police and people are inherently plural (The police are investigating; People are waiting), while news, mathematics, physics are inherently singular despite their plural form (discussed in a later section). Family, team, staff, crew fluctuate: The team is flying to London (unit) versus The team are arguing among themselves (individuals). In formal writing, consistency within a passage matters; switching from singular to plural for the same collective noun without a clear shift of focus is considered a concord error. Examiners may present a paragraph where the collective noun appears twice, once with a singular verb and once with a plural verb, and ask whether the shift is justified. The answer hinges on whether the context supplies a reason for the change.

Collective Noun Agreement: Singular versus Plural Triggers

Group acts as one body; institutional focusSingularThe government has announced a new policy.
Members act individually; internal disagreementPluralThe government are divided on the issue.
Inherently plural nouns (police, people, cattle)PluralThe police have arrested the suspect.
Inherently singular nouns (news, measles, economics)SingularThe news is encouraging.

Indefinite Pronouns and Quantifying Expressions

4.1 Singular Indefinite Pronouns and Their Invariable Verbs

A large set of indefinite pronouns — everyone, everybody, anyone, anybody, someone, somebody, no one, nobody, each, either, neither — are grammatically singular and invariably take a singular verb. This rule holds even when the pronoun appears to refer to multiple entities notionally. Everyone is expected to attend uses is because everyone is singular in form; Neither of the candidates has withdrawn uses has because neither is singular. The singular agreement persists despite the plural noun in the following of-phrase (of the candidates). The grammatical reason is that these pronouns are historically compounds of every, any, some, no with one, body, thing, all of which are singular heads. Examiners frequently test this by inserting a plural noun between the pronoun and the verb (Each of the books are versus Each of the books is) to lure candidates into proximity-based error.

4.2 Quantifiers Governed by the Noun Following 'of'

Quantifying expressions such as most, some, all, any, none, half, part, rest, a lot of, a great deal of do not carry inherent number. Instead, the verb agrees with the noun that follows the preposition of. Most of the work is finished takes a singular verb because work is uncountable and singular; Most of the students are present takes a plural verb because students is plural. This principle, sometimes called the "noun-after-of" rule, applies uniformly across the quantifier set. The logic is that the quantifier merely specifies a portion of the noun; the noun itself remains the semantic and syntactic head of the subject phrase. Candidates must therefore look past the quantifier to the noun it quantifies.

4.3 The Special Cases of 'None', 'All', and 'Most'

None deserves particular attention because it can be singular or plural depending on meaning. Traditional grammar treats none as a contraction of not one and prescribes a singular verb (None of the students was late). Modern usage, however, widely accepts plural agreement when the sense is "not any" (None of the students were late). Both forms are now considered standard in reputable style guides, though formal examinations may still prefer the singular in "not one" contexts. All follows the noun-after-of rule strictly: All of the money is gone (singular), All of the coins are missing (plural). Most behaves identically. The expression more than one is an exception: it takes a singular noun and a singular verb (More than one student was absent) despite its plural meaning, because the head one is singular. Similarly, many a governs a singular noun and verb (Many a candidate has failed). These idioms are high-yield examination items because they contradict the notional plurality.

Special Noun Categories: Form versus Meaning

5.1 Nouns Plural in Form but Singular in Meaning

Several nouns end in -s — the typical plural marker — yet function as singular concepts and take singular verbs. These include names of academic disciplines (mathematics, physics, economics, politics, statistics, linguistics, ethics, civics), diseases (measles, mumps, rickets, shingles), games (billiards, darts, dominoes), and the word news. Mathematics is a difficult subject and The news was shocking illustrate the pattern. The plural form is a historical accident: many of these words derive from Greek or Latin neuter plurals that were reanalysed as singular in English. A few, notably economics and politics, can shift to plural when they refer to separate aspects rather than the discipline as a whole: The economics of the project are uncertain (meaning the financial details). Candidates should memorise the core list and the exceptional plural use for economics/politics.

5.2 Nouns Always Plural in Form and Agreement

Conversely, a set of nouns exists only in plural form and always governs plural verbs. These are typically items consisting of two joined parts (scissors, trousers, pants, shorts, jeans, spectacles, glasses, binoculars, tongs, pliers) or collective nouns lacking a singular counterpart (goods, clothes, alms, premises, thanks, regards, riches, wages, outskirts, surroundings, belongings). The scissors are blunt and His clothes are dirty are correct; The scissor is or A clothe is are impossible. To express singular quantity, English uses a pair of: A pair of scissors is on the table. Here the subject becomes the singular pair, so the verb shifts to singular. This pair of construction is a favourite examination device: A pair of trousers was bought versus The trousers were bought.

5.3 Expressions of Quantity: 'A Number of' versus 'The Number of'

The phrases a number of and the number of illustrate how the definite article can flip verb number. A number of functions as a quantifier meaning "several" or "many"; the true head is the plural noun following of, so the verb is plural: A number of students are absent. The number of refers to a statistical total; the head is the singular number, so the verb is singular: The number of students is fifty. The same contrast appears with a majority of (plural when meaning "most of the members") versus the majority of (singular when referring to the collective majority as a unit), though usage varies. The article test — a for plural, the for singular — provides a reliable heuristic for these expressions.

Inversion, Intervening Phrases, and Relative Clauses

6.1 Intervening Phrases and the Real Subject

A common source of concord error is the insertion of a prepositional phrase or other modifier between the subject and the verb. The verb must agree with the head noun of the subject phrase, not with the noun inside the intervening phrase. In The box of chocolates is expensive, the subject head is box (singular), so the verb is is; the plural chocolates is merely the object of the preposition of. Similarly, The quality of the mangoes is good takes is because quality is singular. Longer interruptions — The collection of rare stamps, which he inherited from his uncle, is valuable — do not change the rule. The grammatical reason is that agreement is a relation between the verb and the subject head; modifiers are structurally subordinate and cannot control verb form. Examination sentences often pile multiple phrases between subject and verb to test whether the candidate can isolate the head noun.

6.2 Inverted Sentences Beginning with 'Here' and 'There'

Sentences that open with here or there followed by a form of be (or occasionally other verbs) place the real subject after the verb. This inversion does not alter the agreement rule: the verb still agrees with the post-verbal subject. Here comes the bus (singular) versus Here come the buses (plural); There is a book on the table versus There are two books on the table. The expletive there is not the subject; it is a placeholder that allows the true subject to follow. In questions, the same principle applies: Where is the key? versus Where are the keys? Candidates must identify the noun after the verb and match the verb to it, ignoring the introductory here/there.

6.3 Relative Pronouns and Antecedent Agreement

When a relative pronoun (who, which, that) functions as the subject of a relative clause, its verb agrees with its antecedent — the noun or pronoun the relative clause modifies. In This is one of the best books that have been written, the antecedent of that is books (plural), so the verb is have. In This is the only book that has been written, the antecedent is book (singular), so the verb is has. The distinction between one of the (plural antecedent) and the only (singular antecedent) is a classic examination trap. The rule extends to other antecedents: He is one of those leaders who inspire confidence (plural leaders → inspire) versus He is the only one of the leaders who inspires confidence (singular one → inspires). The verb in the relative clause must reflect the number of the specific noun the relative pronoun refers to, not the number of the main-clause subject.

Mastery of subject-verb agreement requires not merely memorising rules but developing the habit of locating the true subject head in every sentence, regardless of intervening material, inversion, or quantifying expressions. The principles outlined here — basic number and person matching, coordination and proximity, collective noun nuance, indefinite pronoun invariability, quantifier dependence on the noun after of, form-meaning mismatches, and inversion or relative-clause structures — constitute the complete framework tested in competitive examinations. Consistent application of these principles, reinforced by practice with sentences that layer multiple complexities, will secure accuracy in this high-weight grammar topic.
grammar/articles-prepositions:
Articles (a, an, the)

  • Indefinite article 'a/an': Used before singular countable nouns when mentioning something for the first time or when the noun is not specific. 'a' before consonant sound (a boy, a university — 'u' sounds like 'yu'), 'an' before vowel sound (an apple, an hour — 'h' silent, vowel sound). Choice depends on sound, not spelling letter.
  • Definite article 'the': Used before a particular person/thing already mentioned or known (the book I bought), unique things (the sun, the moon, the earth), superlatives (the best, the tallest), musical instruments (the piano), rivers/seas/ranges (the Ganga, the Indian Ocean, the Himalayas), newspapers (the Hindu), holy books (the Gita), and nationalities (the Indians).
  • Omission of articles: No article before proper nouns (Delhi, John), abstract nouns used generally (Honesty is best policy), material nouns (Gold is precious), languages (Hindi is easy), meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner), bed/church/college/hospital/prison/school when used for primary purpose (go to school = study; go to the school = visit building), plural countable nouns used generally (Cars are expensive).
  • 'A/an' vs 'The': 'A man and a woman were walking. The man was tall.' (first mention = a/an, second = the).

Prepositions

  • Time: at (exact point — at 5 o'clock, at noon, at night), in (period — in May, in 2024, in the morning), on (day/date — on Monday, on 15th August, on Christmas day). 'In' for longer periods, 'on' for specific days, 'at' for exact points.
  • Place: at (point — at the door, at the station), in (enclosed space — in the room, in Delhi, in the box), on (surface — on the table, on the wall, on the floor).
  • Movement/direction: to (towards — go to school), into (enter — go into the room), onto (on top — jump onto the bed), towards (direction — walk towards the market), through (pass from one side to other — walk through the tunnel), across (from one side to other — swim across the river), along (follow length — walk along the road), against (touching and opposing — lean against the wall), among (more than two — divide among three), between (two — divide between Ram and Shyam).
  • Instrument/agent: by (agent — killed by a thief; mode — travel by bus), with (instrument — cut with a knife; accompaniment — go with a friend), in (manner — write in ink), on (basis — depend on).
  • Other common prepositions: about (concerning — talk about politics), above (higher than — above the roof), below (lower than — below the poverty line), over (covering — a roof over the head), under (below — under the table), before (earlier than — before 5 pm), after (later than — after lunch), since (point in past — since Monday), for (duration — for 3 hours), from (starting point — from Monday to Friday), till/until (up to — wait till 6), during (within a period — during the holidays), within (before end — within a week), without (lacking — without water), unlike (different from — unlike his brother), like (similar to — like his father), beside (next to — sit beside me), besides (in addition to — besides English, she knows French), except (excluding — all except John), including (including — including tax).

Important Preposition Pairs/Rules

  • In vs On vs At (place): at (point) < in (enclosed) — I live at No. 5, in Delhi, in India.
  • In vs On vs At (time): at (exact) < on (day) < in (month/year) — at 5 pm, on Monday, in January.
  • Between vs Among: between = two (between you and me), among = more than two (distribute among the poor).
  • Since vs For: since = point (since 2010), for = duration (for 10 years). Both used with perfect tenses.
  • By vs With: by = agent/doer (killed by a thief), with = instrument (cut with a knife).
  • Beside vs Besides: beside = next to (sit beside me), besides = in addition to (besides English, she knows Hindi).
  • From vs Since: from = starting point (works from 9 to 5), since = point in past continued to present (works here since 2010 — with perfect tense).
  • Into vs In: into = movement entering (jump into the well), in = position (swim in the pool).
  • On vs Upon: upon is more formal/literary (once upon a time; upon reflection).
  • Above vs Over: above = higher than, no contact (flags above the building); over = covering/moving across (a roof over us, flew over the city).
  • Below vs Under: below = lower than, no contact (below the poverty line); under = directly below/contact (under the table).
  • Between vs From...to: between two points (between Delhi and Mumbai), from...to (from Monday to Friday).

Conjunctions

  • Coordinating conjunctions: join equal elements — and, but, or, nor, for, so, yet (FANBOYS).
  • Subordinating conjunctions: join dependent clause — because, although, though, since, if, unless, until, while, when, before, after, as, as if, as though, lest, so that.
  • Correlative conjunctions (pairs): either...or, neither...nor, both...and, not only...but also, whether...or, scarcely...when, no sooner...than, rather...than.
  • Important rules:
    • No sooner...than (No sooner did he arrive than it started raining — inversion).
    • Scarcely/Hardly...when (Scarcely had he reached when it rained — inversion, past perfect).
    • Lest = that...not, followed by should (Walk carefully lest you should fall).
    • Unless = if not (Unless you work hard, you will fail — no 'not' with unless).
    • Both...and takes plural verb (Both Ram and Shyam are present).
    • Not only...but also — verb agrees with nearer subject (Not only the teacher but also the students were present).
Technique: Article choice
Question: "___ honest man is respected by all." Choose article.
Answer: 'honest' starts with silent 'h' but vowel sound /ɒn/ → use 'an'. "An honest man is respected by all."
Technique: Since vs For
Question: "She has been living here ___ 2015." Choose preposition.
Answer: 2015 is a point in time → 'since'. "She has been living here since 2015."

Common Traps

  • Using 'a/an' before uncountable nouns (a milk, a furniture — wrong; milk is uncountable).
  • Using 'the' before proper nouns (the Delhi — wrong; Delhi is correct).
  • Confusing 'in' and 'at' for time/place.
  • Using 'between' for more than two people/things.
  • Using 'unless' with 'not' (unless you don't work — wrong; unless you work — correct).
  • Using 'the' before names of meals used generally (I take the breakfast — wrong; I take breakfast — correct).

Memory Tricks

  • Articles: a/an = first mention, general; the = specific, unique, second mention.
  • Sound rule: 'a university' (consonant sound), 'an hour' (vowel sound) — depends on sound, not letter.
  • Preposition place/time: at → on → in (smallest → largest unit).
  • Between vs Among: Between = 2; Among = 3+.
Articles/prepositions exam strategy
In error spotting, check articles before countable nouns, preposition choice (since/for, in/on/at), and 'unless' without 'not'. Read the sentence for meaning — wrong prepositions often change meaning entirely.
grammar/sentence-correction:
1. Foundations of Sentence Structure

1.1 The Core Elements of a Sentence

A sentence in English is built around a subject and a predicate, and the relationship between them determines whether the construction is grammatically sound. The subject may be a simple noun phrase, a pronoun, a gerund phrase, or a clause, while the predicate must contain a finite verb that agrees with the subject in number and person. When a writer omits the subject, uses a non‑finite verb as the main verb, or inserts an extra clause without proper subordination, the result is a fragment or a run‑on that examiners flag as an error. Understanding that every complete sentence requires at least one independent clause, and that dependent clauses cannot stand alone, provides the diagnostic framework for spotting structural faults in error‑spotting questions.

1.2 Clause Types and Their Functions

Independent clauses express a complete thought and can function as standalone sentences, whereas dependent clauses — whether nominal, adjectival, or adverbial — rely on a main clause for meaning. Nominal clauses often serve as subjects or objects, adjectival clauses modify nouns, and adverbial clauses indicate time, cause, condition, or concession. Errors arise when a dependent clause is punctuated as a sentence, when a relative pronoun is omitted in a restrictive clause, or when a subordinating conjunction is used incorrectly, such as placing “because” at the start of a sentence without a following main clause. Recognising the syntactic role of each clause type allows a test‑taker to locate the exact point where the grammar breaks down.

1.3 Sentence Patterns and Word Order

English follows a relatively fixed Subject‑Verb‑Object (SVO) order, but variations appear in questions, inversions, and emphatic constructions. Inversion after negative adverbials (“Never have I seen such a mess”) or in conditional clauses without “if” (“Had he known, he would have acted”) is a frequent source of error because candidates often retain the declarative order. Similarly, misplaced adverbs can change the meaning of a sentence (“He only eats apples” versus “Only he eats apples”). Mastery of the standard patterns and their licensed deviations equips the learner to judge whether a given word order is permissible or constitutes a grammatical violation.

2. Agreement and Concord

2.1 Subject‑Verb Agreement with Simple Subjects

The most basic concord rule requires a singular subject to take a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb. This principle operates even when the subject is separated from its verb by intervening phrases such as prepositional phrases (“The box of chocolates is open”) or relative clauses (“The student who won the prize is here”). The verb must agree with the head noun of the subject phrase, not with the noun nearest to it. Errors of attraction occur when the writer mistakenly matches the verb to the closer noun, producing forms like “The quality of the mangoes are good.” Recognising the head noun and ignoring distractors is the first line of defence in error detection.

2.2 Agreement with Compound and Collective Subjects

When two or more nouns are joined by “and”, the subject is usually plural and demands a plural verb (“The director and the producer have arrived”). However, if the coordinated nouns refer to a single entity or a unified concept, a singular verb is appropriate (“Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast”). Collective nouns such as “team”, “committee”, “family”, or “audience” can take either singular or plural verbs depending on whether the group is viewed as a unit or as individuals; British usage often prefers the plural (“The committee are divided”), while American usage leans toward the singular (“The committee is divided”). The test‑taker must infer the intended sense from context, because the exam rarely supplies an explicit cue.

2.3 Agreement with Indefinite Pronouns and Quantifiers

Indefinite pronouns fall into three categories: those that are always singular (“each”, “everyone”, “somebody”, “nothing”), those that are always plural (“both”, “few”, “many”, “several”), and those that vary with the noun they refer to (“all”, “any”, “most”, “none”, “some”). Quantifiers such as “a number of” take a plural verb (“A number of students are absent”), whereas “the number of” takes a singular verb (“The number of students is rising”). The distinction hinges on whether the phrase emphasises the individual members or the collective quantity. Misidentifying the category leads to errors like “Each of the boys have a pen” instead of “has”.

Indefinite Pronouns and Their Verb Agreement
PronounNumberExample
each, everyone, somebody, nothingSingularEveryone is ready.
both, few, many, severalPluralFew have arrived.
all, any, most, none, someDepends on referentAll of the cake is gone. All of the cakes are gone.

2.4 Proximity and Attraction Errors

Proximity attraction is the tendency of a verb to agree with a nearby noun rather than the true subject. This phenomenon appears frequently in sentences where a singular subject is followed by a plural noun in a prepositional phrase (“The list of items are long”) or where a plural subject precedes a singular noun in a relative clause (“The players who is injured”). The rule is absolute: the verb must agree with the grammatical subject, not with any noun that happens to be closer. Training the eye to locate the subject head noun before checking the verb eliminates the majority of attraction errors in competitive examinations.

Subject‑Verb Agreement with Intervening Phrase
Identify the error: "The bouquet of roses smell sweet."
The subject is "bouquet" (singular); the prepositional phrase "of roses" does not change the number. Correct sentence: "The bouquet of roses smells sweet."
Exam‑Day Insight
When a sentence contains a long modifier between subject and verb, mentally strip the modifier and test the core subject‑verb pair; this isolates attraction errors instantly.

3. Tense, Aspect, and Voice

3.1 Consistency of Tense within a Discourse

A coherent passage maintains a consistent time frame unless a shift is signalled by a time adverbial or a change in narrative perspective. Unmotivated tense shifts — such as moving from past simple to present perfect without a clear reason — create confusion and are marked as errors. For instance, “He entered the room and sees the letter” mixes past and present; the correct form is either “entered … saw” or “enters … sees”. The principle of tense consistency extends to subordinate clauses: when the main clause is in the past, subordinate clauses typically backshift (“She said she was tired”), except when expressing a universal truth (“He said the earth revolves around the sun”).

3.2 Sequence of Tenses in Reported Speech

Reported speech follows a systematic backshifting pattern: present simple becomes past simple, present perfect becomes past perfect, past simple becomes past perfect, and modal verbs shift to their past equivalents (“can” → “could”, “will” → “would”). The reporting verb’s tense governs the shift; a present reporting verb (“He says”) does not trigger backshift. However, if the reported clause contains a timeless fact or a still‑valid future arrangement, the original tense may be retained (“She said she will join us tomorrow”). Mastery of this sequence prevents the common error of leaving the reported verb in its original form when the reporting verb is past.

3.3 Conditional Structures and Their Time References

English conditionals are classified by the reality and time of the condition. The first conditional (real present/future) uses “if + present simple, will + base verb” (“If it rains, I will stay”). The second conditional (unreal present/future) uses “if + past simple, would + base verb” (“If I were you, I would go”). The third conditional (unreal past) uses “if + past perfect, would have + past participle” (“If he had studied, he would have passed”). Mixed conditionals combine time references, such as “If I had taken the job, I would be living in London” (past condition, present result). A frequent trap is inserting “will” or “would” into the if‑clause, which is never permitted in standard grammar.

3.4 Active and Passive Voice Transformations

Changing voice requires the object of the active sentence to become the subject of the passive, the verb to adopt a form of “be” plus the past participle, and the original subject to appear in a “by” phrase if retained. Errors arise when the past participle is omitted (“The letter was send”), when the auxiliary “be” does not match the tense (“The work is completed yesterday”), or when intransitive verbs are forced into passive (“The accident was happened”). Only transitive verbs with a direct object can be passivised, and the tense of the passive must mirror the tense of the active original.

4. Articles, Determiners, and Prepositions

4.1 Definite and Indefinite Articles with Countable and Uncountable Nouns

The indefinite article “a/an” appears only before singular countable nouns, signalling non‑specific reference (“a book”). The definite article “the” marks specific or previously mentioned nouns, whether countable or uncountable (“the water in this bottle”). Uncountable nouns never take “a/an” (“an advice” is incorrect; “advice” or “a piece of advice” is correct). Plural countable nouns use “the” for specific reference and zero article for generic reference (“Dogs are loyal” versus “The dogs next door bark”). Errors such as “The milk is spoilt” (when speaking generically) or “The Delhi is big” (proper nouns usually take zero article) stem from misapplying these rules.

4.2 Zero Article and Generic Reference

Zero article is used with plural countable nouns and uncountable nouns when making generalisations (“Gold is precious”, “Children need love”). It also appears with institutions and meals when they are referred to in their primary function (“at school”, “in hospital”, “at breakfast”). However, when the same nouns are particularised, “the” returns (“The school he attends is famous”). The distinction between generic and specific reference is a frequent source of error because the same noun can appear with or without an article depending on context.

4.3 Preposition Selection after Verbs and Adjectives

Many verbs and adjectives govern specific prepositions, and substituting another preposition changes meaning or creates an ungrammatical construction. “Depend on” (not “depend in”), “good at” (not “good in”), “interested in” (not “interested on”), “afraid of” (not “afraid from”) are fixed collocations. The preposition is part of the lexical entry of the verb or adjective; learning these collocations as whole units reduces errors. Some verbs allow two prepositions with a shift in meaning (“arrive at” a building, “arrive in” a city), and the test may probe this nuance.

4.4 Since versus For, In versus On versus At, Between versus Among

“Since” marks a point in time (“since 2010”), while “for” marks a duration (“for ten years”). “In” is used with months, years, seasons, and parts of the day (“in July”, “in the morning”), “on” with days and dates (“on Monday”, “on 15 August”), and “at” with precise times (“at 5 p.m.”). “Between” applies to two distinct entities (“between you and me”), whereas “among” distributes over three or more (“among the members”). Misusing these prepositions is a hallmark of non‑native writing and appears regularly in error‑spotting sections.

Time Prepositions: Point versus Duration
