Modern India (1750-1947 CE)

Advent of Europeans & Consolidation of British Power

  • European arrival: Vasco da Gama (1498, Portuguese), Dutch (1595), French (1667), British East India Company (1600, Royal Charter, first factory at Surat 1608).
  • Battle of Plassey (1757): Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daulah (with Mir Jafar's betrayal) - beginning of British political power.
  • Battle of Buxar (1764): Company defeated Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah, Shah Alam II - Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar, Orissa (1765).
  • Dual Government (1765-1772): Company had Diwani (revenue), Nawab had Nizamat (administration) - administrative paralysis, exploitation.
  • Wars: Anglo-Mysore (Haider Ali, Tipu Sultan), Anglo-Maratha (three wars), Anglo-Sikh (two wars), Anglo-Nepal, Anglo-Burmese, Anglo-Afghan.
  • Doctrine of Lapse (Lord Dalhousie): Annexed Satara (1848), Sambalpur (1849), Udaipur (1852), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), Awadh (1856 - misrule).

Company Rule: Administration & Policies

  • Regulating Act 1773: First parliamentary control, Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings), Supreme Court at Calcutta.
  • Pitt's India Act 1784: Dual control - Board of Control (political), Court of Directors (commercial).
  • Charter Acts (1813, 1833, 1853): Ended trade monopoly (except tea), centralised legislation, open competition for civil services.
  • Land revenue: Permanent Settlement (1793, Cornwallis - Bengal, Bihar, Orissa), Ryotwari (Madras, Bombay - direct with cultivators), Mahalwari (North-Western Provinces - village-based).
  • Commercial policies: De-industrialisation, drain of wealth (Dadabhai Naoroji's theory), forced commercialisation of crops (indigo, opium, cotton).

Socio-Religious Reform Movements

  • Brahmo Samaj (1828, Raja Ram Mohan Roy): Abolition of sati (1829), monotheism, opposition to idol worship and caste.
  • Arya Samaj (1875, Dayananda Saraswati): "Back to the Vedas", shuddhi (reconversion), opposition to cow slaughter and caste.
  • Prarthana Samaj (1867, Atmaram Pandurang): Western India, social reform (widow remarriage, women's education).
  • Ramakrishna Mission (1897, Swami Vivekananda): Service to humanity, Vedanta, Chicago Parliament of Religions (1893).
  • Theosophical Society (1875, H.P. Blavatsky & H.S. Olcott; Annie Besant later): Adyar headquarters, revival of ancient religions.
  • Aligarh Movement (Sir Syed Ahmad Khan): Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College (1875), modern education for Muslims, loyal to British initially.
  • Singh Sabha (1873, Amritsar): Sikh reform, Gurdwara reforms, Punjabi language.
  • Satya Shodhak Samaj (Jyotiba Phule): Anti-caste, education for lower castes and women, Satyashodhak marriage.
  • Self-Respect Movement (E.V. Ramasamy 'Periyar'): Anti-Brahminism, rationalism, women's rights, Tamil pride.

Revolt of 1857

  • Causes: Political (Doctrine of Lapse, annexation of Awadh), economic (land revenue, de-industrialisation), military (greased cartridges, disparity in pay & promotion), social (interference in customs, Christian missionary activity), immediate (Enfield rifle cartridges, March 1857, Meerut outbreak May 10).
  • Centres and leaders: Delhi (Bahadur Shah II), Kanpur (Nana Sahib, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh), Faizabad (Maulvi Ahmadullah).
  • Suppression: Delhi recaptured (September 1857), Lucknow (Campbell), Jhansi (Hughes), Kunwar Singh (Hughes).
  • Nature: Debated - sepoy mutiny (British view), first war of independence (Savarkar, nationalist view), collection of grievances without unified leadership.
  • Consequences: End of Company rule (1858), Crown takeover, Queen's Proclamation (1858), end of Doctrine of Lapse, reorganisation of army (proportion of British troops increased), racial antagonism increased.

Indian National Movement - Moderate Phase (1885-1905)

  • Indian National Congress (1885): Founded by A.O. Hume; first session Bombay (W.C. Bonnerjee, president). Early leaders - Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjee, Dinshaw Wacha.
  • Methods: Petitions, prayers, protests, constitutional agitation, educating public opinion.
  • Economic critique: Dadabhai Naoroji's "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India" (drain of wealth), R.C. Dutt's economic history.
  • Demands: Indianisation of services, separation of judiciary from executive, reduction of military expenditure, civil rights, legislative councils with elected members.

Extremist Phase and Swadeshi (1905-1918)

  • Partition of Bengal (1905, Lord Curzon): Divided Bengal into East Bengal and Assam (Muslim-majority) and West Bengal (Hindu-majority) - seen as "divide and rule".
  • Swadeshi and Boycott: Boycott of British goods, promotion of Indian industries (Bengal Chemical, Tata Steel), national education (Bengal National College), Swadeshi steamship company (V.O. Chidambaram Pillai).
  • Extremist leaders: Bal Gangadhar Tilak ("Swaraj is my birthright"), Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal (Lal-Bal-Pal).
  • Muslim League (1906, Dacca): Founded by Nawab Salimullah; supported Partition of Bengal; demanded separate electorates (Morley-Minto Reforms 1909).
  • Home Rule Movement (1916): Annie Besant and Tilak - demanded self-government within the British Empire, on lines of Irish Home Rule.
  • Lucknow Pact (1916): Congress-Muslim League agreement on separate electorates, joint demand for self-government.

Gandhian Era (1919-1947)

  • Rowlatt Act (1919) and Jallianwala Bagh (April 13, 1919): General Dyer fired on unarmed crowd in Amritsar - turning point in Indian politics.
  • Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22): Launched after Khilafat issue and Jallianwala Bagh; boycott of schools, courts, councils, foreign goods; Chauri Chaura (February 1922) led Gandhi to withdraw it.
  • Swaraj Party (1923, Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das): Council entry to obstruct government from within.
  • Simon Commission (1927): All-British commission - boycotted ("Simon Go Back"); Nehru Report (1928) demanding dominion status.
  • Purna Swaraj (1929, Lahore session): Jawaharlal Nehru as president; January 26 declared Independence Day.
  • Civil Disobedience Movement (1930-34): Dandi March (March 12-April 6, 1930), salt law violation; Round Table Conferences (1930-32); Gandhi-Irwin Pact (1931); Poona Pact (1932).
  • Quit India Movement (1942): "Do or Die" (August 8, 1942); mass arrests, underground leadership, parallel governments (Ballia, Tamluk, Satara).
  • INA (Subhas Chandra Bose): Azad Hind Fauj, Provisional Government of Free India (Singapore, 1943), women's regiment (Rani of Jhansi Regiment, Lakshmi Sahgal).
  • Cabinet Mission (1946): Three-tier federal plan, interim government; rejected by League and Congress in parts; led to Direct Action Day (August 16, 1946) and communal violence.
  • Mountbatten Plan / Indian Independence Act 1947: Partition into India and Pakistan; August 15, 1947; princely states given option to join either.

Post-Independence Consolidation

  • Integration of princely states (Sardar Patel): Hyderabad (Operation Polo, 1948), Junagadh (plebiscite), Kashmir (accession, 1947, Article 370), Goa (Operation Vijay, 1961), Pondicherry (French, 1954).
  • States Reorganisation Act 1956: Linguistic states - Andhra (1953, first linguistic state), then reorganisation on language basis.
  • Constitution adopted (1950): Republic declared.
Technique: Movement chronology
Question: Arrange in chronological order: Swadeshi, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India.
Answer: Swadeshi (1905) → Non-Cooperation (1920) → Civil Disobedience (1930) → Quit India (1942). Each escalated in mass participation and British repression.
Technique: Assessing the Moderates
Question: "The Moderates failed because they lacked mass base." Comment.
Answer: Moderates (1885-1905) relied on educated elite, petitions, and British goodwill. Their achievements - economic critique, Council Act 1892, Indianisation of services - were real but limited. Lack of mass mobilisation, faith in British justice, no direct action made them vulnerable to Extremist critique after Partition of Bengal (1905).

Common Traps

  • Confusing Regulating Act (1773) with Pitt's India Act (1784).
  • Thinking 1857 Revolt had unified nationalist ideology - it was collection of regional grievances.
  • Missing that Swadeshi was both economic (boycott British goods) and political (swaraj).
  • Assuming Gandhi withdrew Non-Cooperation only due to Chauri Chaura - also due to fear of losing control, British repression.
  • Confusing Poona Pact (1932, Gandhi-Ambedkar) with Communal Award (1932, Ramsay MacDonald).

Memory Tricks

  • 1857 → 1947: Revolt → Crown rule → INC (1885) → Swadeshi (1905) → Non-Cooperation (1920) → Civil Disobedience (1930) → Quit India (1942) → Independence (1947).
  • Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal - Extremist trio.
  • Three settlements: Gandhi-Irwin (1931), Poona Pact (1932), Cabinet Mission (1946).
Mains exam-day strategy
For modern history, always anchor events with dates, viceroys, and key leaders. Distinguish between causes, course, and consequences. For movement-based questions, discuss leadership, methods, participants, British response, and impact. Avoid hero-worship - critically assess limitations (Moderates' elite base, Gandhian withdrawals).

Constitutional Law of India

Constitutional Framework

  • Constitution of India: Adopted 26 Nov 1949, enforced 26 Jan 1950. Originally 395 Articles in 22 Parts and 8 Schedules; now over 450 Articles in 25 Parts and 12 Schedules.
  • Preamble: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic; Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status and opportunity), Fraternity (assuring dignity of individual and unity and integrity of Nation).
  • Citizenship: Articles 5-11; Citizenship Act 1955; acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory; termination by renunciation, termination, deprivation; CAA 2019 - accelerated citizenship for persecuted minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan.
  • Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35): Right to Equality (14-18), Right to Freedom (19-22), Right against Exploitation (23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (29-30), Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). Right to Property deleted (44th Amendment 1978, Art 300A - legal right).
  • Directive Principles (Part IV, Articles 36-51): Non-justiciable; social, economic, political welfare; Uniform Civil Code (44), separation of judiciary from executive (50), organisation of village panchayats (40), promotion of educational and economic interests of SC/ST/weaker sections (46).
  • Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Article 51A): Added by 42nd Amendment 1976; 11 duties (originally 10, 11th added by 86th Amendment 2002 - parent/guardian to provide education to child 6-14 years).
  • Basic Structure Doctrine: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) - Parliament can amend any part of Constitution but cannot destroy/alter basic structure. Basic features: supremacy of Constitution, republican democratic republic, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, freedom and dignity of individual, unity and integrity of nation.

Union Executive

  • President (Articles 52-62): Indirectly elected by electoral college (MPs + MLAs); 5-year term; re-election eligible; qualifications (citizen, 35+ years, qualified for Lok Sabha); qualifications, conditions (no office of profit), oath, impeachment (Article 61 - violation of Constitution).
  • Vice-President (Articles 63-71): Indirectly elected by electoral college (both Houses); ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha; 5-year term; impeachment (Rajya Sabha resolution passed by majority, agreed by Lok Sabha).
  • Prime Minister & Council of Ministers (Articles 74-75): PM appointed by President (leader of majority/coalition in Lok Sabha); other ministers appointed by President on advice of PM; collectively responsible to Lok Sabha (Art 75); individual responsibility; oath; salaries/allowances determined by Parliament.
  • Attorney General (Article 76): Appointed by President; must be qualified to be Supreme Court judge; holds office during pleasure of President; right to audience in all courts; right to speak in Parliament (but no voting); not a member of Cabinet.

Parliament

  • Parliament (Articles 79-122): Bicameral - President + Rajya Sabha (Council of States) + Lok Sabha (House of the People).
  • Rajya Sabha (245 members): 238 elected by State/UT Legislative Assemblies (proportional representation by single transferable vote), 12 nominated by President (special knowledge/practical experience in literature, science, art, social service). Permanent house - 1/3 retires every 2 years; 6-year term. Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman; Deputy Chairman elected from members.
  • Lok Sabha (545 members): 543 elected by direct election (single member constituencies), 2 nominated by President (Anglo-Indian - abolished by 104th Amendment 2019). 5-year term (can be dissolved earlier); Speaker (elected by Lok Sabha) presides; Deputy Speaker elected from members.
  • Qualifications for MP: Citizen of India; age 25 (LS) / 30 (RS); registered voter; not holding office of profit; not disqualified under 10th Schedule.
  • Disqualification (10th Schedule): Voluntarily giving up membership, voting against party whip, joining another party after election, independently elected member joining party, nominated member joining party after 6 months.
Technique: Article 32 - Right to Constitutional Remedies
Question: 'Article 32 is the heart and soul of the Constitution' - Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. Explain.
Answer: Article 32 provides right to approach Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. It makes Fundamental Rights justiciable/real. Supreme Court can issue writs: Habeas Corpus (produce person), Mandamus (command public official), Prohibition (stop lower court), Certiorari (transfer case), Quo Warranto (by what authority - challenge to public office). Without Art 32, Fundamental Rights would be mere declarations without enforcement mechanism.

Common Traps

  • Confusing Fundamental Rights (justiciable) with Directive Principles (non-justiciable).
  • Thinking President has executive power - President acts on aid & advice of Council of Ministers (Art 74).
  • Missing that Fundamental Duties are not legally enforceable (no penalty for violation).
  • Confusing Article 32 (Supreme Court) with Article 226 (High Court) - both issue writs, but SC jurisdiction is wider for FR enforcement while HC can enforce FR + other legal rights.
  • Overlooking that Emergency provisions (Articles 352, 356, 360) alter normal federal structure and can suspend Fundamental Rights (except Articles 20 & 21).

Memory Tricks

  • FR Articles: 12-35 (Part III); DPSP Articles: 36-51 (Part IV).
  • Fundamental Rights: Right to Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Against Exploitation (23-24), Religion (25-28), Culture & Education (29-30), Constitutional Remedies (32).
  • Emergency Types: Article 352 (National Emergency), 356 (President's Rule), 360 (Financial Emergency).
  • Writs: Habeas Corpus (produce person), Mandamus (command), Prohibition (stop lower court), Certiorari (transfer case), Quo Warranto (challenge to public office).
Mains strategy
Constitutional law answers: constitutional provision (Article number) → judicial interpretation (Supreme Court judgments) → practical application → critical analysis (pros/cons, reforms). Quote landmark judgments: Kesavananda Bharati (basic structure), Maneka Gandhi (right to travel abroad, procedure reasonable), Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (judicial review of elections), Minerva Mills (balance between FR & DPSP), S.R. Bommai (President's Rule limits), Puttaswamy (right to privacy), Navtej Singh Johar (Section 377 decriminalized), Joseph Shine (adultery decriminalized), Anuradha Bhasin (internet suspension), Sabarimala (women's entry), Ayodhya (Ram Janmabhoomi).

Basic Structure Doctrine: The Unamendable Core

In the realm of Indian Constitutional Law, no concept is more pivotal to judicial review than the Basic Structure Doctrine. While Article 368 grants Parliament the power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, it does not explicitly state that this power is unlimited. The Supreme Court, in a landmark shift from the *Berubari Union* case (1960) where it held that amendment power was plenary and unrestricted, evolved the doctrine that Parliament cannot alter the "basic structure" or essential features of the Constitution. This distinction separates mere legislative amendments from constitutional subversion.

The genesis of this doctrine lies in the Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) case. In a historic 7-6 majority judgment, Chief Justice H.R. Khanna articulated that while Parliament has wide powers of amendment, it cannot destroy or change the basic structure. The Court listed features such as secularism, democracy, rule of law, separation of powers, judicial review, and the unity and integrity of India as part of this inviolable core. Subsequently, in Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980), the Court struck down Part IV (Directive Principles) to the extent it conflicted with Part III (Fundamental Rights), reinforcing that there must be a "harmony" between them and that judicial review is itself part of the basic structure.

Evolution of Basic Structure Doctrine
Case NameYearKey Holding
Kesavananda Bharati1973Amendment power is not unlimited; basic structure cannot be altered.
Minerva Mills1980Judicial review and balance between FRs and DPSP are part of basic structure.
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India1994Secularism and democracy are integral to the Constitution; President's Rule cannot be misused.
I.R. Coelho2007Ninth Schedule laws (post-1973) are subject to judicial review if they violate basic structure.
Examiner's trap
A frequent error is claiming that the Supreme Court can strike down any law passed by Parliament. Correction: The Court cannot strike down a law if it falls within the legislative competence and does not violate the basic structure. However, under I.R. Coelho, laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 1973 are NOT immune from judicial review regarding basic structure violations.
Exam Strategy: The "What If" Approach
When answering questions on Basic Structure, do not just list features. Instead, use a hypothetical scenario: "If Parliament were to abolish the office of the President, would it violate the basic structure? Yes, because the separation of powers and federalism are core features." This demonstrates applied understanding rather than rote memorization.

Article 32 vs Article 226: Jurisdictional Hierarchy

While both Article 32 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) and Article 226 (Powers of High Courts) empower courts to issue writs, their jurisdictional scope and nature differ significantly. Article 32 is the "heart and soul" of the Constitution, as Dr. B.R. Ambedkar noted. The Supreme Court's power under Article 32 is original and inherent; it can issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights regardless of whether a corresponding remedy exists in ordinary law. Conversely, Article 226 grants High Courts wider powers: they can issue writs not only for Fundamental Rights but also for any "legal right" or to correct errors of jurisdiction by lower courts or tribunals.

A critical distinction lies in the scope of remedies. Under Article 32, the Supreme Court can grant relief even if no specific provision exists in the Constitution for that particular violation (though usually linked to FRs). High Courts under Article 226 are not limited by this and can intervene in administrative actions violating natural justice or statutory duties. However, once a matter falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32, High Courts generally cannot interfere. The Supreme Court has held that it is not necessary to exhaust remedies under Article 226 before approaching the Supreme Court under Article 32, though in practice, High Courts are often approached first as they are geographically closer and have wider jurisdiction.

The Raj Narain v. State of UP (1975) case clarified that while Article 32 is the primary remedy for FR violations, Article 226 acts as a supplementary mechanism. Furthermore, during a National Emergency under Article 352, the Supreme Court's power under Article 32 remains intact, whereas High Courts' writ jurisdiction under Article 226 can be suspended if the President issues an order suspending the operation of Articles 19 and 226 (though this is rarely done). This hierarchy ensures that while local courts handle day-to-day grievances, the apex court stands ready to protect the constitutional conscience.

The Ninth Schedule: Immunity or Shield?

The Ninth Schedule was inserted into the Constitution by the First Amendment Act of 1951 specifically to protect land reform laws from judicial scrutiny. Its primary purpose was to prevent courts from striking down state legislation aimed at abolishing zamindari systems, which were often challenged on grounds of violating Fundamental Rights (like equality). For decades, it acted as a sanctuary for legislative enactments.

However, the immunity provided by the Ninth Schedule is not absolute. The Supreme Court ruled in I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) that laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 1973 are subject to judicial review if they violate the basic structure of the Constitution. This judgment effectively neutralized the "immunity" myth, aligning with the Basic Structure Doctrine established in Kesavananda Bharati. The Court held that Parliament cannot place a law in the Ninth Schedule to shield it from scrutiny regarding fundamental features like secularism or equality.

This shift was crucial because earlier, during the Emergency era (1975-77), several laws were added to the Ninth Schedule to bypass judicial review. The Coelho judgment restored the balance between legislative power and judicial oversight. It is important to note that laws added before 1973 remain in the Ninth Schedule, but their status is not explicitly protected against basic structure challenges in the same way post-1973 entries are scrutinized. The practical effect is that no law, regardless of its location in the Constitution, can violate the basic structure.

Separation of Powers: A Structural Reality

The Indian Constitution embodies a "quasi-federal" and "mixed" system of government where separation of powers is not absolute but functional. Unlike the USA or UK with strict separations, India's model allows for checks and balances that prevent any single organ from becoming dominant. The judiciary has played a pivotal role in defining these boundaries.

Doctrine of Eclipse and Severability in Fundamental Rights Adjudication

The doctrine of eclipse operates on the premise that a pre‑Constitutional law which conflicts with a Fundamental Right does not become void ab initio; rather, it is rendered dormant — eclipsed — for the duration of the inconsistency. When the constitutional impediment is removed, either by amendment or by judicial interpretation narrowing the right, the law revives automatically. The Supreme Court first articulated this in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of Madhya Pradesh (1955), holding that a law violating Article 19(1)(g) was merely eclipsed and would become operative again if the restriction were lifted. The doctrine applies only to laws enacted before the commencement of the Constitution; post‑Constitutional laws that contravene Fundamental Rights are void under Article 13(2) and cannot be revived by subsequent amendment unless the amendment itself validates them.

Severability, by contrast, permits a court to excise the offending portion of a statute while preserving the remainder, provided the valid part is capable of standing independently and the legislature would have enacted it without the invalid portion. The test was laid down in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) Ltd. v. Union of India (1957): the court must examine whether the unconstitutional provision is so intertwined with the rest of the Act that the legislative intent would be defeated if it were removed. In State of Gujarat v. Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), the Court severed the unconstitutional section of the Bombay Labour Welfare Fund Act, upholding the remaining provisions. A practical distinction for answer‑writing: eclipse concerns the temporal operation of an entire pre‑Constitutional law, whereas severability is a surgical tool applied to any statute, pre‑ or post‑Constitutional, to save its constitutional core.

Examiners often blend the two concepts. A typical twist presents a pre‑Constitutional statute partially inconsistent with a Fundamental Right and asks whether the whole law is eclipsed or only the offending part can be severed. The correct approach: first apply eclipse to the entire statute; if the inconsistency is confined to a severable segment, the court may sever that segment and allow the rest to operate, but the eclipse doctrine does not permit partial revival — either the whole law revives when the constitutional bar disappears, or the invalid part remains void while the valid part continues under severability. Remember that the 24th Amendment (1971) and the 42nd Amendment (1976) attempted to curtail judicial review of amendments, but the Basic Structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) restored the court’s power to examine whether an amendment itself violates the core, thereby indirectly affecting eclipse and severability analyses.

Judicial Review of Administrative Action: Wednesbury Unreasonableness, Proportionality, and Legitimate Expectation

Administrative law in India has evolved three principal standards of review. The Wednesbury unreasonableness test, borrowed from Associated Provincial Picture Houses Ltd. v. Wednesbury Corporation (1948), asks whether a decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have reached it. The Indian Supreme Court adopted this in State of U.P. v. Rajesh Gautam (2000) and reiterated it in Om Kumar v. Union of India (2000), emphasising that the court does not substitute its own judgment but only intervenes where the decision is perverse, irrational, or based on irrelevant considerations.

The proportionality standard, more rigorous, requires that the administrative measure be suitable, necessary, and balanced in relation to the objective pursued. The Court imported this from European jurisprudence in Union of India v. G. Ganayutham (1997) and refined it in K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) (the privacy judgment), holding that any restriction on a Fundamental Right must satisfy the four‑fold test: legitimate aim, rational connection, necessity (least restrictive means), and proportionality stricto sensu. Proportionality now governs review of restrictions on Articles 19 and 21, displacing Wednesbury in rights‑based challenges.

Legitimate expectation arises when a public authority, by representation or consistent practice, creates an expectation in a person that a certain benefit or procedure will be afforded. The doctrine was recognised in Navjot Singh v. State of Punjab (1994) and expanded in Food Corporation of India v. M/s. Kamdhenu Cattle Feed Industries (1993). It does not confer a substantive right but entitles the individual to procedural fairness — a hearing before the expectation is frustrated. The Court balances the expectation against public interest; a mere hope or desire does not suffice.

In practice, the hierarchy of review is: (i) illegality (acting beyond powers), (ii) procedural impropriety (breach of natural justice), (iii) irrationality (Wednesbury), and (iv) disproportionality (where Fundamental Rights are engaged). A decision may be struck down on any one ground. For answer‑writing, identify the nature of the challenge — statutory interpretation, procedural fairness, or rights restriction — and then select the appropriate standard. Cite the leading case that matches the standard to demonstrate doctrinal precision.

Issue‑Spotter: Selecting the Standard of Review
A municipal corporation issues an order cancelling a street‑vendor’s licence without any prior notice or hearing. The vendor challenges the order in the High Court under Article 226. Which standard(s) of review will the court apply, and what must the vendor demonstrate to succeed?
The court will primarily examine procedural impropriety — breach of the audi alteram partem rule — because the order was passed without hearing the affected party. This is a standalone ground; the vendor need not prove unreasonableness. If the corporation argues that the cancellation was based on policy, the court may also assess Wednesbury unreasonableness to see if the policy itself is irrational. Since a licence is a statutory entitlement, not a Fundamental Right, proportionality does not apply unless the vendor can link the cancellation to a violation of Article 19(1)(g). The vendor must show (a) a legitimate expectation of a hearing based on past practice or statutory requirement, and (b) that the absence of a hearing renders the order procedurally flawed. The remedy is usually quashing the order and directing a fresh decision after a fair hearing.
Exam‑Day Strategy: Map Review Standards to Fact Patterns
Create a mental matrix: (1) No hearing → procedural impropriety / legitimate expectation. (2) Decision based on irrelevant factors → Wednesbury. (3) Restriction on speech, movement, privacy → proportionality. (4) Ultra vires statute → illegality. In the exam, tick the relevant box(es) before writing; this prevents the common error of invoking proportionality for a pure procedural lapse.

Treaty‑Making Power and Domestic Implementation under Article 253

Article 253 empowers Parliament to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of India for implementing any treaty, agreement, or convention with any other country or any decision made at any international conference, association, or other body. This provision bridges the dualist tradition — where international obligations do not automatically become part of domestic law — by giving Parliament the legislative competence to transform treaty obligations into enforceable municipal statutes. The executive alone cannot create domestic legal effects; a parliamentary enactment is indispensable unless the treaty is self‑executing, a concept the Indian judiciary has treated cautiously.

In Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969), the Supreme Court held that the Indo‑Pak Agreement on the Rann of Kutch required parliamentary legislation under Article 253 before it could be enforced in Indian courts. The Court clarified that Article 253 confers exclusive legislative power on Parliament, overriding the distribution of legislative subjects in the Seventh Schedule. Consequently, even if a treaty touches a State List subject (e.g., public health), Parliament may legislate to implement it without requiring State consent.

However, the Court in Jolly George Varghese v. Bank of Cochin (1980) recognised that certain treaty provisions, particularly those reflecting customary international law or jus cogens norms, may be directly applicable if they are of a self‑executing nature and do not require further legislative action. The distinction hinges on the treaty’s language: obligations phrased as “shall enact legislation” are non‑self‑executing; those stating “shall ensure” or “shall guarantee” may be self‑executing. In practice, Indian courts presume non‑self‑execution unless the treaty text and the legislative history indicate otherwise.

The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (1969), though not ratified by India, is regarded as reflective of customary law. Article 26 (pacta sunt servanda) and Article 27 (internal law cannot justify failure to perform a treaty) reinforce the duty to implement. The Supreme Court in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) used the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW) — ratified but not legislated — to fill a legislative vacuum, treating the treaty as an interpretive aid for Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21. This demonstrates that even without an Article 253 enactment, ratified treaties can influence judicial reasoning, though they do not create directly enforceable rights.

For answer‑writing, distinguish three scenarios: (i) treaty requires implementing legislation → Parliament must act under Article 253; (ii) treaty is self‑executing → courts may apply it directly; (iii) treaty used as interpretive tool → courts may read domestic law consistently with the treaty. Cite Maganbhai for the legislative requirement, Jolly George for self‑execution, and Vishaka for interpretive use.

State Responsibility and Diplomatic Protection in International Law

The law of state responsibility is codified in the International Law Commission’s Articles on Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA) (2001), which reflect customary international law. An internationally wrongful act requires two elements: (a) conduct attributable to the State under international law, and (b) a breach of an international obligation of the State. Attribution covers acts of State organs (Article 4), persons exercising governmental authority (Article 5), and conduct directed or controlled by the State (Article 8). The breach may arise from treaty obligations, customary law, or general principles.

Once responsibility is established, the responsible State is under an obligation to cease the wrongful act (Article 30) and to make full reparation (Article 31). Reparation takes three forms: restitution (re‑establishing the situation before the breach), compensation (monetary payment for financially assessable damage), and satisfaction (acknowledgement, apology, or other non‑monetary remedies for moral injury). The Chorzów Factory case (PCIJ, 1928) established the principle that reparation must, as far as possible, wipe out all consequences of the illegal act.

Diplomatic protection is the means by which a State espouses the claim of its national against another State for an injury caused by an internationally wrongful act. The classic conditions, articulated in the Mavrommatis Palestine Concessions case (PCIJ, 1924) and reaffirmed in Barcelona Traction (ICJ, 1970), are: (i) the claimant must be a national of the protecting State at the time of the injury and continuously thereafter; (ii) the national must have exhausted local remedies in the respondent State, unless remedies are ineffective or futile; (iii) the claim must not be barred by the nationality of the claimant being the same as the respondent State (the “nationality of claims” rule). The Nottebohm case (ICJ, 1955) added the “genuine link” requirement for naturalised persons, though its scope remains contested.

In contemporary practice, diplomatic protection is increasingly supplemented by investor‑State arbitration under bilateral investment treaties (BITs) and the ICSID Convention, allowing nationals direct access to international tribunals. Nevertheless, the traditional route remains relevant for human rights violations, environmental damage, and denial of justice where no BIT applies. The ILC’s Draft Articles on Diplomatic Protection (2006) codify the customary rules and emphasise the discretionary nature of the protecting State’s decision to exercise protection.

For examination purposes, remember the sequence: attribution → breach → cessation and reparation → diplomatic protection (nationality, exhaustion of local remedies, genuine link). Cite ARSIWA articles, Chorzów Factory for reparation, Barcelona Traction for the nationality rule, and Nottebohm for the genuine link. Distinguish between the State’s primary responsibility and the secondary procedural step of diplomatic protection.

Emergency Provisions: Article 352, 356, and 360 – Scope, Judicial Review, and Safeguards

The Constitution envisages three distinct emergencies. Article 352 (National Emergency) may be proclaimed on grounds of war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. The 44th Amendment (1978) tightened the procedure: the proclamation must be approved by both Houses of Parliament within one month by a special majority, and it can continue only with periodic parliamentary approval every six months. Crucially, Articles 19 and 21 cannot be suspended during an emergency; only the rights under Article 19 are automatically suspended, while Article 21 remains enforceable. The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) held that the power to proclaim emergency is subject to judicial review on grounds of mala fides or irrelevance.

Article 356 (President’s Rule) allows the President to assume the functions of a State government on receipt of a report from the Governor or otherwise, if satisfied that the State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. The proclamation must be approved by Parliament within two months and can last up to three years with periodic approvals. The landmark S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) laid down stringent guidelines: the President’s satisfaction is justiciable; the proclamation cannot be used for political purposes; the State Legislative Assembly cannot be dissolved before parliamentary approval; and secularism, federalism, and democracy are basic features that cannot be undermined. The Court also mandated a floor test as the preferred method to ascertain majority.

Article 360 (Financial Emergency) empowers the President to declare a financial emergency if the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. It has never been invoked. During such an emergency, the Union can direct States to observe canons of financial propriety, reduce salaries of all or any class of persons serving in the State, and require money bills to be reserved for the President’s consideration. The 44th Amendment removed the provision allowing the President to suspend the enforcement of Fundamental Rights during a financial emergency, reinforcing the principle that economic crises do not justify rights suspension.

Judicial review of all three emergencies focuses on the existence of the factual basis, the procedural compliance (parliamentary approval, special majority), and the proportionality of the measures taken. The Court in State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977) affirmed that the President’s subjective satisfaction is not immune from scrutiny. The 44th Amendment’s safeguards — mandatory parliamentary approval, time limits, and the non‑suspendability of Article 21 — collectively ensure that emergency powers remain exceptional and accountable.

In answer‑writing, structure the response by emergency type, cite the constitutional text, the 44th Amendment changes, and the controlling judgments (Minerva Mills for Article 352, S.R. Bommai for Article 356, and the constitutional text for Article 360). Highlight the distinction: Article 352 affects the entire Union, Article 356 targets a specific State, and Article 360 addresses financial stability. Emphasise that judicial review is available for all three, and that the basic structure doctrine limits the amplitude of emergency powers.

  • Confusing eclipse with severability: eclipse revives the whole pre‑Constitutional law when the constitutional bar lifts; severability saves only the valid part of any statute.
  • Applying proportionality to pure procedural lapses: proportionality governs rights restrictions; procedural fairness is reviewed under natural justice and legitimate expectation.
  • Assuming all treaties are self‑executing: Indian courts presume non‑self‑execution unless the treaty text expressly creates directly enforceable obligations.
  • Overlooking the exhaustion of local remedies rule in diplomatic protection: the claim is inadmissible unless local remedies are exhausted or demonstrably futile.
  • Treating Article 356 as a purely political question: S.R. Bommai made the President’s satisfaction justiciable and imposed procedural safeguards.
  • Mastering these nuances separates a competent answer from an exceptional one.

Indian Penal Code & Criminal Procedure Code

Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860

  • General Exceptions (Sections 76-106): Mistake of fact (s.76), act of judge (s.77), accident (s.78), absence of criminal intention (s.79), necessity (s.81), infancy (s.82-83), unsoundness of mind (s.84), intoxication (s.85-86), consent (s.87-89), necessity (s.81), communication (s.93), compulsion (s.94), slight harm (s.95), right of private defence (s.96-106).
  • Criminal Conspiracy (Section 120A-120B): Agreement between two or more persons to do an illegal act or an act by illegal means; punishment for criminal conspiracy.
  • Offences against the State: Waging war against India (121), waging war against any Asiatic power (123), sedition (124A), collecting arms (s.123), concealing design (s.124A).
  • Offences against Public Tranquillity: Unlawful assembly (141), rioting (146), affray (159), criminal conspiracy.
  • Offences against Human Body: Culpable homicide (s.299), murder (s.300), culpable homicide not amounting to murder (s.299 Exception 1-5), attempt to murder (s.307), causing death by negligence (s.304A), hurt (s.319), grievous hurt (s.322), wrongful restraint (s.339), wrongful confinement (s.340).
  • Offences against Property: Theft (s.378), extortion (s.383), robbery (s.390), dacoity (s.391), cheating (s.415), mischief (s.425), criminal trespass (s.441).
  • Offences relating to Marriage: Bigamy (s.494), adultery (s.497 - decriminalized by Joseph Shine v. Union of India 2018), cruelty by husband/relatives (s.498A).

Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), 1973

  • Constitution of Criminal Courts (Chapter II): Supreme Court, High Courts, Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of First/Second Class, Executive Magistrates, Special Judicial Magistrates.
  • Arrest (Chapter V): Arrest without warrant (s.41 - cognizable offences), arrest with warrant (s.42 - non-cognizable offences), arrest by private person (s.44), procedure on arrest (s.46-49), right to be informed of grounds of arrest (s.50), right to bail (s.50(2)), right to be produced before Magistrate within 24 hours (s.57).
  • Complaints to Magistrate (Chapter XV): Complaint to Magistrate (s.190), taking cognizance (s.190), inquiry by Magistrate (s.200), dismissal of complaint (s.203), issue of process (s.204).
  • Charge (Chapter XVII): Form of charge (s.211), particulars of charge (s.212), alteration of charge (s.216-217), joint trial (s.223).
  • Trial (Chapter XVII-XXIII): Trial before Sessions Court (s.225-237), trial of warrant cases by Magistrate (s.238-250), trial of summons cases (s.251-259), summary trials (s.260-265), attendance of persons (s.254-259), evidence in inquiries/trials (s.266-285), judgment (s.274-276).
  • Judgment (Chapter XXV): Language of judgment (s.275), contents of judgment (s.275), judgment on conviction for offences punishable with death/life imprisonment (s.276), confirmation of death sentence (s.366-368), confirmation of sentence (s.368).
  • Appeal (Chapter XXIX): Appeal from sentences (s.374-377), appeal from orders (s.379-380), appeal against acquittal (s.378), appeal against conviction (s.374).
  • References: Reference to High Court (s.394-395), case stated (s.395), case referred to Supreme Court (s.397).

Indian Evidence Act, 1872

  • Relevancy (Chapter II): Relevancy of facts (s.5-16), admissibility of evidence (s.165), facts forming part of same transaction (s.7), facts relating to occurrences (s.8), facts of body or mental state (s.11), motive (s.8), conduct (s.8).
  • Admissions & Confessions (Chapter II): Admission (s.17-23), confession (s.24-31), confession made to police officer (s.25), confession made while in custody (s.26), discovery of fact (s.27), confession by co-accused (s.30).

Technique: IPC Sections answer
Question: 'What is the difference between culpable homicide and murder?'
Answer: Culpable homicide (Section 299): causing death by doing an act with intention of causing death, or with intention of causing bodily injury likely to cause death, or with knowledge that act is likely to cause death. Murder (Section 300): culpable homicide is murder if (a) intention to cause death, (b) intention to cause bodily injury likely to cause death, (c) intention to cause bodily injury sufficient to cause death, (d) act imminently dangerous and likely to cause death, with knowledge. All murders are culpable homicide but all culpable homicides are not murder. Exceptions to murder: grave and sudden provocation, private defence, public servant acting in good faith, sudden fight, consent (death of person above 18 years who consents).

Common Traps

  • Confusing culpable homicide with murder - all murders are culpable homicide but not vice versa.
  • Confusing theft with robbery - robbery requires violence or threat of violence.
  • Confusing robbery with dacoity - dacoity requires 5 or more persons.
  • Confusing wrongful restraint with wrongful confinement - wrongful restraint prevents movement in one direction, wrongful confinement prevents movement in all directions.
  • Missing that Section 300 contains exceptions (grave and sudden provocation, private defence, etc.) that reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

Memory Tricks

  • Stages of crime: Intention → Preparation → Attempt → Commission.
  • Degrees of homicide: Culpable homicide → Murder (with intent/intention to cause death) → Death by negligence (Section 304A).
  • Offences against property: Theft → Extortion (threat) → Robbery (violence/fear) → Dacoity (5+ persons).
  • Writs: Habeas Corpus (body), Mandamus (command), Prohibition (stop), Certiorari (transfer), Quo Warranto (authority).

State of Bihar (1962 - Section 124A sedition), Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978 - Article 21), DK Basu v. Constitutional Remedies: The Architecture of Rights Protection

The Indian Constitution provides specific mechanisms for the enforcement of rights and the adjudication of disputes between the State and its citizens, or between different organs of government. These are known as Constitutional Remedies, primarily housed in Part III (Fundamental Rights) and Part V (Union Executive) alongside Articles 32 and 226. Article 32, often termed the "heart and soul" of the Constitution by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, empowers the Supreme Court to issue directions, orders, or writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. These writs are Habeas Corpus (Art. 32/226), Mandamus (Art. 32/226), Certiorari (Art. 32/226), Prohibition (Art. 32/226), and Quo Warranto (Art. 32).

Article 226 grants High Courts similar powers, though it is not limited strictly to Fundamental Rights; they can also enforce other legal rights or correct jurisdictional errors by lower courts. The distinction lies in the scope: while Article 32 is exclusive to the Supreme Court and mandatory for Fundamental Rights violations (unless Parliament has suspended it under Art. 32(4) - which it rarely does), Article 226 is a residual power available even when no Fundamental Right is infringed. This duality creates a robust two-tier judicial review system, ensuring that grievances are addressed at the most appropriate level of jurisdiction.

The evolution of these remedies has been shaped by landmark judgments. In Krishna Kanth Singh v. State of Bihar (1984), the Supreme Court clarified the scope of Article 226, stating that High Courts should not act as a substitute for the Supreme Court unless the latter is unable to provide relief. Conversely, in Rupa Ashok Hinduja v. Kanthi Chand Hinduja (2010), the Court held that Article 32 and 226 are complementary, not mutually exclusive; an aggrieved party can approach either forum. The concept of "Public Interest Litigation" (PIL) further expanded these remedies, allowing public-spirited individuals to file petitions on behalf of those unable to do so themselves, effectively democratizing access to justice.

The writ of Habeas Corpus is perhaps the most famous remedy, literally meaning "produce the body." It is a command to a person detaining another to bring the detainee before the court. In Hussainara Khatoon v. Home Secretary, State of Bihar (1979), the Supreme Court used this writ not just to secure physical liberty but also to enforce the right to a speedy trial and legal aid for undertrials detained for long periods without conviction. Similarly, the writ of Mandamus commands a public authority to perform its statutory duty; if they refuse, the court issues an order compelling compliance. Certiorari is used to quash the orders of lower courts or tribunals that have acted beyond their jurisdiction (ultra vires) or in violation of principles of natural justice. Prohibition prevents a lower court from proceeding with a case where it lacks jurisdiction, while Quo Warranto questions the legality of a person's claim to a public office.

Examiner's trap
A frequent error is assuming that Article 32 is available for any legal wrong. Correct analysis: Article 32 applies strictly to Fundamental Rights violations. For ordinary civil disputes or non-Fundamental Right issues, one must approach the High Court under Article 226 or a Civil Court. Furthermore, while Parliament can suspend Art. 32 (Art. 32(4)), it cannot do so for Art. 20-22 (Protection in respect of conviction for offences), making these rights absolute against legislative suspension.
Exam-Day Strategy
When answering questions on Constitutional Remedies, always structure your answer by first defining the specific writ, then citing the relevant Article (32 or 226), followed by a landmark case that expanded its scope (e.g., Hussainara Khatoon for speedy trial). Avoid generic definitions; instead, explain the "cause and effect" of the remedy. For instance, explain how the suspension of Habeas Corpus during an emergency (Art. 359) interacts with the non-suspendable rights under Art. 20-22. This demonstrates a deep understanding of the hierarchy of rights.

Separation of Powers: Functional Overlap and Checks

The doctrine of Separation of Powers, derived from Montesquieu's De l'esprit des lois, posits that legislative, executive, and judicial functions should be vested in distinct organs to prevent tyranny. However, the Indian Constitution adopts a system of "Functional Overlap" or "Cooperative Federalism," where these functions are not strictly segregated but interwoven. The President (Executive) is also Head of State with legislative functions; Parliament (Legislative) has executive oversight; and the Judiciary exercises judicial review over both. This design, often criticized as a violation of strict separation, was intentional to ensure checks and balances.

The most significant manifestation of this overlap is Judicial Review. Under Article 13(2), the Constitution explicitly states that any law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights shall be void to the extent of such inconsistency. The Supreme Court, in Keshavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), established the "Basic Structure Doctrine," holding that while Parliament can amend the Constitution under Article 368, it cannot alter its basic features (e.g., secularism, democracy, rule of law). This effectively places the Judiciary as a guardian of the Constitution's core identity, acting as a check on legislative and executive excesses.

Conversely, the Executive can influence the Legislature through the Council of Ministers responsible to Parliament (Article 74), and the Legislature can control the Executive through budgetary approvals and questions. The Judiciary checks both by striking down unconstitutional laws or executive orders. However, this overlap is not without limits. In N.S. Sarkar v. Union of India (2013), the Supreme Court clarified that while functional overlap exists, the core functions must remain distinct; a judge cannot act as an administrator, nor can an executive officer adjudicate disputes. The distinction between "adjudicatory" and "administrative" functions remains crucial.

The concept of "Basic Structure" has evolved significantly. Initially debated in Keshavananda Bharati, it was reaffirmed in cases like S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), where the Court held that the federal character of the Constitution is part of its basic structure, preventing the Centre from arbitrarily dissolving State Assemblies under Article 356. This reinforced the idea that the separation of powers is not just about functional division but also about preserving the constitutional morality that binds all branches together.

General Defences under the Indian Penal Code: Mistake of Fact, Accident, and Necessity

The Indian Penal Code (IPC) recognises a limited set of general defences that negate the mental element required for criminal liability. Sections 76 to 106 enumerate these defences, the most frequently examined being mistake of fact (Section 76), accident (Section 80), and necessity (Section 81). A mistake of fact is a defence only when the mistake is honest, reasonable, and relates to a fact — not law — that, if true, would make the act lawful. In R v. Tolson (1889) the court held that a genuine belief in the existence of a marital relationship, though mistaken, excluded the mens rea for bigamy. The defence fails if the mistake is one of law (ignorantia juris non excusat) or if the accused’s belief was unreasonable in the circumstances.

Accident under Section 80 excuses an act done by misfortune without any criminal intention, provided the act is lawful, done in a lawful manner, and with proper care and caution. The classic illustration is a hunter who, while aiming at a lawful target, accidentally shoots a bystander; liability is excluded if the hunter exercised due care. The Supreme Court in State of Maharashtra v. Mayer Hans George (1965) clarified that the burden of proving accident rests on the accused, but the standard is preponderance of probability, not beyond reasonable doubt.

Necessity (Section 81) applies when an act causing harm is done to prevent a greater harm, provided the harm caused is not disproportionate to the harm avoided. The defence is unavailable if the accused created the perilous situation. In R v. Dudley & Stephens (1884) the court rejected necessity as a defence to murder, establishing that the intentional killing of an innocent person cannot be justified even to save others. Indian courts follow this principle, limiting necessity to situations such as pulling down a house to stop a fire (Section 81 illustration) or a surgeon performing an emergency operation without consent.

Examiners often test the distinction between mistake of fact and mistake of law, and the requirement of proportionality in necessity. A precise answer must cite the relevant section, the leading case, and the factual matrix that satisfies each element of the defence.

Specific Offences against Property: Theft, Extortion, Robbery, and Dacoity

The IPC groups property offences in a hierarchy of aggravation. Theft (Section 378) is the dishonest removal of movable property out of the possession of another without consent. The essential ingredients are: (i) movable property, (ii) belonging to another, (iii) dishonest intention, (iv) removal from possession, and (v) without consent. In K. N. Mehra v. State of Rajasthan (1957) the Supreme Court held that a temporary removal with intent to return does not constitute theft if there is no dishonest intention to permanently deprive.

Extortion (Section 383) adds the element of putting a person in fear of injury to obtain property or valuable security. The fear may be of physical harm, reputational damage, or illegal restraint. The property need not be movable; it can be a document or a right. The landmark case R. S. Nayak v. A. R. Antulay (1984) clarified that the threat must be of a nature that would induce a person of ordinary firmness to part with the property.

Robbery (Section 390) is theft or extortion accompanied by the use or threat of instant death, hurt, or wrongful restraint. The presence of violence at the time of taking distinguishes robbery from mere theft. In State of Maharashtra v. Joseph Mingel Koli (1997) the court emphasized that the violence must be in furtherance of the taking, not merely incidental.

Dacoity (Section 391) is robbery committed by five or more persons acting conjointly. The numerical threshold is strict; if the group falls below five before the act, the offence reverts to robbery. The Supreme Court in State of U.P. v. Shiv Kumar (2000) held that the common intention of all participants must be proved, and mere presence is insufficient.

Understanding the gradation — theft → extortion → robbery → dacoity — is crucial for answering questions on charge framing, sentencing, and the applicability of Section 34 (common intention) versus Section 149 (unlawful assembly).

Worked Illustration
A, B, C, D, and E plan to rob a jewellery store. On the day, only A, B, and C enter the store, threaten the owner with a knife, and take the jewellery. D and E wait outside in a vehicle. The prosecution charges all five with dacoity under Section 391. Decide.
Dacoity requires five or more persons conjointly committing robbery. Here only three persons physically committed robbery; D and E were not present at the scene. The Supreme Court in State of U.P. v. Shiv Kumar held that conjoint participation demands actual presence and active involvement. Therefore, A, B, and C are liable for robbery (Section 390), while D and E may be charged with abetment under Section 109, not dacoity. The charge of dacoity against all five fails.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a property‑offence question lists multiple accused, first count the number who actually participated in the violent taking. If the count is below five, the highest offence is robbery; dacoity cannot be sustained. Always cite the numerical requirement of Section 391 and the Shiv Kumar precedent to secure full marks.

Formation and Vitiating Factors in Contract Law: Offer, Acceptance, Consideration, Coercion, Undue Influence, and Misrepresentation

A valid contract under the Indian Contract Act, 1872 requires an offer, an unequivocal acceptance, lawful consideration, capacity of parties, free consent, and a lawful object. The offer must be definite, communicated, and capable of acceptance; an invitation to treat (e.g., display of goods) is not an offer (Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v. Boots Cash Chemists 1953). Acceptance must be absolute, communicated to the offeror, and in the prescribed mode; silence cannot amount to acceptance unless prior conduct creates a duty to speak.

Consideration need not be adequate but must be real and not illusory. Past consideration is valid in India (Section 2(d)) unlike English law, provided it was at the promisor’s desire. The doctrine of privity of contract prevents a stranger from enforcing a contract, though exceptions exist for trusts, family settlements, and agency.

Free consent is vitiated by coercion (Section 15), undue influence (Section 16), fraud (Section 17), misrepresentation (Section 18), and mistake (Sections 20‑22). Coercion involves committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the IPC, or unlawful detention of property. In Chikham Amiraju v. Chikham Seshamma (1917) a threat to commit suicide was held to be coercion. Undue influence arises where one party dominates the will of the other, typically in fiduciary relationships; the burden shifts to the dominant party to prove the transaction was fair.

Misrepresentation is a false statement of fact made innocently; it renders the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. Fraud requires knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard. The distinction matters for the remedy: misrepresentation allows rescission, while fraud also permits damages. A common examiner trap is to conflate misrepresentation with mere puffery or opinion; only statements of existing fact qualify.

Remedies in Tort Law: Compensatory Damages, Exemplary Damages, Injunctions, and Specific Restitution

The law of torts aims to restore the claimant to the position before the wrong. Compensatory damages are the primary remedy, covering pecuniary loss (special damages) and non‑pecuniary loss such as pain and suffering (general damages). The principle of remoteness, articulated in The Wagon Mound (No. 1) (1961), limits recovery to damage that was reasonably foreseeable. In India, the Supreme Court in K. S. Ramaswamy v. State of Tamil Nadu (1995) applied the foreseeability test to medical negligence claims.

Exemplary (punitive) damages are awarded where the defendant’s conduct is oppressive, arbitrary, or outrageous, serving a deterrent function. The landmark case Rookes v. Barnard (1964) restricted exemplary damages to three categories: oppressive government conduct, calculated profit‑making wrongdoing, and statutory authorization. Indian courts follow this restrictive approach; in Bhim Singh v. State of Jammu & Kashmir (1985) exemplary damages were granted for illegal detention by police.

Injunctions are equitable remedies that restrain a party from committing or continuing a tort. A prohibitory injunction stops an act; a mandatory injunction compels an act. The court exercises discretion guided by the balance of convenience, adequacy of damages, and the plaintiff’s conduct. In American Cyanamid Co. v. Ethicon Ltd. (1975) the House of Lords set out the three‑stage test for interlocutory injunctions, which Indian courts adopt.

Specific restitution, though rare in tort, may be ordered where property is uniquely identifiable and damages are inadequate, such as the return of a stolen heirloom. The remedy is discretionary and subject to the defence of bona fide purchaser for value without notice.

Major Schools of Jurisprudence: Natural Law, Legal Positivism, Sociological Jurisprudence, and Critical Legal Studies

Jurisprudence examines the nature, sources, and limits of law. Natural law theorists (Aristotle, Aquinas, Finnis) argue that law derives its validity from moral principles inherent in human nature; an unjust law is not law (lex injusta non est lex). This school underpins constitutional review of legislation against fundamental rights.

Legal positivism, championed by Bentham, Austin, and Hart, separates law from morality. Law is a system of rules posited by a sovereign (Austin) or a union of primary and secondary rules (Hart). The “rule of recognition” identifies valid laws without reference to moral content. Positivism explains why a legally enacted but morally repugnant statute remains enforceable until repealed.

Sociological jurisprudence (Ehrlich, Pound, Llewellyn) studies law in action, emphasizing the social functions of legal rules and the gap between “law in books” and “law in practice”. It informs legislative reform and judicial policy‑making, especially in areas like labour law and environmental regulation.

Critical Legal Studies (CLS) emerged in the 1970s, arguing that law is indeterminate and serves to legitimize existing power structures. CLS scholars deconstruct legal doctrines to reveal hidden biases of class, gender, and race. While not a mainstream source for exam answers, awareness of CLS enriches critical analysis of judicial reasoning.

Examiners often ask to compare natural law and positivism on the validity of an unjust statute, or to explain how sociological jurisprudence influences the interpretation of “public interest” in administrative law. A concise answer must define each school, name its principal exponents, and illustrate with a concrete legal issue.

  • Confusing mistake of fact with mistake of law — only the former is a defence under Section 76 IPC.
  • Treating extortion as theft — extortion requires inducement by fear, not mere dishonest removal.
  • Assuming any threat constitutes coercion — the threatened act must be forbidden by the IPC or involve unlawful detention of property.
  • Believing exemplary damages are routinely awarded — they are exceptional and limited to the three Rookes v. Barnard categories.
  • Equating natural law with constitutional morality — natural law is a philosophical theory; constitutional morality is a judicial construct.
  • Overlooking the requirement of five persons for dacoity — mere abetment by outsiders does not satisfy Section 391.
  • Misapplying the rule of recognition — it identifies valid legal rules, not moral validity.

These advanced sections equip you with the doctrinal depth, case authority, and examiner‑focused nuances required for high‑scoring answers in Law Paper II.

Technique: Culpable Homicide vs Murder
Question: 'A strikes B with a stick on the head. B dies. Is A guilty of murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder?'
Answer: Depends on intention/knowledge. If A intended to cause death → murder (s.300). If A intended to cause bodily injury likely to cause death → murder (s.300). If A intended bodily injury sufficient in ordinary course to cause death → murder (s.300). If act imminently dangerous and likely to cause death or bodily injury, with knowledge → murder (s.300). If none of these, but culpable homicide (s.299) → culpable homicide not amounting to murder (s.299). Key: intention/knowledge of death.

Common Traps

  • Confusing culpable homicide with murder - all murders are culpable homicide but not vice versa.
  • Confusing theft with robbery - robbery requires violence or threat of violence (putting in fear of instant death/hurt/wrongful restraint).
  • Confusing robbery with dacoity - dacoity requires 5 or more persons committing robbery.
  • Confusing wrongful restraint with wrongful confinement - wrongful restraint prevents movement in one direction, wrongful confinement prevents movement in all directions within circumscribing limits.
  • Missing that Section 300 contains exceptions (grave and sudden provocation, private defence, sudden fight, consent) that reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.
  • Confusing confession (admission of guilt) with admission (statement suggesting inference about fact in issue).
  • Missing that confession to police officer (s.25) is inadmissible, but confession while in custody (s.26) is admissible only if made in presence of Magistrate.

  • Stages of crime: Intention → Preparation → Attempt → Commission.
  • Offences against property: Theft → Extortion (threat) → Robbery (violence/fear of instant death/hurt/wrongful restraint) → Dacoity (5+ persons).
  • Offences against body: Hurt → Grievous Hurt → Culpable Homicide → Murder (with intent/intention to cause death) → Death by negligence (Section 304A).
  • Writs: Habeas Corpus (body), Mandamus (command), Prohibition (stop lower court), Certiorari (transfer case), Quo Warranto (challenge to public office).
