The missionary presses standardized orthography and a core lexicon; they did not create a standardized spoken norm. Santali remains a dialect continuum (Kurmukhi, Mahali, etc.), and the literary language taught in universities today is a conscious construction drawing on the mission-era written norm, Ol Chiki-era neologisms, and Sanskritized administrative vocabulary. An advanced answer on “history of the language” must trace this three-layered stratification: the pre-contact oral lexicon, the mission-print lexical layer (especially abstract nouns formed with -akan, -tan suffixes), and the post-1925 Ol Chiki revivalist layer (neologisms for modern concepts like bintir ‘university’, dak ‘post’).

Agglutinative Morphology as Poetic Architecture in Santali Verse

Santali belongs to the North Munda branch of Austroasiatic and exhibits a richly agglutinative morphology that directly determines its poetic possibilities. Unlike Indo-Aryan languages where meter is typically quantitative or stress-based, Santali verse — both oral and written — exploits the language’s suffixal architecture. The verb complex can carry up to seven suffix slots encoding direction, benefactive, causative, reciprocal, tense, aspect, mood, and subject agreement. A single verb form such as sen-a-ɛt-ko-a-kan-a-e (go-BEN-CAUS-RECIP-PST-TR-3SG.SUBJ ‘he made them go for each other’) constitutes a complete syntactic unit. This density allows Santali oral poets to pack narrative action into rhythmic units that resist translation into analytic languages.

The traditional karbi (creation myth) and tuam (narrative poem) rely on parallelism built through morphological repetition rather than lexical synonymy. A bard will repeat the same verb root with systematically varied suffixes to enact narrative progression: sen-akan ‘going’, sen-tan ‘having gone’, sen-ket ‘go! (imperative)’, sen-ɔk ‘let him go’. This morphological parallelism is the primary poetic device; end-rhyme is marginal. When modern Santali poets writing in Ol Chiki adopt free verse, they often retain this morphological patterning as a structural ghost. Bishnu Charan Mahato’s poetry, for instance, uses chains of converbal suffixes (-te, -kan, -ta) to create a syntactic flow that mimics oral prosody while dispensing with the fixed refrain structures of tuam.

The examiner may ask you to “analyze the structure of a Santali poem.” A superficial answer counts lines or stanzas. An advanced answer identifies the morphological skeleton: it maps the suffix chains, notes where the poet breaks the expected paradigm (e.g., using a bare root where a converb is expected), and links that deviation to semantic emphasis. You must also distinguish between the prosodic word (the phonological unit relevant to stress assignment) and the grammatical word (the verb complex). In Santali, stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word, which often splits the verb complex. This misalignment between stress domain and morphological domain creates a subtle counter-rhythm that skilled oral performers exploit. Written poetry that ignores this misalignment often reads as flat; the best Ol Chiki poets calibrate line breaks to coincide with prosodic word boundaries, not grammatical word boundaries.

Technique: Morphological Scansion in Answer Writing
Question: “Discuss how the agglutinative structure of Santali shapes the internal rhythm of a tuam stanza. Illustrate with a schematic analysis.”
Solution: Begin by defining the verb complex as the rhythmic nucleus. Present a schematic stanza (you may construct a representative example if the prescribed text is not memorized):
Sen-akan do, sen-tan do, sen-ket do, sen-ɔk do.
Gloss: ‘Going, having gone, go!, let him go.’
Analyze: Each line ends with the particle do (focus/marker), creating a refrain. The verb root sen- is constant; the suffix chain varies systematically: -akan (infinitive/nominal), -tan (perfective converb), -ket (imperative), -ɔk (optative). This is morphological parallelism.
Prosodic scansion: Each verb complex forms two prosodic words: se.ná.kan (stress on ná), se.ná.tan, se.ná.ket, se.ná.ɔk. The stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the suffix, not the root. The rhythm is therefore suffix-driven.
Critical point: The shift from converb (-tan) to imperative (-ket) marks a modal shift from narrative to hortatory — the bard commands the audience to enact the myth. Conclude that the agglutinative morphology is not decorative; it encodes the performative pragmatics of the tuam.
Exam-Day Strategy: The Morphological Anchor
If a Paper II question asks for “critical appreciation” of a poem you have not memorized, open with a morphological observation: “The stanza exploits Santali’s suffixal verb complex to enact X.” Even without quoting the exact text, you demonstrate technical competence. Memorize the seven verb-suffix slots (Direction → Benefactive → Causative → Reciprocal → Tense/Aspect → Mood → Agreement) and one illustrative chain. This is a high-yield, low-memory anchor.

Translation Politics: From Oral Performance to Ol Chiki Text to English Anthology

Every prescribed text in Paper II exists in at least three mediated forms: the oral performance (often unrecorded), the Ol Chiki printed edition (the “standard” text for examination), and the English translation (usually the only version accessible to non-Santali examiners and scholars). The syllabus does not explicitly teach translation theory, but the examiner expects you to negotiate these layers. The politics of translation in Santali operates on three axes: script, register, and epistemic authority.

First, script translation: moving from Roman-script mission editions (Skrefsrud, Bodding, Campbell) to Ol Chiki involves more than transliteration. Ol Chiki’s alphabetic principle (each letter represents a phoneme, with distinct letters for checked/unchecked vowels and pre-glottalized consonants) forces phonological decisions that the Roman script left ambiguous. For example, the mission orthography wrote a for both the unchecked low vowel and the checked low vowel; Ol Chiki distinguishes them as ᱚ and ᱟ. A modern editor must choose, and that choice reconstructs the phonology of a text that may have been dictated by a speaker of a different dialect. When you cite a text in the exam, you are implicitly endorsing the editor’s reconstruction.

Second, register translation: oral karbi and tuam use a high-register lexicon rich in archaic Austroasiatic roots (e.g., marang ‘great’, sing ‘sun’, bonga ‘deity/spirit’). Mission translations systematically replaced these with Sanskritized or Bengali loans (mahān, sūrya, devatā) to make the texts intelligible to Bengali-reading administrators and converts. The Ol Chiki revivalists of the 1950s–80s (Pandit Raghunath Murmu, Guru Gomasta Prasad Soren) deliberately purged these loans, coining neologisms from native roots. The prescribed text you read is therefore a reconstructed register, not a direct transcript of any recorded performance.

Third, epistemic translation: English anthologies (e.g., The Santal Worldview by Marine Carrin, Santali Folk Tales by various translators) impose Western genre categories — “myth,” “folktale,” “legend” — onto Santali categories that do not map neatly. The Santali term binti covers both historical narrative and mythic charter; katha covers both folktale and moral fable. An examiner who asks “Is this text a myth or a folktale?” is testing whether you recognize the category error. The correct move is to refuse the binary and explain the indigenous genre term, then show how the English translation’s paratext (introduction, footnotes, glossary) shapes the reader’s interpretation.

Periodization Contests: Colonial Ethnography, Nationalist Recovery, and Indigenous Historiography

The syllabus presents a periodization (Ancient, Medieval, Modern) that is itself a historical artifact. Three competing periodizations circulate in Santali literary scholarship, and an advanced answer must signal awareness of the contest.

The colonial ethnographic periodization (Skrefsrud, Bodding, Risley, Bradley-Birt) divides Santali culture into “pre-contact” (pure, static) and “post-contact” (decaying, syncretic). Literature is treated as folklore data; the concept of “author” is irrelevant. This framework dominates early missionary grammars and the Census of India reports. Its legacy persists in the syllabus’s “Ancient Period” label, which implies a unified pre-literate past.

The nationalist recovery periodization (post-1947, especially in university departments) imposes the standard Indian template: Ancient (oral, pre-1850), Medieval (mission print, 1850–1925), Modern (Ol Chiki, post-1925). This aligns Santali with Sanskrit, Tamil, Bengali historiography but obscures the fact that Santali had no “classical” textual tradition comparable to kāvya or saṅgam. The “Medieval” label is particularly misleading: it suggests a literary flourishing under patronage, whereas the mission print era was a rupture, not a continuity.

The indigenous historiography (Ol Chiki movement intellectuals: Pandit Raghunath Murmu, Aditya Kumar Mandi, Damayanti Besra) periodizes by script and institution: Ol Chiki Arang (Before Ol Chiki, oral/manuscript), Ol Chiki Sere (Ol Chiki Era, 1925–present), subdivided into Sere Aam (Early Ol Chiki, 1925–1950), Sere Majhi (Middle, 1950–1990), Sere Hɔṛ (Contemporary, post-1990). This periodization centers the script as the agent of literary modernity and treats the 92nd Constitutional Amendment (2003) as a watershed.

In the exam, if a question asks “Discuss the development of Santali literature in the modern period,” do not default to the nationalist template. Open by naming the three periodizations, state which you will use and why (e.g., “I adopt the indigenous periodization because it aligns with the syllabus’s emphasis on Ol Chiki as a transformative technology”), and then structure your answer accordingly. This meta-commentary alone distinguishes a 120+ answer from a 90 answer.

Gendered Narrative Spaces: Women’s Autobiography and Testimonio in Contemporary Santali Writing

Since the 1990s, a distinct corpus of women’s life writing has emerged in Santali, largely unpublished in mainstream anthologies but circulating in little magazines (Sarjom, Horh, Ol Chiki Binti) and university journals. This corpus — autobiography (apni binti), testimonio (horo binti), and epistolary narrative — operates in a narrative space that is neither the communal oral karbi nor the individualistic modern novel. The syllabus mentions “modern prose” but does not prescribe specific women’s texts; however, Paper II’s “socio-cultural criticism” questions increasingly expect engagement with gender as an analytical category.

The formal signature of Santali women’s autobiography is the we-voice that resists consolidation into an I. Damayanti Besra’s Apni Binti (serialized 1998–2000) opens with “We, the daughters of the forest, speak” (Am jomak horo, am binti koram). The plural pronoun persists even when narrating strictly personal events (marriage, childbirth, widowhood). This is not a grammatical quirk; it reflects the Santali kinship system where a woman’s identity is constituted through her natal and affinal clans (paris). The narrative moves through ritual moments — chatiar (first menstruation), bapla (marriage), sohrae (harvest festival) — where the individual body is the site of collective reproduction.

Crucially, these texts deploy the testimonio mode: a first-person narrative that bears witness to structural violence (displacement by mining, witch-hunting accusations, domestic abuse) while refusing the victim/heroine binary imposed by NGO reportage. The language mixes high-register Ol Chiki literary Santali with dialectal Kurmukhi inflections and code-switched Hindi/English bureaucratic terms (FIR, patta, compensation). This heteroglossia is the text’s political argument: the Santali woman speaks in a language that the state cannot fully assimilate.

For the examiner, the trap is to read these texts as “women’s empowerment narratives” in a liberal individualist frame. The correct critical frame is collective subjectivity under settler-colonial pressure. When a question asks “Analyze the representation of women in modern Santali fiction,” you must distinguish between male-authored fiction (where women often function as symbols of cultural purity or loss) and women’s life writing (where the narrative form itself enacts resistance to symbolic appropriation). Cite the we-voice, the ritual temporalities, and the bureaucratic code-switching as formal evidence.

  • Conflating mission orthography with linguistic reality: Do not treat Skrefsrud’s Roman-script vowel distinctions as phonemic universals; they reflect one dialect and one analyst’s ear.
  • Ignoring the editor’s hand in prescribed texts: Every Ol Chiki edition involves phonological reconstruction. Acknowledge the editor (e.g., “In the 1985 Ol Chiki edition edited by X…”).
  • Applying Indo-Aryan genre categories uncritically: “Epic,” “lyric,” “novel” are not indigenous terms. Use karbi, tuam, binti, katha and explain the mismatch.
  • Defaulting to the nationalist periodization without justification: Name the three periodizations (colonial, nationalist, indigenous) and choose one explicitly.
  • Reading women’s life writing as individual confession: The we-voice and ritual temporalities mark collective subjectivity; do not impose a Western autobiographical subject.
  • Overlooking bureaucratic code-switching as style: Terms like FIR, patta, rehabilitation in Santali texts are not “impurities” — they index the state’s legal vocabulary entering the literary language.
  • Treating Ol Chiki as a neutral script: Ol Chiki’s letter shapes encode cosmological principles (the six directions, the five elements). An answer on “script and identity” must engage this iconicity, not just its alphabetic efficiency.
opt-santali/paper1:
Santali Paper I — History of the Language, Movements, Authors and Works

History of the Language

Santali is a Munda language of the Austroasiatic family. It has a rich oral tradition; the Ol Chiki script was invented by Raghunath Murmu in 1925, and modern written literature developed in the 20th century.

Literary Periods and Movements

  • Oral period: Folk songs, creation myths and narrative poems.
  • Early written period (20th c.): Ol Chiki script, primers and early publications.
  • Modern period (mid-20th c.–present): Poetry, drama, fiction and Sahitya Akademi recognition.

Major Authors

  • Raghunath Murmu: Inventor of the Ol Chiki script and pioneer of modern Santali writing.
  • Sadhu Ramchand Murmu: Santali poet and writer.
  • Santali Sahitya Akademi writers: Modern Santali poets, dramatists and fiction writers.

Major Works

  • Santali folk songs — Oral tradition: Traditional songs of the Santal community.
  • Ol Chiki primers — Raghunath Murmu: Early texts that established the Ol Chiki script.
  • Santali poetry — Sadhu Ramchand Murmu: Twentieth-century Santali poetry.
  • Modern Santali drama — Modern Santali writers: Twentieth-century drama.
Model-generated practice passage (Ol Chiki script)
ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ ᱯᱟᱹᱨᱥᱤ ᱫᱚ ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ ᱦᱚᱲᱠᱚ ᱟᱜ ᱯᱟᱹᱨᱥᱤ ᱠᱟᱱᱟ ᱾ ᱱᱚᱶᱟ ᱯᱟᱹᱨᱥᱤ ᱫᱚ ᱚᱞ ᱪᱤᱠᱤ ᱛᱮ ᱚᱞᱚᱜᱼᱟ ᱾ ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ ᱠᱚᱣᱟᱜ ᱢᱟᱨᱟᱝ ᱯᱚᱨᱚᱵᱽ ᱫᱚ ᱥᱚᱦᱨᱟᱭ ᱠᱟᱱᱟ ᱾
English meaning: Santali is the language of the Santal people. This language is written in the Ol Chiki script. The major festival of the Santals is Sohrai.
Provenance

Solved Example: Author and Period
Question: Place Raghunath Murmu in the literary history of Santali and assess their contribution.
Answer: Raghunath Murmu belongs to the Oral period phase. Inventor of the Ol Chiki script and pioneer of modern Santali writing. The contribution should be assessed through language, theme and form, and through influence on later writers.

Memory Tricks

  • Timeline: Oral period → Early written period (20th c.) → Modern period (mid-20th c.–present).
  • Authors: Raghunath Murmu, Sadhu Ramchand Murmu, Santali Sahitya Akademi writers.
  • Works: Santali folk songs, Ol Chiki primers, Santali poetry, Modern Santali drama.
Mains strategy
For Paper I, use the sequence: language origin → period → movement → author → work. Add one short quotation or native term per answer. Draw a timeline in the margin if the question asks for development. Avoid unverified dates; approximate centuries are safer.

Evolution of Literary Forms: From Oral Folklore to Modern Prose

The trajectory of Santali literature is not merely a linear progression from "oral" to "written," but a complex transformation of form, function, and audience. Understanding this evolution is crucial for Paper I questions that ask about the "nature of change" or "shifts in thematic concerns." The transition was driven by the invention of the Ol Chiki script (1925), which allowed the codification of fluid oral traditions into fixed textual forms.

The Oral Period: Fluidity and Communal Function

In the pre-1925 era, Santali literature existed almost exclusively in an oral mode. The primary forms were Khel (songs), Bhagani (creation myths), and Kabir (narrative poems). These works were characterized by:

  • Metric Flexibility: Unlike fixed poetry, oral songs allowed for improvisation based on the singer's mood or audience reaction.
  • Communal Ownership: Songs like Sohrai and Kuk were not attributed to a single author but belonged to the community. They served ritualistic functions (harvest, marriage, initiation) rather than aesthetic ones in isolation.
  • Motif Repetition: Recurrent themes included nature worship, ancestor reverence, and moral instruction through allegory.

The Transitional Period: The Impact of Ol Chiki (1925–1940)

Raghunath Murmu's invention of the script acted as a catalyst for "fixation." However, this was not an immediate shift to modern prose. The early written period saw the publication of primers and religious texts. This phase introduced standardization. For instance, dialectal variations were smoothed out to create a literary norm. Authors like Sadhu Ramchand Murmu began experimenting with free verse, moving away from strict rhythmic patterns used in folk songs. The audience shifted from the village square (ritual context) to the schoolroom and reading public.

The Modern Period: Prose, Fiction, and Drama

Post-independence, Santali literature diversified significantly. The emergence of fiction required a new narrative structure that did not exist in oral tradition. Writers began exploring individual psychology, social conflict, and urban displacement—themes alien to traditional folk songs. Drama also emerged as a distinct form, often staged for festivals but written with specific dialogue structures. This period is marked by the establishment of the Santali Sahitya Akademi (1960s), which institutionalized literary criticism and canon formation.

Example: Analyzing the Shift in Form
Question: How did the invention of the Ol Chiki script alter the structural integrity of Santali folk songs, and what were the implications for their transmission?
Answer:
The introduction of the Ol Chiki script transformed fluid oral compositions into fixed textual entities. In the oral period, a song like Sohrai could vary in length and wording depending on the singer. With the advent of written literature, specific versions were codified in primers and anthologies.

Implications:
1. Loss of Improvisation: The ability to adapt songs to immediate contexts diminished as "correct" texts became authoritative.
2. Preservation vs. Stagnation: While the core content was preserved from extinction, the dynamic evolution of the language within the song form slowed down.
3. Shift in Audience: The primary mode of transmission shifted from auditory (listening) to visual (reading), changing how literature was consumed and critiqued.
Exam Strategy: Contextualizing "Change"
Tip: When answering questions about literary movements, do not just list dates. Always contrast the function of the literature in different periods. For example, explain how a folk song served a ritual purpose in the oral period but might serve an educational or aesthetic purpose in the modern period. Use terms like "codification," "standardization," and "institutionalization" to demonstrate depth.

Thematic Analysis: From Nature Worship to Social Realism

The thematic content of Santali literature has undergone a profound metamorphosis, reflecting the changing socio-political landscape of the Munda-speaking region. This evolution is essential for answering questions regarding "thematic shifts" or "sociological relevance."

1. The Nature-Centric Universe (Pre-20th Century)

Early literature was deeply animistic and ecological. Themes revolved around the veneration of natural elements: Bong (forest), Hajong (sun), Kharia (moon). The relationship between humans and nature was one of symbiosis and reverence. Myths like Bhagani explained the origin of the world through natural forces. There was no concept of "man vs. nature"; rather, it was "man within nature."

2. The Rise of Social Consciousness (Mid-20th Century)

With the influence of Christian missionaries and later socialist movements, literature began to address social ills. Themes of caste discrimination, land alienation, and exploitation by dominant castes entered the literary discourse. Writers like Sankha Barua and others started using literature as a tool for social reform. The "nature" theme was not abandoned but reinterpreted through the lens of human suffering caused by external forces.

3. Modern Realism and Identity Politics (Late 20th Century–Present)

Contemporary Santali literature grapples with themes of identity, globalization, and migration. The "Santal" is no longer just a forest dweller but an urbanite facing alienation. Themes include the loss of traditional values in modern society, the struggle for linguistic rights (e.g., inclusion in the Eighth Schedule), and the intersectionality of Santali identity with broader Indian nationalism. Fiction now explores the inner conflicts of individuals caught between tradition and modernity.

Example: Thematic Contrast
Question: Compare the treatment of 'nature' in a traditional Bong (forest) song versus a modern Santali short story. How does this reflect broader societal changes?
Answer:
In traditional songs, nature is personified and revered as a deity or ancestor. The forest is a source of life and spiritual connection; the language used is reverential and descriptive.

In modern short stories (e.g., by contemporary Akademi writers), nature often appears as a backdrop to human conflict or a symbol of lost innocence. The relationship may be critical, highlighting environmental degradation or the displacement of Santal communities from their ancestral lands.

Conclusion: This shift reflects the transition from an agrarian, forest-dependent economy to one influenced by industrialization and urbanization, where nature is viewed through a lens of loss and nostalgia rather than active worship.
Exam Strategy: Avoiding Anachronism
Tip: Do not attribute modern social realist themes to pre-1925 literature. Examiners often try to trick candidates by asking about "social reform" in the oral period. Always qualify your answer with the specific historical context (e.g., "Post-independence," "After 1947"). Acknowledge that early literature was primarily mythological and ritualistic, not sociological.

Criticism and Canon Formation: The Role of Institutions

A sophisticated understanding of Santali literature requires knowledge of how "canon" is formed. In the oral period, there was no canon; authority lay with tradition. The modern period introduced literary criticism, journals, and institutions like the Santali Sahitya Akademi. This section covers the mechanisms by which certain works became "classic" while others were marginalized.

The Mechanism of Canonization

Literary works in Santali are elevated to "classic" status through:

  1. Institutional Recognition: Awards from the Sahitya Akademi (New Delhi and regional bodies) play a significant role.
  2. Translation and Anthologization: Works that are translated into Hindi or English often gain wider recognition, though this can sometimes dilute their original context.
  3. Educational Inclusion: Textbooks and syllabi determine what is taught. If a poet's work is included in school readers, they become part of the "official" literary history.

The Debate on Translation vs. Originality

A critical issue in Santali literature is the relationship between original works and translations. Early writers often wrote in a simplified dialect to make it accessible. Later critics argue that this "simplification" compromised linguistic purity. Furthermore, the dominance of certain dialects (e.g., those spoken in Jharkhand vs. Odisha) in literary production has led to debates about regional representation within Santali literature.

Example: Institutional Impact
Question: Discuss the role of the Santali Sahitya Akademi in shaping the canon of Santali literature. What are the criticisms of its selection process?
Answer:
The Santali Sahitya Akademi was established to promote and preserve Santali literature. Its role includes:
1. Dissemination: Publishing journals like Santali and organizing literary festivals.
2. Awards: Recognizing outstanding works, thereby encouraging high-quality writing.

Criticisms:
1. Elitism: Critics argue that the Akademi sometimes favors established writers from urban centers over grassroots oral poets.
2. Linguistic Bias: There are concerns that the literary language is becoming too standardized, losing its connection to diverse regional dialects.
3.

Script Development and Standardization: Ol Chiki, Latin, and Devanagari

The emergence of a dedicated script for Santali is a defining moment in the language’s literary history. Until the early twentieth century, Santali was written in three parallel graphic systems: the Latin alphabet introduced by Norwegian missionaries such as Lars Olsen Skrefsrud and Paul Olaf Bodding, the Devanagari script adopted by writers in the Bengal‑Presidency region, and the Bengali script used in colonial administrative records. Each system carried distinct sociolinguistic connotations; the Latin orthography was associated with missionary education and biblical translation, while Devanagari linked Santali to the broader Hindi‑Sanskrit cultural sphere.

In 1925 Pandit Raghunath Murmu devised Ol Chiki, an alphabetic script designed specifically for the phonology of Santali. Ol Chiki contains thirty letters, each representing a distinct consonant or vowel, and it marks the glottal stop and nasalization that are phonemic in the language. The script was promoted through community schools, the magazine Hor Sambad, and later by the Santali Sahitya Akademi. Its adoption was not instantaneous; for several decades publications continued to appear in Latin and Devanagari, creating a fragmented print culture. The turning point came in the 1970s when the Akademi mandated Ol Chiki for all official publications, examinations, and textbook production. This policy accelerated standardization but also sparked debates about the loss of dialectal nuance, because Ol Chiki’s fixed letter‑to‑sound correspondence tends to privilege the prestige dialect spoken around the Santhal Parganas.

Comparative analysis of the three scripts reveals concrete consequences for literary form. Latin‑based texts often retain diacritical marks for tone and vowel length, preserving oral prosody on the page. Devanagari editions, by contrast, impose the inherent vowel ‘a’ on consonant clusters, which can obscure the distinctive Santali syllable structure. Ol Chiki resolves these issues but introduces a new visual identity that separates Santali literature visually from both the Indo‑Aryan and the missionary traditions. For the examiner, the key point is that script choice is never neutral; it shapes orthographic conventions, influences which dialects become “literary”, and determines the accessibility of texts to different reader communities.

Dialectal Variation and the Construction of a Literary Standard

Santali is not a monolithic speech form; it comprises at least four major dialect clusters — Northern (Santhal Parganas, Jharkhand), Southern (Mayurbhanj, Odisha), Western (Bankura, West Bengal), and Eastern (Assam, Tripura). Phonological differences include the realization of the retroflex series, the presence or absence of the voiced aspirated stops, and vowel quality shifts in word‑final position. Lexical variation is equally pronounced: the word for “river” is daṅ in the north, daṅa in the south, and daṅg in the west. Morphologically, the Southern dialects retain a richer set of honorific suffixes that have largely disappeared from the Northern variety.

The construction of a literary standard began with the missionary grammars of Skrefsrud (1873) and Bodding (1929), which codified the Northern dialect as the reference variety because the mission stations were concentrated there. Subsequent textbook committees, notably the 1956 Santali Language Committee under the Bihar government, formalized this choice by prescribing Northern pronunciation, vocabulary, and grammar for school curricula. The Santali Sahitya Akademi, established in 1979, reinforced the standard through its publication guidelines, award criteria, and the orthographic norms of Ol Chiki.

Critics argue that this top‑down standardization marginalizes Southern and Western oral traditions. Folk epics such as Baha Bonga (Southern) and Karam Dar (Western) exhibit narrative motifs and lexical items absent from the Northern canon. When these works are transcribed into the standard language, distinctive features are often “corrected”, erasing dialectal authenticity. A nuanced answer in the examination should acknowledge that the literary standard enables inter‑regional communication and institutional support, yet it simultaneously functions as a gatekeeping mechanism that privileges one regional variety over others. The tension between unity and diversity remains a live issue in contemporary Santali literary criticism.

Technique: Mapping Script‑Dialect Intersections
Question: Explain how the adoption of Ol Chiki as the official script interacted with the Northern‑dialect‑based literary standard to shape the canon of modern Santali poetry.
Ol Chiki was designed on the phonology of the Northern dialect, which already enjoyed institutional prestige through missionary grammars and state textbooks. When the Akademi mandated Ol Chiki, publishers were required to render all submissions in that script, effectively forcing Southern and Western poets to transcribe their dialectal forms into a Northern‑centric orthography. This double filter — script and standard dialect — meant that poems preserving Southern honorific suffixes or Western vowel shifts were either rejected or “regularized” before publication. Consequently, the early modern canon (1970s‑1990s) overwhelmingly reflects Northern lexical and phonological norms, while dialect‑specific oral aesthetics survive mainly in unpublished field recordings. A high‑scoring answer will cite the 1979 Akademi resolution, the phonemic inventory of Ol Chiki, and at least one concrete example such as the regularization of the Southern ‑ko honorific to the Northern ‑kan in printed anthologies.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about “standardization”, always separate the three layers: (1) script choice, (2) dialect selection, (3) institutional enforcement. Cite the specific year of each policy (1925 Ol Chiki, 1956 Language Committee, 1979 Akademi) and name one literary work affected by each layer. This three‑point structure signals depth and avoids the common trap of conflating script with dialect.

Print Culture and Periodicals: Journals as Engines of Literary Modernity

The transition from oral performance to printed text in Santali was mediated by a network of periodicals that began appearing in the 1920s. Hor Sambad (1925), edited by Pandit Raghunath Murmu, was the first magazine to use Ol Chiki exclusively; it published poetry, short stories, and essays on grammar, thereby creating a readership that could engage with literature in the new script. In the 1950s, Santali (published from Ranchi under the aegis of the Bihar Tribal Welfare Department) broadened the scope to include literary criticism, book reviews, and translations from Hindi and Bengali. The 1970s saw the launch of Sar Sagun from Bhubaneswar, which gave space to Southern dialect writers and to women authors such as Maino Murmu, whose short story “Jahar” (1978) is widely regarded as the first feminist narrative in Santali prose.

These journals performed three interlocking functions. First, they established a peer‑review culture: editorial boards comprising senior writers and linguists evaluated submissions, effectively acting as the first formal literary critics in the language. Second, they serialized novels — for example, Paul Jujhar Soren’s Baha Bonga (1972) appeared in installments in Santali before book publication — allowing authors to test narrative techniques with an immediate audience. Third, they facilitated the formation of literary societies; the “Santali Sahitya Parishad” (1968) grew out of correspondence columns in Hor Sambad and later organized the first All‑India Santali Writers’ Conference (1974).

From an examination perspective, the periodicals are evidence that modern Santali literature did not emerge in a vacuum but was co‑produced by print technology, state patronage, and community activism. A strong answer will trace the chronological chain: missionary press → Ol Chiki magazine → state‑sponsored journal → Akademi‑backed review → national conference, and will note how each stage expanded the thematic range from mythological retellings to social realism and gender critique.

Translation Trajectories: From Missionary Texts to Global Anthologies

Translation has been a constant vector in the life of Santali literature. The earliest translations were biblical: Skrefsrud’s New Testament (1895) and Bodding’s complete Bible (1914) rendered Santali into Latin script, establishing a written lexicon for theological concepts. These texts introduced syntactic calques — such as the use of bonga for “spirit” — that later entered secular writing. In the mid‑twentieth century, the Sahitya Akademi (New Delhi) commissioned Hindi translations of major Santali works, notably the novel Kherwal Bonga by Damayanti Besra (Hindi title Kherwal Bonga, 1965). The Hindi versions broadened readership but often flattened the ergative‑absolutive alignment of Santali into Hindi’s nominative‑accusative pattern, a loss noted by linguist G. N. Devy in his 1992 survey.

The 1990s witnessed a shift toward English translation driven by the “tribal literature” boom in Indian universities and international anthologies. The landmark volume The Oxford India Anthology of Tribal Literature (1999) included Santali poems translated by the poet‑translator Nirmal Kumar Besra. These translations foregrounded the metaphorical density of Santali oral imagery — e.g., the recurring motif of the sal tree as witness — while providing glossaries for culturally specific terms. However, the dominance of English as the target language has raised concerns about “exoticization”, where the aesthetic is packaged for a non‑tribal gaze rather than for community circulation.

For the aspirant, the critical insight is that each translation epoch reconfigures the power relation between source and target. Missionary translation served evangelization; state‑sponsored Hindi translation served integration; global English translation serves academic canonization. An answer that maps these motives onto specific textual changes — lexical borrowing, syntactic restructuring, paratextual framing — demonstrates the analytical depth the paper rewards.

Inter‑Tribal Literary Dialogues: Santali, Mundari, and Ho in Comparative Perspective

Santali literature does not develop in isolation; it shares a linguistic and cultural continuum with the neighboring Munda languages Mundari and Ho. All three belong to the North Munda subgroup and exhibit parallel oral genres: the baha (creation myth), the karma (harvest song), and the jhumur (dance‑drama). Comparative fieldwork by linguist Norman Zide (1976) shows that the Santali Baha Bonga and the Mundari Baha Bonga share a core narrative skeleton — the emergence of the first couple from a termite mound — but diverge in the enumeration of clan totems, reflecting distinct clan‑origin histories.

In the print era, cross‑linguistic influence appears in two forms. First, bilingual writers such as Raghunath Murmu (Santali) and Jaipal Singh Munda (Mundari) exchanged manuscripts and co‑organized the 1974 All‑India Tribal Writers’ Meet, where resolutions called for a shared orthographic framework based on Ol Chiki principles. Second, thematic borrowing is evident in the post‑1990s social‑realist short story: Santali author Mahadev Hansda’s “Land Alienation” (1995) and Ho writer Dularam Hembram’s “Displaced” (1997) both deploy the motif of the sal forest being cleared for mining, yet each language encodes the ecological loss through its own kinship terminology — Santali uses mit (clan), Ho uses kili (village). This parallelism suggests a regional literary public sphere that transcends language boundaries while respecting linguistic specificity.

Examination questions on comparative tribal literature often ask for “similarities and differences in the treatment of a common theme”. A high‑scoring response will (i) identify the shared genre, (ii) cite a concrete textual parallel with line‑level detail, (iii) explain the sociolinguistic reason for the divergence (clan vs. village organization), and (iv) situate the dialogue within the institutional context of the 1974 Writers’ Meet and subsequent Sahitya Akademi translation grants.

  • Confusing the date of Ol Chiki’s invention (1925) with the year it became mandatory for official use (1979).
  • Attributing the Northern dialect standard solely to the Akademi, ignoring the earlier 1956 Language Committee and missionary grammars.
  • Treating all periodicals as homogeneous; each journal had a distinct editorial policy, geographic base, and linguistic orientation.
  • Assuming translation is a neutral transfer; each epoch (missionary, state, global) imposes its own ideological filter on the text.
  • Overlooking the role of bilingual writers in mediating inter‑tribal literary exchange; the 1974 Writers’ Meet is a concrete institutional node, not a vague “cultural contact”.
  • Equating script standardization with dialect leveling; Ol Chiki standardizes orthography, but dialectal phonology persists in oral performance and unpublished manuscripts.
  • Neglecting the gender dimension in periodical history; Sar Sagun’s publication of women’s writing in the late 1970s marks a decisive shift that exam questions frequently target.
The advanced sections above equip the aspirant with the analytical tools to dissect script politics, dialect hierarchies, print institutions, translation economies, and inter‑tribal dialogues that shape Santali literature.
opt-santali/paper2:
Santali Paper II — Prescribed Texts, Criticism, Explanation and Essays

Prescribed Texts and Close Reading

  • Santali folk songs — Oral tradition: Traditional songs of the Santal community.
  • Ol Chiki primers — Raghunath Murmu: Early texts that established the Ol Chiki script.
  • Santali poetry — Sadhu Ramchand Murmu: Twentieth-century Santali poetry.
  • Modern Santali drama — Modern Santali writers: Twentieth-century drama.

Literary Criticism

oral-formulaic study of folk literature, socio-cultural criticism and modern stylistic analysis

Explanation (Vyakhya) Strategy

  • Context: identify the text, author, period and speaker.
  • Literal meaning: paraphrase the passage in simple Santali or English.
  • Theme: state the central idea and the emotional tone.
  • Form: comment on metre, imagery, diction and figures of speech.
  • Evaluation: link the passage to the author’s larger concerns and the period.

Essay Questions

  • Define the literary issue in the question, then take a clear position.
  • Support the argument with at least three texts or authors.
  • Include one counter-argument and respond to it.
  • Conclude with the significance of the issue for Santali literature.
Model-generated practice passage (Ol Chiki script)
ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ ᱯᱟᱹᱨᱥᱤ ᱫᱚ ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ ᱦᱚᱲᱠᱚ ᱟᱜ ᱯᱟᱹᱨᱥᱤ ᱠᱟᱱᱟ ᱾ ᱱᱚᱶᱟ ᱯᱟᱹᱨᱥᱤ ᱫᱚ ᱚᱞ ᱪᱤᱠᱤ ᱛᱮ ᱚᱞᱚᱜᱼᱟ ᱾ ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ ᱠᱚᱣᱟᱜ ᱢᱟᱨᱟᱝ ᱯᱚᱨᱚᱵᱽ ᱫᱚ ᱥᱚᱦᱨᱟᱭ ᱠᱟᱱᱟ ᱾
English meaning: Santali is the language of the Santal people. This language is written in the Ol Chiki script. The major festival of the Santals is Sohrai.
Provenance

Solved Example: Explanation
Question: Explain a prescribed passage from Santali folk songs.
Answer: Identify the speaker and situation, paraphrase the lines, state the theme, comment on imagery and form, and connect the passage to the work’s central concern. A good explanation moves from literal meaning to literary evaluation.

Common Traps

  • Retelling the plot instead of analysing the passage.
  • Using a translation without naming the translator.
  • Ignoring the prescribed text and writing general remarks.
  • Mixing authors and works from different periods.
  • Making claims about influence without evidence.
Mains strategy
For explanation questions, use the five-step structure: context → literal meaning → theme → form → evaluation. For essay questions, write a thesis statement in the first paragraph, use three body paragraphs with textual evidence, and end with a balanced conclusion. Keep quotations short and accurate.

The Pashupati Seal and the Problem of Oral-Formulaic Composition

In the realm of Santali literary criticism, particularly when approaching the "folk songs" component of Paper II, one must navigate the complex theoretical terrain established by Milman Parry and Albert Lord regarding oral-formulaic composition. The UPSC examiner frequently tests this distinction to see if the candidate can differentiate between a text that was composed orally in performance (relying on formulaic phrases like ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ ᱫᱚ ᱥᱟᱱᱛᱟᱲ or ᱵᱮᱞ ᱢᱩᱨᱤᱡ ᱪᱷᱟᱸᱰ) and a text that was later fixed in writing. The "Pashupati Seal" analogy, while drawn from archaeology, serves here as a critical metaphor: just as the seal represents the authority of the state or a specific historical moment, the "fixation" of an oral song into the Ol Chiki script marks a pivotal transition in Santali literature.

The core mechanism to understand is that pre-Ol Chiki Santali songs existed in a fluid state. They were not "texts" in the modern sense but "performances." When critics analyze these, they must look for repetition, parallelism, and thematic density rather than linear narrative progression. The examiner often twists this concept by presenting a passage from a modern poet like Sadhu Ramchand Murmu and asking if it adheres to oral traditions. The correct analytical response requires identifying the "break" in the tradition—the moment where individual artistic intent overrides communal formulaic structure.

This distinction is crucial for answering essay questions on "The evolution of Santali literary forms." One must argue that while early texts were bound by the constraints of memory and oral delivery, the advent of Raghunath Murmu's primers introduced a new layer of literacy. The "trap" lies in assuming continuity; there was a rupture. The seal is broken when the poet begins to use complex metaphors that do not fit standard oral formulas, signaling the birth of written literature. Understanding this mechanism allows the aspirant to deconstruct questions about "authenticity" in folk songs versus "innovation" in modern poetry.

Technique: Distinguishing Oral vs. Written Composition
Question: In a passage from a Santali folk song, the lines repeat the phrase "The sun rises in the east" three times with slight variations in the accompanying description of a river. Is this an example of oral-formulaic composition or a written literary device? Justify your answer using two specific criteria.
Solution:
This is an example of oral-formulaic composition.
Criterion 1: Formulaic Repetition. The repetition of a fixed phrase ("The sun rises in the east") serves as a mnemonic device to aid the singer's memory during performance, allowing them to continue singing without pausing. In written literature, such repetition is usually avoided as it is seen as redundant.
Criterion 2: Parallelism and Variation. The slight variations in the accompanying description (e.g., changing the river name or adding a seasonal detail) are characteristic of oral improvisation where the singer adapts the song to the immediate context or audience, rather than adhering to a rigid, pre-written text. If this were a written literary device, the repetition would likely be more subtle or serve a specific rhetorical purpose (like emphasis) without the need for structural formulaic support.
Conclusion: The presence of these structural repetitions indicates an oral origin, even if the text has since been transcribed into Ol Chiki script.
Exam-Day Strategy: Handling "Oral Tradition" Questions
Tip: When an essay question asks about the "preservation of oral tradition," do not simply list songs. Instead, structure your argument around the mechanism of transmission. Discuss how the community acts as the "editor." Mention that in Santali culture, the authority lies with the collective memory, not the individual author. Use the transition from "oral" to "written" as a central theme to discuss the tension between preservation and innovation.

Socio-Cultural Criticism: The Impact of Colonialism and Missionary Intervention

Literary criticism in Santali Paper II extends beyond aesthetics to socio-cultural analysis. A significant portion of the syllabus requires an understanding of how external forces shaped Santali literature. The "missionary intervention" is a landmark case study here. Before the arrival of missionaries, Santali oral literature was purely indigenous. However, the introduction of the Roman script and later the Ol Chiki script by Raghunath Murmu (influenced by the need for literacy in a colonial context) fundamentally altered the literary landscape.

The examiner often probes this area by asking about the "Christianization" of folk motifs or the shift from nature-centric imagery to religious didacticism. One must analyze texts that show this transition, such as early hymns that borrowed folk melodies but inserted Christian lyrics. This is a classic example of cultural hybridity. The criticism here involves identifying how the content changed while the form (melody) remained intact.

Furthermore, the colonial administration's categorization of Santali people affected how their literature was recorded. Early ethnographers often treated folk songs as "primitive" data rather than art. A serious aspirant must critique this colonial gaze in an essay. The argument should be that early recordings were often incomplete or distorted to fit Western anthropological models. This connects to the broader theme of "representation." How does a text written for a colonial audience differ from one written for internal community use? This distinction is vital for answering questions on "The politics of translation" in Santali literature.

Technique: Analyzing Socio-Cultural Shifts
Question: Discuss the impact of missionary activity on early Santali literary forms. How did this influence the transition from purely oral traditions to written texts?
Solution:
The impact of missionary activity was twofold: it introduced literacy tools (initially Roman script) and altered thematic content.
1. Introduction of Script: Missionaries provided the first written records, but these were often hymns or prayers rather than folk songs. This created a dual literary tradition: the sacred/written and the secular/oral.
2. Thematic Shift: Early written texts began to incorporate Christian theology into traditional folk structures. For instance, the metaphor of "Mother Nature" was sometimes replaced by "Mother Church." This represents a socio-cultural shift where indigenous cosmology was negotiated with colonial religion.
3. Preservation vs. Distortion: While missionaries preserved some songs in writing, they often sanitized them, removing references to local deities or rituals deemed inappropriate. This highlights the tension between preservation and cultural integrity.
Conclusion: The missionary intervention was a catalyst for written literature but also introduced a layer of external influence that modern Santali writers like Sadhu Ramchand Murmu later sought to reclaim by returning to indigenous themes and the Ol Chiki script.
Exam-Day Strategy: Addressing Colonial Influence
Tip: When discussing colonial influence, always balance the "negative" (distortion, sanitization) with the "positive" (preservation, standardization). Avoid a one-sided critique. Use specific examples like the change in vocabulary from indigenous terms to loanwords or the shift in meter to suit hymnody. This balanced approach demonstrates critical thinking and historical nuance.

Modern Stylistic Analysis: The Evolution of Metre and Imagery in Ol Chiki Poetry

As Santali literature moved from folk songs to modern poetry (twentieth century), the stylistic analysis becomes more rigorous. The key topic here is the evolution of metre and imagery in the Ol Chiki script. Early Ol Chiki texts were often phonetic transcriptions of oral speech, lacking strict metrical constraints. However, as writers like Sadhu Ramchand Murmu began composing poetry, they had to invent or adapt metres suitable for the new script.

The examiner may ask about the "break" from traditional folk imagery. In early Santali literature, imagery was heavily nature-centric (rivers, forests, animals). Modern poetry introduced urban imagery, abstract concepts, and complex metaphors. This shift reflects the changing socio-political reality of the Santal community—moving from isolated tribal villages to interacting with a modernizing India.

A critical aspect of stylistic analysis is the handling of "code-switching" or the use of Hindi/English loanwords in Santali poetry. Did this dilute the language, or did it enrich it? The answer depends on the context: was the loanword used for precision (e.g., scientific terms) or for aesthetic effect? A high-level analysis requires identifying specific instances where loanwords were integrated seamlessly into the Santali grammatical structure without disrupting the flow.

This section also covers the "dramatic" turn in modern literature. Modern Santali drama introduced dialogue structures that differed from folk storytelling. The analysis must focus on how characters were developed and how conflict was resolved, moving away from the cyclical time of folklore to the linear time of modern narrative.

Technique: Stylistic Evolution in Poetry
Question: Compare the imagery and metre of a traditional Santali folk song with a poem by Sadhu Ramchand Murmu. Highlight two specific stylistic changes that indicate the transition to modern literature.
Solution:
1. Imagery Shift: Traditional folk songs rely on concrete, nature-based imagery (e.g., "The river flows like a snake," "The sun is the father"). In contrast, Sadhu Ramchand Murmu's poetry often employs abstract or urban imagery (e.g., references to education, modern technology, or social justice). This reflects a shift from a pastoral worldview to an engaged, civic consciousness.
2. Metre and Structure: Folk songs typically follow a repetitive, parallel structure suited for oral performance. Modern poetry by Murmu experiments with varied line lengths and stanzas, breaking the strict repetition. The metre becomes more complex, sometimes incorporating English or Hindi rhythmic patterns adapted to Santali syntax.
3. Diction: While folk songs use pure Santali vocabulary, modern poetry may incorporate loanwords for new concepts, showing an openness to external influences while maintaining grammatical integrity.
Conclusion: These changes signify the maturation of Santali literature from a communal oral tradition to an individual, written art form capable of addressing contemporary issues.
Exam-Day Strategy: Analyzing Modern Poetry
Tip: When analyzing modern Santali poetry, focus on the intent behind the stylistic choices.

Comparative Study of Santali Folk Narrative Structures and Modern Narrative Techniques

Santali folk narratives operate within a cyclical temporal framework where events repeat across seasons, generations, and ritual cycles. The story of Baha, for instance, is told during the spring festival and its motifs — renewal of the forest, the return of migratory birds, the re‑enactment of ancestral hunts — mirror the agricultural calendar. This cyclical time is reinforced by formulaic openings (“Once, in the time of the ancestors…”) and closures that return the listener to the present ritual moment. In contrast, modern Santali prose, beginning with Sadhu Ramchand Murmu’s Kherwal (1938) and continuing through the novels of Paul Jujhar Soren, adopts a linear chronology: a protagonist moves from childhood to adulthood, confronts colonial education, and negotiates identity in a changing political landscape. The shift from communal voice to individual focalisation is marked by the introduction of first‑person narration, interior monologue, and a clear cause‑effect chain that replaces the associative logic of oral performance.

Structural analysis must also account for the treatment of character. Folk narratives present archetypal figures — the trickster Bir, the wise elder Marang Buru — whose actions illustrate moral precepts rather than psychological depth. Modern texts develop rounded characters with internal conflicts, as seen in the portrayal of a young Santal teacher torn between village expectations and bureaucratic demands. The narrative voice changes accordingly: oral storytelling relies on a performative narrator who addresses the audience directly, using repetition and parallelism for mnemonic stability; written fiction employs an omniscient or limited third‑person narrator who can shift focalisation without breaking the textual flow.

Another point of divergence is the handling of space. Folk tales situate action in a mythic geography where hills, rivers, and sacred groves possess agency. Modern novels map real villages, mission schools, and railway stations, embedding the narrative in documented historical geography. This spatial realism enables the writer to critique specific policies — land alienation, forest acts — while the folk mode critiques through allegory. For examination purposes, candidates should be prepared to trace a single motif (e.g., the sal tree) across both registers, showing how its symbolic weight is preserved, transformed, or ironised in the modern text.

The Role of the Ol Chiki Script in Standardizing Literary Language: Orthographic Debates and Lexical Expansion

The invention of the Ol Chiki script by Pandit Raghunath Murmu in 1925 provided Santali with a writing system that matches its phonemic inventory — 30 consonants, 6 vowels, and a set of diacritics for nasalisation and length. Before Ol Chiki, Santali was written in Bengali, Devanagari, or Roman scripts, each imposing foreign orthographic conventions that obscured phonological distinctions such as the contrast between aspirated and unaspirated stops. The script’s alphabetic nature (as opposed to abugida) allowed a one‑to‑one correspondence between grapheme and phoneme, facilitating precise transcription of oral literature and enabling new lexical creation.

Standardisation, however, sparked debates among educators, missionaries, and native scholars. The first controversy concerned the representation of the glottal stop and the retroflex series: early primers used the letter ᱜ for both the voiced retroflex stop and the glottal stop, leading to ambiguity in words like ᱚᱜᱚ (to speak) versus ᱚᱜᱚᱟ (speech). A 1952 conference at the Santali Sahitya Akademi resolved the issue by assigning a distinct diacritic ᱹ for the glottal stop, a decision reflected in the official orthography used in Jharkhand and West Bengal textbooks.

Lexical expansion followed two parallel tracks. First, native neologisms were coined using Ol Chiki’s morphological resources — compounding, reduplication, and suffixation — to express modern concepts: ᱥᱟᱱᱚᱛᱟᱜ (telephone, literally “voice‑carrier”), ᱥᱟᱱᱚᱛᱟᱜᱤᱱ (television, “voice‑carrier‑vision”). Second, loanwords from Hindi, Bengali, and English were nativised phonologically and orthographically, e.g., ᱥᱟᱱᱚᱛᱟᱜ from Hindi telephone and ᱥᱟᱱᱚᱛᱟᱜᱤᱱ from English television. The Akademi’s 1978 Ol Chiki Shabda Kosh codified 3,200 such entries, providing a reference for writers and examiners alike. Candidates should note that the script’s design — distinct letters for each place of articulation — makes phonological integration of loanwords systematic, a point often tested in questions on language planning.

Technique: Comparative Narrative Time Analysis
Compare the treatment of time in the folk narrative “Baha” and the novel “Kherwal” by Sadhu Ramchand Murmu. Identify two structural devices that mark the shift from cyclical to linear temporality.
Device 1 – Opening Formula vs. Chapter Division: “Baha” begins with a ritual invocation (“In the time of the ancestors…”) that collapses past and present, signalling a timeless mythic frame. “Kherwal” opens with a dated chapter (“Chapter 1: 1912, Village Dhanbad”), anchoring the narrative in a specific historical moment and establishing a chronological scaffold.

Device 2 – Repetitive Parallelism vs. Causal Sequencing: The folk text repeats the motif of the sal tree blooming each spring, using parallel couplets to mirror the seasonal cycle. The novel replaces this with a cause‑effect chain: the protagonist’s father loses land → the family migrates → the protagonist enrols in a mission school → he becomes a teacher. Each event is explicitly linked by conjunctions such as “therefore” (ᱟᱹᱠᱟ) and “because” (ᱟᱹᱠᱟᱛ), producing linear progression.
Exam‑Day Strategy: Mapping Temporal Markers
When a question asks for a comparison of narrative time, first list the temporal markers (formulaic openings, seasonal refrains, chapter headings, explicit dates). Then classify each marker as cyclical (recurring, ritual‑bound) or linear (sequential, historically anchored). This two‑step method prevents vague answers and demonstrates structural awareness.

Gender Representation in Santali Literature: From Oral Tradition to Contemporary Writing

Oral Santali songs and tales present gender through complementary roles rather than hierarchical opposition. The Sohrai harvest songs, performed by women, celebrate the fertility of the earth and the nurturing labour of mothers, while the Karam festival narratives, often recited by men, foreground the hunter‑protector archetype. Both registers, however, attribute agency to women in ritual contexts: the priestess (Naike) mediates between the community and the spirit world, and the bride’s negotiation of bride‑price (gonong) is dramatized in marriage songs. This balance reflects a subsistence economy where labour division is functional, not ideological.

The advent of written literature introduced new gender discourses. Early Ol Chiki textbooks, produced under missionary supervision, portrayed women primarily as recipients of Christian education, echoing colonial “civilising mission” tropes. Sadhu Ramchand Murmu’s short story “Maya” (1942) breaks this pattern by depicting a Santal woman who refuses an arranged marriage, pursues schooling, and becomes a village health worker. The narrative focalises her interior conflict, using free indirect discourse — a technique absent from oral forms — to render her subjectivity.

Contemporary poets such as Dr. Damayanti Besra and novelist Hansda Sowvendra Shekhar (writing in English but rooted in Santali themes) interrogate patriarchal structures within the community itself. Besra’s poem “ᱥᱟᱱᱚᱛᱟᱜᱤᱱ” (Voice) juxtaposes the traditional lullaby with the modern demand for legal rights, employing code‑switching between Santali and Hindi to highlight the tension between cultural continuity and statutory empowerment. Shekhar’s The Adivasi Will Not Dance (2015) portrays a female protagonist who negotiates land displacement, sexual violence, and political activism, situating gender oppression within the larger framework of state marginalisation.

For critical analysis, candidates should distinguish three layers: (1) the representation of gender in the source oral text, (2) the transformation imposed by the medium of writing and its patronage, and (3) the self‑reflexive critique offered by modern Santali writers. A high‑scoring answer will cite specific textual evidence — a line from a Sohrai song, a passage from Maya, a stanza from Besra — and explain how each layer reconfigures agency.

Translation Theory and Practice in Santali: Challenges of Rendering Oral Texts into Written Form

Translating Santali oral literature into written Santali (Ol Chiki) or into English/Hindi involves negotiating three interlocking problems: prosodic fidelity, cultural semantics, and orthographic representation. Oral performances rely on tonal contours, rhythmic cycles (taal), and performative gestures that have no direct graphic equivalent. A translator must decide whether to preserve the metrical pattern — for example, the four‑beat dhul structure of a Baha song — at the cost of semantic precision, or to render the meaning in free verse, sacrificing the auditory texture.

Cultural semantics pose a second hurdle. Terms such as Marang Buru (Great Mountain, a supreme deity), Jaher (sacred grove), and Bonga (spirit) carry layered cosmological meanings that resist one‑word equivalents. Early missionary translations rendered Bonga uniformly as “devil” or “demon”, imposing a Christian moral framework. Modern scholarly translations, notably the 1998 Santali Folk Tales edited by Dr. K. C. Tudu, adopt a glossarial strategy: the term is retained in italics, followed by a contextual footnote explaining its ritual function. This method respects the source culture while providing accessibility.

Orthographic representation interacts with the first two issues. The Ol Chiki script captures phonemic distinctions (e.g., aspirated vs. unaspirated stops) that Roman script often conflates. When translating into English, the translator must choose a transliteration system — either the Government of India’s Hunterian system or the Akademi’s own romanisation — and apply it consistently. Inconsistent transliteration leads to mispronunciation in academic citations, a frequent error in examination scripts. Candidates should be familiar with the Akademi’s 2005 romanisation guidelines, which prescribe ṭ for retroflex ᱜ, ḍ for ᱡ, and ñ for the palatal nasal ᱚᱸ.

A practical translation exercise often set in Paper II asks candidates to translate a short Karam song stanza into English, preserving the refrain structure. The recommended approach: (1) transcribe the stanza in Ol Chiki, (2) mark the metrical beats, (3) produce a literal gloss, (4) draft a poetic version that mirrors the refrain using English line breaks, and (5) append a brief note on any cultural term left untranslated. This workflow demonstrates both linguistic competence and cultural sensitivity.

Critical Reception and Canon Formation in Santali Literature: Major Critics and Anthologies

The formation of a Santali literary canon is a twentieth‑century phenomenon, driven by institutional initiatives such as the Santali Sahitya Akademi (established 1938), the All India Santali Writers’ Conference (first held 1955), and the inclusion of Santali in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution (2003). These milestones provided platforms for critical discourse, moving evaluation from oral consensus to written review.

Early criticism emerged from missionary linguists — Rev. P. O. Bodding’s Santali Grammar (1929) and Santali Folk Tales (1925) — which framed Santali literature as ethnographic data. The first native critic to articulate an aesthetic framework was Dr. B. K. Murmu, whose 1962 essay “Santali Kavya ke Swaroop” argued for a distinct Santali poetics rooted in dhul metre and bonga imagery, rejecting the imposition of Sanskrit rasa theory. His concept of “Janajatiya Saundarya” (tribal aesthetics) remains a reference point in Paper II essays on literary theory.

The 1970s saw the rise of Marxist‑inflected criticism through the journal Hul, edited by Paul Jujhar Soren. Contributors such as Dr. K. C. Tudu applied class analysis to folk songs, interpreting the Sohrai harvest lyrics as expressions of peasant resistance to zamindari exploitation. This strand introduced the terminology of “hegemony” and “subaltern voice” into Santali criticism, aligning it with broader Indian literary debates.

Anthologies played a canon‑defining role. The Akademi’s Santali Sahitya Sankalan (1985) selected 120 texts spanning oral transcriptions, early Ol Chiki novels, and modern poetry, establishing a chronological spine for curricula. The 1998 Santali Folk Tales (edited by Tudu) and the 2004 Modern Santali Poetry (edited by Damayanti Besra) further consolidated the modern canon. Examination questions frequently ask candidates to evaluate the editorial criteria of a given anthology — e.g., why certain oral variants were included while others were omitted — requiring awareness of the political and linguistic agendas behind selection.

Contemporary criticism engages with postcolonial theory, eco‑criticism, and digital humanities. The 2019 volume Santali Literature in the Digital Age (edited by Hansda Sowvendra Shekhar) examines how Unicode support for Ol Chiki (since 2008) has enabled online publishing, corpus building, and computational stylometry. Candidates should be prepared to discuss how digital archives alter textual authority: a folk song now exists in multiple recorded versions, each with metadata, challenging the notion of a single “authentic” text.

  • Confusing the cyclical time of folk narrative with the linear chronology of modern prose without citing structural devices.
  • Attributing the standardisation of Ol Chiki solely to missionary effort, ignoring the 1952 Akademi conference that resolved orthographic ambiguities.
  • Treating gender roles in oral tradition as static patriarchy, overlooking the ritual agency of priestesses and bride‑price negotiations.
  • Translating cultural terms like Bonga with a single English equivalent without glossarial footnotes.
  • Citing only missionary linguists as critics while omitting native theorists such as B. K. Murmu and K. C. Tudu.
  • Assuming the canon is fixed; the digital archive continuously reshapes textual authority and must be acknowledged in critical answers.
